title: [Feature] RFC for adding CPU support for SGLang
author: mingfeima
body:
### Motivation

Hi, SGLang folks! This is Mingfei from intel pytorch team, our team helps optimize PyTorch performance on CPU. I am also the PyTorch module maintainer for cpu performance. We would like to contribute to SGLang for CPU enabling and performance optimization.

### Targets
Our primary target is to optimize SGLang performance on Intel Xeon Scalable Processors (x86 server CPUs).
* Optimization will be focusing on Xeon with [Intel® Advanced Matrix Extensions](https://www.intel.com/content/www/us/en/products/docs/accelerator-engines/advanced-matrix-extensions/overview.html) support, including Sapphire Rapids(4th gen), Emerald Rapids(5th gen), Granite Rapids(6th gen).
* Native implementations or fallbacks will be provided for CPUs with other ISA to make it functional.
* Providing good performance per dollar.

### Limitations

* Kernels written in **avx512** and **amx-bf16**, requires **GCC11** or above.
* **BFloat16/Float16** will be enabled at the same time on CPU, but we only focus on **BFloat16** performance optimization at the current stage, **Float16** optimization will be added later on.

### Schedule for 25Q1
We will focusing on DeepSeek series at the moment to align with our internal development requirements and extend the model coverage later on.

#### Generic enabling/optimizations for sglang

- [x] CPU device enabling. We intend to enable CPU device with torch native backend first and then gradually replace all the performance critical components with C++ intrinsics kernels. https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/2806
- [x] fused kernels for `rms_norm`, `silu_and_mul`, sampling and so on.
- [x] radix attention kernels for extend and decoding.

#### DeepSeek performance optimizations
(we are currently mapping the work from [DeepSeek Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) Throughput Optimizations](https://lmsys.org/blog/2024-09-04-sglang-v0-3/#deepseek-multi-head-latent-attention-mla-throughput-optimizations))
- [x] MLA decoding kernel optimization with head blocking.
- [x] DeepSeekMoE (FusedMoE)
- [x] fp8 kv cache (experimental)

#### Tensor Parallel
- [x] Map TP to the multiple sockets (numa nodes) on a single node CPU
- [ ] EPMoE

We hope to help more customers to build better user experience with deploying with sglang on CPU devices. Welcome any feedbacks, thanks!

title: [RFC] Support Multi-Stage Awake for RL
author: hebiao064
body:
### Contributor:
- Biao @hebiao064 
- Ata @MrAta 
- Tom @fzyzcjy 
- Chenyang @zhaochenyang20 

### Checklist

- [x] 1. If the issue you raised is not a feature but a question, please raise a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions/new/choose Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [x] 2. Please use English, otherwise it will be closed.

### Motivation

Reduce the peak memory usage by `N` GB to avoid OOM, `N` equals to the memory size of Model Weights.

| Model    |  Before |  After | Improvement | 
| -------- | ------- | ------- | ------- |
| QWen 32B  | 192GB   |  131.8GB   |  **30%** | 
| Llama 8B | 148.9GB    | 134.5GB   |  **10%** |

```
QWen 32B Test (mem_frac = 0.9): Memory: 5.8 → 36.6 → 98.1 → 37.6 → 131.8 GB
Llama 8B Test (mem_frac = 0.9): Memory: 7.1 → 14.7 → 30.1 → 15.7 → 134.5 GB
```



#### Background


In RL Ecosystem which use colocate design like [verl](https://github.com/volcengine/verl/tree/main), we need to offload training model and load serving model & KV Cache frequently.

- Currently SGLang is using [torch_memory_saver](https://github.com/fzyzcjy/torch_memory_saver) to pause and resume.
- [torch_memory_saver](https://github.com/fzyzcjy/torch_memory_saver) is a open source repo that provided easy to use api to hack **cudaMalloc** and **cudaFree** to make sure the virtual address could be consistent after pause and resume, which is critical to ensure CUDA Graph work.
- CUDA Graph is critical to make sure SGLang runs faster in decoding phases.


#### Here is the current behavior of VERL + SGLang

![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/e87e7dd6-f223-4de6-8f07-915eb2030ea8)

1. During Training, we have training model and optimizer state in the GPU Memory, and once training is done, we will offload optimizer state to cpu and keep the model weights in GPU, which is needed in Update Weight.
2. During Update Weight, we awake the SGLang engine, so those paused memory of Model Weights and KV Cache will come back. Then we update model from training model to serving model on the fly using the api: `update_weights_in_tensor`
3. After Model being updated, we delete the training model from GPU Memory.


Above design works pretty well so far, however, this would waste a big chunk of GPU Memory during rollout, which could cause a few issues we've seen so far:
- **Small KV Cache**: We need to use relative lower number of mem fraction ratio (e.g: 0.6), hence our KV Cache has less tokens. Given KV Cache has less tokens, we will hit `RuntimeError: Prefill out of memory. Try to lower your batch size.` when we try prefill large number of requests.
- **Out of Memory**: If we use mem fraction ratio 0.8 and run RL for 32B model on 8 H100, it will OOM during update weight


#### Challenge
- `torch_memory_saver` currently only supports Singleton, hence SGLang will pause and resume KV Cache + Weights together, they are treated as the same group of memory controlled by the singleton `torch_memory_saver` instance

#### Proposal
![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/7fda9638-0dc2-4c14-bc64-cd20616f350f)

1. During Training, we do the same
2. During Update Weight Stage 1, we awake the model weights from SGLang and then update weights
3. During Update Weight Stage 2, we delete the training model weights from GPU Memory
4. Awake the SGLang's KV Cache


![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/f3dab327-dc2e-4ed8-88d7-15e383f77d25)


### Benefit
With above feature, we can train larger model with same GPU, we can also make training/rollout more efficient given we can allocate larger KV Cache

### Option 1: Use two `torch_memory_saver`

- [ ] Support multiple instance of torch_memory_saver: https://github.com/fzyzcjy/torch_memory_saver/pull/17 
- [ ] Support Multiple Stage Awake in SGLang: https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/6962 
- [ ] Support Multiple Stage Awake in verl: https://github.com/volcengine/verl/pull/1911
 
### Option 2: Keep using Singleton and provide tag based pause/resume

- [x] Support tag based resume/pause: https://github.com/fzyzcjy/torch_memory_saver/pull/20 @hebiao064 
- [x] Support Multiple Stage Awake in SGLang: https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/7099 @hebiao064 
- [x] Support Multiple Stage Awake in verl: https://github.com/volcengine/verl/pull/1911 @hebiao064 
- [x] Add e2e test for multi instance multi stage memory release/resume occupuation: https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/7208 @MrAta  
- [x] Clean up VERL Engine related code: https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/7326

### Related resources

_No response_

title: [RFC] Bi-weekly release
author: zhyncs
body:
After thorough internal discussions, the SGLang team has decided to standardize the release cycle as follows:

- A new version will be released every two weeks under normal circumstances (e.g., v0.4.8, v0.4.9).

- If urgent issues or high-priority features arise between regular releases, we may publish a patch release or an additional stable version as needed.

- Bi-weekly releases will typically occur around the middle and end of each month.

- Each release will aim to include a set of planned features, usually discussed and finalized by the SGLang team in advance.

title: 🚧  RFC: Redesign Batch Processing as an Offline Workflow
author: CatherineSue
body:
### **Summary**
This RFC proposes removing the existing `/v1/batches` and `/v1/files` endpoints from the main OpenAI-compatible server and replacing them with a standalone offline batch processing service.

> **Note:** As part of the ongoing OpenAI API refactor, the batch support has already been removed from the main server. This RFC serves to document the rationale and formalize the replacement plan.


---

### Problem

#### 7.1 Fundamental Issues with the Current Batch API (#7068 )

The current design for online batch processing is flawed and not production-safe. Key issues include:

- **Server Stability Risk**: Uploading and processing thousands of requests at once can overwhelm online API servers.
- **Timing Constraints**: Difficult to enforce `completion_window` in a real-time environment.
- **Resource Contention**: Batch jobs run alongside latency-sensitive requests without proper isolation.
- **Architecture Mismatch**: Batch workloads are inherently asynchronous/offline, conflicting with the synchronous nature of standard OpenAI endpoints.

---

### Proposed Solution

#### 1. **Simplify Online Endpoints**
- Remove logic for handling list-wrapped input in `/v1/chat/completions`, `/v1/embeddings`, etc.
- Accept only single request per HTTP call (OpenAI spec-compliant).
- Cleaner code and better performance for common-case usage.

#### 2. **Split Out Batch Service**
Implement batch processing as a **separate offline job runner**, modeled after how vLLM does it.

This batch runner will:
- Accept batch jobs in OpenAI-compatible `.jsonl` format
- Spawn a new process/container to handle the job
- Stream output to a results file (local or presigned S3 URLs)
- Optionally enforce `completion_window` guarantees in the background

#### 3. **Remove from Main Server**
- Remove `/v1/batches` and `/v1/files` routes from the main OpenAI-compatible HTTP server.
- These should live in a separate service (`batch-runner`) to enforce separation of concerns.

---

### 📌 Action Items

- [ ] Finalize and approve this RFC
- [ ] Implement batch runner
- [x] Deprecate online batch endpoints
- [ ] Update docs and integration tests

title: [RFC] Move request disconnection handling out of tokenizer manager
author: CatherineSue
body:
Tokenizer_manager currenctly depends on `fastapi.Request` to handle the abort of a request. This brings a deep coupling between tokenization and fastapi server layer. We should consider removing it. 

> I would also like to point out that currently, apart from the Web Server part, other sections of the SRT code also depend on `fastapi.Request`, and this coupling has caused some difficulties for third-party development. For example, I plan to use Litestar to write a third-party server, but this coupling will lead to type and compatibility issues.  
> 
> Currently, the main dependency on `fastapi.Request` is in `TokenizerManager`. After analysis, most of the `request` objects here are not actually used. The primary use of the `request` object is to check whether the user has actively disconnected, and then call `abort_request` to cancel execution.
> 
> Would it be possible to decouple this dependency? For example:
> 
> - Passing an `is_disconnected_fn` to handle connection state detection, or
> - Letting the server's logic manage cancellation (via decorators, async tasks, etc.). 

 _Originally posted by @YorkSu in [#7068](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/7068#issuecomment-2969356971)_

title: [RFC] Remote KV Connector for SGLang Global Cache Reuse and PD
author: hzh0425
body: co-authors: @yizhang2077 # \[RFC\] Remote KV Connector for SGLang Global Cache Reuse ## 1. Abstract This RFC proposes a Remote KVCache Connector System to enable global KV cache reuse **across SGLang nodes**, solving redundant computation problems in multi-turn conversation scenarios and achieving global compute-to-storage conversion. The system introduces a connector abstraction layer that allows nodes to store and retrieve KV cache data from external storage, enabling prefix-based cache matching and reuse across distributed inference workers. Key benefits include: • **Global KV Cache Reuse**: Reducing redundant computation via cross-node global KV cache sharing through Global Prefix Index Management capabilities, achieving ~50% TTFT reduction in Qwen-32B 4TP multi-turn dialogues • **Flexible Storage Backend**: Supporting diverse storage backends via a universal KVConnector interface; enabling direct RDMA-based HBM KV Cache access for high-throughput data transfer • **Seamless Integration**: - Native integration with SGLang Scheduler through asynchronous external KV Cache read/write - Native integration with PD Disaggregation architecture ## 2. Motivation ### Problem Statement SGLang currently lacks global PrefixCache reuse functionality. In multi-turn conversation scenarios, completed inference KV caches cannot be reused across nodes. When similar prefixes are processed repeatedly across different worker nodes, this leads to significant redundant computation and resource waste. ### Goals * **Goal 1**: Define a universal Remote Connector Interface for SGLang that provides basic KV cache read/write operations, implementing 3FS Connector * **Goal 2**: Enable Normal/Overlap Scheduler to implement async PreFetch and Offload KVCache through Connector without blocking scheduler operations * **Goal 3**: Achieve global cache reuse with measurable performance improvements in multi-turn scenarios * **Goal 4**:Integration with PD separation mode ## 3. Technical Design ### Architecture Overview The overall workflow involves: 1. **First Time Scheduling (A)**: * A2: Query remote prefix matched cache through Connector, returns 0 * A3: Execute model inference, write KVCache to VRAM * A4: Write KVCache and Prefix Key to remote store through Connector 2. **Second Time Scheduling (B)**: * B2: Query remote prefix matched cache through Connector, assume match result is 1024 (first 1024 tokens computed on other nodes) * B3: Execute PreFetch through Connector, pull first 1024 tokens' KVCache to corresponding GPU * B5: Execute model inference * B6: Write inference results back to remote cache ### Key Components #### GlobalRemoteStorage Remote storage engine, can be 3FS/Mooncake/LMCache etc. #### GlobalKVManager Remote global prefix index, responsible for maintaining prefix indices stored in remote storage. GlobalKVManager is an optional plugin - if RemoteStorage itself has prefix query capabilities, GlobalKVManager is not needed. #### RemoteKVConnector Connector component abstracts the API interface required for Scheduler to read/write external KVCache. #### SchedulerRemoteKVQueue Scheduler async schedules read/write of external KVCache through RemoteKVQueue: * **AsyncKVPrefetchQueue**: Requests attempt to match remote prefix tokens through Connector, pre-allocate Token KVCache Slots, and async pull Remote KVCache through Connector * **AsyncKVStoreQueue**: Requests wait for all Chunk KVCache to complete transfer before releasing occupied resources ### Scheduler Overlap Optimization The Scheduler reads/writes external KVCache data through Connector. To optimize overall performance after introducing Connector and avoid blocking Scheduler operations, multi-layered queue overlap between KV cache transfer and computation across independent requests is implemented. This architecture uses a layered queue mechanism to decouple scheduling and transfer: * **Async Pipeline Processing**: PreFetch Queue (async prefetch), Scheduling Queue (scheduling decisions), PostTransfer Queue (async transfer) form a non-blocking task processing pipeline * **Design Goal**: Ensure Scheduler focuses on resource allocation and task distribution, isolating I/O latency through queue buffering and async operations to maximize system throughput * **Example**: When requests 0,1,2,3 initiate PreFetch, requests 4,5 can compute in parallel without waiting; when 4,5 initiate async writeback, 0,1 can also compute in parallel ### Workflow Phases 1. **PreFetch Phase**: * Scheduler adds Req to AsyncKVPrefetch Queue * Queue uses KVConnector.num\_external\_matched\_tokens to determine remote prefix cache length * When exceeding retrieve\_remote\_cache\_threshold, initiate PreFetch * Allocate Token KVCache Page Slots and read remote cache via KVConnector.retrieve\_kv\_async 2. **Forward Phase**: * Execute model inference workflow * For each produced Chunk KVCache, async send via KVConnector.store\_kv\_async 3. **Transfer Phase**: * After inference completion, place Req in AsyncKVStore Queue * Wait for all Chunk transfers to complete ![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/097e83b7-d7a1-4ae9-b9fa-8a25a5d703ba) ### Connector Interface Definition ```python class RemoteKVConnector(ABC): """ Base class for all connectors. A connector is responsible for storing and retrieving KV caches from the external storage. """ @abstractmethod def __init__(self, metadata: ConnectorMetadata): """ Initialize the connector with the metadata. Args: metadata: The specific metadata for the connector. """ pass @abstractmethod def register_kv_buffers(self, kv_args: KVArgs): """ Initialize with the KV caches. Useful for pre-registering the KV Buffers (e.g. KV ptrs) into the KVConnector (e.g. for NIXL, Mooncake). """ pass @abstractmethod def store_kv_async( self, req_id: str, page_to_tokens_mapping: list[tuple[int, slice]], tokens_list: list[int], **kwargs ) -> tuple[Future, int]: """ Async store the KV cache of the given token range to the connector. This method stores KV cache data for tokens organized by page indices. Each page contains a list of tokens that need to be stored together. Args: req_id: Unique request identifier for tracking this store operation. page_to_tokens_mapping: A list of tuples, where each tuple contains: - page_index: The index of the KV cache page - token_index_range: List of tokens associated with this page tokens_list: The complete token list. **kwargs: Additional arguments for the store operation. Returns: tuple[Future, int]: A tuple containing: - Future: The future object that indicates success or failure of the store operation. - int: The end index of the stored tokens, indicating the last token position that was successfully stored in this operation. """ pass @abstractmethod def retrieve_kv_async( self, req_id: str, page_to_tokens_mapping: list[tuple[int, slice]], tokens_list: list[int], **kwargs, ) -> Future: """ Async retrieve the KV cache from the connector to the given kv indices. This method retrieves KV cache data for tokens organized by page indices. Each page contains a list of tokens that need to be retrieved together. Args: req_id: Unique request identifier for tracking this retrieve operation. page_to_tokens_mapping: A list of tuples, where each tuple contains: - page_index: The index of the KV cache page - token_index_range: List of tokens associated with this page tokens_list: The complete token list. **kwargs: Additional arguments for the retrieve operation. Returns: Future: The future object that indicates success or failure of the retrieve operation. """ pass @abstractmethod def num_external_matched_tokens( self, req_id: str, tokens: list[int], num_local_computed_tokens: int, **kwargs ) -> int: """ Get number of new tokens that can be loaded from the external KV cache beyond the num_local_computed_tokens for a batch of inputs. Args: req_id: Unique request identifier for tracking this operation. tokens: The tokens to match against the external KV cache. num_local_computed_tokens: The number of locally computed tokens. **kwargs: Additional arguments for the operation. Returns: int: The number of new tokens that can be loaded from the external KV cache beyond the num_local_computed_tokens. """ pass @abstractmethod def finish_req( self, req_id: str ): """ Finish the request, release the related resources. """ pass @abstractmethod def close(self): pass ``` ## 4. Implementation Plan ### Phase 1: Core Infrastructure (Weeks 1-2) **Timeline**: 2 weeks   **Deliverables**: * [ ] ✅ Task01: RemoteKVConnector Interface Definition * Define abstract base class with all required methods * [ ] ✅ Task02: RemoteKVManager Interface * Design prefix index management interface * [ ] ✅ Task03: 3FS KVConnector Implementation * Implement 3FS connector   * Implement localfile connector * Add chunking and compression support * Include error handling and retry mechanisms * [ ] ✅ Task4: Mini RemoteKVManager * Basic in-memory prefix index implementation * Thread-safe operations * Implement Restful API ### Phase 2: Queue Infrastructure (Week 3) **Timeline**: 1 week   **Deliverables**: * [ ] ✅  Task5: AsyncKVPrefetchQueue Implementation * Resource allocation management，Token pool allocation for external cache * Async Prefetch kvcache * Completion polling with TP consistency guarantees * [ ] ✅  Task6: AsyncKVStoreQueue Implementation * Chunked transfer management with configurable thresholds * Completion polling with TP consistency guarantees * Resource cleanup and error recovery ### Phase 3: Scheduler Integration (Weeks 4-6) **Timeline**: 3 weeks   **Deliverables**: * [ ] ✅  Task7: Core Scheduler Logic Integration * Integrate AsyncPrefetch/StoreQueue into event loops * Add remote KV cache configuration options * Implement polling mechanisms in normal/overlap modes ### Phase 4: Testing and Optimization (Weeks 7-8) **Timeline**: 2 weeks   **Deliverables**: * [ ]  Task8: Performance Evaluation * Multi-turn dialogue scenario testing with Qwen/DeepSeek models * TTFT reduction measurement (target: ~50% improvement) * Throughput comparison against baseline * [ ]  Task9: Stability Testing * Long-running conversation scenarios * Error injection and recovery testing * Memory leak detection and prevention * [ ]  Task10: Documentation and Examples * Configuration guides for different storage backends * Performance tuning recommendations * Troubleshooting documentation ## 5. Long-Term Vision With PD Upon completion of this RFC, the Connector mode can be integrated with SGLang's PD (Prefill-Decode) separation architecture.  Options include: • Reusing Remote Cache via Connector during Prefill • Direct KVCache transfer between PD nodes through Connector ## 6. Different with HiRadixCache HiRadixCache​ is another highly efficient multi-tier storage implementation from the SGLang community. Extending HiRadixCache appropriately to schedule the ​Remote Cache​ is also a viable design option. This solution also draws inspiration from the concepts of HiRadixCache. Its main differences from HiRadixCache are: 1. Current Solution:​ It ​forming a ​completely independent schedule pipeline. It interacts ​directly with the GPU​ without intermediate buffering in DRAM, enabling ​direct transfer of KVCache via RDMA. 2. Current Solution:​ It employs a ​dedicated Global KVCacheManager​ component to uniformly manage ​global prefix indexing. Crucially, the underlying storage ​does not require​ native support for prefix query capabilities. ## 7. References 1. **SGLang PD Disaggregation Design** * [Internal Design Document](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1rQXJwKd5b9b1aOzLh98mnyMhBMhlxXA5ATZTHoQrwvc/edit?tab=t.0#heading=h.i3s2t1j0e1ik) 2. **SGLang Scheduler Implementation** * `python/sglang/srt/managers/scheduler.py` 3. **Memory Pool and Cache Systems** * `python/sglang/srt/mem_cache/memory_pool.py` * `python/sglang/srt/mem_cache/radix_cache.py` * `python/sglang/srt/mem_cache/hiradix_cache.py` ### Related resources _No response_

title: [RFC] DRI for every module
author: zhyncs
body:
SGLang now has a wide range of features and modules, with many efforts happening in parallel across new features, optimizations, and bug fixes. Each module already has an internal DRI (Directly Responsible Individual), but these assignments haven’t been made public. As a result, some community pull requests have experienced delays, and contributors often don’t know who to reach out to.

We plan to make the DRI list public over the next two weeks and will actively follow up in a dedicated public channel. We're looking forward to working more closely with the community! Cheers!

title: [RFC] Multi-framework support for sglang
author: wangtiance
body: ## Motivation Currently, PyTorch is the only supported framework for sglang. We would like to propose supporting different frameworks in addition to PyTorch for the following reasons: - Optimizations in specific fields. For example, TF/Jax and MindSpore both made a lot of optimizations on static graphs. Also Jax works well with XLA on TPU. In the case of Ascend, currently sglang has some support on Ascend NPU through torch_npu, but MindSpore can bring performance benefits such as graph/op fusion and integrated compilation, as well as developer friendly Triton op support. - Each framework has its own user groups and ecosystems. Supporting multiple frameworks makes sglang more accessible to them compared with torch-exclusive LLM serving frameworks. The core philosophies are: 1. **Co-existence of torch and the new framework**: Now that PyTorch is deeply integrated into the project structure, replacing it with another framework would be rather expensive. Instead, new framework can focus on model running and the attention backend. Tensors can be converted across frameworks through [dlpack](https://github.com/dmlc/dlpack). 2. **Maximal reuse**: Frontend language, scheduler, tokenizer/detokenizer, sampler, etc. are reused without change. 3. **Avoid intrusive changes**: Current code stucture is kept intact. Codes relevant to the new framework are clustered in a separate directory. ## Design ### Model Execution In a single forward call, the oringal call stack is: ``` Engine -> Scheduler -> TpModelWorker -> Model Runnner -> Model/Model Loader -> Layer/Ops/Attn ``` The new framework takes over from model runner onward. After the model returns the hidden states, ### Code Structure Suppose we want to support framework A, we add the following directories. There are 2 plans, we'd like to know which one the community prefers: Plan 1: ``` /python /sglang /srt ... /distributed_A /layers_A /models_A /model_loader_A ``` Plan 2: ``` /python /sglang /srt ... /srt_A /distributed /layers /models /model_loader ... ``` Scripts will also be added to /examples and /tests ## Proof of Concept We made some early attempts on running a MindSpore model on Ascend NPU. Currently it uses torch CPU and mindspore native attention implementation. We can now successfully run a basic inference sample with a single device (Atlas 800I A2). ### Current Modifications ``` HEAD detached at v0.4.9 Changes not staged for commit: (use "git add ..." to update what will be committed) (use "git restore ..." to discard changes in working directory) modified: python/sglang/srt/configs/load_config.py modified: python/sglang/srt/layers/quantization/compressed_tensors/compressed_tensors_moe.py modified: python/sglang/srt/layers/quantization/utils.py modified: python/sglang/srt/model_executor/model_runner.py modified: python/sglang/srt/model_loader/loader.py modified: python/sglang/srt/server_args.py Untracked files: (use "git add ..." to include in what will be committed) ms_example/ python/sglang/srt/models/ms_model/ ``` That includes: ms_model: the mindspore model implementation, and corresponding wrapper to process ForwardBatch as input. server_args, load_config, loader: make a new load option for mindspore, and corresponding mindspore model loader. quantization: resolve some import conflicts with vllm and sgl_kernel model_runner: some changes for distributed init, not related to single-card inference. ### Pytorch-MindSpore conversion: In the current POC implementation, we get KV Cache from ForwardBatch of pytorch in the first run, then cache and maintain it on the device by mindspore for the next steps. For each step we convert the input tensor from torch on cpu to mindspore on npu. In future we'll eliminate the conversion through dlpack. ### Experiment We run a Qwen2.5 7B model with the following script: ``` import sglang as sgl def main(): llm = sgl.Engine(model_path="/home/ckpt/qwen2.5-7b-hf", device="cpu", load_format="mindspore", max_total_tokens=20000, disable_overlap_schedule=True, tp_size=1, dp_size=1) prompts = [ "Hello, my name is", "The president of the United States is", "The capital of France is", "The future of AI is", ] sampling_params = {"temperature": 0.01, "top_p": 0.9} outputs = llm.generate(prompts, sampling_params) for prompt, output in zip(prompts, outputs): print("===============================") print(f"Prompt: {prompt}\nGenerated text: {output['text']}") if __name__ == "__main__": main() ``` Screenshot of the result: As for the performance analysis, mindspore will compile the graph twice (for prefill and decode) which takes time. For prefill we use flashattention kernel for ascend. For decode we use a mindspore implementation similar to the TorchNativeAttnBackend. Here is the time for each forward including torch-to-ms conversion. ``` ms run time: 17.34398579597473 ms run time: 0.014678716659545898 ms run time: 15.733514785766602 ms run time: 0.057671546936035156 ms run time: 0.054368019104003906 ms run time: 0.05373978614807129 ms run time: 0.05384349822998047 ms run time: 0.054900407791137695 ms run time: 0.055121660232543945 ms run time: 0.052907705307006836 ms run time: 0.05253124237060547 ``` ## Roadmap We hope this work will be included in the H2 Roadmap of sglang. We have the current tentative schedule: Q3: - create branch for MindSpore - basic functionalities including RadixAttention, model runner, device communicators - implement mainstream LLMs - benchmark, profiling, documentations etc. Q4: Full-feature support including all parallelisms (DP/TP/EP/PP), PD disaggregation, quantization, speculative decoding, LoRA, etc.

title: [RFC] Support FFN-Attention Disaggregation Strategy for scientific research and low capable NIC devices
author: yiakwy-xpu-ml-framework-team
body: ### Checklist - [x] 1. If the issue you raised is not a feature but a question, please raise a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions/new/choose Otherwise, it will be closed. - [x] 2. Please use English, otherwise it will be closed. ### Motivation ## Motivation & background Traditional HPC application kernel-level optimization pays more attention to - the memory accessing (sparsity, low bits, memory hierarchy caching, reigsters level accum ...) and - workload balancing (persitent, stream-k, split-k ...) Complementary to the proposal in https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/22799, however there is trend that communication between chips becomes more and more important and **Decoding Stage FFN-Attention Model Sharding Pipelining without PMF** (noted as Attention-FFN Disaggregation (AFD) in step3) opened up this opportunity for the future, especially useful for scientific research even though we are not confident it will bring immediate benefits to our infra. Growth of NIC and scales for MoE model Sparisty is amost double each product release: - bandwith up 1.5x (600 GB/s -> 900 GB/s) from Ampere to Hopper , and 2x (900 GB/s -> 1.8 TB/s) from Hopper to Blackwell - higher FLOPS but lower utilization, everything else is bounded by network - reduction inside switches when routing data from one node to another node cross switches Hence, in a broader future, for performance lead, we should support this feature with faster and faster IB/RoCE network communication speed. Both researchers from NVIDIA and AMD recently utilized the latest communication powerness and released **Two Shot** communication libraries among devices, long before that, **one shot** communication pattern dominates in the area device-device communciation, which unlock the future of more complex pipelining schemes. Morover FFN-Attention Model Sharding itself exposes some interesting parts to inferences worloads . In **decoding stage**, attention may be either bounded by computing ceilings (MLA) or memory ones (GPT-OSS 8:1 GQA for example ~ 1 TFlops over tens of GB bytes): 1. for current computing bound attention arch (deepseek v3), and a single micro batch size, MoE FFNs are distributed to all cards in Expert parallel (dp), and attention is distributed to the same group of cards in TP parallel. 2. for those memory bounded attention, flops of GEMM (here we refer to MoE FFN) in decoding stage has nothing do with historical token lengths and is computing bound. And flops of memory bound Attn, such as GQA, in decoding stage, is linearly affected by historical token lengths; 3. compared to MoE Expert parallel, sharding experts to a different groups of cards do not have load-balance problems, with the expenditures communication time. Consider GPT-OSS for example as we calculated [1], MoE parallel is much faster than sharding Attn and FFN to distinct gorups of cards. But for expensive routing (domestic NIC cards), we cannot easily draw solution theoretically, by supporting this feature we can verify immediately. ## Proposal Content We are discussing details here : https://docs.google.com/document/d/1QNYSQP5-KEdOD8cfptaL9eftrIBjDwiH1Tr1TmdtQFU/edit?tab=t.0 Notes : 1. PoC & MVP a. In this stage, we want to demonstate for most available and capable environments, NV/AMD cards, we can shard experts FFN and attention to different groups cards; b. We can create communication ops for consecutive FFN and attention ops; Since IB is an important environment for evaluation, RoCE only solution should not be prioritized; c. We can schedule FFN, Attn in different micro batches to pipeline the whole computatation. 2. Efficient Ping-Pong Pipliner Unlike MoE Expert parallel, sharding FFN and Attn to two distinct groups of GPUs needs pipelining to improve device utilization. Optimizing this pipelining is not a trival thing for a given model. [1] we will release a report separately ## Design of Pipelining of FFN-ATTN Model Sharding In this RFC, we propose Dynamo graph based transformer/Pass to implement Pipelining of FFN-ATTN by rescheduling data flow of arbitrary computation graph: - Since each role has less resources to process data, it is well estimated that the e2e latency will be increased if we implement FFN-ATTN parallel (FAP) with modules replication. - This implements M (streams) : 1 (GPU) relationship with 1 (Process) : N (GPUs in diffrent roles) mapping. The topological order of modules will be fully resolved with our Constrained Topological Sorter module. ## Related resources _No response_

title: [RFC] Consolidate SGLang environment variables
author: vincentzed
body:
# Note
Basically, an extension of https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/9607. We could build on top of it (Or land it quickly, and get on to working on this). #9607 easily shows all of the most convenient sites to replace.

# Issue and background

Environment variable handling in SGLang has become fragmented and inconsistent across the codebase. Direct calls to `os.getenv()` and `os.environ.get()` are scattered throughout modules, creating maintenance overhead and increasing the likelihood of bugs. We need a unified approach.
More importantly, we sacrifice discoverability with the current approach. There's no single place to understand what environment variables the system recognizes or how they're interpreted.

Solution: Something like the following.

We should establish a single canonical source for all environment variable access. The infrastructure is already there; we just need to complete the migration and prevent regression.
A new environment_variables dictionary serves as both a registry and an accessor. When someone imports from this module, they get properly parsed values with consistent defaults. More importantly, the __dir__() function makes all available environment variables discoverable through standard Python introspection.
This centralized approach offers several practical benefits. Type safety improves because each variable has a defined type and parsing logic. Debugging becomes easier because there's a single place to add logging or modify behavior. Documentation becomes possible because all variables are visible in one location.
# Proposition
```python
import hashlib
import logging
import os
import sys
import tempfile
from typing import TYPE_CHECKING, Any, Callable, Optional

logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)

# Track warned environment variable keys
_warned_bool_env_var_keys = set()


def get_bool_env_var(name: str, default: str = "false") -> bool:
    value = os.getenv(name, default)
    value = value.lower()

    truthy_values = ("true", "1")
    falsy_values = ("false", "0")

    if (value not in truthy_values) and (value not in falsy_values):
        if value not in _warned_bool_env_var_keys:
            logger.warning(
                f"get_bool_env_var({name}) see non-understandable value={value} and treat as false"
            )
        _warned_bool_env_var_keys.add(value)

    return value in truthy_values


def get_int_env_var(name: str, default: int = 0) -> int:
    value = os.getenv(name)
    if value is None or not value.strip():
        return default
    try:
        return int(value)
    except ValueError:
        return default


def get_default_cache_root():
    return os.getenv(
        "XDG_CACHE_HOME",
        os.path.join(os.path.expanduser("~"), ".cache"),
    )


def get_default_config_root():
    return os.getenv(
        "XDG_CONFIG_HOME",
        os.path.join(os.path.expanduser("~"), ".config"),
    )


def maybe_convert_int(value: Optional[str]) -> Optional[int]:
    if value is None:
        return None
    return int(value)


def maybe_convert_bool(value: Optional[str]) -> Optional[bool]:
    if value is None:
        return None
    return bool(int(value))

def __getattr__(name: str):

    if name in environment_variables:

    raise AttributeError(f"module {__name__!r} has no attribute {name!r}")


def __dir__():

def is_set(name: str):
    """Check if an environment variable is explicitly set."""
    if name in environment_variables:
        return name in os.environ
    raise AttributeError(f"module {__name__!r} has no attribute {name!r}")

```

# Migration Strategy
The migration should be straightforward and incremental. Replace direct os.getenv() calls with imports from sglang.srt.utils. This will require a lot of manual work.

For example:
```python
# Before
MAX_TOKENS = int(os.getenv("MODELOPT_MAX_TOKENS_PER_EXPERT", "65536"))

# After  
from sglang.srt.utils import MODELOPT_MAX_TOKENS_PER_EXPERT
MAX_TOKENS = MODELOPT_MAX_TOKENS_PER_EXPERT
```

# Prevent Regression
Add a pre-commit like:
```python
# In .pre-commit-config.yaml, add a custom hook
def check_env_var_usage(filenames):
    pattern = r'os\.getenv|os\.environ\.'
    violations = []
    for filename in filenames:
        if 'utils.py' in filename:  # Skip the central module
            continue
        # Check for direct os.getenv usage
        # Suggest using sglang.srt.utils instead
```

# Docs
Add a note, like the following.
> Environment Variables: All environment variable access should go through ---X---. This module provides type-safe accessors with consistent defaults and validation. To add a new environment variable, define it in the environment_variables dictionary with appropriate parsing logic.

title: RFC: SGLang Benchmarking Script Consolidation and Reliability Improvements
author: vincentzed
body:
# Summary
We should make scripts consistent, hackable, and easily extendable. Fix existing bugs and issues, and maybe build a dedicated interface. Multi-person, multi-week effort.

# Issue Background
In our repository, we have four distinct scripts that serve as the main benchmarking utilities. They have many issues, but as of right now, they generally work for most purposes. However, the main concerns are with overlapping functionality, inconsistent interfaces, and reliability issues that can make them less effective for performance evaluation. These scripts have mostly evolved organically based on needs and ad hoc changes. While there's no way around this, it has led to some fragmentation in script consistency, and some unification would be very helpful.

bench_one_batch: Single static batch without server (offline, GPU-synchronized)
bench_one_batch_server: Single batch via HTTP server (online, client-observed)
bench_offline_throughput: Offline engine throughput testing
bench_serving: Online serving with dynamic request patterns

Some scripts contain bugs that can be reliably triggered under normal usage patterns. For example, some parameters in the scripts have name errors because they reference variables out of scope. Some calculations result in division by zero when a metric capture fails, and other similar issues pop up when testing for edge cases in the benchmarking scripts. At least in our case, reliability issues don't really exist with the scripts since when they fail, the benchmark result was invalid anyways. But in many cases, when we have inconsistency, we don't let the user know. The scripts don't have much in terms of consistency and visibility for the benchmarking users.

They also have pretty inconsistent CLI interfaces, making them very disparate tools. Instead of being a relatively cohesive benchmarking suite, this aspect definitely can be improved. For example, flag naming varies very arbitrarily across scripts.
Eg, from just comparison bench_serving vs bench_one_batch, we have: --result-filename versus --output-file, there are many other examples.

Tokenization handling also diverges between scripts: some use `sglang.get_tokenizer` while others rely on `transformers.autotokenizer`. There are differences in token counting that change how benchmarks work. While benchmarks currently aren't cross-compared, we should definitely resolve this inconsistency.

One suggestion that has come up is to have unified sglang subcommand functionality, but this would be a more complex job than unifying and making benchmarking consistent across scripts. Ideally, we’d start off with:
A. Making existing scripts the most correct they can be.
B. Design a bench interface that supports the most important and widely used benchmarks.
C. Finally, deprecate the existing benchmark scripts.
Design note: a new benchmark suite should be relatively ‘hackable’ -insofar that users would be able to design / create their own benchmarks on custom datasets easily, with their own metrics. This requires some smart design. Users should easily be able to fork and customize scripts for their specific needs.
We should make it easy enough to understand so that despite not being backwards compatible, users should have no problem migrating. In this case, I reason that the improvement is large enough to warrant such a change.

# Documentation
The docs https://docs.sglang.ai/developer_guide/benchmark_and_profiling.html can stay basic, but the current strategy of code as documentation is still quite complex / requires lots of overhead to view and extend.

# Practical Notes
This would work as a multi-week effort depending on the stages we implement.

title: RFC: Command-Line Interface Architecture for SGLang
author: vincentzed
body:
# RFD: Unified `sglang` Command-Line Interface

## Status

Draft

## Summary

SGLang’s current invocation pattern requires users to run Python modules directly, for example:

```bash
python -m sglang.launch_server
python -m sglang.bench_latency
```

This is workable but brittle: it is easy to mistype, hard to discover, and forces users to memorize internal module names that we may want to refactor. This RFD proposes a first-class `sglang` CLI with a small set of well-named commands, and an internal structure that can scale without turning into a bespoke CLI framework.

This document leans heavily on a close study of vLLM’s CLI, because vLLM is a good preview of what happens when an inference engine accumulates years of flags, modes, and “just one more option” requests. The goal here is not to imitate vLLM; it’s to learn from its successes and avoid inheriting its pain.

## Context and motivation

We repeatedly see users struggle with “what exact incantation do I need?” and “which module path is correct?” because SGLang exposes multiple operations as separate Python module entrypoints with no unified discovery mechanism. The net effect is that the interface leaks implementation details: users are coupled to our package structure.

A unified CLI should make common workflows obvious and stable. It should also give us a place to enforce consistent validation and error messages, rather than distributing that responsibility across multiple `__main__` blocks and scripts.

## Proposed interface

The entry point is `sglang`. The initial command surface is:

```text
sglang launch
sglang chat
sglang complete
sglang batch
sglang bench <subcommand>
```

Benchmarks are intentionally grouped as a subtree so they remain discoverable without polluting unrelated command help:

```text
sglang bench latency
sglang bench serving
sglang bench throughput
```

Whether the canonical verb is `launch` or `serve` is open; if we pick one, we should almost certainly provide the other as an alias for familiarity across ecosystems.

## Design principles

This CLI should be discoverable via `--help`, stable under internal refactors, and responsive for trivial operations like `--version` and `--help`. It should fail fast on invalid combinations of flags before expensive initialization. It should also be maintainable: the CLI will grow over time, and we should be wary of designs that force us into thousands of lines of plumbing or a proliferation of one-off parsing hacks.

The vLLM study is relevant here because vLLM demonstrates both ends of the spectrum: they have real rigor in validation and reuse, and they also show how a CLI can accumulate framework-wrestling code once it reaches a certain scale.

## Architecture

This proposal separates the CLI into three layers: a command framework, a command registry, and a configuration layer. The layers are small, but the separation matters, because it determines whether the CLI remains a thin interface or becomes a second system.

### Command framework (parsing, help, completion)

The command framework is responsible for parsing options, rendering help, and dispatching to the correct subcommand. The recommendation is Typer (built on Click), rather than argparse.

This recommendation is directly informed by vLLM. vLLM uses argparse and has clearly invested substantial engineering to keep it usable at scale. That investment is instructive. Their CLI lives under `vllm/entrypoints/cli/`, and their OpenAI-server-facing CLI args are built in `vllm/entrypoints/openai/cli_args.py`. The net result is functional, but it is also an example of “argparse at scale” creating its own engineering surface area: custom action classes, help filtering utilities, parallel parser construction for docs, and explicit command wiring.

In vLLM, the amount of code dedicated to “making argparse behave like a modern CLI” is not incidental; it is the dominant cost once the CLI becomes featureful. This RFD’s bias toward Click/Typer is essentially a decision to not re-implement that layer ourselves.

There is also a responsiveness concern. vLLM’s `vllm/entrypoints/cli/main.py` has explicit lazy import structure to keep `--version` and `--help` fast. The fact that they had to do that is not a criticism; it’s an honest signal about what happens if CLI parsing is tightly coupled to importing the world. We should treat “help must be fast” as a design constraint from the start, regardless of framework.

### Command registry (structure, dispatch, lazy imports)

The registry organizes subcommands and dispatches execution. The important design point is that dispatch should support lazy imports so that running `sglang --help` does not import or initialize GPU/model-related code.

vLLM provides two notable patterns here. First, they use a top-level list of command modules (`CMD_MODULES`) and import them only when needed in `vllm/entrypoints/cli/main.py`. This keeps the CLI responsive, but it also creates a manual wiring point: every new command requires editing a central list. That is easy to forget, and it is an example of “mechanical friction” that tends to show up as user-visible incompleteness (“why doesn’t my command appear?”) rather than a clean failure.

Second, vLLM uses a base class shape for subcommands (`CLISubcommand` in `vllm/entrypoints/cli/types.py`) and an argparse pattern where a callback is injected into the parsed namespace via `set_defaults()`, then executed after parsing. This works, but it ties command dispatch to argparse’s data model, and it subtly encourages the command’s “definition” and “execution” to be scattered (parser building in one place, validation elsewhere, execution somewhere else).

For SGLang, the intent is to keep the registry explicit but low-friction. If we use Typer/Click, subcommand registration is naturally structural (functions grouped under commands), and help is scoped by default without filtering hacks. We still need to be disciplined about imports: the handler for `launch` should import the server implementation only when invoked, not at module import time.

### Configuration layer (mapping flags to validated config)

The configuration layer maps CLI options into typed configuration objects that are used by the engine/server. This is where we get reuse (CLI and programmatic entrypoints share the same config) and where we can place validation in one coherent location.

vLLM does something genuinely good here. They centralize a large portion of CLI option definition and reuse through `FrontendArgs` and related configuration constructs, and they reuse parser construction between the CLI and the API server entrypoint rather than duplicating flags by hand. The compositional pattern in `make_arg_parser()` (in `vllm/entrypoints/openai/cli_args.py`) is a strong signal that “one configuration definition reused across entrypoints” is the right direction.

However, vLLM also demonstrates the cost of marrying that configuration layer to argparse. Where options require structured parsing, they end up with bespoke argparse Action classes such as `LoRAParserAction` to support multiple input formats, and various workarounds for JSON-like values. None of this is conceptually difficult, but it forces parsing logic into framework-specific corners, which makes it harder to test, harder to read, and easier to accidentally break.

This RFD therefore proposes that SGLang’s configuration layer should be framework-agnostic. The CLI can adapt options into a typed configuration object; validation then happens on that object before we do expensive initialization. The CLI framework should not be the place where we encode half of our configuration semantics.

## vLLM study: what we should explicitly learn from

vLLM’s strongest pattern is fail-fast validation before expensive work. Their serve command validates parsed args (for example, ensuring option combinations are coherent) before model loading. This is exactly the user experience we want: if the configuration is invalid, the user should learn that immediately, not after waiting for GPU initialization and model load.

Their second strong pattern is import discipline. The explicit lazy import scaffolding in their CLI entrypoint is a sign that performance and reliability matter even for mundane CLI operations. A CLI that occasionally triggers heavyweight imports during `--help` will feel “broken” even if it’s technically correct.

Their third strong pattern is composition of argument sources: serving options, frontend options, engine options are assembled together, which reduces duplication.

Where vLLM appears to struggle is in all the code that exists purely to compensate for argparse ergonomics at scale. Help filtering is an especially telling example: once commands have 100+ flags, you either accept overwhelming help output or you build your own filtering layer. vLLM builds a filtering layer. That’s a rational outcome, but it’s also an outcome we can avoid by choosing a framework that naturally scopes help to the relevant command and supports grouping without custom introspection.

Similarly, documentation generation pressure shows up as parallel parser construction (`create_parser_for_docs()`), which is a classic drift risk. This is not a vLLM-specific mistake; it is a common failure mode when “the runtime definition” and “the documentation definition” are not the same artifact. We should design SGLang’s CLI so that docs can be generated from the actual commands without reconstructing them.

Finally, manual dispatch wiring (the need to register commands in a central list) is not catastrophic, but it is the kind of tax that accumulates as the command set grows. It is also the kind of tax that disproportionately affects contributors, because the “happy path” is to implement the command logic, not to remember to edit a registry file. Our design should bias toward structures where commands appear by construction, not by ceremony.

## Implementation details

Command handlers should be thin adapters. Each handler should construct a configuration object from the CLI options, validate it, and then call an internal API to do the real work.

The key non-negotiable is that configuration validation happens before expensive initialization. That includes validating cross-flag constraints, file existence, template compatibility, and any “mode implies constraint” rules. vLLM’s validation pattern is a good example to follow here; we just want it expressed in our configuration layer rather than scattered across parsing glue.

Benchmarks should be implemented as nested subcommands with a discovery mechanism that does not require heavyweight imports for top-level help. vLLM’s benchmark subtree uses subclass-based discovery, which is clever and keeps wiring minimal, but it relies on imports that may or may not be cheap depending on module structure. For SGLang, the requirement is simpler: entering `sglang bench --help` can afford to import benchmark command definitions; `sglang --help` should not.

## Backward compatibility

Existing module-based invocations should remain supported for at least one deprecation window, but should warn and point users to the new CLI. Internally, the module entrypoints should become thin wrappers around the same functions used by the new CLI, so we do not maintain two logic paths.

## Alternatives considered

Argparse is the obvious alternative, and vLLM proves it can be made to work. The reason to not choose it is that the long-term steady-state appears to require a non-trivial amount of framework-specific plumbing: custom parsing actions, help filtering, doc parser duplication, and manual dispatch scaffolding. Choosing Click/Typer is a decision to avoid re-learning those lessons.

Keeping module-based invocation avoids work in the short term but keeps the user experience coupled to internal code structure and does not address discoverability.

## Risks and tradeoffs

A unified CLI is a user-facing contract. Once users adopt `sglang launch ...`, we need to treat option names and semantics as stable and versioned. That argues for being deliberate now, especially about naming, defaults, and grouping.

Lazy imports improve responsiveness but require discipline in module boundaries. vLLM’s explicit lazy import work is a reminder that this is not optional if we want a CLI that feels reliable.

Unifying configuration will require some refactoring. The payoff is that validation, reuse, and documentation become tractable rather than duplicated.

## Open questions

We should decide whether the canonical verb is `launch` or `serve`, and whether we want aliases.

We should decide whether a config-file format is in scope for the first iteration. Even if we defer it, we should ensure the configuration layer makes it easy to add later.

We should decide how much extensibility we want for benchmarks: internal-only is simplest; plugin-style is powerful but adds surface area.

## Determination

We should build a unified `sglang` CLI. The design should incorporate vLLM’s clear successes—fail-fast validation, argument composition, and import discipline—while avoiding the long-term argparse complexity that vLLM’s codebase demonstrates in practice. The CLI should be a thin layer over typed configuration and internal APIs, not a second implementation of SGLang’s behavior.

title: [RFC] SGLang unified kernel fusion and torch compile optimisations
author: DevashishLal-CB
body:
### Motivation
To achieve the best possible performance across diverse hardware, workloads, and scale. Heavily optimized hand tuned kernels are often required. This requirement makes it harder for model developers (that just want to focus on the model architecture) to easily integrate there models into inference engines like sglang. Currently models need to be reimplemented using the set of optimized kernels provided by sgl-kernel and other kernel libraries. Not only does this duplicate a lot of code related to invocation of the kernels across different models it just adds more for the models authors to get the best performance.

With torch compile model authors don't need to care about the specifics of optimized kernels and can let the compiler do it for them.
### Solution
For pure pytorch models torch compiles works great, all you need to do is decorate a function with `@torch.compile` and it will trace the tensor operations to generate a computation graph which is then compiled to optimized triton kernel (depending on the inductor backend). torch compile with just native pytorch code get you pretty far in terms of performance but seek out the last bit of performance custom hardware kernels are still required. torch compile can easily be extended with custom fusion passes completely decoupling model architecture from kernel optimisations and these passes can be reused across models
### What does a custom fusion pass look like
Torch compile provides multiple way to perform surgery on the fx graph, we can drop down at the node level and perform matching and replacement manually but inductor ships with a nice pattern matcher (`torch._inductor.pattern_matcher`) which can make implementation quite clean and simple, as an example a [fused swiglu](https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.05202) pass would like the following
```python
import torch._inductor.pattern_matcher as pm

patterns = pm.PatternMatcherPass()

def fused_swiglu_pattern(x, w):
    mm = torch.ops.aten.mm.default(x, w)
    result = torch.ops.aten.empty.memory_format(
        [mm.shape[0], mm.shape[1] // 2],
        dtype=mm.dtype,
        device=mm.device,
        pin_memory=False,
    )
    at = auto_functionalized_v2(
        torch.ops.sgl_kernel.silu_and_mul.default,
        input=mm,
        _out_base_index=0,
        _all_bases=[result],
    )
    return at[1]


def fused_swiglu_replacement(x, w):
    return torch.ops.sglang.fused_swiglu.default(x, w)


example_inputs = [
    torch.empty(16, 16).half().cuda(),
    torch.empty(16, 16).half().cuda(),
]

pm.register_replacement(
    fused_swiglu_pattern,
    fused_swiglu_replacement,
    example_inputs,
    pm.fwd_only,
    patterns,
)
```

Patterns can be found by looking at the dynamo graph, and as long the replacement is registered as a torch operator with [torch compile support](https://docs.pytorch.org/tutorials/advanced/cpp_custom_ops.html#adding-torch-compile-support-for-an-operator), registration for the above operator looks like the following
```python
from sglang.srt.utils import direct_register_custom_op

def fused_swiglu(
    x: torch.Tensor,
    w: torch.Tensor,
    x_scale: Optional[torch.Tensor] = None,
    w_scale: Optional[torch.Tensor] = None,
    o_scale: Optional[torch.Tensor] = None,
) -> torch.Tensor:
	# actual implementation
	...
	pass


def fused_swiglu_fake(
    x: torch.Tensor,
    w: torch.Tensor,
    x_scale: Optional[torch.Tensor] = None,
    w_scale: Optional[torch.Tensor] = None,
    o_scale: Optional[torch.Tensor] = None,
) -> torch.Tensor:
    # fake implementation is to just inform the compiler of the outputs
    # if this is an inplace operator this function would be blank
    M, N, K = x.shape[0], x.shape[1], w.shape[1] // 2
    return torch.empty((M, K), device=x.device, dtype=x.dtype)


direct_register_custom_op(
    op_name="fused_swiglu",
    op_func=fused_swiglu,
    mutates_args=[],
    fake_impl=fused_swiglu_fake,
)
```
Fake implementations are used by the compiler to check graph if a particular fusion pass can fit in the computation graph, using a fake implementation avoids the execution of actual operators during the compilation which would just slow down the compilation.

Finally you need to tell torch compile about the pattern matcher you just created
```python
def sglang_fusion_passes(graph):
    num_matches = patterns.apply(graph)
    return num_matches

# actual registration into the backend
torch._inductor.config.post_grad_custom_post_pass = sglang_fusion_passes
```

With this any function/module passed to or decorated with `torch.compile` would run our fusion passes
### Example of fusion passes
Here are just a few examples of possible fusions, lot more should be possible especially with different quant schemes
- SiLU and Mul (and other actications)
- SiLU and Mul + Quant (FP8)
- UpProject + SiLU and Mul (and other actications)
- UpProject + SiLU and Mul (and other actications) + Quant (FP8)
- FusedMOE + SiLU and Mul
- Attention + Quant (FP8)
- RMSNorm + Quant (FP8)
- Allreduce + RMSNorm
- Allreduce + RMSNorm + Quant (FP8)
### Implementation (Proposed)
To get started we just need `PassManager` where custom passes can be registered, but I would like to lay down the foundation for features that may be adopted down the road, just on top of my head and looking at [vllm's implementation](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/tree/main/vllm/compilation)
- Easily configurable, user should be able to tweak sglang specifc or general torch compilation config as well as enable/disable specific passes
- Usable with or without cuda graphs, currently torch.compile is only supported with cuda graph
- Inductor cache management for faster starts, inductor can do a lot of this for us need to look further do we need manual management
- Cuda graph integration, Piecewise graphs, I understand sglang manages cudagraphs for decode on it's own (`cuda_graph_runner.py`) torch compile could do this too, I need too look more into this to fully understand which would be the best way
- Observability and monitoring, we should easily be able to gets stats on which passes ran and how many replacements were done
- Unit testing, writing unit tests for custom fusion passes and testing them on actual model should be easy
#### Compilation Config
responsible for resolving the current config from server_args and env vars for torch compile as well as individual passes, this config object's hash would be used for cache invalidation if need manual management. any required validation and model specific tweaks to the config to be done here
#### Compilation Manager
Entry point for the compilation, responsible for registering the pass manager with inductor post grad passes and collecting compilation stats and metrics
#### Pass Manager
Responsible for registering individual passes custom passes based on compilation config
#### SGLang Inductor Pass
base class for defining passes, ideally passes should be composable in nature as logically similar passes could be registered with multiple variation (i.e with or without quant or multiple types of quant), sole purpose of this class is to provide utilities to enable the composable nature and avoid duplication of code
#### Operator registration
As required existing kernels and triton ops would need to be register as torch ops with torch compile support to avoid graph breaks and facilitate pattern replacement, e.g registration for the triton decode attention
```python
def decode_attention_fwd_impl(
    q: torch.Tensor,
    k_buffer: torch.Tensor,
    v_buffer: torch.Tensor,
    o: torch.Tensor,
    kv_indptr: torch.Tensor,
    kv_indices: torch.Tensor,
    attn_logits: torch.Tensor,
    attn_lse: torch.Tensor,
    num_kv_splits: torch.Tensor,
    max_kv_splits: int,
    sm_scale: float,
    logit_cap: float = 0.0,
    sinks: Optional[torch.Tensor] = None,
    xai_temperature_len: int = -1,
) -> None:
    assert max_kv_splits == attn_logits.shape[2]
    assert q.shape[0] <= kv_indptr.shape[0] - 1
    assert q.shape[0] <= attn_logits.shape[0]

    kv_group_num = q.shape[1] // v_buffer.shape[1]

    if kv_group_num == 1:
        # MHA
        decode_attention_fwd_normal(
            q,
            k_buffer,
            v_buffer,
            o,
            kv_indptr,
            kv_indices,
            attn_logits,
            attn_lse,
            num_kv_splits,
            max_kv_splits,
            sm_scale,
            logit_cap=logit_cap,
            sinks=sinks,
            xai_temperature_len=xai_temperature_len,
        )
    else:
        # GQA/MQA/MLA
        decode_attention_fwd_grouped(
            q,
            k_buffer,
            v_buffer,
            o,
            kv_indptr,
            kv_indices,
            attn_logits,
            attn_lse,
            num_kv_splits,
            max_kv_splits,
            sm_scale,
            logit_cap=logit_cap,
            sinks=sinks,
            xai_temperature_len=xai_temperature_len,
        )


def decode_attention_fwd_fake(
    q,
    k_buffer,
    v_buffer,
    o,
    kv_indptr,
    kv_indices,
    attn_logits,
    attn_lse,
    num_kv_splits,
    max_kv_splits,
    sm_scale,
    logit_cap=0.0,
    sinks=None,
    xai_temperature_len=-1,
):
    pass


def decode_attention_fwd(
    q,
    k_buffer,
    v_buffer,
    o,
    kv_indptr,
    kv_indices,
    attn_logits,
    attn_lse,
    num_kv_splits,
    max_kv_splits,
    sm_scale,
    logit_cap=0.0,
    sinks=None,
    xai_temperature_len=-1,
):
    torch.ops.sglang.decode_attention_fwd(
        q,
        k_buffer,
        v_buffer,
        o,
        kv_indptr,
        kv_indices,
        attn_logits,
        attn_lse,
        num_kv_splits,
        max_kv_splits,
        sm_scale,
        logit_cap,
        sinks,
        xai_temperature_len,
    )


direct_register_custom_op(
    op_name="decode_attention_fwd",
    op_func=decode_attention_fwd_impl,
    mutates_args=["o", "attn_lse"],
    fake_impl=decode_attention_fwd_fake,
)
```
#### Usage of auto functionalize v2
functionalization is required for torch compile to optimise the IR, for mutable operators auto functionalize v1 achived functionalization using extra copies and an extra defunctionalization pass was required to get rid of these copies post compilation (https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/vllm/compilation/fix_functionalization.py), auto functionalize v2 does this for us under the hood. for a better explanation refer the following: https://dev-discuss.pytorch.org/t/a-new-strategy-for-automatic-custom-operators-functionalization/2733

### Overview of vLLM's implementation
This is the execution flow of the complete compilation process according to the snooping around I have done
- starts with the `support_torch_compile` decorator which is added to model architecture for which custom passes are supported
- this calls the custom dispatcher `TorchCompileWrapperWithCustomDispatcher` which inits the `VllmBackend` based on compilation config and calls torch.compile with the initialized backend
- `VllmBackend` on init creates the `graph pool` (probably for the piecewise graphs), `compilation manager` (responsible for the actual compilation), `pass manager` (this where post grad passes get registered)
- `VllmBackend` when executed first computes get's the config has, this is used by the compilation manager to either load existing compiled cache (skip the compilation) or compile and save a new cache, then the backend creates the piece wise graphs (each of these will be a compiled cuda graph) this is done as all graphs breaks can't be avoided
- Each graph is handled by a `PiecewiseCompileInterpreter(torch.fx.Interpreter)` which internally calls the compilation manager
- `CompilerManager` is just a wrapper around existing inductor backend, this is done through `CompilerInterface` which is implemented by `InductorStandaloneAdaptor` or `InductorAdaptor` other than executing inductor compilation, CompilerManager also manages create or loading the cache for the sub graph it's targeting

### References
- https://blog.vllm.ai/2025/08/20/torch-compile.html
- https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.05202
- https://docs.pytorch.org/tutorials/advanced/cpp_custom_ops.html#adding-torch-compile-support-for-an-operator
- https://dev-discuss.pytorch.org/t/a-new-strategy-for-automatic-custom-operators-functionalization/2733
- https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/tree/main/vllm/compilation

title: [Feature] RFC: Integrating checkpoint engine into SGLang
author: stmatengss
body:
### Checklist

- [ ] 1. If the issue you raised is not a feature but a question, please raise a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions/new/choose Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [ ] 2. Please use English, otherwise it will be closed.

### Motivation

Two key scenarios can benefit from this PR:
- Reinforcement Learning (RL) Workloads – including RLHF, DPO, and continual pre-training – where model weights are updated frequently. Current methods for synchronizing these updates into the inference engine introduce significant latency, creating a bottleneck. This underutilizes GPUs during weight updates and slows the overall training-inference loop.
- Bulk Deployment – The boot time is a performance bottleneck when launching multiple SGLang instances. 

Proposal: Motivated by #8215, we aim to integrate [ckpt-engine](https://github.com/moonshotai/checkpoint-engine)into SGLang to accelerate model loading and weight synchronization.

ckpt-engine is a lightweight library optimized for large-scale distributed training. It uses a parameter server architecture (ps.py, worker.py) and supports both co-located and disaggregated deployments. Its core innovation is an asynchronous, pipelined data transfer mechanism built on the Mooncake transfer engine. This allows SGLang to offload weight updates to background workers, effectively hiding I/O and communication latency.

CC. @ShangmingCai @zhyncs @james0zan @XucSh @zxpdemonio

### Related resources

Develop Roadmap:
1. Stage one: While booting sglang instance, load model (i.e., update weights) from ckpt engine.
2. Stage two: support online update weights, and related fastAPI
3. Stage three: support saving weights to ckpt engine in sglang side.

Code Changes (Stage One):
1. a new ckpt engine connector (CkptEngineConnectot) in python/sglang/srt/connector/skpt_engine_connector.py
2. a new model load (CkptEngineModelLoader) in  python/sglang/srt/model_load/loader.py, and add a new  load_format in get_model_loader()
3. In class ModelRunner (model_runner.py), 
    a. Add extra configs as new parameters for initialization of ParameterServer.
    b. Init class ParameterServer (self.ps = ParameterServer(auto_pg=False)) in __init__. 
    c. In load_model(), if self.server_args.load_format == LoadFormat.CKPT_ENGINE, invoke load_model_from_ckpt_engine()
    d. In load_model_from_ckpt_engine(), use methods split_checkpoint_files() and update_weights() to load weights from ckpt engine.
4. add a new load_format option (ckpt_engine) in server_args.py, and extra_config for endpoint
5. According to https://github.com/MoonshotAI/checkpoint-engine/blob/main/examples/update.py, add a new tool named save_model_to_ckpt_engine_util.py

WorkFlow:
1. Use the tool (save_model_to_ckpt_engine_util.py) to emulate the training side, save model weights to ckpt engine.
2. Run inference side: python -m sglang.launch_server --load-metas-file global_metas.pkl 
--ckpt-engine-endpoint http://ip:port
--load-format ckpt-engine

title: [RFC] [Feature] Improving request-level timing and performance metrics
author: scottjlee
body:
### Checklist

- [x] 1. If the issue you raised is not a feature but a question, please raise a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions/new/choose Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [x] 2. Please use English, otherwise it will be closed.

### Motivation

## Motivation
When using SGLang in production, it is important to be able to analyze problematic request(s) based on a number of criteria (TTFT, TPS, speculative decoding effectiveness, etc) in order to debug bottlenecks and other issues. Moreover, it's useful to export the results in a standardized format (e.g. JSON) so that other services can use them (e.g. for monitoring & alerting, data analysis, etc). To achieve these goals, we propose the following additions:

- [x] 1. **Metrics exporter [[PR](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/10973)]:** Add an abstract `RequestMetricsExporter` interface which exports request-level metrics collected by SGLang to arbitrary data sinks. Also included is a concrete implementation which writes JSON-format strings (one for each request) to files on disk; the data in these files can then be asynchronously ingested by databases or data platforms. Alternatively, users can also extend the `RequestMetricsExporter` interface and implement an appropriate utility for their data sink of choice.

- [ ] 2. **Identifier fields [[PR](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/11108)]:** Add identifier fields (`user_id`, `external_request_id`) to be able to trace a request from an external caller (with their provided request ID) through SGLang, without overwriting the SGLang internal `rid` field. It can also be useful to analyze the set of requests from a certain user, enabled by a `user_id` field. It's possible to further abstract this to accept a generic dict of "identifier fields", but wanted to start with this concrete use case first. 

- [x] 3. **Timing metrics [[PR](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/11119)]:** Add additional timing metrics to breakdown how long a request spends in major phases of inference (validation, queue, prefill, decode). In addition, having timestamps of key points of the request lifecycle (request received, request scheduled, response sent) can be helpful to analyze latencies between external callers.

- [x] 4. **Speculative decoding metrics [[PR](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/11441)]:** Add metrics for evaluating effectiveness of speculative decoding: per-request acceptance rate and average acceptance length.

~- [ ] 5. **Prefix cache hit rate [[PR](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/11146)]:** Add per-request prefix cache hit rate for evaluating effectiveness of prefix cache.~ Will not do -- defer to router/middleware/user to calculate from `cached_tokens / prompt_tokens`

- [x] 6. **Retraction count [[PR](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/11177)]:** Add per-request retraction count for identifying retracted requests.
