title: [RFC] Faster loading for MoE models using TP
author: nvjullin
body:
### Checklist

- [x] If this is not a feature request but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [x] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

# Problem
For the purposes of this discussion, the majority of weights is in MoE and we'll be ignoring the rest.

When loading models such as deepseek-R1 using TP8, the loading times can be extremely long (~1hour), bottlenecked at disk IO. In contrast, when using TEP8/DEP8, the loading time is significantly shorter (~2min). However, all three settings read the same number of bytes on each rank, so the main culprit is the access pattern.

Safetensors are stored parameter-by-parameter, meaning each safetensor stores several parameters contiguously. In EP, the access pattern is simple: either read an entire parameter or skip it. In TP, the weights are striped. For example, for TP2, the two gemm weights look like
```
+----------+         +-----------+
|#####-----|         |###########|
|#####-----|         |###########|
|#####-----|         |-----------|
|#####-----|         |-----------|
+----------+         +-----------+
```
This pattern is horrible for disk IO, even with all the mmap and caching involved.

# Solution

A solution is to load in a pattern that is disk IO friendly. Namely, we can load weights as-if using EP, then use device-to-device (D2D) memory transfers to restore the weights into what TP needs. A proof-of-concept implementation (including a unit test) can be found at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/compare/main...nvjullin:sglang:claude-tp-to-ep.

This solution is premised on several factors:
1. EP weight loading is fast, which varies with the disk setup
2. TP weight loading is slow, which varies with the disk setup
3. D2D is fast, which varies with GPU topology

So it's not a universal solution for all setups. In our setup, the solution makes weight loading go from ~1hour to ~2min because D2D is virtually free.

This solution does not work generically across models. Diffusion models won't benefit from this, but the same principle can be ported over (with effort).

There is a slight memory overhead of additional buffers used during D2D. It is on the order of the weights of a single layer. For deepseek-R1 with 61 layers, this is ~2% overhead, which is unlikely to be problematic.

# Alternative Solutions

#19758 implements an alternative format InstantTensor. I am not familiar with its technical details.
It doesn't describe what scenario it excels at, nor its solution.

title: [RFC] Refactor server_args.py
author: Fridge003
body:
### Motivation

Following the discussion in #19139 and #20285, this issue provides a more detailed plan of how to refactor `server_args.py`, which has grown to more than 5k lines.

**Caution: Most of this doc is generated with Claude Opus under instruction. It's prone to change in some details (but the overall idea doesn't change)**

## Part 1: Analysis of `server_args.py`

The file is **5,787 lines** and almost entirely occupied by a single class `ServerArgs` (lines 280-6082). Here is a breakdown by section:


| Section                                     | Lines  | % of File |
| ------------------------------------------- | ------ | --------- |
| Constants and choice lists (top-level)      | ~200   | 3.5%      |
| Field definitions (dataclass attributes)    | ~435   | 7.5%      |
| `__post_init__` + 38 handler methods        | ~2,550 | 44%       |
| `add_cli_args` (static method)              | ~2,290 | 40%       |
| Other methods (check, validate, properties) | ~517   | 9%        |


The single largest handler method is `_handle_model_specific_adjustments` at **601 lines** (~10% of the entire file), containing per-architecture if/elif branches for DeepSeek, Llama4, Gemma, Qwen3, Falcon, etc.

## Part 2: Overall Refactoring Ideas

1. **Mixin classes as code-organization units** — Each argument domain (model, parallelism, cache, etc.) becomes a mixin class that defines its fields, its `add_cli_args` contribution, and optionally its own validation. `ServerArgs` inherits from all mixins via multiple inheritance, so fields are registered directly as member variables — no `__getattr__` delegation, no sub-object access, and no mutation-sync issues. This keeps `server_args.model_path` working as a direct attribute while co-locating each field with the CLI definition that populates it.

   ```python
   # arg_groups/groups/model_args.py
   @dataclasses.dataclass
   class ModelArgsMixin:
       model_path: str = ""
       tokenizer_path: Optional[str] = None
       tokenizer_mode: str = "auto"
       # ... fields for this domain

       @staticmethod
       def add_cli_args(parser: argparse.ArgumentParser):
           group = parser.add_argument_group("Model and tokenizer")
           group.add_argument("--model-path", "--model", type=str, ...)
           ...
   ```

   ```python
   # server_args.py
   @dataclasses.dataclass
   class ServerArgs(ModelArgsMixin, ParallelArgsMixin, CacheArgsMixin, ...):
       # Only fields that don't belong to any domain, or orchestration overrides
       ...

       @staticmethod
       def add_cli_args(parser):
           ModelArgsMixin.add_cli_args(parser)
           ParallelArgsMixin.add_cli_args(parser)
           CacheArgsMixin.add_cli_args(parser)
           ...
   ```

2. **Extract handler methods into modules** — The 38 `_handle_*` methods (2,550 lines) should be grouped into handler modules under `python/sglang/srt/arg_groups/handlers/`. Each handler module contains closely related functions. `__post_init__` remains on `ServerArgs` but calls imported handler functions, using **lazy (inline) imports** so that unused handler modules (e.g., NPU-specific handlers on CUDA machines) incur no import cost.

3. **Split `_handle_model_specific_adjustments`** — This 601-line function should become a **dispatch table** (registry pattern) of per-architecture handler functions. Each architecture (DeepSeek, Llama4, Qwen3, etc.) gets its own function. This replaces the giant if/elif chain with O(1) lookup and makes it trivial to add new architectures without touching the dispatch function, genuinely reducing cyclomatic complexity.

4. **Move validation methods** — `check_server_args`, `check_lora_server_args`, `validate_buckets_rule`, etc. move to a dedicated `validators.py`.

5. **Preserve backward compatibility** — `ServerArgs` remains the single public interface with all fields directly on it. The `arg_groups/` sub-modules are internal code-organization. All existing imports (`from sglang.srt.server_args import ServerArgs`) and all existing attribute access patterns (`server_args.model_path`) continue to work with zero runtime overhead. A `compat.py` module provides deprecation warnings for any public symbols that move. See Part 5 for details.

6. **Phase the migration in small, safe increments** — This is a large refactor touching ~100+ consumer files. Do it in **4 stages across multiple releases**, each stage independently mergeable and revertable. No stage should break downstream consumers. See Staged Rollout Plan below.

## Part 3: Proposed File Structure

```
python/sglang/srt/
├── server_args.py                          # ServerArgs dataclass inheriting all mixins
│                                           #   + __post_init__ (calling handler modules)
│                                           #   + add_cli_args (delegating to mixins)
│                                           #   + __all__ re-exports for backward compat
│                                           #   (~300-500 lines, down from 5,787)
└── arg_groups/
    ├── __init__.py                         # Re-exports all arg group mixins
    ├── constants.py                        # All choice lists (LOAD_FORMAT_CHOICES, etc.)
    │                                       #   and add_*_choices() helpers
    ├── compat.py                           # Deprecation shims for downstream protection
    ├── validators.py                       # check_server_args, check_lora_server_args,
    │                                       #   validate_buckets_rule, etc.
    ├── utils.py                            # prepare_server_args, get/set_global_server_args,
    │                                       #   LoRAPathAction, DeprecatedAction, etc.
    ├── port_args.py                        # PortArgs class (currently at line 6137)
    ├── groups/                             # All mixin classes — one per domain
    │   ├── __init__.py
    │   ├── model_args.py                   # ModelArgsMixin: model_path, tokenizer_*,
    │   │                                   #   load_format, revision, etc. + add_cli_args
    │   ├── parallel_args.py                # ParallelArgsMixin: tp_size, pp_size, dp_size,
    │   │                                   #   ep_size, dist_init_addr + add_cli_args
    │   ├── serving_args.py                 # ServingArgsMixin: host, port, api_key,
    │   │                                   #   max_req_len, etc. + add_cli_args
    │   ├── memory_args.py                  # MemoryArgsMixin: mem_fraction_static,
    │   │                                   #   max_running_requests, etc. + add_cli_args
    │   ├── cuda_graph_args.py              # CudaGraphArgsMixin: disable_cuda_graph,
    │   │                                   #   cuda_graph_*, etc. + add_cli_args
    │   ├── kernel_backend_args.py          # KernelBackendArgsMixin: attention_backend,
    │   │                                   #   sampling_backend, etc. + add_cli_args
    │   ├── speculative_args.py             # SpeculativeArgsMixin: speculative_*,
    │   │                                   #   eagle_*, etc. + add_cli_args
    │   ├── lora_args.py                    # LoraArgsMixin: lora_paths, max_loras,
    │   │                                   #   etc. + add_cli_args
    │   ├── moe_expert_args.py              # MoeExpertArgsMixin: enable_ep_moe,
    │   │                                   #   expert_*, etc. + add_cli_args
    │   ├── cache_args.py                   # CacheArgsMixin: chunked_prefill_size,
    │   │                                   #   enable_radix_cache, etc. + add_cli_args
    │   ├── disagg_args.py                  # DisaggArgsMixin: disaggregation configs
    │   │                                   #   + add_cli_args
    │   ├── quantization_args.py            # QuantizationArgsMixin: quantization,
    │   │                                   #   kv_cache_dtype, etc. + add_cli_args
    │   ├── logging_args.py                 # LoggingArgsMixin: log_level, log_*,
    │   │                                   #   etc. + add_cli_args
    │   └── misc_args.py                    # MiscArgsMixin: remaining fields that
    │                                       #   don't fit elsewhere + add_cli_args
    └── handlers/
        ├── __init__.py
        ├── memory_handlers.py              # handle_gpu_memory_settings,
        │                                   #   handle_piecewise_cuda_graph, etc.
        ├── parallel_handlers.py            # handle_data_parallelism,
        │                                   #   handle_context_parallelism, etc.
        ├── device_handlers.py              # handle_hpu_backends, handle_cpu_backends,
        │                                   #   handle_npu_backends
        ├── attention_handlers.py           # handle_attention_backend, etc.
        ├── moe_handlers.py                 # handle_moe_settings, etc.
        ├── speculative_handlers.py         # handle_speculative_decoding, etc.
        ├── disagg_handlers.py              # handle_disaggregation, etc.
        ├── cache_handlers.py               # handle_cache_settings, etc.
        ├── misc_handlers.py                # handle_deprecated_args, handle_ssl, etc.
        └── model_specific/
            ├── __init__.py                 # dispatch_model_specific_adjustments()
            │                               #   with architecture registry
            ├── deepseek.py                 # DeepSeek V3, R1, V3.1, V3.2 (NSA/DSA)
            ├── llama4.py                   # Llama 4 family
            ├── qwen3.py                    # Qwen3 MoE + dense
            ├── gemma.py                    # Gemma 2/3/3n
            ├── mamba_hybrid.py             # Mamba/Jamba hybrid
            └── misc_models.py              # Falcon, GPT-BigCode, other small handlers
```

### Key design decisions

**Mixin inheritance instead of delegation:**

`ServerArgs` inherits from all `*ArgsMixin` classes. Python's MRO flattens the fields into a single class, so `server_args.model_path` is a direct `__dict__` lookup — identical performance to today. Each mixin co-locates its fields with its CLI definition, making it self-documenting which arguments belong together. No `__getattr__`, no sub-object nesting.

**Balanced directory structure:**

All `*_args.py` mixin files live under `arg_groups/groups/`, and all handler files live under `arg_groups/handlers/`. This keeps the `arg_groups/` root clean (only `constants.py`, `compat.py`, `validators.py`, `utils.py`, `port_args.py`) and avoids the imbalance of mixing 15+ arg files with handler directories at the same level.

**Folder naming — `arg_groups` not `args`:**

The folder is named `arg_groups` instead of `args` to avoid shadowing the common Python variable name `args` and potential conflicts with test fixtures or other modules.

## Part 4: Handler Module Design

Each `_handle_*` method on `ServerArgs` becomes a standalone module-level function that takes `server_args` (the `ServerArgs` instance) as its first argument, plus any extra parameters the original method received. The function reads and mutates `server_args` fields directly — since all fields are flat on `ServerArgs`, this works identically to `self.field_name`.

### 4.1 General handler pattern

Every handler file follows the same convention:

```python
# arg_groups/handlers/parallel_handlers.py
from __future__ import annotations

import logging
from typing import TYPE_CHECKING

if TYPE_CHECKING:
    from sglang.srt.server_args import ServerArgs

logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)


def handle_data_parallelism(server_args: ServerArgs) -> None:
    if server_args.dp_size == 1:
        server_args.enable_dp_attention = False
        server_args.enable_dp_lm_head = False

    if server_args.enable_dp_attention:
        server_args.schedule_conservativeness *= 0.3
        assert server_args.tp_size % server_args.dp_size == 0
        server_args.chunked_prefill_size = (
            server_args.chunked_prefill_size // server_args.dp_size
        )
        logger.warning(
            f"DP attention is enabled. Chunked prefill size adjusted to "
            f"{server_args.chunked_prefill_size}."
        )

    if server_args.enable_dp_lm_head:
        assert server_args.enable_dp_attention, (
            "Please enable dp attention when setting enable_dp_lm_head."
        )


def handle_context_parallelism(server_args: ServerArgs) -> None:
    ...


def handle_pipeline_parallelism(server_args: ServerArgs) -> None:
    ...
```

Key rules:

- Each function's signature is `(server_args: ServerArgs, ...) -> None`.
- Use `TYPE_CHECKING` guard for the `ServerArgs` import to avoid circular imports.
- Functions that the original method called with extra arguments (e.g., `_handle_gpu_memory_settings(self, gpu_mem)`) keep them: `handle_gpu_memory_settings(server_args, gpu_mem)`.
- Helper functions that were only used internally (e.g., `_generate_cuda_graph_batch_sizes`, `_set_default_nsa_backends`) become private module-level functions in the same file.

### 4.2 How `__post_init__` calls the handlers (with lazy imports)

`ServerArgs.__post_init__` becomes a thin orchestrator that uses **inline imports** so that handler modules are only loaded when they are actually needed. This is especially important for device-specific handlers (HPU, NPU, CPU) that import heavy backend libraries — they should not be loaded on machines that don't use them.

```python
# server_args.py
def __post_init__(self):
    # Always-needed handlers — imported at top of function
    from sglang.srt.arg_groups.handlers.misc_handlers import (
        handle_load_balance_method,
        handle_ssl_validation,
    )

    handle_load_balance_method(self)
    handle_ssl_validation(self)

    if self.model_path.lower() in ["none", "dummy"]:
        return

    from sglang.srt.arg_groups.handlers.misc_handlers import (
        handle_deprecated_args,
        handle_missing_default_values,
    )
    handle_deprecated_args(self)
    handle_missing_default_values(self)

    # Device-specific handlers — lazily imported based on device type
    if self.device == "hpu":
        from sglang.srt.arg_groups.handlers.device_handlers import handle_hpu_backends
        handle_hpu_backends(self)
    elif self.device == "cpu":
        from sglang.srt.arg_groups.handlers.device_handlers import handle_cpu_backends
        handle_cpu_backends(self)
    elif self.device == "npu":
        from sglang.srt.arg_groups.handlers.device_handlers import handle_npu_backends
        handle_npu_backends(self)

    from sglang.srt.arg_groups.handlers.memory_handlers import (
        handle_piecewise_cuda_graph,
        handle_gpu_memory_settings,
    )
    handle_piecewise_cuda_graph(self)

    gpu_mem = get_device_memory_capacity(self.device)
    handle_gpu_memory_settings(self, gpu_mem)

    # Model-specific dispatch — lazy per-architecture loading
    from sglang.srt.arg_groups.handlers.model_specific import (
        dispatch_model_specific_adjustments,
    )
    dispatch_model_specific_adjustments(self)

    # ... remaining handlers in same order as today
```

### 4.3 Model-specific handler design (registry with lazy loading)

The 601-line `_handle_model_specific_adjustments` is split into per-architecture files under `handlers/model_specific/`. A registry in `__init__.py` dispatches based on model architecture, using **lazy imports** so only the matched architecture's module is loaded.

**Registry and dispatch:**

```python
# arg_groups/handlers/model_specific/__init__.py
from __future__ import annotations

import importlib
from typing import TYPE_CHECKING, Callable

if TYPE_CHECKING:
    from sglang.srt.server_args import ServerArgs

# Maps architecture name -> (module_path, function_name)
# Only the matched architecture's module is imported at runtime.
MODEL_ARCH_HANDLERS: dict[str, tuple[str, str]] = {
    # DeepSeek family (+ KimiK25, MistralLarge3, Pixtral, GlmMoeDsa)
    "DeepseekV3ForCausalLM": ("sglang.srt.arg_groups.handlers.model_specific.deepseek", "handle_deepseek"),
    "KimiK25ForConditionalGeneration": ("sglang.srt.arg_groups.handlers.model_specific.deepseek", "handle_deepseek"),
    "MistralLarge3ForCausalLM": ("sglang.srt.arg_groups.handlers.model_specific.deepseek", "handle_deepseek"),
    "PixtralForConditionalGeneration": ("sglang.srt.arg_groups.handlers.model_specific.deepseek", "handle_deepseek"),
    "GlmMoeDsaForCausalLM": ("sglang.srt.arg_groups.handlers.model_specific.deepseek", "handle_deepseek"),
    # Llama4
    "Llama4ForConditionalGeneration": ("sglang.srt.arg_groups.handlers.model_specific.llama4", "handle_llama4"),
    # Gemma
    "Gemma2ForCausalLM": ("sglang.srt.arg_groups.handlers.model_specific.gemma", "handle_gemma"),
    "Gemma3ForCausalLM": ("sglang.srt.arg_groups.handlers.model_specific.gemma", "handle_gemma"),
    "Gemma3ForConditionalGeneration": ("sglang.srt.arg_groups.handlers.model_specific.gemma", "handle_gemma"),
    "Gemma3nForCausalLM": ("sglang.srt.arg_groups.handlers.model_specific.gemma", "handle_gemma"),
    "Gemma3nForConditionalGeneration": ("sglang.srt.arg_groups.handlers.model_specific.gemma", "handle_gemma"),
    ...
}


def _resolve_handler(module_path: str, func_name: str) -> Callable:
    """Lazily import the handler module and return the function."""
    mod = importlib.import_module(module_path)
    return getattr(mod, func_name)


def dispatch_model_specific_adjustments(server_args: ServerArgs) -> None:
    from sglang.srt.connector.utils import ConnectorType, parse_connector_type
    from sglang.srt.configs.model_config import is_deepseek_nsa

    if parse_connector_type(server_args.model_path) == ConnectorType.INSTANCE:
        return

    hf_config = server_args.get_model_config().hf_config
    model_arch = hf_config.architectures[0]

    entry = MODEL_ARCH_HANDLERS.get(model_arch)
    if entry is not None:
        handler = _resolve_handler(*entry)
        handler(server_args, hf_config, model_arch)

    # Shared post-arch logic (e.g., TRTLLM AllReduce Fusion) that applies
    # across multiple architectures based on feature flags, not arch name.
    _handle_cross_arch_adjustments(server_args, hf_config, model_arch)
```

**Per-architecture handler example:**

```python
# arg_groups/handlers/model_specific/gemma.py
from __future__ import annotations

import logging
from typing import TYPE_CHECKING

if TYPE_CHECKING:
    from sglang.srt.server_args import ServerArgs

logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)


def handle_gemma(server_args: ServerArgs, hf_config, model_arch: str) -> None:
    logger.warning(
        f"Disable hybrid SWA memory for {model_arch} as it is not yet supported."
    )
    server_args.disable_hybrid_swa_memory = True
```

**Handling shared code across architectures:**

Some logic in the original function applies across multiple architectures (e.g., the TRTLLM AllReduce Fusion block at lines 1963-1988 checks `model_arch in [...]` plus hardware/config conditions). These become a `_handle_cross_arch_adjustments` function called after the per-arch dispatch, keeping the feature-flag-based logic separate from architecture-specific logic.

### 4.4 Complexity reduction analysis

The original concern: *"The current design doesn't decrease the complexity of the codebase."*

The updated mixin + registry design reduces complexity along several axes:

| Metric | Before | After | Why it matters |
|--------|--------|-------|----------------|
| `server_args.py` lines | 5,787 | ~300-500 | Cognitive load per file |
| Max function cyclomatic complexity | 601 lines / ~45 branches (`_handle_model_specific_adjustments`) | ~30 lines per arch handler, O(1) dispatch | Adding a new arch = new file, no touching dispatch |
| Field-to-CLI coupling | Fields at line ~300, their CLI defs at line ~3000 | Co-located in same mixin class | Can understand a domain by reading one file |
| Cross-domain coupling in `__post_init__` | 38 methods interleaved, all on one class | Grouped by domain in separate modules, called in sequence | Each handler module is independently testable |
| Import cost for device-specific code | All handlers loaded unconditionally | Lazy imports for HPU/NPU/CPU handlers | Faster startup on common CUDA path |

The key insight: moving code to separate files alone doesn't reduce complexity — but **co-locating related concerns** (mixin pattern) and **replacing branching with dispatch** (registry pattern) genuinely do.

## Part 5: Downstream Compatibility

This refactor must not break downstream repos that depend on SGLang's `ServerArgs`.

### 5.1 Stable public interface

`ServerArgs` remains importable from its current location, with all fields as direct attributes:

```python
# This continues to work — it's the only public API.
from sglang.srt.server_args import ServerArgs
args = ServerArgs(model_path="meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct", tp_size=4)
print(args.model_path)  # direct attribute access
```

### 5.2 Re-exports via `__all__`

Any public symbol that moves from `server_args.py` to a sub-module (e.g., `PortArgs`, `prepare_server_args`) is re-exported from `server_args.py` so existing imports don't break:

```python
# server_args.py
from sglang.srt.arg_groups.port_args import PortArgs
from sglang.srt.arg_groups.utils import prepare_server_args

__all__ = ["ServerArgs", "PortArgs", "prepare_server_args", ...]
```

### 5.3 Deprecation shims in `compat.py`

If any public function signature or constant is renamed/removed, `compat.py` provides a shim with a deprecation warning:

```python
# arg_groups/compat.py
import warnings

def old_function_name(*args, **kwargs):
    warnings.warn(
        "old_function_name is deprecated, use new_function_name instead. "
        "It will be removed in v0.X.0.",
        DeprecationWarning,
        stacklevel=2,
    )
    from sglang.srt.arg_groups.utils import new_function_name
    return new_function_name(*args, **kwargs)
```

### 5.4 Downstream CI validation

Before merging each stage, run integration tests against known downstream consumers (if available) to verify nothing breaks. Document the public API surface in `arg_groups/__init__.py` docstring.

## Staged Rollout Plan

Each stage is an independently mergeable PR (or small set of PRs). Stages are designed to be safe to ship in separate releases, so that downstream consumers have time to adapt.

---

**Stage 1: Extract constants + `compat.py` scaffolding** *(low risk, no behavioral change)*

- Create `arg_groups/` directory with `__init__.py`, `constants.py`, `compat.py`
- Move all choice lists (`LOAD_FORMAT_CHOICES`, etc.) and `add_*_choices()` helpers to `constants.py`
- Re-export everything from `server_args.py` — zero consumer changes needed
- **Validation:** `pre-commit` + existing test suite passes with no import changes

---

**Stage 2: Extract arg group mixin classes + CLI definitions** *(medium risk)*

- Create `arg_groups/groups/*.py` — one mixin per domain with fields + `add_cli_args`
- `ServerArgs` inherits from all mixins; fields are now defined in mixins
- `ServerArgs.add_cli_args` delegates to each mixin's `add_cli_args`
- **Validation:** `python -c "from sglang.srt.server_args import ServerArgs; print(ServerArgs.__dataclass_fields__.keys())"` produces identical output; `--help` output is identical; full test suite passes
- This removes ~2,500 lines from `server_args.py`

---

**Stage 3: Extract handler methods** *(medium risk)*

- Move each `_handle_*` method into `arg_groups/handlers/*.py` as standalone function
- `__post_init__` imports and calls handler functions with lazy imports
- Split `_handle_model_specific_adjustments` into per-architecture modules with registry dispatch
- **Validation:** Unit test that constructs `ServerArgs` for each supported model and compares all field values against a baseline snapshot (generated before the refactor)
- This removes another ~2,550 lines from `server_args.py`

---

**Stage 4: Extract validators, utilities, and `PortArgs`** *(low risk)*

- Move `check_server_args`, `check_lora_server_args`, `validate_buckets_rule` to `validators.py`
- Move `PortArgs`, `prepare_server_args`, `get/set_global_server_args` to their own files
- Update `server_args.py` re-exports
- **Validation:** `grep -r "from sglang.srt.server_args import" .` — all existing imports still resolve
- This removes the remaining ~500 lines of non-field code from `server_args.py`

---

### Release boundary recommendation

- **Stage 1** can ship immediately (pure code movement of constants).
- **Stages 2 + 3** are the core refactor — consider shipping together in the same release to avoid an intermediate state where fields are in mixins but handlers are still methods.
- **Stage 4** is cleanup — can ship in a follow-up release.

### Related resources

_No response_

title: [RFC] Release cuda 13.0 docker image as default
author: rainj-me
body:
### Checklist

- [x] If this is not a feature request but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [x] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

### Motivation

**1. Purpose**
This proposal outlines the integration of FlashAttention 4 (FA4) into the SGLang runtime. The primary objective is to leverage FA4’s performance enhancements (particularly for SM90/Hopper architectures) while managing the transition from CUDA 12 to CUDA 13 requirements.

**2. Background and Drivers**
With the official release of FlashAttention 4, the underlying dependency tree has shifted. Notably, FA4 requires nvidia-cutlass-dsl 4.4.1, which establishes CUDA 13 as the mandatory toolchain.

Currently, SGLang utilizes CUDA 12.9 as the default Docker environment, with CUDA 13.0 offered as an experimental or secondary option. To fully support the FA4 API and SM90-specific optimizations, our environment strategy must evolve.

**3. Proposed Changes**
**3.1 Build System & Compatibility**
I propose a hybrid build strategy managed via pyproject.toml. This will allow the runtime to serve two distinct user tiers:

Next-Gen (Default): Tailored for CUDA 13/FA4 environments.

Legacy (Optional): Maintained for CUDA 12 users who cannot yet migrate.

**3.2 Kernel-Level Refactoring**
Integration will require source-level modifications to accommodate the FA4 API, specifically:

Updating kernel dispatch logic to support new FA4 entry points.

Ensuring robust SM90-specific pathing to exploit Hopper architecture improvements.

**3.3 Docker and Environment Defaults**
To align with the latest industry performance standards, I propose flipping the default Docker image to CUDA 13.0.

New Default: CUDA 13.0 (with FA4 enabled by default).

Optional/Legacy: CUDA 12.9 (accessible via a dedicated tag or sgl-fa4 legacy flag) to ensure backward compatibility for existing deployments.

**4. Impact Assessment**
Performance: Significant throughput improvements on H100/H200 clusters via FA4.

Complexity: Increased CI/CD matrix to validate both CUDA 12 and 13 build targets.

User Migration: Users on older drivers may need to explicitly pin the CUDA 12.9 image if they cannot upgrade to a CUDA 13-compatible driver.

Note: Maxwell, Pascal, and Volta support were dropped in CUDA 13, but currently, SGLang requires > SM 75 in the CUDA environment due to incompatibilities with `sgl-kernel`, so functionally there should be no issues for end users device compatibility with respect to CUDA environment support.

title: [RFC] NVIDIA ModelOpt Quantized Diffusion & Video Model Deployment in SGLang
author: Edwardf0t1
body:
## Summary

This RFC proposes end-to-end support for deploying **NVIDIA ModelOpt-quantized diffusion and video generation models** in SGLang's multimodal generation pipeline (`multimodal_gen`). ModelOpt handles model optimization and quantization (FP8, NVFP4), and SGLang handles high-performance deployment — together providing a seamless pipeline from quantized checkpoint to production inference.

The initial prototype ([PR #20082](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/20082)) demonstrates FP8 FLUX deployment. This issue tracks the broader initiative covering additional quantization formats, model architectures, and the overall design direction.

## Background and Motivation

**The problem:** Diffusion and video generation models are compute-intensive, making quantization essential for practical deployment. NVIDIA [ModelOpt](https://github.com/NVIDIA/TensorRT-Model-Optimizer) provides state-of-the-art post-training quantization (PTQ) for these models, producing checkpoints with `quantization_config` metadata (e.g., `quant_algo: "FP8"`, `quant_method: "modelopt"`). However, there is limited deployment path that can natively consume these checkpoints and leverage hardware-accelerated quantized kernels.

**Why SGLang:** SGLang's `multimodal_gen` runtime already supports a broad set of diffusion models (FLUX, Sana, Qwen) and video generation models (WAN, HunyuanVideo, LTX-2), along with a modular quantization layer (`layers/quantization/`) and high-performance FP8/FP4 GEMM kernels on the LLM side (`sgl_kernel`). This makes SGLang the natural deployment target — we can reuse existing infrastructure rather than building from scratch.

**Key benefits:**
- **Zero-friction deployment:** Auto-detect `quantization_config` from the checkpoint — no special CLI flags needed (`sglang generate --model-path <modelopt-fp8-checkpoint>` just works)
- **Hardware-accelerated inference:** Reuse SGLang's existing CUTLASS FP8/FP4 GEMM kernels (`sgl_kernel.fp8_scaled_mm`) for Ada/Hopper/Blackwell GPUs
- **Broad model coverage:** A single quantization integration path that works across image and video generation models
- **Community value:** Provides ModelOpt users a direct deployment path; provides SGLang users access to state-of-the-art quantized models

## Design Overview

### Architecture

The integration follows SGLang's existing quantization plugin pattern:

```
ModelOpt Checkpoint (quantization_config in config.json)
        │
        ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Quantization Config Registry           │
│  (__init__.py: "modelopt" → Config)     │
│  (__init__.py: "modelopt_nvfp4" → ...)  │
└──────────────┬──────────────────────────┘
               │
        ┌──────┴──────┐
        ▼             ▼
┌──────────────┐ ┌──────────────────┐
│ ModelOptFp8  │ │ ModelOptNvfp4    │
│ Config       │ │ Config (planned) │
│ LinearMethod │ │ LinearMethod     │
└──────┬───────┘ └───────┬──────────┘
       │                 │
       ▼                 ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Shared LLM Kernel Infrastructure       │
│  • sgl_kernel.fp8_scaled_mm (CUTLASS)   │
│  • FP4 GEMM backends (planned)          │
│  • apply_fp8_linear / fp4 utilities     │
└─────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

### Key Design Decisions

1. **Config-driven auto-detection:** The `quantization_config` in the model's `config.json` drives method selection. Each ModelOpt quant format registers a config class that parses the checkpoint metadata and returns the appropriate linear method.

2. **Ignore-list layer exclusion:** ModelOpt checkpoints specify layers that should remain in full precision (e.g., normalization layers, embedders). The config implements glob-based pattern matching against the ignore list to route these layers to `UnquantizedLinearMethod`.

3. **Auto-dequantization in the loader:** Some modules (e.g., diffusers' `AdaLayerNormZero`) contain linear layers that are quantized in the checkpoint but use standard `nn.Linear` in the model definition. The FSDP loader auto-detects dtype mismatches (FP8 checkpoint weight → bfloat16 parameter) and dequantizes using the per-tensor `weight_scale`.

4. **Kernel reuse from LLM runtime:** Rather than introducing new kernels, we reuse SGLang's battle-tested FP8 and FP4 GEMM infrastructure. The diffusion quantization methods call `apply_fp8_linear` and will similarly reuse FP4 utilities.

### Components per Quantization Method

Each new quantization method requires:
| Component | Location | Purpose |
|-----------|----------|---------|
| `ModelOpt<Format>Config` | `layers/quantization/modelopt_<format>.py` | Parse checkpoint config, ignore-list matching |
| `ModelOpt<Format>LinearMethod` | Same file | `create_weights`, `process_weights_after_loading`, `apply` |
| Registry entry | `layers/quantization/__init__.py` | Map method name → config class |
| Loader support | `loader/fsdp_load.py` | Handle dtype mismatches for non-quantization-aware modules |

## Roadmap

### Phase 1: FP8 Image Generation (In Progress)
- **FP8 FLUX** — [PR #20082](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/20082)
  - `ModelOptFp8Config` + `ModelOptFp8LinearMethod`
  - Auto-dequantization in FSDP loader
  - Per-tensor static FP8 quantization using CUTLASS kernels
  - Status: Prototype PR open, functional, generating correct images

### Phase 2: NVFP4 Image Generation
- **NVFP4 FLUX**
  - `ModelOptNvfp4Config` + `ModelOptNvfp4LinearMethod`
  - Leverage existing FP4 GEMM backends on the LLM side (`fp4_utils.py`, FlashInfer cuDNN/CUTLASS)
  - Block-wise scaling with group_size=16 (NVFP4 format)
  - Target: Ada/Hopper/Blackwell GPUs

### Phase 3: Video Generation Models
- **FP8 + NVFP4 for Wan 2.2**
  - Extend quantization support to `wanvideo.py` / `causal_wanvideo.py`
  - Handle video-specific architectural differences (temporal attention, 3D convolutions)
- **FP8 + NVFP4 for LTX-2**
  - Extend to `ltx_2.py`
  - Validate accuracy on video generation benchmarks

### Phase 4: Optimization and Hardening
- Performance benchmarking across all supported models and quantization formats
- Mixed-precision strategies (e.g., FP8 attention + NVFP4 FFN)
- Unit test coverage for all quantization configs, linear methods, and loader paths
- Documentation and user guides

## Execution Plan

| Phase | Deliverable | PR(s) | Dependencies |
|-------|------------|-------|--------------|
| 1 | FP8 FLUX deployment | [#20082](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/20082) | None |
| 1 | Unit tests for FP8 config + loader | TBD | #20082 merged |
| 2 | NVFP4 FLUX deployment | TBD | Phase 1, FP4 kernel availability in multimodal_gen |
| 3a | FP8/NVFP4 Wan 2.2 | TBD | Phase 1-2 |
| 3b | FP8/NVFP4 LTX-2 | TBD | Phase 1-2 |
| 4 | Benchmarks, docs, mixed-precision | TBD | Phase 1-3 |

### Open Questions

1. **NVFP4 kernel routing:** The LLM side has multiple FP4 backends (FlashInfer cuDNN, CUTLASS, TRT-LLM, CuTeDSL). Which should be the default for diffusion models, and do we need any diffusion-specific tuning?
2. **Tensor parallelism:** The current prototype assumes single-GPU (no TP). For large video models, do we need TP-aware quantization weight sharding?
3. **Mixed-precision policies:** Should we support per-layer quantization format selection (e.g., FP8 for attention, NVFP4 for feed-forward)?

---

We welcome feedback from the SGLang maintainers on the design direction, priority ordering, and any architectural concerns. cc @sgl-project/sglang-maintainers

/cc @Edwardf0t1 @Fridge003 @Qiaolin-Yu @JustinTong0323 @Ying1123 @merrymercy @nvpohanh @hlu1

title: [RFC][Diffusion] Intel Auto-Round x SGL Diffusion Quantization Support (2026 H1)
author: WeiweiZhang1
body:
### Checklist

- [ ] If this is not a feature request but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [ ] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

### Motivation

###  Overview

This RFC proposes adding support for directly loading **pre-quantized AutoRound diffusion models**.

This work integrates **Intel AutoRound**, a post-training quantization (PTQ) toolkit that supports **large language models (LLMs), vision-language models (VLMs), and diffusion models**. which performs gradient-based optimization of weight rounding and clipping, allowing models to be quantized to low bit widths (2–4 bits) while maintaining strong generation quality.

AutoRound already supports quantization for diffusion models such as **Flux** and **FramePack**, with competitive accuracy results demonstrated in prior experiments. Support for **Omni models** is currently under development.


For more details, please check the [AutoRound repo](https://github.com/intel/auto-round) and our [blog](https://medium.com/@NeuralCompressor/diffusion-in-autoround-low-bit-quantization-for-video-and-image-generation-models-952d00b064d0).


### Motivation for Offline Quantization Support
- **Performance**: Static quantization removes runtime quantization overhead. 
- **Accuracy**: Accuracy: Leverage advanced quant algorithms to reduce quantization error compared to naive round-to-nearest.


### Quantization Schemes
- [ ] `WxA16_INT` (prioritize `W4A16`)
- [ ] `w8A16_FP8`


### Target Model List
prioritize text‑to‑image models
- [ ] Flux
- [ ] Qwen-Image
- [ ] Qwen-Omni

title: [Feature] [RFC] HiCache retention slots
author: lawrence-harmonic
body:
### Checklist

- [x] If this is not a feature request but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [x] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

### Motivation

## Motivating use case

Consider an RL system where we have a fixed set of K rollout workers, each of which runs 1 multi-turn rollout at a time with a max context length of N, and an sglang server which can fit T tokens in HiCache. In this scenario, we have at most K * N tokens of active context, so we hope to be able to scale K up to T / N while maintaining zero evictions of active context.

In reality, this does not happen, due to the following scenario:

Worker A starts rollout 1
Worker B starts and finishes rollout 1
Worker B starts and finishes rollout 2
Worker A finishes rollout 1

In this scenario, Worker A rollout 1 is pre-empted by up to 2 * N tokens. In general we see violations of the assumption that the rollout will be preempted by at most K * N tokens, and this causes cache misses which spiral into more cache misses. The issue is more severe for linear attention, since a rollout is pre-empted by a full Mamba state per request (#20144).

## Why pinning, priority, and TTL are not enough

retention_seconds is implemented in https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/21045. However, in our example above:
* all rollouts are equal priority and should have equal TTL a priori
* we cannot know that worker B rollout 1 cache is stale until rollout 2 starts

Since we cannot proactively determine an appropriate TTL, we need to retroactively unpin or deprioritize previously cached requests as new requests are cached.

## Potential solutions

### Option A: retention slots

We may let the client specify a "retention_slot". Then any of the following would solve our problem, though with different behaviors in general:
* Option 1: Introduce an EvictionStrategy which first evicts nodes which are stale within their slot. We define staleness as follows: If there have been n requests within the retention_slot, and a node was last refreshed by the mth request within the slot, then the staleness is (n - m) within the slot. Hence, in our example above, as soon as Worker B starts making requests for rollout 2, its cache nodes from rollout 1 become stale, whereas Worker A's cache nodes are not stale despite being older.
* Option 2: Introduce an EvictionStrategy which first evicts from the retention_slot with the most tokens
* Option 3: Accept a retention_slot_size along with retention_slot. If inserting tokens under the retention_slot would exceed the retention_slot_size, evict tokens under the retention_slot.

Note:
* In all of these options, the case of nodes belonging to multiple slots needs to be handled
* Can be combined with TTL so that slots are not leaked

### Option B: session refs

Use /open_session and /close_session (already exist). But rather than use streaming session memory layout, still use HiCache and let the session hold a HiCache ref counter. 

In this case, the client would manually open/close session for every rollout, rather than keep one retention_slot across all rollouts which automatically clears previous rollouts.

### Related resources

## Related work

Streaming sessions (https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/19171) allow rollouts to be cleaned up as they finish. However, this is tied to a feature which is oriented around low-latency append-only sessions cached on-device. Our use case is different: we don't care about low-latency or avoiding Radix Cache and prefix matching, but we do care about throughput, utilization of HiCache, and non-append-only.

## Notes

Since sglang is agnostic to L3 backend and does not have an interface for evicting from L3, a solution for L3 may be nontrivial.

title: [RFC][NPU] Ascend NPU A5 Support for MXFP8/MXFP4 Quantization
author: YChange01
body:
### Checklist - [x] If this is not a feature request but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed. - [x] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed. ### Motivation As part of the ongoing effort to expand hardware backends and optimize inference performance (tracked in #14424), we are working on the MXFP8/MXFP4 support for the Huawei Ascend NPU ecosystem, specifically targeting the new Ascend A5 architecture. The Ascend A5 introduces robust hardware-level support for Microscaling Formats (MXFP8/MXFP4). By leveraging these formats, we can significantly reduce memory bandwidth bottlenecks, lower memory footprint, and accelerate computation while maintaining near-lossless accuracy. This RFC proposes a detailed, phased implementation plan to support MXFP8/MXFP4 quantization across different model architectures in sglang, starting with Diffusion Models, followed by LLMs, and finally VLMs. ### Scope & Objectives The implementation will cover three major model families. For each family, we will support specific quantization schemes (W8A8, W4A8, W4A4) and architectural variants (Dense vs. MoE). ```mermaid graph LR Root[Supported Configurations
Ascend NPU A5 MXFP] %% 分支 1: Diffusion Root --> Diff[1. Diffusion Models] Diff --> Wan[Wan2.2 DiT] Wan --> Wan_W8A8(W8A8) Wan --> Wan_W4A4(W4A4) %% 分支 2: LLM Root --> LLM[2. Large Language Models] LLM --> Q3_Dense[Qwen3 Dense] LLM --> Q3_MoE[Qwen3 MoE] Q3_Dense --> L_D_W8A8(W8A8) Q3_Dense --> L_D_W4A8(W4A8) Q3_Dense --> L_D_W4A4(W4A4) Q3_MoE --> L_M_W8A8(W8A8) Q3_MoE --> L_M_W4A8(W4A8) Q3_MoE --> L_M_W4A4(W4A4) %% 分支 3: VLM Root --> VLM[3. Vision-Language Models] VLM --> Q35_Dense[Qwen3.5 Dense] VLM --> Q35_MoE[Qwen3.5 MoE] Q35_Dense --> V_D_W8A8(W8A8) Q35_Dense --> V_D_W4A8(W4A8) Q35_Dense --> V_D_W4A4(W4A4) Q35_MoE --> V_M_W8A8(W8A8) Q35_MoE --> V_M_W4A8(W4A8) Q35_MoE --> V_M_W4A4(W4A4) ``` ### Phased Implementation Plan #### Phase 1: Diffusion Models - Wan2.2 Establishing the foundational MXFP matrix multiplication (GEMM) kernels on Ascend A5 and adapting them to the Diffusion Transformer (DiT) architecture. 1. Core Kernel Development: Implement and optimize Ascend C / CANN custom operators for MXFP8 and MXFP4 GEMM. Ensure stable compilation and linking of these custom kernels within the PyTorch NPU ecosystem. 2. DiT Block Optimization: Apply the new MXFP kernels to the dense linear layers and attention mechanisms within Wan2.2 DiT blocks. 3. W8A8 Support: Target stable generation with standard 8-bit MX format. [diffusion][npu][quant] Add MXFP8 quantization support for Wan2.2 Diffusion on Ascend NPU #20922 4. W4A4 Support: Extreme quantization for max throughput, focusing on mitigating image quality degradation during the diffusion steps. [[diffusion][npu][quant] Add MXFP4 quantization support for Wan2.2 Diffusion on Ascend NPU #22338](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/22338) #### Phase 2: Large Language Models (LLM) - Qwen3 Extending the core MXFP kernels to support autoregressive text generation and complex routing mechanisms. 1. Dense Model Support (Qwen3-Dense): Implement W8A8 (Weight-8bit, Activation-8bit) inference. [[llm][npu][quant] Add W8A8 MXFP8 quantization support for Qwen3 Dense on Ascend NPU #22352](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/22352) Expand to W4A8 [[llm][npu][quant] Add W4A8 MXFP quantization support for Qwen3 Dense on Ascend NPU #23650](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/23650) and W4A4 [llm][npu][quant] Add W4A4 [MXFP4 quantization support for Qwen3 Dense on Ascend NPU #23795](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/23795) inference pipelines. Verify accuracy (Perplexity) and benchmark throughput. 2. MoE Model Support (Qwen3-MoE): Optimize expert routing and fused expert GEMMs for MXFP formats. Address load-balancing overhead in low-precision formats. Enable W8A8, W4A8, and W4A4 for MoE layers. #### Phase 3: Vision-Language Models (VLM) - Qwen3.5 Integrating the work from Phase 2 with vision components for a complete multimodal MXFP pipeline. 1. Vision Encoder Quantization: Apply MXFP8/MXFP4 to the Vision Transformer (ViT) components. 2. Cross-Modality Alignment: Ensure the projection layers (adapters) between the vision encoder and language model maintain accuracy under quantization. 3. Dense Model Support (Qwen3.5-Dense): Complete W8A8, W4A8, W4A4 end-to-end multimodal pipeline. 4. MoE Model Support (Qwen3.5-MoE): Enable W8A8, W4A8, W4A4 specifically for multimodal MoE routing. Looking forward to the community's thoughts and feedback! I will link the respective Draft PRs to this RFC as development progresses.

title: [RFC] AMD Quark Quantized Diffusion Image&Video Model Deployment in SGLang
author: ColinZ22
body:
## Summary

End-to-end support for deploying AMD Quark-quantized diffusion and video generation models in SGLang's `multimodal_gen` pipeline. Supports **MXFP4** and **FP8** quantization (online and offline) with algorithms like **SVDQuant**, maximizing performance on AMD GPUs by reusing and further tuning aiter GEMM kernels.

Initial work includes **FP8/MXFP4 online quantization for multimodal generation** ([PR #21431](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/21431)). Roadmap includes advanced algorithms for image and video model quantization and AMD Quark offline quantized model support.

---

## Background and Motivation

AMD Quark is a comprehensive cross-platform deep learning toolkit designed to simplify and enhance the quantization of deep learning models. Supporting both PyTorch and ONNX models, AMD Quark empowers developers to optimize their models for deployment on a wide range of hardware backends, achieving significant performance gains without compromising accuracy. However, there lacks a high-performance deployment runtime for multimodal generation that can natively consume these checkpoints and leverage hardware-accelerated quantized kernels.

SGLang's `multimodal_gen` runtime already supports 20+ diffusion models and video generation models, along with a modular quantization layer ([layers/quantization/](sglang/python/sglang/multimodal_gen/runtime/layers/quantization/)) and high-performance quantization and GEMM kernels via **aiter** (used in SGLang's LLM inference). This makes SGLang the natural deployment target — providing AMD Quark users a direct deployment path and SGLang users access to state-of-the-art quantized models optimized for AMD hardware.

---

## Design Overview

**Online and Offline Quantization Support:** Both modes are fully supported and optimized. Online quantization allows quantizing unquantized BF16/FP16 checkpoints at load time via `--quantization`. Offline quantization consumes pre-quantized checkpoints (produced by AMD Quark) with `quant_method` metadata in config.json, enabling seamless deployment.

**Advanced Quantization Algorithms:** Other advanced algorithms (e.g. SVDQuant) will be integrated, allowing for further compression, accuracy recovery, and performance gains.

**Optimized Kernels for AMD Hardware:** Leverages aiter's ROCm-native Triton kernels (low-bit GEMM, dynamic/static quantization, etc.) tuned for AMD GPUs to maximize inference performance.

---

## Roadmap

| Milestone | Models | Quantization | Mode | Status |
|-----------|--------|-------------|------|--------|
| **Z-Image-Turbo** | Z-Image-Turbo | MXFP4 + FP8 | Online | Ready |
| **Wan2.2 Video** | Wan2.2-T2V, Wan2.2-TI2V | MXFP4 + FP8 | Online | In Progress |
| **Offline Quantization** | Selected Models (TBD) | MXFP4 + FP8 | Offline (pre-quantized) | Planned |
| **SVDQuant & Advanced Algorithms** | Selected Models (TBD) | Advanced Algorithms | Online + Offline | Planned |

---

## Open Questions

1. **Per-layer Quantization Scheme:** Should we support per-layer quantization format selection (e.g., FP8 for attention, MXFP4 for feed-forward) as a future optimization?

2. **Standarize Evaluation Datasets and Methods:** Which dataset should be used when it comes to evaluating diffusion model generation quality? Standardizing this (and which metrics, like CLIP, FID, etc.) can be very helpful.


---

Feedback, comments, and concerns regarding the design are welcomed!
@sgl-project/sglang-maintainers

title: [Feature][RFC] SPECTRE: Parallel Speculative Decoding with a Multi-Tenant Remote Drafter
author: zhangfeiyu5610
body: ### Checklist - [x] If this is not a feature request but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed. - [x] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed. ### Motivation We propose SPECTRE (Parallel **Spec**ulative Decoding with a Multi-**T**enant **Re**mote Drafter), a novel system architecture for Speculative Decoding in SGLang , inspired by recent parallel speculative-decoding efforts such as [Pearl](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.11850) and [SSD](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.03251). By decoupling the tightly-bound Drafter and Verifier into independent, asynchronously communicating SGLang services (via ZMQ), SPECTRE resolves the high sequential latency and poor resource utilization of traditional implementations through two core features: **Cross-Round Parallel Overlap**: Breaking the strict, synchronous "draft-then-verify" loop that leads to low GPU utilization, SPECTRE employs optimistic concurrency control. Assuming high draft acceptance, the Drafter generates tokens for round k+1 concurrently while the Verifier validates round k. This completely overlaps the forward passes of both models and effectively hides drafting latency. **Drafter Dual-Mode Coexistence**: Instead of dedicating an underutilized GPU solely to the Drafter, SPECTRE treats it as a multi-tenant service. It processes internal draft requests from the Verifier alongside its own standalone user traffic within the same continuous forward batch. This maximizes GPU utilization and drastically lowers the serving cost for production environments. **paper link**: (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2605.08151) ## Architecture Overview To break free from this co-located synchronous trap, SPECTRE shifts speculative decoding into a **distributed, asynchronously coordinated pipeline**. SPECTRE keeps both sides operationally familiar: - The **Verifier** is a standard SGLang HTTP server that handles user requests and performs token verification with the large model. It acts as the authoritative serving endpoint. - The **Drafter** is also a standard SGLang HTTP server. However, operating in **Dual-Mode**, it accepts remote draft-generation requests from the Verifier *in addition* to serving its own standalone traffic. Both traffic streams are mixed into the same GPU batch. - The two sides communicate over **ZMQ**, with messages serialized as `SpectreRequest` objects through a C++ pybind11 transport layer. ![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/36f76fc6-df8d-431e-a47c-4c46ee6a8220) As shown in the image above, SPECTRE can achieve overlap between the verifier and drafter computation results. Furthermore, drafter can simultaneously support the computation of both verifier requests and normal requests. --- ## Implementation Footprint SPECTRE is implemented against SGLang `0.5.10rc0`. Most new code is isolated under `python/sglang/srt/speculative/spectre/`, with only a small set of integration points in the existing serving stack. ```text python/sglang/srt/speculative/spectre/ | |- spectre_protocol.py # SpectreRequest, SpectreAction, SpecType |- spectre_communication.py # SpectreConfig, SpectreZMQCommunicator | |- verifier/ | |- spectre_target_scheduler_mixin.py # SpectreTargetSchedulerMixin, DraftCircuitBreaker | `- spectre_worker.py # SpectreWorker | |- drafter/ | |- spectre_draft_scheduler_mixin.py # SpectreDraftSchedulerMixin | |- spectre_state_manager.py # SpectreDraftState, SpectreDraftStateManager | `- spectre_kv_rollbacker.py # SpectreKVRollbacker | `- cpp_zmq/ |- src/ | |- spectre_zmq.cpp | `- spectre_zmq_serialization.cpp `- setup.py ``` ### Main integration points in the existing codebase ```text srt/server_args.py spectre_* CLI arguments and ServerArgs fields srt/speculative/spec_info.py SPECTRE detection, worker import, and routing to the SPECTRE event loop srt/managers/scheduler.py scheduler mixin integration, init_spectre_communication(), event_loop_normal_spectre_draft/target(), and state reset on flush srt/model_executor/cuda_graph_runner.py spectre_ntpb_options for CUDA graph batch-size variants ``` The C++ ZMQ extension is built once before launch: ```bash bash python/sglang/srt/speculative/spectre/cpp_zmq/scripts/build_cpp_zmq.sh ``` --- ## Protocol Design All communication uses a `SpectreRequest` dataclass serialized through msgpack via the C++ ZMQ layer. ### Key fields | Field | Type | Description | | ------------------ | --------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | `request_id` | `str` | SGLang request ID (`req.rid`) | | `spec_cnt` | `int` | Per-request speculative round counter used to correlate messages and discard stale responses | | `action` | `SpectreAction` | `DRAFT`, `FINISH`, `ABORT`, or `REJECT` | | `spec_type` | `SpecType` | `DRAFT_REQUEST` or `DRAFT_RESPONSE` | | `draft_token_ids` | `List[int]` | Draft tokens proposed by the Drafter | | `input_ids` | `List[int]` | Full prompt token IDs, sent on `spec_cnt == 0` | | `output_ids` | `List[int]` | Tokens generated so far | | `num_draft_tokens` | `int` | Number of draft tokens requested by the Verifier | ### Action semantics | `SpectreAction` | Direction | Meaning | | --------------- | ------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------- | | `DRAFT` | Verifier -> Drafter and Drafter -> Verifier | Normal draft request / response | | `FINISH` | Verifier -> Drafter | Request completed normally; Drafter cleans up state | | `ABORT` | Verifier -> Drafter | Request aborted; Drafter cleans up state | | `REJECT` | Drafter -> Verifier | Drafter is overloaded; Verifier should back off | --- ## Transport Layer ### ZMQ transport selection `SpectreConfig` chooses the transport automatically based on `--spectre-zmq-addr`: | `zmq-addr` value | Transport | Rationale | | ------------------------ | --------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------- | | `127.0.0.1` or `0.0.0.0` | **IPC** | Avoids unnecessary network stack overhead for same-machine deployment | | Any other IP | **TCP** | Enables cross-machine communication | ### Socket roles The current design uses: - **Verifier**: binds a **Router** socket - **Drafter**: connects with a **Dealer** socket This choice keeps the Verifier in a coordination role and makes it possible to extend toward one-to-many topologies, where a single Verifier can talk to multiple Drafter instances. That matters because SPECTRE is intended to scale outward cleanly. The transport is not just point-to-point glue; it is the foundation for a future multi-drafter deployment model. ### C++ transport layer SPECTRE uses a C++ pybind11 extension for ZMQ plus msgpack serialization. This keeps message handling predictable and efficient in the serving path, avoiding Python-level control flow overhead for every transport operation. The communication layer is kept thin, explicit, and production-friendly — it is not an additional infrastructure dependency but a narrow binding on top of well-established primitives. --- ## Scheduling, Fault Tolerance, and State Management ### Circuit breaker on the Verifier The Verifier maintains a `DraftCircuitBreaker` so that Drafter failures do not stall user-visible generation. | State | Behavior | | ----------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | `CLOSED` | Normal operation. Draft requests are sent every round. | | `OPEN` | Too many consecutive timeouts. The Verifier falls back to single-token decoding for `SPECTRE_COOLDOWN_ROUNDS` rounds. | | `HALF_OPEN` | Cooldown expired. One probe request is sent. Success returns to `CLOSED`; failure reopens the breaker. | This gives SPECTRE a critical operational property: when remote drafting is unhealthy, the system degrades to standard autoregressive decoding instead of amplifying latency or deadlocking progress. SPECTRE accelerates the happy path without holding the serving stack hostage to the remote path. ### Drafter scheduling modes Because draft tokens are highly time-sensitive, the Drafter exposes two scheduling strategies. **Mixed mode** (default): - Draft requests are merged into the Drafter's normal running batch. - This maximizes overall GPU utilization. - It works well when Drafter load is light or moderate. - It offers no strong isolation, so under heavy load the Verifier may see occasional timeouts. **Draft-Priority mode** (`--spectre-draft-priority`): - The Drafter runs a dedicated draft batch for up to `--spectre-max-draft-priority-steps` steps before serving normal requests each iteration. - This bounds draft latency more tightly. - It protects Verifier throughput when the Drafter is busy. - The trade-off is slightly higher tail latency for the Drafter's ordinary user traffic. This mode split reflects an actual serving trade-off rather than hiding it: SPECTRE can optimize for utilization or for speculative responsiveness, depending on deployment goals. --- ## User-Facing API ### CLI arguments #### Shared arguments | Argument | Type | Default | Description | | -------------------------- | ----- | ------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------- | | `--spectre-role` | `str` | `None` | `target` for the Verifier or `draft` for the Drafter | | `--spectre-zmq-addr` | `str` | `None` | ZMQ address. `127.0.0.1` selects IPC automatically; other IPs use TCP | | `--spectre-zmq-port` | `str` | `None` | ZMQ port used by both sides | | `--spectre-max-batch-size` | `int` | `32` | Overload threshold for sending `REJECT` | #### Verifier-side arguments | Argument | Type | Default | Description | | -------------------------------- | ------- | ------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | `--speculative-algorithm` | `str` | `None` | Must be `SPECTRE` | | `--speculative-num-steps` | `int` | `None` | Draft tree depth | | `--speculative-num-draft-tokens` | `int` | `None` | Total draft tokens verified per round | | `--spectre-reject-interval` | `int` | `500` | Decode rounds to skip after a `REJECT` before retrying | | `--spectre-no-draft-ratio` | `float` | `0.5` | Fraction of requests without drafts that triggers batch fallback to autoregressive decoding | | `--spectre-retry-fail-ratio` | `float` | `0.5` | Fraction of pre-verify failures required to trigger inline retry | | `--spectre-retry-min-count` | `int` | `4` | Minimum failed-request count required before retry logic activates | #### Drafter-side arguments | Argument | Type | Default | Description | | ------------------------------------ | ----- | ------- | ----------------------------------------------------------- | | `--spectre-draft-priority` | flag | `False` | Enable draft-priority scheduling | | `--spectre-max-draft-priority-steps` | `int` | `0` | Maximum dedicated draft steps per iteration; `0` means auto | ### Environment variables | Variable | Side | Default | Description | | ------------------------------- | -------- | ------- | --------------------------------------------------------------- | | `SPECTRE_RECV_TIMEOUT_MS` | Verifier | `200` | Max time to wait for draft tokens on receive | | `SPECTRE_FAILURE_THRESHOLD` | Verifier | `30` | Consecutive timeout rounds before opening the circuit breaker | | `SPECTRE_COOLDOWN_ROUNDS` | Verifier | `100` | Rounds to stay in `OPEN` before probing again | | `SGLANG_DRAFT_CLEANUP_INTERVAL` | Drafter | `500` | Forward cycles between stale-state cleanup sweeps | | `SPECTRE_DEBUG` | Both | `0` | `1` enables info-level ZMQ logs; `2` enables per-message timing | ### Launch example #### Step 1: Start the Drafter ```bash python -m sglang.launch_server \ --model-path /path/to/small-model \ --tp 1 \ --host 0.0.0.0 \ --port 3008 \ --spectre-role draft \ --spectre-zmq-port 30090 \ --spectre-draft-priority \ --spectre-max-draft-priority-steps 5 \ --spectre-max-batch-size 320 \ --disable-overlap-schedule ``` #### Step 2: Start the Verifier ```bash python -m sglang.launch_server \ --model-path /path/to/large-model \ --tp 1 \ --host 0.0.0.0 \ --port 30000 \ --speculative-algorithm SPECTRE \ --spectre-role target \ --speculative-num-steps 3 \ --speculative-eagle-topk 1 \ --speculative-num-draft-tokens 4 \ --spectre-zmq-addr 127.0.0.1 \ --spectre-zmq-port 30090 \ --spectre-max-batch-size 160 \ --attention-backend fa3 ``` For same-machine deployment, `127.0.0.1` selects IPC automatically. For cross-machine deployment, replace it with the Drafter's reachable IP and the transport switches to TCP. --- ## Performance We compared Autodecode, Eagle3, StandAlone, and Pearl with Spectre on SGLang, and all showed certain performance gains. --- To reproduce our results： ### Dedicated traffic ```bash python3 -m sglang.bench_serving \ --backend sglang \ --dataset-name random \ --random-input-len 4000 \ --random-output-len 1000 \ --random-range-ratio 1 \ --request-rate 8 \ --max-concurrency 32 \ --num-prompts 128 \ ``` Target model: `Qwen3-32B` Draft model: `Qwen3-0.6B` Eagle3 model: `Zhi-Create-Qwen3-32B-Eagle3` | | Autodecode | Eagle3 | Standalone | Spectre | |--|---------:|--------:|-----------:|----------:| | Output token throughput (tok/s) | 715.97 | 925.88 | 992.00 | **1258.82** | | Speedup | 1.00x | 1.29x | 1.38x | **1.76x** | StandAlone: Spectre: ### Mixed traffic in drafter We sent bench serving to Verifier and Drafter(with Draft-Priority mode) respectively. Verifier: ```bash python3 -m sglang.bench_serving \ --backend sglang \ --dataset-name random \ --random-input-len 4000 \ --random-output-len 1000 \ --random-range-ratio 1 \ --request-rate 8 \ --max-concurrency 32 \ --num-prompts 128 \ ``` Drafter: ```bash python3 -m sglang.bench_serving \ --backend sglang \ --dataset-name random \ --random-input-len 1000 \ --random-output-len 1000 \ --random-range-ratio 1 \ --request-rate 32 \ --max-concurrency 8 \ --num-prompts 1000 \ ``` | | Autodecode | Eagle3 | Standalone | Spectre-verifier | | ------------------------------- | ---------- | ------- | ---------- | ---------------- | | Output token throughput (tok/s) | 715.97 | 925.88 | 992.00 | **1244.71** | | Speedup | 1.00x | 1.29x | 1.38x | **1.74x** | | | Origin-drafter | Spectre-drafter | | ------------------------------- | ---------------|--------------- | | Output token throughput (tok/s) | 3291.44 | 2869.87 | | Speedup | 1.00x | **0.87x** | The numbers support a system-level win (Verifier throughput up) at the cost of lower peak Drafter throughput—worth it if the goal is serving efficiency and end-user latency/throughput, not maximizing the draft worker’s standalone score. --- ## Reference [PEARL: Parallel Speculative Decoding with Adaptive Draft Length](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.11850) [Speculative Speculative Decoding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.03251) --- ## Team @feng397 @xq25478 @GoGoldenx @zhangfeiyu5610 We welcome all interested developers to join us. ### Related resources _No response_

title: [RFC]: Internal Process-level Fault Tolerance for SGLang
author: gaidandawang-afk
body:
## Motivation Large MoE models are typically deployed across multiple physical nodes through DP, EP, and related parallel strategies. While this deployment model improves throughput, it also raises the reliability requirement substantially. In large-scale cluster inference, any single-point failure may directly interrupt the whole serving instance, amplifying request failures, service instability, and recovery cost. Therefore, we believe the inference framework itself needs an engine-level fault tolerance mechanism so that local faults do not immediately escalate into full service interruption. At present, SGLang handles faults either by **exiting directly** or by **isolating failed ranks** with FT backends such as [Mooncake](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/10423). In the latter case, the forward pass can continue automatically so that inference proceeds without the failed rank. However, there are two main limitations: 1. The current architecture embeds fault handling inside the inference workflow itself, which makes fault recovery tightly coupled with execution logic. This prevents the engine from coordinating its components in a unified way to handle failures, and it also prevents upper-layer services from observing the engine's actual fault state through explicit interfaces. As a result, the engine behaves as a black box during failures and cannot be controlled in a systematic manner. 2. Real-world faults require policy-driven recovery rather than a single built-in action such as direct scale-down through the FT backend. Different failure modes, including transient network jitter, node power loss, and uncorrectable memory errors (UCEs), may require different recovery policies, but the inference engine alone lacks the context and mechanisms needed to select the right policy. ## Proposed Change We propose to introduce a **Fault-Tolerance Framework** inside the SGLang runtime. As discussed above, we do not view fault tolerance as a mechanism that should live entirely inside the inference engine. Instead, it should be completed jointly by the data plane, the control plane, and the decision plane: ```mermaid flowchart TB SF[Serving Framework
Decision Plane] FW[SGLang FT Framework
Control Plane] BE[FT Backend
Data Plane] FW -->|Fault reporting| SF SF -->|Recovery decision| FW BE -->|Fault collection| FW FW -->|Link repair| BE ``` **Fault Tolerance Architecture (Data / Control / Decision Planes)** - **Data Plane (FT Backends)** The data plane fault tolerance is built on FT-enabled backends (e.g., Mooncake-EP, Nixl-EP). It provides in-kernel fault detection (e.g., timeouts) and rank-level isolation via mechanisms such as the active rank mask. Upon a single-rank failure, healthy ranks can continue execution without being blocked in collective communication, while failed ranks are masked out to enable continued execution. - **Control Plane (SGLang FT Framework)** The control plane is implemented by the SGLang FT framework. It is responsible for maintaining runtime state (e.g., per-rank health), aggregating fault signals from the data plane, and exposing standardized control and observation interfaces (e.g., status queries and fault-handling APIs). Importantly, SGLang does not make recovery decisions itself; instead, it provides the necessary abstractions and control hooks for external systems to perform fault-tolerant orchestration. - **Decision Plane (Serving Framework)** The decision plane is implemented by the upper-layer serving framework. It consumes the runtime state exposed by SGLang, integrates cluster-level signals, and makes recovery decisions (e.g., retry, scale, restart). It also orchestrates the recovery process across engines and system components. **Delegating fault recovery decisions to the serving framework provides several key benefits.** - First, it cleanly separates mechanism from policy: SGLang focuses on exposing accurate runtime state and control primitives, while the serving layer retains flexibility to implement different recovery strategies. - Second, the serving framework has a global view of the system (e.g., multiple engines, cluster health, and SLA requirements), enabling more informed and coordinated decisions that go beyond a single runtime instance. - Third, it allows seamless integration with existing infrastructure such as autoscaling, scheduling, monitoring, and alerting systems. This design avoids embedding complex recovery logic into the runtime, improves extensibility, and enables production systems to evolve their fault-tolerance policies independently without modifying SGLang itself. ## Overall Architecture We follow the same fault-tolerance separation of responsibilities already validated in vLLM [#27866](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/27866). Similar to vLLM, SGLang follows the same control pattern of combining a centralized manager with local fault-handling agents for fault reporting and upper-layer instructions. The main difference is that vLLM organizes this pattern around a single `EngineCore`, whereas SGLang map it onto the components in its multi-process serving pipeline. In our architecture, the HTTP Server, TokenizerManager, Scheduler, and DetokenizerManager remain on the main serving path. To match this runtime structure, each scheduler rank is paired with a local `Sentinel`, and all local sentinels report to a centralized `SentinelManager`, which is a subprocess of the Engine and communicates with the other Sentinels through ZMQ sockets. ## Interface Design To integrate with an upper-layer serving framework for fault observation, decision-making, and coordinated recovery, we propose the following interfaces. ### Status Interface | **Method** | **Endpoint** | **Description** | | --- | --- | --- | | **GET** | **/fault_tolerance/status** | Returns per-rank health state in JSON format for the upper-layer serving framework, such as `healthy`, `dead`, or `paused`. The response can be extended with additional fields in the future as needed. | ### Control Interface | **Method** | **Endpoint** | **Description** | | --- | --- | --- | | **POST** | **/fault_tolerance/apply** | Applies a fault-tolerance control instruction through an instruction type together with optional parameters. | Example control actions include: - `pause`: Pause frontend components from accepting requests, stop the engine's inference workflow, and wait for further instructions. - `retry`: Resume the engine runtime context, handle requests that may have been interrupted, and allow frontend components to start accepting requests again. - `scale_down`: Identify and isolate failed ranks, and notify the remaining healthy ranks to continue working. ## Plan **1. Milestone1: Fault reporting** Upon a failure in any inference-related component, the SGLang runtime no longer exits immediately. Instead, it stays alive for a configurable timeout window and exposes internal fault state through newly introduced `APIs`, so that the upper-layer serving framework can observe the failure and coordinate subsequent recovery. **2. Milestone2: Pause-on-error** Introduce a `Pause` instruction to suspend healthy ranks when one rank fails, in order to prevent cascading failures. When a pause event is received, the sentinels immediately set a pause flag, and key components such as the scheduler and modelrunner check this flag to halt the workflow in a controlled manner. **3. Milestone3: Fault handling interface** Based on the previous two capabilities, the upper-layer serving framework can choose an appropriate recovery strategy such as `Retry` and `Scale_down` for each fault scenario. When a recovery instruction is issued, the runtime context is restored and failed components are isolated if needed so that inference can continue. Combined with the existing FT backend, this further reduces recovery time. ### Related resources No response ### Feedback Period No response ### CC List @UNIDY2002 @tzulingk ### Any Other Things co-authors: @fangyuchu

title: [RFC]: Real-Time Streaming Audio Input for ASR Models
author: SammLSH
body:
# RFC: Real-Time Streaming Audio Input for ASR Models ## Motivation This RFC addresses the second item of issue #22025: streaming input design and implementation. The first item, Qwen3-ASR model support, was resolved by PR #22073. PR #22089 added server-side chunked streaming output to sglang's transcription endpoint: clients upload a complete audio file with `stream=true` and receive partial transcripts over SSE. That improves TTFT for offline file uploads, but it does not cover live audio input. PR #22181 introduced the `TranscriptionAdapter` interface that encapsulates per-model ASR streaming state and formatting. This RFC builds on that foundation. Live captioning, voice assistants, and real-time meeting transcription need to push audio incrementally as it is captured, instead of uploading a completed audio file. This RFC proposes a WebSocket-based realtime transcription path that accepts incremental PCM audio input and emits transcript deltas during the session. The current M1 implementation is PR #22848. It implements the realtime ASR path through `WS /v1/realtime` and aligns the wire protocol with OpenAI's Realtime transcription API, while keeping ASR-specific streaming state in the existing transcription adapter layer. ## Proposed Change Add a WebSocket realtime transcription endpoint: ```text WS /v1/realtime ``` The endpoint implements the transcription subset of the OpenAI Realtime API. It is not intended to implement the full realtime chat/audio conversation stack in M1. At a high level: 1. Client opens a WebSocket connection to `/v1/realtime`. 2. Server sends `session.created`. 3. Client sends `session.update` to configure a transcription session. 4. Client sends repeated `input_audio_buffer.append` events containing base64-encoded PCM audio. 5. Server buffers audio and runs ASR once enough new audio has accumulated. 6. Server emits `conversation.item.input_audio_transcription.delta` events as partial transcript text becomes available. 7. Client sends `input_audio_buffer.commit` to finalize the current audio item. 8. Server emits the canonical commit cluster: `input_audio_buffer.committed` → `conversation.item.created` → final delta(s) → `conversation.item.input_audio_transcription.completed`. 9. After `completed`, the WebSocket connection remains open and the client may begin a new audio item without reconnecting. Subsequent `input_audio_buffer.committed` events chain via `previous_item_id`, so a single WebSocket session can host multiple independently-committed transcription items. 10. Client may send `input_audio_buffer.clear` at any time before commit to discard the current uncommitted audio buffer and reset the current item id. The WebSocket path reuses the existing `StreamingASRState`, `process_asr_chunk`, and `TranscriptionAdapter` interface introduced by PR #22181. The new code is limited to the realtime transport and protocol layer: WebSocket lifecycle, session validation, audio buffering, PCM conversion, event parsing, and error envelopes. Streaming ASR behavior such as prefix rollback, deduplication, transcript finalization, and model-specific formatting remains in the transcription adapter / shared streaming ASR layer. This avoids lifting model-specific ASR behavior into a generic realtime connection layer. ## Architecture ```mermaid flowchart TB HTTP["HTTP /v1/audio/transcriptions
file upload + optional SSE"] WS["WebSocket /v1/realtime
base64 PCM in JSON"] subgraph RT["openai/realtime package"] H["handler.py
accept + semaphore + cleanup"] S["session.py
RealtimeConnection state machine"] P["protocol.py
typed realtime event schemas"] end SSE["serving_transcription.py
HTTP chunked ASR path"] PAC["process_asr_chunk
shared inference driver"] subgraph State["StreamingASRState"] CT["confirmed_text
chunk-local rollback"] ET["emitted_text
monotonic emitted prefix"] UF["update() / finalize()"] end ADP["TranscriptionAdapter"] TM["tokenizer_manager"] HTTP --> SSE WS --> H H --> S S -.validates with.-> P SSE --> PAC S --> PAC PAC --> State PAC --> ADP PAC --> TM style RT fill:#e1f5ff,stroke:#0288d1,stroke-width:2px style PAC fill:#f5f5f5,stroke:#999 style State fill:#f5f5f5,stroke:#999 ``` The realtime package has three responsibilities: | File | Responsibility | |---|---| | `handler.py` | WebSocket accept/reject, concurrent session gating, safe send/close, cleanup. | | `session.py` | Per-connection state machine: `session.update`, `append`, `commit`, `clear`, inference dispatch, delta emission. | | `protocol.py` | Typed event schemas and sglang-specific protocol extensions around OpenAI Realtime transcription events. | The HTTP SSE path and WebSocket path both call the same shared ASR inference driver.
