title: [RFC] In-Tree Support for Cambricon MLU Backend
author: chenxb002
body:
### Checklist

- [x] If this is not a feature request but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [x] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.


## Summary

SGLang has become a widely adopted inference framework with built‑in support for multiple hardware backends, including GPUs, TPUs, CPUs, NPUs and Moore Threads GPUs. This RFC proposes adding native in‑tree support for Cambricon MLU series AI accelerators, integrating Cambricon’s hardware ecosystem directly into the main SGLang repository.  
Beyond the technical proposal, this RFC aims to clarify the community’s general stance on continuously expanding in‑tree hardware backends and the expected contribution process for such additions.

---

## Motivation

- **SGLang already provides a solid foundation for hardware diversity**  
  The project’s existing support for various hardware types demonstrates strong architectural extensibility. Adding Cambricon MLU – a widely deployed AI chip – would further broaden SGLang’s ecosystem coverage and benefit a larger user base.

- **Cambricon is actively pursuing upstream contributions**  
  We are adapting SGLang to run efficiently on Cambricon MLUs and intend to follow community best practices by contributing the backend code directly in‑tree. This approach reduces fragmentation and provides users with out‑of‑the‑box support.

- **Community guidance will help ensure a smooth contribution**  
  Before submitting substantial code, we would like to understand the community’s preferences regarding in‑tree hardware backends and the expected contribution process. This will help us align our efforts with the project’s direction from the start.

---

## Proposed Approach (High‑Level)

1. **Backend Implementation**  
   - Add a new hardware backend module for Cambricon MLU within the SGLang codebase, covering device management, memory handling, and operator execution.  
   - Follow existing hardware abstraction patterns in SGLang to ensure consistency and maintainability.

2. **Build and Integration**  
   - Use conditional compilation so that the MLU backend is only enabled when a Cambricon environment is detected, without impacting other backends.

> **Note**: Detailed aspects such as testing strategy, CI integration, and long‑term maintenance will be discussed in follow‑up RFCs or PRs once the overall direction is confirmed.

---

## Open Questions (Requesting Community Feedback)

We would like to gather the community’s input on the following:

**Contribution Process**  
- What is the preferred high‑level workflow for proposing and landing a new hardware backend? (e.g., RFC discussion → PoC branch → implementation → review → merge)  
- Are there any specific architectural or organisational guidelines we should follow early on to facilitate acceptance?

---

## Next Steps

1. Collect community feedback on the open questions above.  
2. Based on the discussion, decide whether to proceed with an in‑tree contribution and define a detailed implementation plan.  
3. Publish a proof‑of‑concept branch for further evaluation once ready.

We look forward to your thoughts and a constructive discussion.

### Related resources

_No response_

title: [RFC] TensorCast KV backend integration
author: zhou-yuhan
body:
## Background 👋 Hello SGLang community. This is TensorCast team. [TensorCast](https://tensorcast.ai/) is a high-performance tensor management layer built for LLM inference. Its ultimate goal is to provide a unified tensor layer in a serving cluster to handle model weights, KV cache, and more. We have recently open-sourced TensorCast https://github.com/tensorcast-ai/tensorcast and implemented some preliminary integration with SGLang. In this RFC, we focus on integrating TensorCast into HiRadixCache as a new KV backend as the first step. In the long run, we would like to bring the full features of TensorCast into SGLang as a long-term plan. ## KV Backend Integration TensorCast can be used to load/update model weights and transfer/reuse KV cache, with a Python SDK used inside inference engines or external App callers (e.g., a request router). The architecture overview of TensorCast can be found [here](https://tensorcast.ai/architecture/architecture-overview/). As a first step, we choose to integrate it as a new KV backend in SGLang's HiRadixCache because: - A KV backend is the first step towards more flexible and programmable KV management brought by TensorCast. See [Tensor Programmability Designs](https://github.com/tensorcast-ai/tensorcast/blob/main/docs/designs/0055-programmable-framework.md) for more details. In short words, TensorCast Python SDK provides a fancier control plane for KV cache management, and this integration will build the data plane. - HiRadixCache provides a modular interface to support multiple KV backends. Therefore, this integration would technically only add a new `tensorcast_store` inside `mem_cache/storage/`. ### Implementation Details We have already implemented the integration in a [branch forked from v0.5.8](https://github.com/tensorcast-ai/sglang/tree/yuhan/tensorcast-kv-hicache). Clearly, we need to do some cleanup, merging, and cherry-picking efforts to catch up with the latest main. The implementation of `TensorcastStore` is very similar to mooncake: - It inherits from `HicacheStore`, implementing `batch_[exists|get|set]` methods. - It connects to a [TensorCast Daemon](https://tensorcast.ai/architecture/architecture-overview/#2-store-daemon) located on the same node using the Python SDK on instance rank launch. - The connected daemon exports a shard memory slab (a CPU memfd) for `TensorcastStore` to read/write KV pages. The slab is owned by the daemon with chunked RDMA MR pre-registration. - The daemon handles distributed and sharded KV page placements.

### Benchmark Results We have benchmarked our KV backend integration. We use 2, 4, and 8 nodes, where one node receives prompts from the LongBench dataset (~35k tokens per prompt) and publishes KV pages to the cluster. Later, all other nodes receive the same prompts and fetch KV pages from the cluster concurrently. Each node runs an SGLang instance serving a Qwen-32B model with 2 x H800 GPUs (TP=2). We show the TTFT reduction results below:

w/ RDMA

w/o RDMA

TensorCast shows similar and better performance compared to Mooncake with RDMA and TCP, respectively. Because we use userspace mTCP and perform some optimizations for non-RDMA communications. ## Long Term Integration Plan TensorCast aims to manage all tensor workloads in a serving cluster by a unified tensor layer. It can be further integrated as: - [ ] Model weight loader & updater: - Load and update model weights from a distributed tensor pool (VRAM, DRAM, SSD), instead of a distributed file system or other sglang instance (RFork). This can be especially useful in RL post-training where a trainer publishes the new weights to the cluster, and lots of rollout workers fetch them concurrently. - TensorCast supports slicing the tensor on the fly; therefore, each TP/PP rank can only fetch the needed weight slice instead of the whole tensor. - We have implemented a [preliminary version](https://github.com/tensorcast-ai/sglang/tree/yuhan/tensorcast-model-loader) of model weight loader/updater integration. It outperforms distributed file system (JFS) but needs more testing & cleanup. - [ ] Programmable KV management: - TensorCast Python SDK provides [a set of APIs](https://github.com/tensorcast-ai/tensorcast/blob/main/docs/designs/0056-programmable-framework-adv.md) like `publish, prefetch, hydrate` to let users write Python programs to manually transfer and reuse KV cache in the TensorCast cluster. This can be useful for external controllers like a KV-aware request router. - We have implemented a [naive version](https://github.com/tensorcast-ai/sglang/tree/yuhan/tensorcast-kv-programmability) of this feature inside SGlang. It is still under development.

title: [RFC] SGLang IR A Functional Intermediate Representation for SGLang Operators
author: pre-master
body:
- **Status**: Draft
- **Target project**: SGLang
- **Authors**: TBD
- **Created**: 2026-06-01
- **Tracking issue / PR**: TBD
- **Related work**:
  - vLLM RFC: [vLLM IR: A Functional Intermediate Representation for vLLM](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/32358)
  - vLLM implementation PR: [[vLLM IR] 1/N Implement IR skeleton and rms_norm op](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/33825)
  - SGLang RFC: [Unified kernel fusion and torch.compile](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/10118)
  - SGLang RFC: [Building towards a Hardware Abstraction Layer in SGLang](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/26426)
  - SGLang issue: [Implement defunctionalization for sgl_kernel ops](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/21550)
  - SGLang issue: [Replace memory-bound custom CUDA kernels](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/21855)
  - SGLang issue: [Triton RMSNorm kernel underutilizes T4/A10G/A100 SMs](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/24353)

> **Attribution**: This RFC is explicitly inspired by and structurally references vLLM PR [#33825](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/33825), which implements the initial vLLM IR skeleton and an `rms_norm` IR operator. The proposed SGLang design adapts the same high-level ideas鈥攆unctional IR operators, native semantic definitions, implementation registration, priority-based dispatch, and lowering鈥攊nto SGLang's serving, kernel, and compilation architecture. This RFC does not propose copying vLLM code verbatim; it proposes adopting the architectural pattern where it fits SGLang.

---

## 1. Summary

This RFC proposes introducing **SGLang IR**, a functional intermediate representation for selected SGLang operators such as `rms_norm`, `fused_add_rms_norm`, `rope`, `activation`, `quant`, `kv_cache_store`, and other memory-bound or fusion-sensitive operators.

The key idea is to separate:

1. **Operator semantics**: what the operator means mathematically.
2. **Operator implementations**: how the operator is implemented on CUDA, ROCm, XPU, Triton, CUTLASS/CuTe, FlashInfer, `sgl-kernel`, or native PyTorch.
3. **Dispatch policy**: which implementation should be selected for a given platform and argument set.
4. **Compilation representation**: what `torch.compile` / FX / Inductor should see before lowering.
5. **Lowering**: when and how the high-level IR operator is replaced by a concrete implementation.

Instead of exposing many backend-specific custom operators directly to model code and compiler passes, SGLang IR would expose stable high-level functional operators. Compiler passes can then match these IR operators directly, and a later lowering pass can choose the concrete kernel implementation.

---

## 2. Motivation

SGLang already contains multiple kernel paths and optimization efforts around custom kernels, Triton kernels, CUDA graph capture, `torch.compile`, fusion, and hardware abstraction. These efforts expose a recurring architectural problem: high-level operator semantics are often coupled with backend-specific implementations.

This makes the system harder to optimize, test, and extend.

### 2.1 Current pain points

#### 2.1.1 Compiler passes see implementation details too early

When model code calls concrete custom kernels directly, `torch.compile` and FX passes may see backend-specific operators or decomposed PyTorch graphs instead of stable semantic operators.

For example, an RMSNorm operation may appear as:

- a native PyTorch decomposition,
- an `sgl-kernel` custom op,
- a Triton implementation,
- a FlashInfer-backed implementation,
- a fused variant,
- or an implementation hidden behind Python dispatch logic.

This makes fusion and pattern-matching fragile. A compiler pass that wants to optimize `RMSNorm + residual add` should not need to know every backend-specific implementation detail.

#### 2.1.2 Operator semantics and kernel implementations are coupled

SGLang supports and experiments with multiple kernel providers. However, when operator calls are wired directly to specific providers, it becomes difficult to define a single source of truth for correctness.

For example, a single operator such as RMSNorm has subtle semantic details:

- whether weight is optional,
- whether computation is performed in fp32,
- whether output dtype follows input dtype,
- whether residual input is mutated,
- whether the operation is in-place, out-of-place, or maybe-in-place,
- whether shape constraints differ across backends.

Without a semantic IR layer, each implementation can silently encode slightly different assumptions.

#### 2.1.3 Backend selection is scattered

SGLang increasingly needs to select among different backend implementations depending on:

- GPU architecture,
- CUDA / ROCm / XPU availability,
- tensor dtype,
- tensor shape,
- sequence length,
- capture mode,
- compilation mode,
- whether an implementation is available in the current build,
- and user preferences.

A unified IR-level priority mechanism would make this selection explicit, configurable, testable, and easier to reason about.

#### 2.1.4 Existing SGLang issues point to the same need

Recent SGLang discussions already point toward similar requirements:

- kernel fusion and `torch.compile` require operators to be represented in a compiler-friendly way;
- a hardware abstraction layer requires platform-dependent modules to be wrapped behind a dispatcher;
- defunctionalization is needed to avoid unnecessary tensor copies around custom in-place kernels;
- memory-bound decode-path kernels such as RMSNorm, RoPE, q/k normalization, and KV-cache stores remain important optimization targets.

SGLang IR would provide a common abstraction for these efforts.

---

## 3. Goals

SGLang IR should provide:

1. **Stable operator semantics**  
   Each IR operator has a native semantic implementation that defines correctness.

2. **Functional representation**  
   IR operators are represented as functional operators by default, so compiler passes can reason about them safely.

3. **Implementation registration**  
   Backend providers can register concrete implementations for an IR operator.

4. **Priority-based dispatch**  
   SGLang can choose the best available implementation through platform defaults and user overrides.

5. **Compiler-friendly tracing**  
   `torch.compile` should see high-level SGLang IR operators before lowering, not a mixture of unrelated backend-specific kernels.

6. **Late lowering**  
   IR operators should be lowered to concrete implementations after high-level fusion and transformation passes.

7. **Incremental migration**  
   The system should allow one operator at a time to migrate into SGLang IR without requiring a full rewrite.

8. **Out-of-tree extensibility**  
   External kernel packages should eventually be able to register implementations without modifying SGLang core.

---

## 4. Non-goals

This RFC does not propose:

1. Replacing all SGLang kernels immediately.
2. Rewriting the entire model execution stack.
3. Replacing `torch.compile`, FX, Inductor, Triton, or `sgl-kernel`.
4. Defining a general-purpose MLIR dialect.
5. Requiring every operator to become an IR operator.
6. Removing backend-specific optimized kernels.
7. Guaranteeing that the first implementation improves latency.

The first milestone should focus on infrastructure correctness and low-risk migration, using `rms_norm` as the initial operator.

---

## 5. Design overview

The proposed architecture follows this pipeline:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Model code calls sg_ir.ops.rms_norm] --> B[Dynamo / FX tracing]
    B --> C[FX graph contains torch.ops.sgl_ir.rms_norm.default]
    C --> D[High-level SGLang compiler passes]
    D --> E[IR fusion / transformation]
    E --> F[SGLang IR lowering pass]
    F --> G{Priority-based implementation selection}
    G --> H1[sgl_kernel implementation]
    G --> H2[Triton implementation]
    G --> H3[FlashInfer / vendor implementation]
    G --> H4[Native PyTorch fallback]
    H1 --> I[Inductor / runtime execution]
    H2 --> I
    H3 --> I
    H4 --> I
```

The essential design is:

- `register_op` defines an IR operator and its native semantics.
- `register_impl` registers concrete implementations.
- `supports_args` determines whether a concrete implementation can handle the current arguments.
- `ir_op_priority` determines implementation preference.
- eager mode dispatch selects an implementation at runtime.
- compiled mode keeps the IR op visible until a lowering pass replaces it with the selected implementation.

---

## 6. Proposed API

### 6.1 Defining an IR operator

An IR operator is registered with a native semantic implementation.

```python
# python/sglang/ir/ops/layernorm.py

import torch
from torch import Tensor

from sglang.ir import register_op


@register_op("rms_norm")
def rms_norm_native(
    x: Tensor,
    weight: Tensor | None,
    eps: float,
) -> Tensor:
    """Native semantic definition of RMSNorm.

    This implementation is the semantic source of truth.
    Backend implementations must match this behavior.
    """
    variance = x.to(torch.float32).pow(2).mean(dim=-1, keepdim=True)
    out = x * torch.rsqrt(variance + eps)

    if weight is not None:
        out = out * weight

    return out.to(dtype=x.dtype)
```

The native implementation has three roles:

1. **Correctness reference** for tests.
2. **Fallback implementation** when no optimized implementation is available.
3. **Semantic definition** for all backend providers.

### 6.2 Calling an IR operator from model code

Model code should call the IR operator rather than a provider-specific kernel.

```python
from sglang import ir

hidden_states = ir.ops.rms_norm(hidden_states, weight, eps)
```

In eager mode, this call dispatches to the selected implementation.

In compiled mode, this call should trace as a high-level IR op:

```python
torch.ops.sgl_ir.rms_norm.default(hidden_states, weight, eps)
```

### 6.3 Registering an implementation

Concrete implementations are registered against the IR operator.

```python
# python/sglang/kernels/rms_norm.py

from sglang import ir
from sglang.kernels import sgl_kernel_rms_norm


def supports_sgl_kernel_rms_norm(x, weight, eps):
    return (
        x.is_cuda
        and x.dtype in (torch.float16, torch.bfloat16)
        and x.shape[-1] <= 8192
    )


@ir.ops.rms_norm.register_impl(
    provider="sgl_kernel",
    supports_args=supports_sgl_kernel_rms_norm,
    inplace=False,
)
def rms_norm_sgl_kernel(x, weight, eps):
    return sgl_kernel_rms_norm(x, weight, eps)
```

### 6.4 Registering a Triton implementation

```python
@ir.ops.rms_norm.register_impl(
    provider="triton",
    supports_args=lambda x, weight, eps: (
        x.is_cuda and x.dtype in (torch.float16, torch.bfloat16)
    ),
    inplace=False,
)
def rms_norm_triton(x, weight, eps):
    return triton_rms_norm(x, weight, eps)
```

### 6.5 Registering a native fallback

The native implementation is automatically available as `native`.

```python
# Conceptually available by default:
provider = "native"
implementation = rms_norm_native
```

The native implementation should be the last fallback in most priority lists.

---

## 7. Priority-based dispatch

SGLang should provide an IR op priority configuration.

### 7.1 CLI

Proposed CLI:

```bash
python3 -m sglang.launch_server \
  --model-path meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct \
  --ir-op-priority.rms_norm=sgl_kernel,triton,native
```

Multiple operators can be configured independently:

```bash
python3 -m sglang.launch_server \
  --model-path meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct \
  --ir-op-priority.rms_norm=sgl_kernel,triton,native \
  --ir-op-priority.rope=triton,sgl_kernel,native \
  --ir-op-priority.activation=triton,native
```

### 7.2 Python config

```python
server_args.ir_op_priority = {
    "rms_norm": ["sgl_kernel", "triton", "native"],
    "rope": ["triton", "sgl_kernel", "native"],
}
```

### 7.3 Platform defaults

Platforms can define default priorities.

```python
CUDA_DEFAULT_IR_OP_PRIORITY = {
    "rms_norm": ["sgl_kernel", "triton", "native"],
    "fused_add_rms_norm": ["sgl_kernel", "triton", "native"],
    "rope": ["sgl_kernel", "triton", "native"],
}

ROCM_DEFAULT_IR_OP_PRIORITY = {
    "rms_norm": ["triton", "native"],
    "fused_add_rms_norm": ["triton", "native"],
}

CPU_DEFAULT_IR_OP_PRIORITY = {
    "rms_norm": ["native"],
}
```

User-provided priority should be prepended to platform defaults, then deduplicated.

Example:

```text
User priority:      rms_norm=triton
Platform default:   rms_norm=sgl_kernel,triton,native
Effective priority: rms_norm=triton,sgl_kernel,native
```

### 7.4 Dispatch algorithm

```python
def dispatch(ir_op, *args, **kwargs):
    priority = ir_op.get_effective_priority()

    for provider in priority:
        impl = ir_op.get_impl(provider)

        if impl is None:
            continue

        if not impl.is_supported_platform():
            continue

        if not impl.supports_args(*args, **kwargs):
            continue

        return impl(*args, **kwargs)

    raise RuntimeError(
        f"No valid implementation found for IR op {ir_op.name}. "
        f"Priority={priority}."
    )
```

`supports_args` should only check stable properties such as:

- device type,
- dtype,
- rank,
- hidden size,
- alignment,
- optional argument presence,
- compile-mode support,
- capture-mode support if statically known.

It should not branch on dynamic batch size, request count, or values that would create unstable compile guards.

---

## 8. Functionalization and maybe-in-place operators

Some SGLang kernels mutate outputs or reuse input buffers for performance. However, compiler passes are easier to reason about when operators are functional.

This RFC proposes two overload modes:

1. `default`: functional, no mutation visible to the graph.
2. `maybe_inplace`: allows buffer donation or reuse when safe.

### 8.1 Example

```python
hidden_states = ir.ops.rms_norm.default(hidden_states, weight, eps)

hidden_states = ir.ops.rms_norm.maybe_inplace(
    hidden_states,
    weight,
    eps,
    donated_inputs=(0,),
)
```

### 8.2 Compiled-mode behavior

In compiled mode:

1. `maybe_inplace` is first represented as an IR op.
2. A SGLang functionalization pass rewrites it to `default`.
3. The pass records donation metadata.
4. Later clone-elimination or defunctionalization can restore memory reuse where safe.
5. The final lowering pass selects a concrete implementation.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[maybe_inplace IR op] --> B[Functionalization]
    B --> C[default IR op + donation metadata]
    C --> D[Optimization passes]
    D --> E[Clone elimination / defunctionalization]
    E --> F[Lowering to concrete kernel]
```

This design aligns with SGLang's existing need to avoid unnecessary copies around custom in-place kernels while preserving compiler correctness.

---

## 9. Lowering pass

SGLang should add an IR lowering pass that runs after high-level IR fusion and transformation passes.

### 9.1 Lowering responsibilities

The lowering pass should:

1. Find `torch.ops.sgl_ir.*` nodes in the FX graph.
2. Resolve the effective priority list for each IR op.
3. Select the first compatible implementation.
4. Replace the IR op node with the selected implementation graph or custom op call.
5. Preserve metadata needed by Inductor, CUDA graph capture, and runtime execution.
6. Include lowering-affecting configuration in the compile cache key.

### 9.2 Example before lowering

```python
def forward(hidden_states, weight):
    return torch.ops.sgl_ir.rms_norm.default(hidden_states, weight, 1e-6)
```

### 9.3 Example after lowering

```python
def forward(hidden_states, weight):
    return torch.ops.sgl_kernel.rms_norm(hidden_states, weight, 1e-6)
```

or:

```python
def forward(hidden_states, weight):
    return triton_rms_norm(hidden_states, weight, 1e-6)
```

or, if no optimized implementation supports the arguments:

```python
def forward(hidden_states, weight):
    return rms_norm_native(hidden_states, weight, 1e-6)
```

### 9.4 Compile cache key

The lowering output depends on:

- selected provider,
- provider priority list,
- implementation source,
- implementation version,
- platform defaults,
- relevant feature flags,
- and possibly CUDA / ROCm / XPU capability.

Therefore, the compile cache key should include an IR lowering fingerprint.

```python
def ir_lowering_fingerprint():
    return hash((
        effective_ir_op_priority,
        registered_impl_uuids,
        platform_name,
        platform_capability,
        relevant_feature_flags,
    ))
```

This prevents reusing a compiled graph that was generated under a different IR implementation policy.

---

## 10. Proposed package structure

```text
python/sglang/
  ir/
    __init__.py
    op.py
    registry.py
    config.py
    lowering_pass.py
    functionalization.py
    clone_elimination.py
    ops/
      __init__.py
      layernorm.py
      activation.py
      rope.py
      quant.py
      kv_cache.py
  kernels/
    ir_impls/
      __init__.py
      rms_norm_sgl_kernel.py
      rms_norm_triton.py
      rope_sgl_kernel.py
      activation_triton.py
```

### 10.1 Core modules

| Module | Responsibility |
|---|---|
| `sglang.ir.op` | Defines `IrOp`, `IrOpImpl`, overloads, dispatch helpers |
| `sglang.ir.registry` | Global registry for IR ops and implementations |
| `sglang.ir.config` | CLI and Python config for IR priority |
| `sglang.ir.lowering_pass` | FX graph lowering from IR ops to concrete implementations |
| `sglang.ir.functionalization` | Rewrites maybe-in-place IR ops into functional form |
| `sglang.ir.clone_elimination` | Removes redundant clones introduced by functionalization |
| `sglang.ir.ops.*` | Native semantic definitions of IR operators |
| `sglang.kernels.ir_impls.*` | Provider-specific registered implementations |

---

title: [Feature] [RFC] Fast Recovery for sglang engine
author: QiuMike
body:
### Checklist

- [ ] If this is not a feature request but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [ ] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

### Motivation

Nowadays, Sglang has been successfully deployed in production environments. However, when encountering bugs or heavy loads, the only solution is often to restart the entire engine — which, in most cases, means restarting the Pod. This process can be time-consuming due to the lengthy Kubernetes workflow.
Taking Qwen3-235B FP8 as an example, when all the weights are stored on SSD, reloading them alone takes around 5 minutes on average. Additional overheads include NCCL collective group initialization, Python package imports, model warmup, and CUDA Graph capture.

Our goal is to reduce the total restart time to under 10 seconds vs
We are introducing three or more major modifications:

1. GPU-based Weight Caching
This approach separates the weight loading process from the model runner, and runs it as a long-lived daemon process on the GPU (with minimal code logic). This makes the system simple and stable.
The actual model runner connects to the daemon and maps the weights into its own address space via mmap.
As a result, model loading during restart can be completed in under 1 second.
✅ A working prototype has been implemented:

https://github.com/QiuMike/sglang/tree/fast_recovery

2. Warmup and CUDA Graph Caching
The initial startup already performs warmup and CUDA Graph capture. We aim to persist these results and restore them after a restart.
The main challenge lies in restoring the CUDA Graph. We need to modify the graph node handling logic(replace the addresses,etc.)
🚧 This is currently under development by @QiuMike.

3. Optimization of Python Imports and Initialization (e.g., Torch Distributed)
This phase includes Python package imports and the initialization of the main process (e.g., Torch Distributed setup).
For Qwen3-235B FP8 with TP4 on H20 GPUs, this currently takes 12–15 seconds.
🚧 Optimization is ongoing by @liusy58.

4. Other Optimizations
We are also exploring additional optimizations to further reduce the restart overhead.




### Related resources

_No response_

title: [RFC] GPU Memory Service (GMS) integration for out-of-process GPU memory management in SGLang
author: galletas1712
body:
> **Update:** rewritten after the merge of #27139. This RFC now builds directly on the merged weight cache. cc @QiuMike @liusy58 @ShangmingCai ## Summary SGLang now has fast engine recovery through the weight cache daemon (#27139): a per-rank daemon holds post-quantized weights and serves them to restarting engines over CUDA IPC. We (NVIDIA Dynamo) built a system in the same design space: the [GPU Memory Service (GMS)](https://github.com/ai-dynamo/dynamo/tree/main/lib/gpu_memory_service), an out-of-process GPU memory owner based on CUDA VMM with stable virtual addresses. This RFC proposes two things: 1. **One small, engine-neutral extension point**: a configurable `torch_memory_saver` hook mode / backend, so that any external weight-memory provider (the in-tree weight cache or an out-of-tree allocator like GMS) plugs in through the same seam. Nothing GMS-specific lands in SGLang. 2. **A two-phase evolution of the weight cache daemon**: first swap legacy CUDA IPC for VMM FD handles (a transport change only, no new components), then optionally let the daemon allocate through a shared memory owner and commit (config 2 below). Each phase unlocks concrete capabilities from the #27052 roadmap: weight sleep/wake, CUDA graph restore, weight updates without reload, and standby engines. The matrix in section 7 shows exactly which capability each phase flips. Nothing here removes or changes the merged design. ## 1. Background: two systems in the same design space The merged weight cache (#27139) keeps a per-rank daemon alive on the GPU. The daemon loads the model itself (full pipeline: disk → TP shard → quantize → `process_weights_after_loading`), holds the result in GPU memory, and serves CUDA IPC handles to engines over a Unix socket. A restarting engine builds the model on the meta device and maps each parameter onto the daemon's memory; weight loading drops from minutes to about a second. GMS approaches the same problem from the memory side. It is a small per-GPU server, built on CUDA VMM (`cuMem*`), that owns physical GPU memory on behalf of client processes. Clients attach over a Unix domain socket, lease memory read-write or read-only, and map it into stable virtual-address ranges. The intended interface is via a PyTorch CUDAPluggableAllocator/mempool. It ships as a standalone wheel, similar in spirit to `torch_memory_saver`, and does not depend on any other component in Dynamo. In fact, it only has CUDA and PyTorch as dependencies. Both systems answer the same question: **how do model weights outlive an engine process, so the next engine start doesn't pay the disk load?** The designs differ in two ways that turn out to be independent of each other: 1. **the memory transport**: legacy CUDA IPC vs. VMM shareable handles; and 2. **which process/component runs the model loader code**: the daemon vs. the engine. ## 2. Why the transport matters Legacy CUDA IPC (`cudaIpcGetMemHandle` / `cudaIpcOpenMemHandle`, which is what torch tensor serialization uses under the hood) has two structural limitations: **No address control.** The importer maps IPC memory at a driver-chosen address, different on every attach, and cannot unmap or remap physical backing while keeping a pointer valid. 1. *CUDA graphs surviving a restart.* Captured graphs bake in raw device pointers. The Phase 2 plan in #27052 (serialize graph metadata, patch addresses by a constant offset) can plausibly handle the graph's own memory pool, but weight pointers land at fresh arbitrary addresses on every IPC attach, so each graph would need full pointer relocation surgery, per graph, per model. 2. *Weight sleep/wake and in-place weight updates become difficult.* Releasing weights and getting them back later requires every existing pointer (including ones baked into CUDA graphs) to stay valid across the unmap/remap. That needs a stable VA with swappable physical backing, and legacy IPC cannot provide this. This is why #27139 had to hard-error on `release_memory_occupation` / `resume_memory_occupation` and `update_weights` while the cache is active. **Lifetime is tied to the exporter.** When the exporting process dies, the importer's mappings dangle. #27139 handles this the only way it can: a watchdog thread in `ipc_loader.py` that SIGKILLs the engine when the daemon's PID disappears, because "forward passes would read freed GPU memory → illegal-address crashes or silent garbage" (quoting the code comment). This means weight cache daemon death propagates to the consuming processes also dying. VMM fixes both properties. VA reservations are stable: you can unmap physical backing, keep the reserved address range, and remap later (or remap different backing) with every pointer still valid. And physical memory created with `cuMemCreate` is exported as an OS file descriptor: FDs are kernel-refcounted, so an importer's mapping stays valid even if the exporter dies. One thing worth stressing: **SGLang already depends on these exact VMM properties.** `torch_memory_saver`'s pause/resume for the KV cache is implemented with `cuMem*` for precisely the pointer-stability reason. What we are describing is the same technique applied to weights, with the physical handles made shareable across processes. This transport swap is phase 1 of ask 4.2: it changes no interfaces and no architecture, removes the watchdog-SIGKILL failure mode, and is the prerequisite for graph restore, weight updates, and standby engines later. Legacy IPC stays available as a fallback for platforms without VMM support (non-NVIDIA backends where torch tensor IPC works today). ## 3. Who owns the memory vs. who loads the weights It helps to name three roles explicitly: - the **owner** holds physical memory and its lifetime, and admits clients; - the **writer** produces the contents: loads from disk, applies updates, commits the result; - the **readers** import resident weights and serve. The current design from #27139 assigns owner = writer = daemon. GMS separates them: the owner is a dumb memory server that never runs a kernel and holds no CUDA context; the writer is whichever client currently holds the RW lease. Given this separation, there are three deployment strategies that are possible: | Config | Owner | Writer | Readers | |---|---|---|---| | **1. Daemon-owned** (#27139) | daemon | daemon | engines | | **2. Daemon-published** | GMS server | daemon | engines | | **3. Engine-published** | GMS server | first engine to boot | later engines | Note that config 1 can run on either transport: as merged (CUDA IPC), or after the phase-1 VMM swap. The matrix in section 7 lists them separately, because several capabilities depend only on the transport. A few words on why each configuration earns its place: **Config 1** is the baseline, and it remains the right answer where VMM is not available (torch tensor IPC works on non-NVIDIA backends today) or where deploying any external service is unacceptable. Nothing in this proposal removes or changes it. **Config 2** keeps the daemon doing what only a daemon can do: warm a GPU *before* any engine exists, keep the cache fresh independently of engine lifecycles, and act as the delivery agent for RL weight updates (more on that below). The daemon keeps its loading pipeline, its `CacheConfig` fingerprint, its socket and discovery. The difference is that it allocates through a different owner and commits, instead of owning the memory itself. Its crash then costs nothing: the committed weights outlive it. The daemon can restart and reconnect to the owner and continue to update the weights, or if no weight updates are necessary, it can also be ephemeral. We expect this to be the workhorse configuration for most deployments. **Config 3** needs no extra resident component at all. The first engine loads normally (its allocations are routed into owner-managed memory), commits, and from then on every restart imports in seconds. The cache is warmed as a side effect of a normal boot; a crashed engine's weights survive it. Because the writer *is* the serving engine, the cached layout always matches the engine build, so a version upgrade self-heals: the first new-version engine notices the mismatch, disk-loads once, and republishes. This is the natural fit for plain crash/rolling restarts and colocated RL (where the engine receives updated weights directly from the trainer and can republish them itself). Note the writer role is a lease, not a static assignment: a deployment running config 2 day-to-day is in config 3 whenever an engine takes the RW lease to republish. The key observation for this RFC: **the engine-side requirements of configs 2 and 3 are identical.** In both, the engine must be able to (a) route weight allocations through a pluggable allocator backend, and (b) import read-only onto a meta-initialized model. (a) is ask 4.1 below; (b) already exists in-tree from #27139 (the weight-cache import path itself). ## 4. What we're asking for Two asks. The first is a small engine-side seam where the pluggability itself lives in `torch_memory_saver`, not in SGLang. The second is an evolution of the in-tree `weight_cache` component, which we propose as a phased collaboration with the #27139 authors. ### 4.1 Engine: configurable `torch_memory_saver` hook mode / backend **Proposal:** a server argument (e.g. `--memory-saver-hook-mode`) that `TorchMemorySaverAdapter` passes through to `torch_memory_saver`, and that skips `configure_subprocess()` when the mode is not `preload`. Context: TMS supports two hook modes, `preload` (LD_PRELOAD interception) and `torch` (pluggable allocator), but SGLang hard-codes the `preload` singleton. An out-of-process VMM allocator cannot coexist with `preload` interception for the tags it owns. Once fzyzcjy/torch_memory_saver#79 lands (`register_hook_mode`), routing can also be per-tag: `weights` → external backend, `kv_cache` / `cuda_graph` → preload, so pauseable CUDA graphs keep working exactly as they do today. Note that this seam already encloses model loading: `load_model_with_memory_saver` wraps the stock loader inside `memory_saver_adapter.region(GPU_MEMORY_TYPE_WEIGHTS)`, so an allocator backend sees every weight allocation **without any loader-level hook**. This means we don't need another custom model loader, and the meta-init import path is already covered by the weight-cache loader (see section 5). This is also the mechanism by which the *existing* `release_memory_occupation` / `resume_memory_occupation` API starts working for externally-owned weights. No new engine API is needed for weight sleep/wake: the plumbing already exists, it just needs a backend that can honor it. One optional refinement, in the same spirit as the existing per-tag `enable_cpu_backup` option: let a backend advertise that pause preserves tensor contents (a VA-stable owner keeps the committed backing alive on the server side). The scheduler could then skip the static-state stash (`_export_static_state` / `_import_static_state`) around weights release/resume. This is purely an optimization, not a requirement: with our backend the named buffers live on the ordinary torch allocator, so the stash round-trip is redundant but harmless. We mention it because a sleeping engine should hold as little GPU memory as possible, and the stash works against that. ### 4.2 Weight cache daemon: VMM transport, then a shared owner Both phases touch the in-tree `weight_cache` package, so we file them as asks rather than doing out-of-tree work. We're happy to drive the implementation, with review from the weight-cache authors. **Phase 1: transport swap.** The daemon allocates weights via VMM and exports FD-based shareable handles instead of legacy CUDA IPC blobs (legacy IPC remains as a fallback where VMM is unavailable). This is the change motivated in section 2. No architecture change, no new components, no new dependencies. It removes the daemon-death → engine-death coupling, and it makes weight sleep/wake and stable VAs possible while the daemon remains the owner. In the section 7 matrix, this phase alone flips four rows for config 1. **Phase 2: shared ownership (config 2).** The daemon allocates through a shared memory owner (GMS) and commits its allocations read-only, instead of owning the memory itself. The daemon keeps everything that makes it the weight cache: the loading pipeline, the `CacheConfig` fingerprint, the socket protocol, discovery, and the tensor manifest. The mechanical change is small: per manifest entry, the CUDA IPC handle blob becomes an allocation reference (ID + offset) into the owner. What it unlocks is not small: cache contents that survive daemon crashes and restarts, an ephemeral pre-warm mode, and epoch-based weight updates through the owner's RW/RO leases. Section 5 details this. Phase 2 is where the two systems genuinely converge, and we would not want to design it unilaterally: the manifest format and the daemon protocol should stay fully SGLang-owned. ## 5. What phase 2 unlocks: the daemon as publisher Once the daemon speaks VMM, letting a shared owner hold the memory is a small step: the daemon loads through a client memory pool of the owner, then commits its allocations read-only. Everything the daemon is *for* survives intact: the loading pipeline, the `CacheConfig` fingerprint, the socket protocol, the ready-file discovery. Per manifest entry, the CUDA IPC handle blob is replaced by an allocation reference (ID + offset) into the owner. The meta-init import path stays exactly where it is today (the weight-cache loader); it just gains a pluggable transport. What emerges is a clean split into two planes: ```mermaid flowchart LR subgraph metadata["Metadata plane (SGLang-versioned)"] D["weight cache daemon
loads, fingerprints,
serves the tensor manifest,
republishes on updates"] end subgraph memory["Memory plane (engine-agnostic)"] S["memory owner (GMS server)
allocation IDs + handles,
RW/RO leases, no CUDA context"] end D -- "RW lease: load, commit" --> S E1["engine (reader)"] -- "manifest" --> D E1 -- "import RO, map" --> S E2["engine (reader)"] -- "manifest" --> D E2 -- "import RO, map" --> S ``` We think this split puts each kind of knowledge where it belongs: - **Model-level metadata** (tensor names → allocation/offset/shape/dtype, quant fingerprints) is engine-version-specific. It should live in SGLang code, versioned with SGLang, i.e. in the daemon. Frankly, this fixes a weakness of our own current design, where reconstruction metadata lives in the memory service and can skew against engine versions. - **The memory owner stays dumb**: IDs, sizes, handles, leases. It never parses model metadata. For config 3 (no daemon), the writer engine attaches the manifest as an *opaque blob at commit time*; a fresh reader fetches blob → meta-init → map. Same mechanism, daemon optional. The operational consequence: cache contents now survive daemon crashes *and* engine crashes. The daemon can even exit after committing, which gives you pre-warmed GPUs with zero resident loader processes. ### Convergent evolution Meta-model reconstruction is the part of this problem that requires deep, version-specific engine knowledge: which tensors exist after quantization, which buffers are non-persistent, which attributes are views that need rewiring (`_rebuild_stale_views` is hardcoded per model class for a reason). #27139 put that logic where it belongs, in-tree next to the model code that defines it, but coupled it to memory ownership over a transport that limits what ownership can do (section 2). GMS started from the other end: memory ownership done right with VMM, but with reconstruction metadata living in the memory service, where it inevitably drifts out of sync with engine versions. Our next-generation core draws the consequence and deletes reconstruction from the memory service entirely; the owner keeps only allocation IDs, handles, and leases, and engines are restored from process snapshots instead of ever being rebuilt. The phase-2 composition takes the strong half of each. SGLang keeps the reconstruction path and the manifest: engine-versioned, in-tree, maintained next to the model code, which is the only place it can be maintained correctly. The owner keeps only engine-agnostic memory state, which is why one owner implementation can serve any engine. And notably, the composition removes the snapshot prerequisite from our side for SGLang: a fresh engine is rebuilt from the daemon's manifest instead of restored from a snapshot. (One asterisk: a fresh-attach-by-manifest entry point is a small addition on the owner side; the underlying import and mapping primitives already exist.) Snapshot then becomes a purely additive optimization to pursue later (section 6), not a dependency of anything in this RFC. ### Weight updates without reload Today `update_weights*` is rejected while the weight cache is active (a transport limit, per section 2). With a VA-stable owner, updates become an epoch handoff, and the daemon becomes the weight *delivery agent* (it already knows how to join collectives): ```mermaid sequenceDiagram participant T as trainer participant D as daemon (writer) participant S as memory owner participant E as engines (readers) T->>D: push new weights (NCCL/RDMA) E->>S: pause weights tag (unmap, release RO lease) D->>S: acquire RW lease (writer priority) D->>S: write new epoch, commit RW→RO E->>S: re-acquire RO, remap at saved VAs Note over E: same shapes → same addresses →
existing pointers and captured CUDA graphs stay valid E->>E: resume serving ``` Because remapping happens at the same virtual addresses, engines resume with every pointer still valid, including pointers baked into captured CUDA graphs. No graph recapture on a weight update. In the colocated-RL case (trainer and engine share the node and weights arrive in-process), the engine itself holds the writer lease and republishes: that's config 3, same protocol, no daemon in the loop. ## 6. Meta model reconstruction Nonetheless, meta-device reconstruction stays brittle in every configuration discussed here. Configs 1, 2, and 3 all rebuild the model skeleton and rebind storages, so the `conv_weights`-style edge cases remain a shared, per-model-architecture tax. The only approach that eliminates the class is snapshot-based process restore (CRIU + cuda-checkpoint over a VA-stable owner), which also restores CUDA graphs and warmup state, but it is still fairly limited today and we are deliberately keeping it out of scope for this RFC (although we will open another RFC for snapshot support in SGLang soon). The phase-2 split also opens up a clean seam for the snapshot approach: the same engine-agnostic owner serves both the manifest-driven reconstruction path described here and, later, a snapshot-restore path that skips reconstruction entirely. ## 7. Which configs support which scenarios Deployments usually want several of these at once, so instead of one "recommended config" per scenario, here is what each configuration can and cannot do. "1 + VMM" is config 1 after the phase-1 transport swap (same architecture, different handles); "2" assumes phase 2. | Capability / scenario | 1 (as merged) | 1 + VMM (4.2 phase 1) | 2 (4.2 phase 2) | 3 | |---|---|---|---|---| | Fast restart after engine crash | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | | Pre-warm before any engine exists / fleet cold start | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ | | Warm-standby engine failover | ⚠️ ¹ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | | Engines survive daemon/owner crash | ❌ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | | Cache survives daemon crash/restart | ❌ | ⚠️ ² | ✅ | n/a (no daemon) | | Weight sleep/wake via release/resume | ❌ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | | Weight updates without engine reload | ❌ | ⚠️ ³ | ✅ ⁴ | ✅ ⁴ | | Stable VAs for CUDA graph restore (#27052 Phase 2) | ❌ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | | Non-NVIDIA backends | ✅ | ❌ | ❌ | ❌ | | No external service beyond SGLang | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ | ❌ | ¹ Works today: the standby maps shared weights at zero marginal cost and parks KV/graphs via the existing memory saver. But daemon death SIGKILLs primary and standby together, so the failover pair shares a fault domain with the daemon. ² Attached engines keep serving (their mappings stay valid), but new engines must disk-load until the daemon reloads. ³ Possible in principle (the daemon owns writable memory), but requires designing an update/coordination protocol inside the daemon. With a shared owner this comes for free from the RW/RO lease epochs. ⁴ Config 2: the daemon delivers trainer-push updates (disaggregated RL). Config 3: the engine takes the writer lease itself (colocated RL). These are per-deployment choices on one protocol, not competing systems, and the writer role can move between daemon and engine at runtime via the lease. ## 8. Open questions 1. How should an out-of-tree memory-saver backend be selected for plain `sglang.launch_server`: a server argument, TMS-side registration (fzyzcjy/torch_memory_saver#79), or both? 2. If the pause-preserves-contents refinement (section 4.1) is wanted, should it be a property of the TMS backend or a per-tag region option, like `enable_cpu_backup` today? 3. For 4.2 phase 2: what should the manifest schema and versioning look like? We propose it stays fully SGLang-owned; the memory owner stores it as an opaque blob. ## 9. Proposed next steps We're happy to send a PR for 4.1 (it's small), and to drive 4.2 phase 1 with review from the weight-cache authors. For 4.2 phase 2 we'd propose co-designing the manifest format first, so the daemon owns it end to end. If there's interest, we can also share what worked and what didn't from walking this path in GMS.

title: [RFC] Host-Backed Deferred Device KV Allocation for PD Disaggregation
author: aooxin
body: # Host-Backed Deferred Device KV Allocation for PD Disaggregation ## Summary This RFC proposes a PD direct-to-host decode KV transfer path for disaggregated serving. Today, decode-side preallocation reserves device KV cache before the prefill-to-decode KV transfer completes. For agentic long-context workloads with high HiCache hit rates, this can cause many preallocated and in-transfer requests to occupy decode GPU memory before they are ready to run, reducing the device KV capacity available to the active decode batch. The proposal is to stage transferred KV cache in pinned host memory on the decode node and delay device KV allocation until the request is close to decode execution. The decode node then asynchronously moves KV cache from host to device before admitting the request into the running batch. This shortens device KV residency for preallocated and in-transfer requests, separates transfer staging capacity from active decode execution capacity, and can improve running batch size under decode-side device KV pressure. The tradeoff is an additional host-to-device staging step, which may increase TTFT in uncongested cases. ## Motivation Agentic workloads often have very long input contexts and high HiCache hit rates. In this setting, the prefill node can process many concurrent long-input requests and sustain very high input-token throughput. In a PD disaggregated deployment, however, each of these requests still needs decode-side destination KV capacity before the prefill-to-decode KV transfer can complete. This makes decode-side preallocation scale with prefill input throughput, not just with the number of requests that are actually ready to run decode. Compared with traditional shorter-context workloads, agentic workloads can therefore reserve a much larger amount of decode GPU memory for preallocated and in-transfer requests, squeezing the memory available to the active running batch. This creates several issues. ### 1. Long Device KV Residency for Preallocated and In-Transfer Requests A large portion of decode GPU memory can be occupied by requests that have not entered the running batch yet. In agentic long-context workloads, this effect is amplified because high prefill input throughput continuously creates new decode-side preallocation demand. As a result, the active running batch size can stay far below the configured upper bound even when decode compute still has headroom. #### Example on H20e Consider an H20e decode node with a device KV pool of about `5M` tokens. For requests with roughly `100K` input tokens, the pool has a nominal capacity of about `50` request-contexts before accounting for output growth, fragmentation, and scheduler constraints. In production traces, however, requests in this input-length range show that about `33%` of decode-side device KV residency is spent before the request enters the active running batch, including preallocation, transfer in-flight, and post-transfer waiting. In capacity terms, this means that a significant fraction of the `5M` token pool can be occupied by requests that are not yet generating tokens. With a `33%` pre-running residency share, the effective KV budget available to active decode is: ```text 5M * (1 - 0.33) = 3.35M tokens ``` At `100K` tokens per request, this corresponds to roughly `33` active running requests, instead of the nominal `50` request-contexts. The remaining capacity is not wasted permanently, but it is temporarily held by requests that are still being prepared for decode execution. For long-context workloads with high prefill throughput, this temporary residency can be large enough to keep the running batch well below its configured limit even when decode compute still has headroom. ### 2. Decode-Side Prealloc Queueing Can Increase TTFT Under Device KV Pressure When decode-side device KV is scarce, requests may wait in the prealloc queue before KV transfer can proceed. In those congested cases, queueing directly increases time-to-first-token. In uncongested cases, direct device transfer may still have lower TTFT because it avoids the extra H2D staging step. ### 3. Transfer Staging Capacity and Active Decode Capacity Become Tightly Coupled The scheduler must balance memory reserved for preallocated or in-transfer requests against memory available for active decode execution. If too little memory is available for preallocation, not enough requests can be prepared to keep decode compute busy. If too much memory is occupied by preallocated or in-transfer requests, the running batch cannot grow large enough to saturate the GPU. This makes KV capacity implicitly control compute concurrency. The core observation is that a request does not need to occupy device KV memory for the entire period between decode-side preallocation and actual decode execution. By staging transferred KV in host memory and allocating device KV only before H2D, we reduce each request's device-memory residency window. This reduces aggregate decode-side device KV pressure and can improve active running batch size for long-context workloads, while trading off an additional host-to-device staging step. ## Proposed Changes Introduce a new decode-side transfer mode, tentatively called **PD direct-to-host**. ### Current Path ```text decode prealloc queue -> allocate device KV slots -> prefill node transfers KV to decode device KV -> transfer complete -> request enters decode waiting/running batch ``` ### Proposed Path ```text decode prealloc queue -> allocate pinned host transit KV slots -> prefill node transfers KV to decode host memory -> transfer complete -> decode node allocates device KV slots -> async H2D copy -> H2D complete globally across TP ranks -> request enters decode waiting/running batch ``` ### Main Changes - Add decode-only `--enable-pd-direct2host` mode. - Add a pinned host transit KV pool on the decode node. - Register host KV buffers with the transfer backend when direct-to-host is enabled. - During decode preallocation, allocate host KV slots instead of device KV slots. - After prefill transfer completes, allocate device KV only when H2D is ready to start. - Use a dedicated CUDA stream for host-to-device KV copy. - Keep requests in the transfer queue until H2D is complete across all TP ranks. - Free host transit slots after H2D completion. - Preserve existing fallback behavior when direct-to-host is disabled. This change does not reduce the final device KV requirement of an active decode request. Instead, it reduces the amount of time a non-running request occupies device KV memory. ## Usage Example decode-side options: ```bash --disaggregation-mode decode \ --enable-pd-direct2host \ --pd-direct2host-host-ratio 2.0 ``` Optional fixed host pool size: ```bash --pd-direct2host-host-size ``` ### Expected Constraints - Decode mode only. - Mutually exclusive with decode KV cache offload in the initial implementation. - Mutually exclusive with hierarchical cache in the initial implementation. - Requires enough pinned host memory on decode nodes. - Transfer backend must support registering and writing to host buffers. ### Expected Effects - Reduce decode-side device KV residency for preallocated and in-transfer requests by staging transferred KV in host memory and allocating device KV only before H2D. - Increase active running batch size for long-context workloads. - Lower TTFT when decode-side prealloc queueing is the bottleneck, at the cost of an extra H2D staging step in uncongested cases. - Better separate transfer staging capacity from active decode execution capacity. ## Known Deployment Caveat In current testing, PD direct-to-host may require setting: ```bash export NCCL_GRAPH_MIXING_SUPPORT=0 ``` The direct-to-host path introduces non-CUDA-graph H2D work on a dedicated stream while normal decode may still use CUDA graph replay. Disabling NCCL graph mixing has been necessary in the current test environment to make graph and non-graph execution coexist reliably. This is treated as a deployment caveat for the initial implementation, not a settled long-term requirement. We still need to evaluate its impact on correctness, performance, NCCL scheduling behavior, and mixed graph/non-graph production workloads. ## Roadmap ### 1. Prototype Direct-to-Host Transfer Path Implement host transit KV pools, host buffer registration, decode-side H2D scheduling, and request lifecycle handling. ### 2. Add Metrics and Observability - Host transit pool usage. - H2D in-flight request count. - H2D latency. - Prealloc queue time. - Transfer queue time. - Device KV residency time. ### 3. Evaluate Performance Benchmark long-context workloads, focusing on: - Running batch size. - TTFT. - ITL. - Throughput. - GPU utilization. - Host memory usage. - H2D bandwidth overhead. ## Open Questions - What should the default host transit pool size be: fixed GB, ratio to device KV pool, or dynamically computed from traffic shape? - How much pinned host memory is acceptable in production deployments, and should the feature degrade gracefully when host memory is insufficient? - What is the impact of disabling `NCCL_GRAPH_MIXING_SUPPORT`? In current testing, graceful coexistence between CUDA graph and non-CUDA graph execution requires turning this off. We need to evaluate its effect on correctness, performance, NCCL scheduling behavior, and mixed graph/non-graph workloads in production.

title: [RFC] ParisKV2 sparse attention integration for SGLang
author: amy-77
body:
# [RFC] ParisKV sparse attention integration for SGLang

## Background

👋 Hello SGLang community. We are the **ParisKV** team.

### Why ParisKV2 matters (TL;DR)

ParisKV2 is a **production-ready, model-agnostic** long-context decode stack that combines **CPU offload**, **high-recall sparse retrieval**, and **SOTA speed** — on dense and sparse models alike:

| Claim | What we deliver |
|-------|-----------------|
| **Offload** | Retrieval zone (100K+ tokens) lives in **CPU pinned memory**; GPU holds only sink + local + update buffer. Enables 130K+ decode on a single GPU without OOM. |
| **High recall at top‑100** | At `K=100` on ~130K LongBench-v2 contexts: **~87% candidate recall, ~83% final recall** (ParisKV2) vs **~8% for Quest-only** (Table 7 ablation). |
| **No task accuracy drop** | Downstream scores on LongBench-v2 / RULER / AIME match **full attention** at practical budgets (`top_k=100`), while sparse baselines (Quest, ShadowKV, etc.) degrade. |
| **Drift-resistant** | Per-step **query-dependent** hierarchical Quest coarse + KIVI rerank (not a static page mask); **dynamic index update** flushes new tokens into the retrieval zone; sink + local window cover attention drift during generation. |
| **SOTA speed** | **~22 ms TPOT** at `K=100` on 130K contexts (Qwen3-8B, bs=1) — faster than ParisKV v1 (~34 ms), ShadowKV, RetroInfer, and full attention on the same GPU budget; scales to bs=24 within ~76 ms. |

> Speed numbers above are measured with `POLAR_PIPELINE_RECALL=0`. Recall-instrumented runs (exact q·k oracle per step) are **not** latency benchmarks.

**ParisKV** is a Polar ANN-based KV cache system for long-context LLM inference. ParisKV2 extends the original RaBitQ stack with a **Quest-style hierarchical coarse stage** and **KIVI 4-bit CDS rerank**. Core prototype: `cache_hub/polar_cache_kivi_quest_density_seperate_kernel.py`; CUDA kernels under `cache_hub/quest/`, `cache_hub/kivi/`, `cache_hub/rerank/`, `cache_hub/topk/`.

Architecture details, parameters, and evaluation setup: **[ParisKV README](https://github.com/amy-77/ParisKV/blob/main/README.md)**

We have been running ParisKV2 on Qwen3 / LongBench-v2 (130K+ tokens) and would like to upstream it into SGLang as a first-class sparse-attention backend.

**Positioning:** ParisKV2 is closest to SGLang's **`QuestAlgorithm`** on the *algorithm* side, and closest to **`HiSparse`** on the *offload* side — but it is **model-agnostic**. Unlike `--enable-hisparse` (DSA / DeepSeek-V3.2 / GLM-5 / DSV4 only, model-native indexer), ParisKV2 brings **external Quest-style retrieval + CPU offload** to **any** attention model — dense GQA (Qwen3), and sparse/DSA architectures alike.

---

## How ParisKV relates to existing SGLang components

SGLang today has three relevant pieces. ParisKV is **not** a replacement for HiCache; it extends the [Quest algorithm path ](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/main/python/sglang/srt/mem_cache/sparsity/algorithms/quest_algorithm.py) with production offload.

| | **Quest** (`mem_cache/sparsity`) | **HiSparse** (`--enable-hisparse`) | **HiCache** (L1/L2/L3) | **ParisKV** |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Primary role** | Decode sparse **algorithm** (bbox page scorer) | Decode **memory** offload for DSA models | Cross-tier **prefix KV** storage & reuse | Decode sparse **algorithm + offload** |
| **Model support** | Generic (framework exists, not wired to main path) | **DSA / DSV4 only** — uses model-native indexer | Model-agnostic (storage layer) | **Model-agnostic** — external retrieval, no native sparse head required |
| **Retrieval method** | Page min/max bbox + `sparsity_ratio` topk | Model indexer selects top‑k | N/A (full KV pages) | Hierarchical Quest coarse + CDS + KIVI rerank |
| **Offload** | Not implemented (`SparseCoordinator` TODO) | CPU host pool + GPU device buffer + swap-in | GPU → host → external L3 | Sink + local (GPU) + retrieval (CPU pinned) |
| **When it helps** | Reference sparse decode | Long DSA decode under PD disagg | Multi-QA, shared prefixes | Single 100K–1M token prompts on **any** model |
| **Attention** | Top‑k pages via FlashAttention | Top‑k via DSA + flashmla backends | Full attention on cached prefix | Top‑K tokens: sink + local + retrieved |

**Takeaway for maintainers:**

1. **Compare ParisKV primarily against Quest** — same bbox coarse idea, same `mem_cache/sparsity` hooks (`construct_representations`, `retrieve_topk`). ParisKV is a production upgrade, not a new problem class.
2. **HiCache is orthogonal** — prefix reuse across instances (TensorCast / Mooncake L3). ParisKV does per-request decode retrieval; the two compose (RadixAttention + HiCache + ParisKV).
3. **HiSparse is the closest offload analogue, but ParisKV does not inherit its model gate** — we reuse similar sink/local/retrieval zoning and async D2H, without requiring DSA or PD disaggregation.

---

## Why integrate into SGLang?

SGLang's `mem_cache/sparsity/` framework already defines the right algorithm interface (`QuestAlgorithm`, `BaseSparseAlgorithmImpl`, `SparseCoordinator`) but ships only a **reference Quest scorer** — flat page bbox, PyTorch topk, no offload, and `create_sparse_coordinator()` is not yet wired into the main decode path.

Meanwhile, production offload exists only under **`--enable-hisparse`**, which is gated to DSA models and relies on each model's built-in sparse indexer.

ParisKV fills the gap: **Quest-grade external retrieval + HiSparse-style offload, for any model.**

What ParisKV adds on top of SGLang Quest:

- **Hierarchical coarse stage** — two-level chunk tree (large chunk → small chunk) to avoid scoring all small chunks globally on 100K+ contexts
- **CDS dense/sparse classify** — centroid-based chunk density split before per-token rerank
- **KIVI 4-bit stage-2 rerank** — on-the-fly dequant + fused per-chunk top‑K + global top‑K gather (CUDA)
- **Built-in offload** — sink + local on GPU, retrieval zone in CPU pinned memory, async D2H, UVA H2D gather (no DSA requirement)
- **Flat mode toggle** — `hierarchical=false` for ablation / short-context fallback

Integrating ParisKV would give SGLang a **turn-key long-context decode path for dense models** (Qwen3, Llama, etc.) and an **alternative sparse path for DSA models** that do not want to depend solely on the native indexer — without a separate inference fork.

---

## Proposed integration

### Phase 1 — `ParisKVAlgorithm` in `SparseCoordinator` (recommended first step)

Add `pariskv` (alias `polar_ann`) to `_ALGORITHM_REGISTRY` in `mem_cache/sparsity/factory.py`, subclassing `BaseSparseAlgorithmImpl` (Quest-derived). Wire `create_sparse_coordinator()` into the decode attention path — this is required for **both** Quest and ParisKV, and is separate from the DSA-only `--enable-hisparse` gate.

**Mapping from ParisKV → SGLang interfaces**

| ParisKV component | SGLang hook | Closest existing analogue |
|---|---|---|
| `_compute_and_store_chunk_minmax` | `construct_representations` / `update_representations` | Quest `_compute_page_representations` |
| `_quest_pick_coarse_indices_hierarchical` / `_flat` | `retrieve_topk` stage-1 | Quest `_retrieve_page_scores` + `topk` |
| `_cds_dense_sparse_select` + `collision_based_topk_batch` | `retrieve_topk` stage-2 | *(not in Quest)* |
| Sink + local + retrieval zoning | `SparseCoordinator` device buffer + host retrieval pool | HiSparse host/device split *(pattern only)* |
| `flash_attn_with_kvcache_compat` on gathered KV | `FlashAttentionAdaptor` sparse path | Quest backend path |

**New server flags (draft)**

We propose a **model-agnostic** entry point, distinct from `--enable-hisparse`:

```bash
--enable-sparse-attention          # new flag; NOT gated on DSA
--sparse-attention-config '{
  "algorithm": "pariskv",
  "top_k": 2048,
  "page_size": 16,
  "min_sparse_prompt_len": 8192,
  "sparse_extra_config": {
    "large_chunk": 256,
    "large_ratio": 0.4,
    "small_ratio": 0.3,
    "hierarchical": true,
    "sink_size": 4,
    "local_size": 512,
    "dynamic_update_interval": 512,
    "cds_dense_ratio": 0.3,
    "cds_dense_topk": 16,
    "cds_sparse_topk": 8,
    "kivi_bits": 4,
    "align_offload": true
  }
}'
```

> **Note:** Reusing `--enable-hisparse` is possible mechanically (it already parses `hisparse_config` JSON), but today that flag **asserts DSA model class** in `validate_hisparse()`. ParisKV integration should either add a new flag or relax that gate when `algorithm=pariskv`. We welcome maintainer guidance here.

**Kernel packaging**

We propose vendoring (or publishing as `sgl-kernel` extension) the following CUDA ops already used in production:

- `quest_chunk_score`, `quest_sub_chunk_score`, `quest_map_back`
- `partial_chunk_kivi_qk_dense_sparse_cuda`
- `partial_chunk_density_scores_cuda`, `dense_mask_from_topk_cuda`
- `float_topk_3d`, `float_topk_gather_concat_3d`
- UVA `h2d_gather` for CPU retrieval zone

Initial target: **bf16, head_dim=128, GQA models (Qwen3 family)** — matching our current speed path.

### Phase 2 — Optional HiCache host pool backing

ParisKV already implements its own CPU pinned retrieval zone (functionally similar to HiSparse's host pool). Phase 2 is an **allocator swap**, not a feature prerequisite:

- Optionally allocate the retrieval zone from `HostKVCache` (HiCache L2) instead of a private `unified_keys_cpu` buffer
- Reuse HiCache IO backends (`kernel` / `direct`) for page-aligned host↔device movement
- Keep sparse metadata (per-chunk min/max/centroid, KIVI packed codes) as **sidecar tensors** per page, similar to Quest's `page_k_min` / `page_k_max`

This composes with HiCache prefix caching but does **not** replace it. No new `HiCacheStorage` L3 backend is required.

### Phase 3 (optional) — Compressed KV sidecar for HiCache L3

Longer term, ParisKV's KIVI-packed chunk representation (~4× smaller than bf16 K) could be exposed as an optional **compressed pool** in `PoolTransfer`, enabling cross-node shipping of ANN-ready KV rather than raw pages. This is analogous in spirit to TensorCast's page export, but optimized for sparse decode rather than full-prefix replay.

---

## Architecture overview

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                     SGLang Decode Step                       │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  SparseCoordinator                                           │
│    └─ ParisKVAlgorithm                                       │
│         ├─ Steady zone (GPU): sink + local + update buffer   │
│         ├─ Retrieval zone (CPU/L2): full history K/V         │
│         ├─ Stage-1 Quest: hierarchical chunk bbox score    │
│         │     large_chunk=256 → top 40% → sub_chunk=16      │
│         │     → global top ~12% small chunks               │
│         ├─ Stage-2 CDS+KIVI: dense/sparse per-chunk rerank │
│         └─ Gather top-K tokens → FlashAttention sparse     │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

**Memory zones (per layer)**

| Zone | Typical size | Location | Attention |
|------|-------------|----------|-----------|
| Sink | 4 tokens | GPU | Full |
| Local | 512 tokens (+ aligned tail) | GPU | Full |
| Retrieval | up to ~130K tokens | CPU pinned | Sparse top‑K |
| Update buffer | `dynamic_update_interval` | GPU | Merged into retrieval on flush |

---

## Implementation plan

### Milestone 1 — Algorithm port + decode wiring

- [ ] Add `ParisKVAlgorithm` under `mem_cache/sparsity/algorithms/` (Quest-derived)
- [ ] Port chunk min/max/centroid maintenance from `_compute_and_store_chunk_minmax`
- [ ] Wire hierarchical + flat coarse pickers behind `sparse_extra_config`
- [ ] Register `"pariskv"` in `_ALGORITHM_REGISTRY`
- [ ] Wire `create_sparse_coordinator()` into decode path for generic (non-DSA) models
- [ ] Unit tests against existing `quest` reference + offline `test_hierarchical_vs_flat.py` fixtures

### Milestone 2 — CUDA kernel build 

- [ ] Integrate kernels into `sgl-kernel` build or standalone `pariskv_ops` extension
- [ ] CI smoke test: 1 LongBench-v2 sample, 40 decode steps, `top_k=2048`

### Milestone 3 — HiCache host pool 

- [ ] Optional `--pariskv-use-hicache-host` to allocate retrieval zone from `HostKVCache`
- [ ] Validate with `--hicache-io-backend kernel` and `page_first` layout

### Milestone 4 — Benchmark & docs 

- [ ] LongBench-v2 easy/long, RULER, multi-turn QA
- [ ] Compare against native `quest` algorithm and full FlashAttention baseline
- [ ] Document tuning guide (chunk sizes, ratios, top_k, local_size)

- [ ] Add same-environment SGLang full-attention baseline: Qwen3-8B, ~128K prompt, bs=1, 40 decode steps
- [ ] Report TPOT / TTFT / peak GPU memory / OOM threshold for full attention vs ParisKV2
- [ ] Add sparse inference speed baselines where runnable: SGLang Quest, ShadowKV, RetroInfer, and DSA-only HiSparse on a compatible model
- [ ] Keep recall-instrumented runs separate from latency benchmarks
- [ ] LongBench-v2 easy/long, RULER, multi-turn QA
- [ ] Document tuning guide (chunk sizes, ratios, top_k, local_size)
---



## Preliminary results

### Recall ablation (instrumented runs — **not** speed benchmarks)

Recent internal logs (`POLAR_PIPELINE_RECALL=1`, `LOG_EVERY=1`) on Qwen3-8B, LongBench-v2 easy/long, ~131K tokens, `final_topk=2048`, 40 decode steps:

| Config | CoarsePool R@2048 | Final R@2048 |
|--------|-------------------|--------------|
| Hierarchical `l0.4 s0.3` | ~76% | ~74% |
| Flat `cand_ratio=0.12` | ~78% | ~75% |

These runs intentionally compute **exact q·k recall** every decode step (full ~130K retrieval zone × 36 layers × Final + CoarsePool). The logged TPOT (~12 s/token) reflects that instrumentation overhead and **must not** be quoted as inference latency.

### Production speed (recall off — from published eval)

With `POLAR_PIPELINE_RECALL=0`, representative TPOT on ~130K LongBench-v2 contexts (Qwen3-8B, bs=1):

| Method | K=100 | K=512 | K=1024 | K=2048 |
|--------|-------|-------|--------|--------|
| ParisKV (v1) | 33.6 ms | 35.8 ms | 33.8 ms | 34.8 ms |
| **ParisKV2** | **22.0 ms** | **22.0 ms** | **22.0 ms** | **25.6 ms** |

Batch-scaling smoke (same workload, bs=1→32): ParisKV2.0 TPOT stays in the **~22–76 ms** range up to bs=24; Full Attention OOMs at bs≥8 on the same GPU budget.

Recall ablation takeaway: at similar CoarsePool recall, hierarchical stage-1 avoids scoring all small chunks globally (~16× fewer bbox evals vs flat), which is why ParisKV2 achieves higher recall **and** lower TPOT than ParisKV v1.


### Planned SGLang speed baselines

To make the speed comparison reproducible for SGLang maintainers, we will add same-environment baselines on Qwen3-8B with ~128K prompt length and 40 decode steps. All latency numbers will be measured with recall instrumentation disabled.

| Method | Model scope | Attention / retrieval path | TPOT @ bs=1 | TTFT @ bs=1 | Peak GPU memory | OOM threshold | Status |
|---|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
| SGLang full attention / FlashAttention | Generic dense models | Full KV on GPU, dense attention | --| -- | -- | -- | Planned |
| SGLang Quest | Generic sparse framework | Page bbox scorer + top-k pages | -- | -- | -- | -- | Planned if generic sparse path is available |
| SGLang HiSparse | DSA / DSV4-style models | Model-native sparse indexer + host/device split | N/A for Qwen3-8B | N/A | N/A | N/A | Separate DSA-model benchmark |
| **ParisKV2** | Generic dense/sparse models | Hierarchical Quest + CDS + KIVI rerank + CPU offload | **22.0 ms @ K=100** | -- | -- | -- | Existing published eval |

Benchmark setup:

- Model: Qwen3-8B
- Prompt length: ~128K tokens
- Decode length: 40 generated tokens
- Batch size: bs=1 first, then bs scaling if memory allows
- Metrics: TPOT, TTFT, peak GPU memory, and OOM threshold
- ParisKV latency mode: `POLAR_PIPELINE_RECALL=0`
- Hardware / software: same GPU, same SGLang version, same tokenizer, same prompt set, same measurement script

The primary comparison will be ParisKV2 vs vanilla SGLang full attention under the same hardware, model, prompt length, decode length, and measurement script. We also plan to include sparse inference baselines where they are runnable in SGLang or reproducible from public implementations. Recall-instrumented runs will remain separate from latency benchmarks.

---

## Differences from Quest and HiSparse

### vs SGLang Quest (primary comparison)

SGLang's `QuestAlgorithm` ([`quest_algorithm.py`](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/main/python/sglang/srt/mem_cache/sparsity/algorithms/quest_algorithm.py)) is the closest algorithmic baseline. ParisKV extends it:

| Capability | SGLang Quest | ParisKV |
|---|---|---|
| Coarse scoring | Flat page bbox | Hierarchical (large→small) or flat |
| Fine selection | Bbox only (`sparsity_ratio` page topk) | CDS classify + KIVI 4-bit token rerank |
| Recent tokens | `num_recent_pages` | Explicit sink + local window |
| Offload | None | CPU pinned retrieval zone + async D2H |
| Kernels | PyTorch loop | Fused CUDA (`quest_*`, `kivi_*`, `topk_*`) |
| Wired to decode | No (`create_sparse_coordinator` unused) | Target: full decode integration |

### vs SGLang HiSparse (offload analogue, different model scope)

| Capability | SGLang HiSparse | ParisKV |
|---|---|---|
| Memory layout | Host pool + GPU device buffer | Sink/local (GPU) + retrieval (CPU) |
| Top‑k source | **Model-native DSA indexer** | **External Quest+KIVI pipeline** |
| Model gate | DSA / DSV4 only + PD disagg | **Any dense or sparse model** |
| Algorithm plug-in | No (`HiSparseCoordinator` is separate) | Yes (`ParisKVAlgorithm` in sparsity registry) |

### vs HiCache (complementary, not competing)

HiCache solves **prefix KV reuse** across GPU/host/L3. ParisKV solves **per-request decode sparse attention**. They compose: HiCache holds full pages, ParisKV selects which pages/tokens to attend to at decode time.

---

## Open questions for maintainers

1. **Flag design** — new `--enable-sparse-attention` vs reusing `--hisparse-config` with a relaxed DSA gate when `algorithm=pariskv`?
2. **Wiring `SparseCoordinator`** — preferred hook point in `model_runner` / attention backend for generic (non-DSA) models?
3. **Kernel distribution** — upstream into `sgl-kernel` vs optional `pip install pariskv-ops`?
4. **Page size alignment** — ParisKV uses `quest_chunk_size=16` by default; OK to require `page_size % 16 == 0` when `algorithm=pariskv`?
5. **DSA coexistence** — on DSA models, should ParisKV be an alternative to the native indexer, or run alongside HiSparse?
6. **Interaction with RadixAttention** — on prefix hit, skip retrieval-zone construction for the shared portion?

---

## Multi-chip support matrix

ParisKV targets **multi-vendor hardware support** beyond NVIDIA. The table below tracks backend portability status — data will be backfilled as PRs land.

### Component × Backend status (single layer)

| Quest chunk scorer (coarse) | — | — | — | — | — | — | — | — | — | — | — | — |

| CDS dense/sparse classify | — | — | — | — | — | — | — | — | — | — | — | — |
| Top-K gather (fused) | — | — | — | — | — | — | — | — | — | — | — | — |
| CPU offload (D2H / H2D) | — | — | — | — | — | — | — | — | — | — | — | — |
| FlashAttention (sink + local) | — | — | — | — | — | — | — | — | — | — | — | — |

### End-to-end performance

---

## Long-term vision

- **Unified long-context stack**: RadixAttention (prefix reuse) + HiCache (host/L3) + ParisKV (decode sparse retrieval on any model)
- **Dense-model sparse decode**: Qwen3 / Llama / Mistral long-context without native sparse heads
- **DSA-model flexibility**: optional external retrieval path alongside native HiSparse indexer

We are happy to start with a minimal Milestone 1 PR (algorithm skeleton + PyTorch fallback path) and iterate with the SGLang team on kernel packaging and CI.
