title: [RFC] Beyond Passive Byte Stores: Scheduler-Aware Multi-Tier KV Caching for SGLang with MORI-UMBP
author: TianDi101
body: # [RFC] Beyond Passive Byte Stores: Scheduler-Aware Multi-Tier KV Caching for SGLang with MORI-UMBP --- ## 1. Summary This RFC proposes integrating **MORI-UMBP** (Unified Memory & Bandwidth Pool — the tiered-storage, distributed KV component of AMD's MORI library) into SGLang as a HiCache L3 storage backend **plus** a KV-event feed that the request scheduler/router can consult. Existing L3 backends (file, Mooncake, NIXL, HF3FS, …) are passive byte stores: SGLang pushes pages down and pulls pages up, and everything the system knows about cache placement, temperature, and access economics is invisible to the layer that needs it most — the scheduler. UMBP differs in four ways: 1. **Scheduler-friendly, co-designed with mori-sched.** The UMBP master is a cluster-wide KV placement directory covering *all* tiers (engine HBM, host DRAM, UMBP DRAM pool, SSD). Beyond placement, it exposes per-key historical access counts, routing hit counters, last-access time, per-node capacity/utilization, access bandwidth histograms, and RPC latency — so a router can build a real *cost model*: not just "who has the prefix" but "who can serve it fastest". 2. **Customizable KV cache management policy.** Offload (put-routing), load (get-routing), eviction, and (planned) replication are pluggable strategy interfaces. Policy authors get access to the same rich metrics, so cache management becomes a developer surface instead of a hard-coded LRU. 3. **(WIP) Agent-aware hints.** TTL, session pinning, and priority hints flow from the serving API through HiCache into UMBP, so agentic workloads with known revisit patterns can shape cache retention explicitly. 4. **AMD hardware affinity by design.** UMBP explores software–hardware codesign opportunities with AMD GPU/CPU/NIC — examples include IBGDA and SDMA transports, AMD Infinity Storage (AIS), and GPU-initiated NVMe. The data plane already runs daily in our PD-disaggregation benchmarks (`--hicache-storage-backend mori`). This RFC documents the design and proposes the remaining integration work in phases. --- ## 2. Design ### Architecture The L3 data path (`UMBPStore` ↔ `IUMBPClient`, zero-copy RDMA) and the KV-event feed (KV events ↔ master ↔ router) are decoupled: each is useful alone, and together they close the loop — engine reports placement → master indexes and accumulates history → router routes on the cost model (Pillar 1) → routing trains the hit history → placement / eviction / replication policies consume it (Pillar 2) → agent hints override where the workload knows better (Pillar 3). A prefix that fell out of every engine's HBM but survives in the UMBP pool remains routable and is fetched from the nearest replica over RDMA instead of being recomputed. The whole loop rides on a data plane codesigned with AMD hardware (Pillar 4). --- ## 3. Implementation details This section describes the current state of the integration, which runs in our fork and is exercised daily by the PD-disaggregation benchmarks. Everything in §3.1–§3.5 is implemented; §3.6 lists the work still pending. ### 3.1 Where the code lives | Concern | SGLang touchpoint | Backing MORI call | | --- | --- | --- | | L3 byte store | `mem_cache/storage/umbp/umbp_store.py` (`UMBPStore`) | `BatchGet` / `BatchPut` / `BatchExistsConsecutive` | | L2 host buffer | `memory_pool_host.py` (`UMBPHostTensorAllocator` hook) | host KV tensor registration | | KV-event feed | `KVEventsSubscriber` in `umbp_store.py` ← `ZmqEventPublisher` (no engine changes) | master external-KV index | | Routing | mori-sched (`umbp_cache_aware` policy) | master query per request | The backend is registered as `mori` in `StorageBackendFactory` and selected with `--hicache-storage-backend mori`. The whole integration is flag-gated and import-guarded, so a build without UMBP is unaffected. ### 3.2 L3 backend (`UMBPStore`) - **Interface.** Implements the zero-copy v1 `HiCacheStorage` interface: - `batch_exists` → `BatchExistsConsecutive` (the prefetch probe). - `batch_get_v1` / `batch_set_v1` → pointer-based `BatchGet` / `BatchPut` issued directly against the host KV page buffers (no intermediate copy). - **Key scheme.** Key construction and MHA / MLA / split-heads handling mirror `MooncakeStore`, so existing layouts are reused rather than reinvented. - **Compatibility.** Existing write / prefetch policy knobs are unchanged. ### 3.3 Deployment modes - **Standalone (default).** Per-rank local DRAM + SSD with automatic rank isolation (per-rank SSD dirs, MLA+TP shared-SSD leader/follower, DP+SPDK tenant quotas). - **Distributed (`master_address` set).** Each rank joins the master-led pool with a per-rank identity, the host KV buffer registered once for RDMA zero-copy (staging-buffer fallback for capped-MR NICs), `dram_page_size` auto-derived so one Put/Get = one page = one RDMA op, and cross-DP-rank duplicate puts deduped by the master. ### 3.4 L2 host allocator Opt-in `UMBPHostTensorAllocator` hook in `memory_pool_host.py`. It allocates a hugepage-backed, NUMA-bound, prefaulted host KV tensor. Beyond the allocation itself, this layout is what makes the one-shot RDMA registration (§3.3) reliable on AINIC / ROCm. ### 3.5 KV-event feed With `kv_events_subscriber=true`, the `KVEventsSubscriber` in `umbp_store.py` mirrors L1/L2 `BlockStored`/`BlockRemoved` events from SGLang's existing `ZmqEventPublisher` into the master's external-KV index (no engine changes); mori-sched reads it back via `MatchExternalKv` for the `umbp_cache_aware` routing policy, closing the Pillar-1 loop. --- ## 4. TODO - [ ] **Benchmark results.** Publish end-to-end numbers (hit rate, TTFT / ITL, throughput) for UMBP vs. existing L3 backends across standalone/distributed modes and the HBM / DRAM / SSD tiers. - [ ] **More test coverage.** Extend beyond smoke/unit tests to zero-copy get/set correctness across MHA / MLA / split-heads, depth-aware eviction, distributed multi-rank dedup + RDMA registration, and policy-interface conformance. - [ ] **mori-scheduler integration.** Promote `umbp_cache_aware` from prefix-match to the full §2 cost model and wire the pluggable policies (Pillar 2) and agent hints (Pillar 3) through to mori-sched. --- Related PR: https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/25377

title: [RFC] A Policy-Programmable Scheduling Interface for SGLang Diffusion
author: tie-pilot-qxw
body:
## 1. Summary

This RFC proposes a policy-programmable scheduling interface for SGLang diffusion.

The goal is to let the diffusion backend schedule semantically complete tasks, such as
conditioning, denoising chunks, and decoding, through a pluggable policy interface. This
gives SGLang diffusion an explicit scheduling boundary at diffusion task boundaries, rather
than forcing all scheduling decisions to happen only at request admission.

The first milestone introduces:

- a task-centric representation of diffusion requests;
- a runtime state object that tracks task dependencies and worker availability;
- a policy interface that selects ready tasks for dispatch;
- an event-driven control loop that reacts to new requests, newly runnable tasks, and
  worker events;
- a default policy that preserves the current request-level scheduling behavior.

## 2. Motivation: request-level head-of-line blocking

Diffusion requests can be long-running, especially during denoising. If a diffusion backend
schedules only at request granularity, a long request can keep occupying execution resources
while later short requests wait, even though the long request naturally reaches boundaries
where the runtime could safely reconsider scheduling.

A diffusion request already has semantically meaningful execution boundaries:

```text
conditioning / encoder
        ↓
denoising step or denoising chunk
        ↓
denoising step or denoising chunk
        ↓
...
        ↓
decoder / postprocessing
```

At these boundaries, the request state is well-defined. The runtime can safely decide whether
to continue the same request or dispatch another ready task.

For example, consider a long video-generation request followed by several short
image-generation requests. With request-level scheduling, the short requests wait until the
long request finishes or reaches an implementation-specific yield point. With task-boundary
scheduling, the runtime regains control after a denoising chunk completes and can ask a
policy what to run next.

This RFC proposes the scheduling interface needed to express that choice inside SGLang
diffusion.

## 3. Design

The proposed design has four components.

### 3.1 RequestCompiler

`RequestCompiler` converts an incoming diffusion request into a task graph.

A task graph consists of semantically complete diffusion tasks and dependency edges between
them. A simple graph may look like:

```text
TEXT_ENCODE
    ↓
DENOISE_CHUNK_0
    ↓
DENOISE_CHUNK_1
    ↓
...
    ↓
VAE_DECODE
    ↓
FINALIZE
```

The model adapter chooses the task granularity. For example, a denoising task may represent
one denoising step or a fixed-size chunk of consecutive denoising steps.

### 3.2 RuntimeState

`RuntimeState` maintains the scheduler-visible state of the diffusion runtime:

- submitted requests;
- task graphs;
- task dependency state;
- ready tasks;
- running tasks;
- completed tasks;
- worker availability;
- request metadata such as priority, deadline, shape, or estimated cost.

The runtime owns dependency resolution. When a task's inputs become available, the runtime
marks the task as ready and exposes it to the scheduling policy.

### 3.3 SchedulerPolicy

`SchedulerPolicy` selects ready tasks to dispatch.

A policy observes the current `RuntimeState` and a set of ready tasks. It returns the tasks
that should be dispatched next. The runtime then validates and dispatches those tasks through
the existing execution path.

A possible interface is:

```python
class SchedulerPolicy(ABC):
    def on_request_submitted(
        self,
        state: RuntimeState,
        graph: TaskGraph,
        ready_tasks: Iterable[Task],
    ) -> Iterable[Task]:
        ...

    def on_tasks_runnable(
        self,
        state: RuntimeState,
        ready_tasks: Iterable[Task],
    ) -> Iterable[Task]:
        ...

    def on_worker_event(
        self,
        state: RuntimeState,
        event: TaskEvent,
        ready_tasks: Iterable[Task],
    ) -> Iterable[Task]:
        ...
```

The policy interface is task-level. Returning a task means that the policy
wants the runtime to dispatch that ready task now, subject to current worker availability and
runtime validation.

The policy does not execute model code directly. It only selects from tasks that the runtime
has already determined to be runnable.

### 3.4 TaskExecutor

`TaskExecutor` executes one task through SGLang's existing model-execution path.

For each dispatched task, the executor:

- prepares the task inputs from runtime-managed request state;
- invokes the corresponding model stage or denoising chunk;
- records the produced outputs;
- emits lifecycle events back to the control loop.

The executor is the bridge between the task-centric scheduler and the existing diffusion
model implementation.

## 4. Event-driven execution model

The proposed runtime separates scheduling control from GPU execution.

```text
   control plane                                execution plane
 ┌─────────────────────────────┐   dispatch   ┌────────────────────────┐
 │ RequestCompiler             │ ───────────► │ TaskExecutor + workers  │
 │ RuntimeState                │              │ async GPU execution     │
 │ SchedulerPolicy             │ ◄─────────── │ task lifecycle events   │
 └─────────────────────────────┘    events    └────────────────────────┘
            ▲                                             │
            └────────────── async event monitor ──────────┘
```

The control plane owns request graphs, dependency tracking, worker state, and policy
invocation. The execution plane runs tasks on GPU workers and emits lifecycle events.

Typical task events include:

```text
queued → launched → completed
                 ↘ failed / cancelled
```

When an event arrives, the control loop updates `RuntimeState`, computes newly ready tasks,
invokes the policy, and dispatches selected tasks when workers are available.

This event-driven structure is the mechanism that exposes diffusion task boundaries to the
scheduler. A policy can be invoked when:

- a new request is submitted;
- a task completes and makes downstream tasks ready;
- a worker becomes available;
- request metadata changes, such as priority or deadline.

## 5. First milestone

The first milestone wires the policy-programmable scheduling interface into one SGLang
diffusion path.

The implementation includes:

1. **Task graph construction.**
   Add a request compiler for one reference diffusion model or pipeline.

2. **Runtime state tracking.**
   Track submitted requests, task readiness, running tasks, completed tasks, and worker
   availability.

3. **Event-driven scheduling loop.**
   Dispatch tasks asynchronously and drive scheduling from request-submission and
   worker-event callbacks.

4. **Policy interface.**
   Add the `SchedulerPolicy` interface and route ready-task selection through it.

5. **Default policy.**
   Provide a default policy that follows current request-level execution semantics.

6. **Example policy.**
   Provide at least one simple alternative policy, such as shortest-ready-task first or
   priority-first, to validate that policies can be swapped without modifying model
   execution code.

7. **Feature flag.**
   Enable the task-centric scheduler through an explicit configuration flag.

## 6. Example policies

The interface supports different scheduling policies over the same task graph and execution
backend.

### 6.1 Current-behavior policy

The default policy preserves current request-level semantics by continuing the admitted
request's tasks in order until completion, subject to the existing backend behavior.

### 6.2 Priority policy

A priority policy prefers ready tasks from higher-priority requests.

### 6.3 Shortest-ready-task policy

A shortest-ready-task policy uses estimated task cost to prioritize tasks that are expected
to finish quickly, reducing head-of-line blocking for short requests.

## 7. Validation plan

The first implementation should validate the interface rather than claim end-to-end
scheduling gains.

Validation should include:

1. **Correct execution.**
   A request is compiled into a task graph, executed through the event-driven loop, and
   completed successfully.

2. **Default-policy parity.**
   The default policy follows current request-level scheduling semantics.

3. **Policy replaceability.**
   An alternative policy can be enabled without modifying model-execution code.

4. **Task-boundary scheduling.**
   The runtime invokes the policy at request submission, task completion, and
   worker-availability events.

5. **Control-plane overhead.**
   Measure the overhead of task-graph bookkeeping, policy invocation, and event handling.

## 8. Future milestones

After the policy interface is integrated, the same scheduling boundary can support richer
diffusion-serving policies.

Possible follow-up milestones include:

- cost-model-driven scheduling;
- priority and deadline-aware scheduling;
- stage-aware scheduling across conditioning, denoising, and decoding;
- layout-aware task dispatch;
- dynamic execution-layout selection;
- online artifact movement across task boundaries;
- elastic parallelism for diffusion tasks.

The key point is that these mechanisms can build on the same task-centric policy interface
introduced by the first milestone.

## 9. Relation to GF-DiT

This RFC is informed by GF-DiT: Scheduling Parallelism for Diffusion Transformer Serving
(https://arxiv.org/html/2606.13501v1).

GF-DiT studies task-centric and policy-programmable scheduling for DiT serving. This RFC
extracts the scheduling-interface part of that design and proposes a minimal SGLang
integration path: expose diffusion task boundaries, route ready-task selection through a
policy interface, and drive scheduling through asynchronous worker events.

## 10. Questions for maintainers

Feedback is especially useful on the following points:

1. Is this the right abstraction boundary for SGLang diffusion scheduling?
2. Where should the task graph and policy interface live in the SGLang codebase?
3. What is the preferred configuration mechanism for enabling the task-centric scheduler?

title: [RFC] Optimize RadixKey.match with native prefix comparison
author: merrymercy
body:
## Summary

`RadixKey.match()` in `python/sglang/srt/mem_cache/radix_cache.py` is a CPU-side hot path for prefix-cache lookup/insert. The current implementation avoids a Python per-token loop by using exponential search plus binary search over Python `array` slices, but each probe materializes temporary slices and then compares them.

Proposal: add a native C++ fast path for contiguous `array('q')` token buffers to compute the common-prefix length without Python slice allocation, using `memcmp`/vectorized block comparison plus a small in-block mismatch search. Keep the existing Python implementation as the fallback.

## Current behavior

Current code shape:

```python
while lo < n:
    hi = lo + step if lo + step < n else n
    if t0[lo:hi] != t1[lo:hi]:
        while hi - lo > 1:
            mid = (lo + hi) // 2
            if t0[lo:mid] == t1[lo:mid]:
                lo = mid
            else:
                hi = mid
        matched_tokens = lo
        break
    lo = hi
    step *= 2
```

If one slice comparison `t0[a:b] == t1[a:b]` is modeled as cost `b - a`, the algorithm is still `O(n)` for `n = min(len(t0), len(t1))`, with worst-case coefficient bounded by about `2n - 1` compared logical elements. In practice the constant is worse because each slice probe allocates/copies temporary `array` objects before comparison.

This matters most for long shared prefixes, equal prefixes, and mismatches near the end. Those are exactly the cases prefix caching tries to exploit.

## Proposal

Add an optional native helper, roughly:

```python
raw_matched_tokens = native_radix_prefix_match(t0, t1)
```

Requirements:

- Accept Python buffer-compatible contiguous arrays, initially `array('q')` / signed int64 token buffers.
- Return the first raw-token mismatch index in `[0, min(len(t0), len(t1))]`.
- Preserve current `RadixKey.match()` semantics:
  - `extra_key` compatibility check remains in Python.
  - normal mode returns raw matched-token count rounded down by `page_size`.
  - bigram mode converts raw matched tokens to logical bigram units with the existing `max(0, min(matched_tokens - 1, len(self), len(other)))` rule.
  - page-size rounding stays unchanged.
- Fall back to the current Python implementation if the native extension is unavailable or receives unsupported buffers.
- Avoid adding CUDA/GPU requirements. This is a CPU prefix-cache optimization.

Implementation options:

1. Preferred: a small packaged CPU extension, so there is no first-request JIT compile cost on production servers.
2. Acceptable experiment: a JIT C++ extension guarded by lazy loading and fallback, to validate speedup before deciding whether to package it.

C++ comparison strategy:

- Fast path: compare large contiguous blocks with `std::memcmp` to skip equal regions without Python allocation.
- When a block mismatches, locate the first differing `int64_t` inside that block using a simple scalar loop or smaller binary/block search.
- For fully equal prefixes, this is one contiguous native scan and returns `n`.

A plain `memcmp(a, b, n * sizeof(int64_t))` alone is not sufficient because it only says equal/not equal, not the first mismatch position. The helper needs either chunked `memcmp` or a native element loop after detecting the mismatching region.

## Benchmark plan

Add a microbenchmark for `RadixKey.match()` comparing current Python vs native fast path across:

- lengths: 0, 1, 8, 64, 512, 4096, 32768+
- mismatch position: first token, middle, last token, fully equal
- modes: normal and `is_bigram=True`
- `page_size`: 1 and a representative paged value

Measure:

- wall time per call
- temporary allocations if practical
- first-call overhead separately from steady-state if using JIT

Also run at least one prefix-cache-heavy serving/replay workload to confirm the microbenchmark improvement shows up in end-to-end latency or scheduler CPU time.

## Correctness tests

Add tests for:

- empty inputs
- full match
- mismatch at index 0, middle, and last
- one key being a strict prefix of the other
- `page_size` rounding
- `is_bigram=True` off-by-one behavior
- mismatched `extra_key` still raising `ValueError`
- fallback path behavior when native helper is disabled/unavailable

## Open questions

- Is the current `array('q')` representation guaranteed for all callers of `RadixKey`, or should the helper handle additional item sizes/type codes?
- Should this live under existing `python/sglang/jit_kernel` infrastructure, or should it be a tiny CPU utility extension outside GPU/JIT-kernel paths?
- What prefix length distribution do production traces show? If most calls are tiny, native-call overhead may dominate and we may want a threshold before calling into C++.

title: [RFC] Migrate UnifiedRadixCache logical backbone to Rust
author: ispobock
body:
## Summary

SGLang's radix caches (`RadixCache`, `SWARadixCache`, `MambaRadixCache`, `HiRadixCache`, `HiMambaRadixCache`) are consolidating into one `UnifiedRadixCache` that covers the full matrix: Hybrid (SWA / Mamba) and HiCache (L2 / L3) in any combination.

This roadmap migrates `UnifiedRadixCache`'s logical backbone to Rust: the pure CPU-bound control flow and bookkeeping that never touches the GPU (tree topology, key matching, per-component indices, LRU, locking, eviction, split, host-tier bookkeeping). Only genuine GPU compute and IO-bound orchestration stay in Python. The radix tree is the heaviest CPU-bound data structure in the scheduler, and taking it off the hot path's CPU budget is its instance of the broader non-GPU Rust migration (#23206).

Backward compatible: the external `BasePrefixCache` interface and its semantics are unchanged, and the Python implementation is kept as a parity oracle and fallback.

## Motivation

Long-context serving re-sends a large shared prefix with a small new increment each step (multi-turn chat, agentic loops). The GPU only prefills the new tokens, but the radix tree's CPU work does not shrink the same way: each step re-walks the whole prefix from root, so its cost grows with context length even as the GPU's share of the step stays small. Chunked prefill hits the same wall inside a single long request, each chunk re-walking the prefix the previous chunks built. As GPUs get faster while the scheduler's host work stays single-threaded, this CPU cost takes a growing share of each step.

The tree is walked several times per step: a match when the request is scheduled, an insert plus a re-match in `cache_unfinished_req` (repeated for every chunked-prefill chunk), and a final insert in `cache_finished_req`. Each walk descends the full current prefix, and in long context every insert grows the path the next walk has to descend. Every descent pays:
- per-node key slicing
- a full `torch.cat` to assemble the matched indices
- per-node component hooks

It is worst exactly where it matters most: Hybrid (SWA / Mamba) + HiCache, where per-component logic and host-tier bookkeeping ride on every node.

This is one layer of a broader move: SGLang's non-GPU side is already going to Rust (the router and gRPC paths today), and #23206 tracks taking more of the engine's CPU-bound hot paths the same way. The dividing line stays the same throughout: genuine GPU compute in Python, pure CPU-bound control flow and bookkeeping a migration target.

## Goals
- Make per-turn tree CPU cost independent of prefix depth, off the prefix-cache hot path's critical budget.
- Cover the full matrix at parity with Python: Hybrid (SWA / Mamba) + HiCache (L2 / L3), any combination.
- Stay backward compatible: external cache API and semantics byte-identical, Python kept as parity oracle and fallback.

## Non-Goals
- Keep in Python: genuine GPU compute and IO-bound orchestration (HiCache controller, storage backends, prefetch, async transfer, session, Req glue, KV-event emission). Everything else, the pure CPU-bound control flow and bookkeeping, is in scope.
- Do not change the external cache API or any model-visible behavior.

## Design

**Load-bearing invariant.** A walk's control flow depends only on key length and each component value's presence and length, never on the value's contents. That lets *decide* (pure tree state, in Rust) and *execute* (pool and tensor IO, in Python) split cleanly:

- One walk in Rust makes every decision and returns an `ActionBatch`. Python applies the physical effects afterward (pool free, SWA translate, mamba CoW, host backup).
- Nothing heavy crosses FFI, and one hot entry is one crossing. Matched indices are written into a caller-provided buffer (`out_ptr = tensor.data_ptr()`) rather than returned as a list. Node identity crosses as an opaque `u64` handle (held in `req.last_node`, with lock tickets keyed on it), never as a Python object.

**Component-aware backbone.** A node carries `[ComponentSlot; N]`, and the validator, cascade, and lock are generic over the slots, so SWA / Mamba / HiCache become slots on one backbone instead of five parallel trees. Components land incrementally, FULL first, then SWA → Mamba → HiCache, each gated and parity-checked against the Python implementation.

**Swappable backend.** The tree logic lives behind a `TreeBackbone` interface with two implementations: `PyBackbone` (today's logic moved behind the interface, byte-for-byte unchanged) and `RustBackbone`. The backend is selected at construction by an env flag and falls back to Python on an unsupported config, so `UnifiedRadixCache`'s external `BasePrefixCache` surface never changes.

## Roadmap

- **PoC**: Rust core + parallel adapter, FULL / SWA / Mamba parity (fuzz + small deterministic runs), HiCache L2 core cycle unit-tested, tree-CPU microbench
- **Step 0** (independent, pure-Python): drop redundant `match`, offset-based slicing (no per-node key copy), resume from `last_node`
- **Step 1**: extract a backbone interface and move today's tree logic behind it (pure refactor, zero behavior change), converge physical effects into one `ActionBatch` consumer
- **Step 2**: Rust backbone (FULL), absorb the PoC, differential-fuzz vs Python in CI, perf comparison, opt-in
- **Step 3**: migrate components, each gated and parity-checked: SWA → Mamba → HiCache L2 (controller wiring) → HiCache L3
- **Cross-cutting**: registered CI tests, hit-rate parity, real-tree perf on target platform

Move to https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/20415.

## References

- https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/20415
- https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/23206

title: [RFC][NPU][DLLM] Add fused tracker and coreset kernels for LLaDA2 JointThreshold
author: leedongkun30-arch
body:
# [RFC][NPU][DLLM] Fused tracker and coreset kernels for LLaDA2 JointThreshold

## Summary

Two NPU-only fused kernels for the LLaDA2.1-mini dLLM JointThreshold decode path on Ascend,
replacing per-layer small-op swarms in MoE expert tracking and coreset keep-mask selection with
single kernels, behind a runtime flag with a pure-Torch fallback. On GSM8K (n=50) they deliver
**+5.14% output throughput at identical accuracy (92.0%)**. This RFC proposes kernel placement and
the kernel → release → integration upstream sequence.

## Motivation

In the JointThreshold decode loop, two operations run per MoE layer per denoising forward:
1. the history-gate tracker max + EMA update, and
2. the per-call coreset keep-mask selection (softmax-sum score → group-balanced top-q).

On NPU these are dispatch-bound: each is a handful of small kernels whose host launch cost
dominates their compute, so the device idles between launches. Fusing each path into one kernel
removes those launches from the decode critical path without changing the selection semantics.

## Proposed kernels

1. **`moe_gate_max_update`** — fuses the per-expert running-max update and the EMA update into
   one NPU kernel (replaces a `torch.maximum(...)` + `mul_`/`add_` pair per layer).
2. **`moe_shortlist_mask`** — computes the per-call coreset selection (bf16-rounded softmax-sum
   score; exact top-q-per-group with lowest-index tie-break, matching `torch.topk(q)`), writes the
   keep-set, and masks dropped experts, in one HBM round-trip (replaces ~6–10 small vector ops per
   layer).

Both are NPU-only and shape-specialized to the current LLaDA2 MoE (E=256, 8 groups). The Python
integration uses them only when enabled; otherwise the existing Torch path runs unchanged.

## Upstream sequence (kernel / release / integration)

Kernel source and the SGLang Python caller land as separate PRs because the kernel package is
released separately:

1. **[sgl-kernel-npu] Kernel source PR** — add the two ops + bindings + a correctness test.
2. **[sgl-kernel-npu] Release** — a maintainer ships a release containing the new ops.
3. **[sglang] Python integration PR** — env-gated NPU-only call sites with Torch fallback, depending
   on the sgl-kernel-npu release that contains the ops.

Target repos: kernels → `github.com/sgl-project/sgl-kernel-npu`; Python → `github.com/sgl-project/sglang`.

## Guarded-fallback design (integration PR)

The integration is NPU-only and guarded; CUDA/default execution is structurally untouched because
the kernels are NPU-only. The call site checks: `device.type == "npu"`, fp32 dtype + contiguity, op
availability (`hasattr(torch.ops.npu, "moe_gate_max_update")` / `"moe_shortlist_mask"`), and
the runtime flag — otherwise it runs the existing Torch path. The model still loads and serves
when the kernels are not present; the Torch path simply runs.

## Evidence

GSM8K (n=50), Ascend 910B3, LLaDA2.1-mini, SGLang dLLM JointThreshold. Control runs the identical
recipe and runtime-flag stack with the two new kernels off (`TRACKER_MAX_UPD_KERNEL=0`,
`PERCALL_KEEP_KERNEL=0`).

| Run | Accuracy | Output TPS | Elapsed |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Control (kernels off) | 46/50 = 92.0% | 355.107 | 42.68 s |
| + tracker-max-update + coreset-keep kernels | 46/50 = 92.0% | 373.346 | 40.60 s |

Δ = **+18.24 tok/s (+5.14%)** at identical accuracy. Next: extend to n ≥ 100 and add a per-op
fallback equivalence test.

Excluded from this RFC: cbout, maxfold, tracker sum-update, and deferred-flush variants. They were
tested locally but were not reproducible release candidates.

## Environment

| Component | Version |
| --- | --- |
| NPU | Ascend 910B3 |
| CANN | 9.0.0 (V100R001C10SPC001B250) |
| torch / torch_npu | 2.10.0 / 2.10.0 |
| dtype / attention / max-running-requests | bfloat16 / ascend / 1 |

## Open questions

1. Should these kernels live under the existing `sgl-kernel-npu` layout, or a dLLM-specific submodule?
2. What is the release/version mechanism for sgl-kernel-npu — how should the integration PR pin the
   release that contains these ops?

## Reviewers / references

NPU backend: @ping1jing2 @iforgetmyname @whybeyoung · DLLM: @ClawSeven @btw616

Style references: #27127 (guarded NPU-only fallback), #21094 (before/after dLLM throughput evidence),
#18485 (how-to-run + benchmark evidence), #27144 (concise NPU dLLM PR with GSM8K evidence).

title: [RFC] Porting ReplaySSM to SGLang: faster decode and speculative decoding for hybrid (GDN/KDA) models
author: yuan-luo
body:
## Summary

[ReplaySSM](https://dao-lab.ai/blog/2026/replayssm/) (Dao AI Lab, 2026) is a technique that makes the **recurrent decode step of linear-attention / SSM layers faster** by turning a *read + write* of the full recurrent state every step into a *read-only* step plus a periodic *flush*. The recurrent update is linear, so the state can be reconstructed on demand from a checkpoint plus a tiny ring buffer of the last `L` steps' `(d, k, g)` records — and the output can be read out **without ever materializing the full state matrix** on non-flush steps.

This is a **bandwidth** optimization for a **memory-bound** kernel: GDN decode at batch ≥ 64 runs at 70–79% of peak HBM bandwidth, so halving per-step state traffic translates almost directly into speedup.

This RFC tracks porting ReplaySSM to SGLang in two independently-shippable parts:

| Part | Scope | Resource won | Status |
|------|-------|--------------|--------|
| **A** | Buffered output-only GDN **decode** kernel + integration | HBM **bandwidth** → decode speedup | **Implemented** — [#28451](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/28451) |
| **B** | ReplaySSM **spec-decode** verify (chunked, ring across verify steps) | bandwidth at high batch | **Implemented** — [#28695](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/28695) |
| (rel.) |  Compact linear spec cache | spec-decode **memory footprint** | **In review** — [#27658](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/27658) |

Upstream reference: vLLM ReplaySSM (commit `3c85112`), files `fused_recurrent_replayssm.py` (decode) and `gdn_replayssm_spec_decode.py` (spec).

> **Figure credit.** All figures below are reproduced from the [Dao AI Lab ReplaySSM blog](https://dao-lab.ai/blog/2026/replayssm/) for illustration. Credit to the original authors; see the blog for full context, methodology, and additional results.

---

## Background & motivation

### The problem

GDN (Gated DeltaNet, the Qwen3.5 / Qwen3-Next lineage) and KDA (Kimi Delta Attention) decode maintain a fixed-size recurrent state `S` of shape `[HV, V, K]` per slot per layer (~1 MB in bf16 for `HV=32, K=V=128`). The standard packed decode kernel reads `S` from HBM, applies a rank-1 update, and writes `S` back **every** decode step — roughly `2 * |S|` of state traffic per step (read + write).

This kernel is **memory-bound** at serving batch sizes. Measured on H20-3e (peak copy bandwidth ~3.8 TB/s):

| batch | achieved HBM bandwidth |
|-------|------------------------|
| 1     | 2% (launch/latency bound) |
| 16    | 29% |
| 64    | **70%** |
| 256   | **79%** |

When a kernel is this bandwidth-bound, **reducing bytes moved per step ≈ reducing runtime**.

![Latency breakdown showing the SSM decode step is dominated by state memory traffic](https://dao-lab.ai/assets/img/2026-06-15-replayssm/motivation-latencybreakdown.png)

*Latency breakdown (Nemotron-3-Super-120B-A12B-NVFP4, batch 256, single B300) — the recurrent state traffic dominates the step. From the [Dao AI Lab ReplaySSM blog](https://dao-lab.ai/blog/2026/replayssm/).*

### The idea

Keep the last flushed state `S0` (the **checkpoint**) frozen, and a small per-slot **ring buffer** of the last `L` steps' `(d, k, g)`. On a non-flush step, append the new `(d, k, g)` and reconstruct the readout from `S0` + the ring. Only every `L` steps **flush**: fold the ring into `S0` and write the full state back.

`S0` is still **read** every step, but the full-state **write** is amortized from every step to every `L` steps. Per-step state traffic drops from read+write (`~2|S|`) to read-only (`~|S|`) plus tiny ring appends — roughly halved. The ring records are negligible compared to the `[V, K]` state.

![ReplaySSM caches recent SSM inputs in a ring buffer and reconstructs state on the fly, writing back only on flush](https://dao-lab.ai/assets/img/2026-06-15-replayssm/headline_approach.png)

*ReplaySSM caches recent SSM inputs instead of storing the recurrent state every step, reconstructing states on the fly and writing back only when the buffer is full. From the [Dao AI Lab ReplaySSM blog](https://dao-lab.ai/blog/2026/replayssm/).*

---

## Core algorithm

Single head, single decode step (matches `fused_recurrent_gated_delta_rule_packed_decode` exactly):

$$\alpha = \exp(g)$$
$$d = \beta (v - \alpha (S k))$$
$$o = \alpha (S q) + d (k^\top q)$$
$$S' = \alpha S + d k^\top$$

Because the state update is **linear** in `S`, after `m` buffered steps the state before the current token unrolls to:

$$S = A \cdot S_0 + \sum_{j} w_j \cdot d_j k_j^\top$$

$$A = \prod_i \alpha_i \qquad\text{(total decay)} \qquad w_j = \prod_{i > j} \alpha_i \qquad\text{(replay decay of entry } j)$$

The bookkeeping is one rule: the checkpoint `S0` is decayed by **all** buffered `\alpha`; each older entry `j` is decayed by every `\alpha` that came **after** it.

**Output-only readout.** The output needs only `S q` and `S k`, both matrix-vector products. Substituting the unrolled `S`:

$$S q = A (S_0 q) + \sum_j w_j (k_j^\top q) d_j$$

`(k_j^\top q)` is a **scalar**, computed first; the `[V, K]` outer product `d_j k_j^\top` is **never built in HBM** on a non-flush step. The reconstruction sum is a small GEMM, run on **tensor cores** (see Precision below).

![Two routes to the same output: build the full state then read it, versus form the key-query scalar first](https://dao-lab.ai/assets/img/2026-06-15-replayssm/output_only.png)

*Two routes to the same output. The state-and-output route builds the full state then reads it; the output-only route forms the scalar key-query product first, so the state matrix is never materialized. From the [Dao AI Lab ReplaySSM blog](https://dao-lab.ai/blog/2026/replayssm/).*

**Degenerate L=1.** The ring is always empty and every step is a flush, so the reconstruction term vanishes, `A = 1`, and the kernel reduces *algebraically and numerically* to the baseline packed decode — a bit-exact anchor for testing.

---

## Scope & work breakdown

### Part A — buffered output-only GDN decode (implemented)

A standalone decode kernel plus full runtime integration. **Implemented in [#28451](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/28451).**

- New kernel + wrapper: `fused_recurrent_gdn_replayssm_decode(...)`, ported from vLLM `3c85112` with SGLang's packed GDN decode layout.
- Memory pool: per-slot ring buffers `replayssm_{d,k,g}` and a persistent `replayssm_write_pos`; reset at slot alloc and on COW.
- Backend dispatch: `TritonGDNKernel.packed_decode` routes to the ReplaySSM kernel when ring kwargs are present.
- CUDA-graph safety: static per-bs `write_pos` buffer, refreshed/advanced outside capture.
- Radix coordination: device-side `force_flush` aligned byte-for-byte to the mamba radix track snapshot condition (zero off-by-one), so the ring is folded into the checkpoint on exactly the step the radix cache reads `temporal[slot]`.
- Server args: `--enable-gdn-replayssm`, `--gdn-replayssm-cache-len` (default 16).

Files touched: the new kernel/test/bench, `mem_cache/memory_pool.py`, `attention/hybrid_linear_attn_backend.py`, `attention/linear/gdn_backend.py`, `attention/linear/kernels/gdn_triton.py`, `attention/mamba/mamba2_metadata.py`, `configs/mamba_utils.py`, `server_args.py`.

### Part B — ReplaySSM spec-decode verify (proposed, gated)

The upstream `gdn_replayssm_spec_decode.py` is **not** a state-cache tweak — it is a full **chunked verify forward** kernel that:

- computes verify outputs for all draft tokens via the chunked delta-rule UT-transform `(I + A)^{-1}`,
- reconstructs the carried state output-only from a **circular ring carried across verify steps**,
- flushes the full state only **every `L` committed tokens** (not every verify step),
- runs the reconstruction on tensor cores.

This would convert spec-decode's full-state write from **every verify step** to **every `L` committed tokens** — a bandwidth win at high batch. It also makes rejected-draft rollback a pointer move on the ring rather than a state write-back:

![ReplaySSM caches each draft's raw inputs, so rolling back rejected drafts is a pointer move with no state write-back](https://dao-lab.ai/assets/img/2026-06-15-replayssm/rollback_solution.png)

*ReplaySSM caches each draft's raw inputs, so rolling back rejected drafts is just a pointer move with no state write-back. From the [Dao AI Lab ReplaySSM blog](https://dao-lab.ai/blog/2026/replayssm/).*

**Relationship to #27658 (important).** #27658 ("compact linear spec cache replay") already captured the **memory** half of this idea for spec-decode: it stores compact `(k, Δv, decay)` per draft token instead of full intermediate states (2.32 GB → 0.06 GB), replays the accepted state once at the accept boundary in full fp32, and integrates the radix track snapshot + KDA. It explicitly reports **no throughput change** (verify was not bandwidth-bound at its 32–64-concurrency test point). Part B is **complementary, not a replacement**: it would add the bandwidth/speed half on top of #27658's memory/correctness infrastructure.

**Decision gate (do this before writing Part B code).** Measure the achieved HBM bandwidth of the spec-decode verify GDN forward at the *target* serving batch:
- ≥ ~70% → the full-state-write amortization is a real speedup; Part B is worth prototyping.
- < ~30% → same conclusion as #27658; the rewrite buys no time. Do not build it.

The upstream blog's own breakdown shows where the spec-decode gain comes from (kernel vs verify forward vs full decode step) and the orthogonal concurrency benefit — useful priors for what to expect:

![Speedup over the spec-decode baseline at kernel, verify-forward, and full-decode-step levels](https://dao-lab.ai/assets/img/2026-06-15-replayssm/spec-speedupbreakdown.png)

*Speedup over vLLM's speculative-decoding baseline at the kernel, verify forward pass, and full decode step levels. From the [Dao AI Lab ReplaySSM blog](https://dao-lab.ai/blog/2026/replayssm/).*

![Maximum decode concurrency under a fixed HBM budget with speculative window 4](https://dao-lab.ai/assets/img/2026-06-15-replayssm/spec-maxconcurrency.png)

*Maximum decode concurrency under a fixed HBM budget (speculative window 4) — the memory axis that #27658 already addresses. From the [Dao AI Lab ReplaySSM blog](https://dao-lab.ai/blog/2026/replayssm/).*

If built, Part B should: base on #27658's branch / its successor in `main` (**not** the Part A decode branch — Part A shares no spec logic with #27658, only the abstract idea; the real spec infra lives in #27658); reuse #27658's compact cache / radix track / KDA wiring; port the **early-flush invariant** exactly (`max_cache_len >= 2 * max_spec_len`, flush one window early so the circular cache never overflows the spec window — an overflow feeds the rejection sampler an uninitialized logit and desyncs the committed state); be gated behind a flag and default off.

### Out of scope (possible follow-ups)

- KDA decode (shares the backend; different gating — not wired in Part A).
- Lower-precision (bf16/fp8) ring/checkpoint to stack additional traffic savings.
- Batch-adaptive `L` (fall back to `L=1` at small batch where ReplaySSM cannot help and its extra reconstruction compute would otherwise be a small net loss).

---

## Design & integration concerns

The kernel is the easy half; the hard part is wiring a stateful, ring-buffered kernel into continuous batching + CUDA graphs + the radix prefix cache.

1. **`write_pos` is a per-slot decode cursor, not derivable from `seq_len`.** It must track the physical mamba slot (reset to 0 at slot alloc, when the post-prefill checkpoint is correct and the ring is logically empty), and advance **once per forward** (shared by all GDN layers of a step), not per layer.
2. **CUDA-graph safety.** `write_pos` is a static per-bs buffer captured by the graph and advanced in-place outside capture; the advance is guarded by `not in_capture` so warmup/capture do not corrupt the persistent counter.
3. **Radix `force_flush` alignment.** The radix cache snapshots `temporal[slot]` at fixed track boundaries; between flushes the checkpoint is stale. `force_flush` forces a flush on exactly those steps, computed from the identical condition the scheduler uses (zero off-by-one). `cache_valid` still uses the true `write_pos` — never fake `write_pos = L-1` to force a flush, or the kernel reads uninitialized ring entries.
4. **COW reset.** On a prefix-cache hit, `MambaPool.copy_from` copies the (always-flushed) snapshot into the private slot and resets that slot's `write_pos` to 0 so the destination ring starts empty.

---

## Precision & correctness

- **Mathematically lossless** — the reconstruction is an exact algebraic identity.
- **Not bit-exact in floating point** — the reconstruction GEMM runs on tensor cores (TF32 for fp32, bf16 tensor cores for bf16) and reassociates the recurrence, so it differs from the sequential baseline at the `~1e-4` (TF32) / `~1e-3` (bf16) level. This matches the upstream vLLM kernel, which uses the same tensor-core path and validates at the same tolerances (fp32 `atol 1e-4`, bf16 `atol 2e-2`).
- **Accuracy-neutral end-to-end** — per-step decay `\alpha < 1` attenuates old reconstruction error (bounded, re-anchored at each flush). Note that baseline GDN inference is already non-bit-exact across batch/chunk sizes; this introduces no new error class.
- Forcing IEEE precision on the reconstruction dot would make it bit-exact but disables tensor cores and makes the kernel **10–20× slower** — bit-exactness and the speedup are mutually exclusive by construction.

---

## Validation methodology (Part A)

Layered, weakest-to-strongest:

| Layer | Method | Result |
|-------|--------|--------|
| Kernel math | unit test vs `..._packed_decode` | fp32 `L=1` bit-exact (`atol 2e-6`); `L>1` within tensor-core tolerances; `force_flush` mid-buffer passes |
| Integration plumbing | short greedy decode, flag-on vs baseline | byte-identical (eager / CUDA-graph / radix all on) |
| **End-to-end correctness** | **GSM8K, radix + CUDA-graph on** | **flag-on 0.900 vs baseline 0.850 — within noise, no regression** |
| Performance | microbench + bench_serving | see below |

The standalone kernel test caught the tensor-core trap (an `input_precision="ieee"` dot that silently disabled tensor cores → 15× slowdown) **before** any integration work.

---

## Performance (honest, model-dependent)

- **Kernel microbench:** 1.2–1.5× at batch ≥ 16 with `L=8`; slightly slower at batch 1 (overhead-bound, not an operating point — the reconstruction compute is not hidden when there is no bandwidth pressure).
- **End-to-end (Qwen3.5-35B-A3B, 128 concurrent):** ~2.3% TPOT improvement.

The e2e gain is much smaller than the kernel gain because Qwen3.5-35B-A3B is **MoE-heavy**: the GDN linear layers (where the kernel wins) are a small fraction of decode cost, diluted by MoE and full-attention layers. **GDN-dense models would gain substantially more.** This is a model-dependent optimization, not a universal speedup.

The theoretical ceiling is `~0.57×` traffic (`L=8`) → `~1.75×`; the realized 1.2–1.5× reflects <100% bandwidth utilization, the still-every-step `S0` read, the added reconstruction compute, and ring traffic.

For reference, the upstream blog reports the same shape — strong kernel-level speedup that dilutes to a smaller end-to-end gain on MoE models, and a clear dependence on buffer size `L` and batch:

![Kernel-level and end-to-end per-step speedup over the vLLM baseline across Nemotron-3 and Qwen3.5 families](https://dao-lab.ai/assets/img/2026-06-15-replayssm/ar-e2espeedup.png)

*Kernel-level and end-to-end per-step speedup over vLLM's baseline (Nemotron-3 and Qwen3.5 families). From the [Dao AI Lab ReplaySSM blog](https://dao-lab.ai/blog/2026/replayssm/).*

![Kernel speedup for buffer sizes 4, 8, 16, 32 at batch sizes 64 and 256](https://dao-lab.ai/assets/img/2026-06-15-replayssm/ar-buffersize.png)

*Kernel speedup vs buffer size (`L` = 4, 8, 16, 32) at batch 64 and 256 — informs our `--gdn-replayssm-cache-len` default. From the [Dao AI Lab ReplaySSM blog](https://dao-lab.ai/blog/2026/replayssm/).*

---

## Task tracking

- [x] Part A: buffered output-only GDN decode kernel + wrapper
- [x] Part A: memory pool ring buffers + `write_pos` lifecycle (alloc/COW reset)
- [x] Part A: CUDA-graph-safe `write_pos`
- [x] Part A: radix `force_flush` alignment
- [x] Part A: server args + validation (unit / byte-identical / GSM8K) — **PR: [#28451](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/28451)**
- [x] Decision gate: measure spec-decode verify GDN forward HBM bandwidth at target batch
- [x] Part B: ReplaySSM spec-decode verify kernel (chunked, ring-across-steps, early-flush) — **PR:  [#28695](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/28695)**
- [ ] Follow-up: KDA decode coverage

---

## Open questions / risks

1. **Is spec-decode verify bandwidth-bound at realistic serving batch?** This single number decides whether Part B is worth building (see Decision gate). Spec-decode is often latency-focused (low batch), where the win may be marginal.
2. **Part B integration risk is high** — it is a forward-kernel rewrite (~650 lines, chunked UT-transform) with a subtle early-flush correctness invariant, not a surgical cache swap like #27658.
3. **Tensor-core precision** — accepted as accuracy-neutral (GSM8K parity), but worth a config escape hatch for anyone who needs the slow bit-exact path.
4. **Scope of models** — Part A is GDN-only; KDA shares the backend but has different gating.

---

## References

- ReplaySSM blog (Dao AI Lab) — https://dao-lab.ai/blog/2026/replayssm/ (source of all figures in this RFC)
- ReplaySSM reference implementation — https://github.com/Johnny-Liou/ReplaySSM
- Upstream vLLM ReplaySSM kernels (commit `3c85112`): `fused_recurrent_replayssm.py`, `gdn_replayssm_spec_decode.py`
- Marconi: Prefix Caching for Hybrid LLMs (arXiv 2411.19379) — background on hybrid-model state caching


### Related resources

_No response_

title: Deprecate Marlin FP8 quantization, QServe, FBGEMM FP8
author: b8zhong
body:
To reduce the complexity of the quantization paths, we plan to deprecate this feature.

Here is the reasoning for why we would be removing these quantization features, in terms of utilization:

| Quantization | What it is | Why it's removable |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Marlin FP8** | Weights-only FP8 on A100, 3090. | Utilization for SM80 is quite low, and we can still use the INT8 path |
| **QServe (qoq)** | W4A8 QServe/QoQ format | It seems there has been no feature development of this quantization format, as it was mostly experimental |
| **FBGEMM FP8** *(fpgemm_fp8)* | FBGEMM per-channel FP8 linear, only used by official Llama 405B FP8 checkpoint. | ModelOpt FP8, or compressed-tensors FP8 |


Feedback time: 3 weeks.

title: [RFC] Weight loading: separate loading from completeness verification
author: EazyReal
body:
## Problem

Several `Model.load_weights(weights)` implementations both copy tensors and check that a full checkpoint initialized every parameter. That is correct after a full checkpoint load, but the same method is reused by partial update paths such as online/RL weight updates and pinned-cache reloads. Those callers intentionally pass only a subset of tensors, so model-local completeness checks produce false missing-weight warnings, errors, or asserts.

The operations are different:

- load these `(name, tensor)` pairs into the model
- verify that this full checkpoint initialized all required parameters

## Proposed Contract

Make `load_weights(weights)` the tensor-loading primitive:

- accepts any iterable of `(name, tensor)` pairs
- copies recognized tensors
- returns the set of model parameter/buffer names it loaded
- does not decide whether the input was a complete checkpoint

Full checkpoint loaders do the completeness check after loading:

```python
loaded = model.load_weights(weights)
if loaded is not None and getattr(model, "verify_weights_on_load", False):
    missing = required_parameters - loaded - optional_parameters
    if missing:
        raise RuntimeError(...)
```

Models contribute data only:

- `verify_weights_on_load = True` once their `load_weights` returns a complete loaded-name set
- `is_optional_weight(name)` for rank/config-specific omissions, such as PP-distributed heads or quantization scales

Partial update and pinned-cache paths can call `model.load_weights(partial_weights)` directly, without an `is_full_load` flag.

## Implementation Options

- #29323 is the final-state implementation: loader verifier plus Gemma4, DeepSeek, and Llama4 migrations.
- #28962 is the small staged loader slice: dormant mechanism only, no model behavior change.
- #28519 and #28560 are interim `is_full_load` stopgaps if maintainers want a short-term fix before the loader contract lands.

## Open Questions

1. Is loader-side completeness verification the right long-term contract?
2. Should opted-in models fail fast on missing required full-checkpoint parameters?
3. Do maintainers prefer landing the final-state stack directly, or the staged loader-only slice first?

title: [RFC] Add SM89/L20 support for DeepSeek-V4-Flash-FP8
author: xesdiny
body:
## Motivation

We would like to add an SM89/Ada-compatible path for running DeepSeek-V4-Flash-FP8 on NVIDIA L20 GPUs in SGLang.

We validated a local patch on 8x NVIDIA L20 (SM89), TP=8, with DeepSeek-V4-Flash-FP8. The goal is to upstream this as a focused SGLang code change rather than relying on external deployment patches.

## Observed Issues on SM89/L20

When running the current DeepSeek-V4-Flash-FP8 path on L20/SM89, we observed compatibility issues with kernels that appear to target SM90+ paths:

- `paged_mqa_metadata.cuh:113: CUDA error: invalid argument`
  - This still triggers in eager mode after disabling CUDA graph, so it is not CUDA-graph-only.
- `topk_v2.cuh` build/runtime failure:
  - `__cluster_dims__ not supported`
  - `cooperative_groups::this_cluster()` unavailable
  - This appears to rely on CUDA thread block cluster features available on SM90+, but not on SM89/Ada.

The current workaround for deployment uses environment variables to avoid these paths, but we would prefer an upstream source-level SM89 path.

## Proposed Direction

We are considering a focused PR with the following changes:

1. Add explicit SM89 detection for DeepSeek-V4 attention/indexer paths.
   - Use CUDA capability `(8, 9)`.
   - Avoid broad checks such as `not SM90 and not SM120`, so other CUDA architectures are not affected.

2. Route DeepSeek-V4 Flash attention on SM89 to a fallback path that avoids SM90-only FlashMLA kernels.

3. Add a Triton FP8 paged MQA logits kernel for SM89.
   - The kernel computes paged MQA logits page-by-page instead of materializing the large PyTorch fallback intermediate.
   - This avoids the memory amplification we saw during long-context prefill.

4. Dispatch the DeepSeek-V4 FP8 indexer to the SM89 Triton kernel only on SM89.

5. Keep existing paths unchanged for:
   - SM90 / Hopper
   - SM100 / SM120
   - AMD / HIP
   - FP4 indexer
   - TileLang and AITER indexer paths

## Local Validation

Local validation has been completed outside upstream CI:

- Hardware: 8x NVIDIA L20, SM89
- Model: DeepSeek-V4-Flash-FP8
- Parallelism: TP=8
- Base image used for validation: `lmsysorg/sglang:v0.5.13` with local source mounted

Validation results:

- Import smoke for the SM89 helper/path passed.
- Registered pytest for SM89 helper/import coverage passed: `2 passed`.
- Manual Triton paged MQA logits correctness passed on L20 for 3 cases, max diff `0.000000`.
- Service startup succeeded on 8xL20 after allowing full model load time.
- Short chat completion request passed.
- Long-context request with `max_tokens=4096` passed:
  - prompt tokens: 9388
  - completion tokens: 2074
  - total tokens: 11462
  - finish reason: `stop`
- Triton kernel grid search selected:
  - `num_warps=4`
  - `num_stages=4`

We do not claim separate ablation results for each internal patch. The validation is for the combined SM89 support path.

## Testing Plan for the PR

Because upstream CI may not have L20/SM89 runners, the PR would include CI-safe tests plus local L20 validation evidence:

- Import and dispatch tests for the new SM89 helper/path.
- Mocked CUDA capability tests:
  - `(8, 9)` should select the SM89 path.
  - `(9, 0)`, `(12, 0)`, `(8, 0)`, `(8, 6)` should not select it.
- Existing DSV4 tests should continue to pass or skip according to local dependency availability.
- Local L20 service validation results would be included in the PR body.

## Question for Maintainers

Would maintainers be open to a focused PR adding this SM89/L20 path for DeepSeek-V4-Flash-FP8 in SGLang Python/Triton code, with CI-safe dispatch tests and local L20 validation results?

If there is a preferred place for the SM89 capability helper or a preferred test registration pattern for this hardware-specific path, we would be happy to follow it.

title: [RFC] Disaggregated request preprocessing
author: sagearc
body:
### Motivation Before a model runs, the serving system often needs to know what the request will look like to the model: - A router places and sizes work before a request reaches a GPU: how long the request is, whether its prefix is already cached, and whether its media is already processed. - A disaggregated pipeline prepares a request once and hands the model the tokens, instead of re-tokenizing at each hop. For both cases, the prepared request has to match what the model actually runs. When it does not, cache lookups can miss and token counts can be wrong (#26555, #27386, [llm-d-router#1072](https://github.com/llm-d/llm-d-router/issues/1072)). This proposal exposes that request view before execution, so routing and model servers do not rely on approximations. ### Proposal

The goal is to expose the same preprocessing path used by SGLang inference as a lightweight standalone service that returns the prepared generate request without running the model. In particular, this should: - Run as a CPU-light preprocessing-only server. - Share the exact preprocessing logic used by normal SGLang inference endpoints. - Return a generate request, not just raw token IDs, with the metadata needed for tokens-in/tokens-out. - Include multimodal hashes and related metadata in the tokenize/preprocess output, so encoder-disaggregated setups can route and reuse MM encoder work consistently. **Before and after:** Today, chat and completions requests can be tokenized through one dedicated `/tokenize` endpoint: ``` chat / completions | v /tokenize | v token ids + count - no mm features (no hashes, no positions) - no /responses or /messages support ``` Proposed, the same request becomes the full input the model runs: ``` request (chat / completion / messages / ...) | v preprocessing (same logic used by serving entry points) - chat template, tools, reasoning - tokenization - media identity and token positions | v generate request - token ids - request metadata - multimodal fields needed by the generate path | v model (token ids in -> token ids out) ``` The model accepts this generate request directly, so preprocessing and execution can run in one process or on separate machines. The rest of the request, such as the sampling settings and any cache key, rides along unchanged for the model to run. ### Usage The standalone mode could be exposed either as: ```bash sglang serve renderer ``` or as a dedicated command: ```bash sglang renderer ``` For HTTP APIs, the clearest option is to expose preprocess-specific endpoints that mirror the serving APIs, for example: ``` /v1/chat/completions/render /v1/completions/render /v1/responses/render /v1/messages/render ``` These endpoints would accept the same request format as the corresponding serving endpoint, but return the prepared generate request instead of running the model. ### Phasing 1. **Shared preprocessing path.** Factor preprocessing into one shared path used by the existing serving entry points. This should not change behavior, and is useful on its own. 2. **Standalone preprocessing service.** Expose the same path as an opt-in service that can run without starting the full serving engine or loading the model (following #27606 in spirit). ### QA **Why not just use the current `/tokenize` endpoint?** `/tokenize` is useful, but it only returns token ids and a count. That is enough for simple text cases, but not for precise routing or token-in/token-out execution. For multimodal requests, we also need media identity and positions in the token sequence. `/tokenize` is also not a lightweight standalone service today: it still requires starting the serving engine, loading the model, and it does not cover all request APIs such as `/responses` or `/messages`. **What is a generate request?** A generate request is the prepared input the model runs on: the token ids, the multimodal inputs if any, and the execution settings that should stay attached to the request. It is not part of the standard OpenAI-compatible API. Each backend defines its own version, so vLLM and SGLang may represent it differently. **How is multimodal handled?** For multimodal requests, preprocessing exposes the information needed before execution: the tokenized request, the media identity, and where each media item appears in the token sequence. Whether heavier processed media data is produced in the standalone service or later in the SGLang server is left as an implementation choice. The important part for this RFC is that routing and model execution use the same media view as full inference. **Why does SGLang need this, instead of one shared preprocessing server for all backends?** The output has to match SGLang's internal model input. Tokenization, chat templates, special tokens, multimodal placeholder handling, and the internal generate-request format can vary by backend and model, so a generic preprocessor would only approximate the result. A shared layer can still normalize user requests before they reach SGLang, but it cannot replace the SGLang-specific preprocessing that produces the model input. **Is this only useful for routing?** No. Similar needs have come up for custom frontends and reinforcement learning. SGLang has related requests for server-mode token IDs and token-ids input (#5653, #12145). ### References This RFC is influenced by parallel vllm work on separating preprocessing from model execution and making the prepared request shape explicit: - [vLLM #35213](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/35213): discussion around standalone / disaggregated preprocessing. - [vLLM #36102](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/36102): adds the command-line entry point for standalone preprocessing. - [vLLM #36166](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/36166): implementation work for standalone preprocessing. - [vLLM #35684](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/35684): returns the prepared generate request and includes multimodal information. Related SGLang issues: - SGLang #5653, #12145: token IDs / token-in needs for server-mode and RL workflows. - SGLang #27606: early standalone-preprocessing entry point. - SGLang #27386: applying the chat template before cache-aware hashing. - SGLang #26555: retokenization drift for pre-tokenized multimodal requests. ### cc @Jiminator @JustinTong0323 @vMaroon @ahg-g @nilig @rahulgurnani

title: [RFC] Agent-aware Session-level Cache Preemption for StreamingSession
author: ykdcai
body:
## 1. Motivation

SGLang's streaming session feature (`StreamingSession`) persists KV cache between turns. When a turn finishes, `cache_finished_req` saves the request's `req_pool_idx` and token indices into a `SessionSlot` dict instead of releasing them. The next turn restores this state instantly via `match_prefix`, bypassing the radix tree entirely.

The side effect is that idle session slots which are sessions waiting between turns hold pool resources **permanently and invisibly** until the client explicitly closes the session or an opt-in timeout fires. Under memory pressure a server with many idle sessions can OOM every new request while session KV stays pinned.

## 2. Limitations of the Current System

The problem of unbounded cache growth and deadlocks in current `StreamingSession` are well documented in this https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/27024


## 3. Design

We introduce **session-level KV preemption**: when the token pool runs low and tree eviction alone cannot satisfy demand, idle session slots are soft-evicted until enough tokens are freed. The session is not closed and only its KV is released. On the next turn the request re-prefills from whatever the radix tree still has cached; no error is surfaced to the client.

The design supports pluggable eviction heuristics (e.g. LRU, length-based, weighted length × recency). The initial implementation will provide **LRU** as the first heuristic: `preempt_session_kv` sorts idle candidates by `last_active_time` (a `time.monotonic()` timestamp recorded at turn-finish in `save_from_req`) and evicts oldest-first until the deficit is covered.

The benefit of  **heuristic extensibility** is that instead of being tightly coupled with the eviction policy of Radix Tree, which is agentic agnostics,  our `preempt_session_kv` interface enabling session-level agent-aware policies the tree cannot express:

- **Recency**: prefer evicting sessions that are cold and are unlikely to receive request soon.
- **Router-initialized signals**: For example, the router injects a priority score at session-open, so VIP or latency-SLA sessions will not be targets of eviction. This is closedly related to https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/27574.
- **Weighted combinations**: tunable combination of recency, size, and router signals.


### Fixing the problems of `StreamingSession`

One cause of the current [problem](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/27024) of `StreamingSession` seems to be the lack of **single source of truth**. Currently, cache-related states of each session are scatter into multiple classes: 
- `SessionSlot`: holds `req_pool_idx`, `kv_allocated_len`, `cache_protected_len`, and `last_node`
- `ReqToTokenPool`: maps `req_pool_idx` to physical KV page indices
- `RadixTree`: holds the same page indices for the shared prefix under a `lock_ref`
Each class is mutating and reading these state and it is hard to keep the updates in sync. 

One way to solve this problem is to have **session-private Prefix Cache**: instead of having all sessions share a single Prefix Cache, initialize one PrefixCache per session whose only role is prefix matching. All other cache-related logic are handled by the `SessionSlot`, which uses `TokenToKVPoolAllocator` to allocate and free pages, and the lifecycle of kv cache is tied to the `SessionSlot` object itself so that we can support session level eviction safely. The tradeoff here is we no longer have inter-session prefix matching, yet this is acceptable because in agentic workloads, most matches happen inside session accorss turns.

However, implementing session-private cache might involve non-trivial refactors of the `Schduler` and `SchdulerBatch`. I am currently trying to come up with a less intrusive approach. We are open to implementing this RFC on top of whichever session architecture the maintainers prefer, rather than continuing to patch `StreamingSession` if a different base is chosen.

## 4. Related Work

### PR #27058: Radix-tree-native session eviction

PR #27058 (`--enable-session-radix-cache`) makes session nodes ordinary evictable radix tree entries tagged with a `session_id`. The tree's own LRU reclaims them at node granularity under pressure; `close_session` scans for the tag to free them on explicit close.

The key difference is the **unit of eviction**. PR #27058 evicts individual nodes by their own `last_access_time`  which is a session's KV can be partially evicted with no agent-level recency concept. Our approach evicts whole sessions ordered by `last_active_time` (when the agent last completed a turn), which is semantically more meaningful for agentic workloads.

title: [RFC] Add Top-nσ (Top-n-sigma) logit truncation as a built-in CustomLogitProcessor
author: Jackie2049
body:
## Motivation

[Top-nσ](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.07641) ("Top-nσ: Not All Logits Are You Need", ACL 2025) is a logit-space dynamic truncation method that uses the **standard deviation** of the logit distribution to set a filtering threshold:

```
threshold = max_logit - n * std_logit
logits[logits < threshold] = -inf
```

Unlike probability-space filters (`top_p`, `min_p`), it operates **before softmax** (SGLang's custom logit processor pipeline already runs before temperature scaling), and adapts the candidate set to the "peakiness" of the distribution:

- **Sharp distribution** (model certain): small std → narrow threshold → fewer candidates
- **Flat distribution** (model uncertain): large std → wide threshold → more candidates

### How it compares to existing methods

| Method | Space | Truncation rule | Adaptive? |
|---|---|---|---|
| top_k | Probability | Keep top-k highest-probability tokens | ❌ Fixed count |
| top_p (nucleus) | Probability | Keep tokens until cumulative prob ≥ p | ✅ Adaptive count only |
| min_p | Probability | Keep tokens with prob ≥ max_prob × min_p | ✅ Relative threshold |
| top_nσ | **Logit** | threshold = max_logit − n × std | ✅ Dual-adaptive |

> Key distinction: top_k/top_p/min_p operate **after softmax** (probability space); top_nσ operates **before softmax** (logit space).

### Why Top-nσ?

- **Truncation before softmax** — top_nσ filters in logit space first, then softmax only processes the surviving candidates. In contrast, top_p/min_p must compute a full-vocab softmax first, then truncate.
- **Dual adaptivity** — the std-based threshold adjusts both *how many* and *how loosely* candidates are kept in one formula. top_k fixes the count; top_p adapts the count but not the threshold tightness.
- **Temperature-stable** — candidate count stays consistent across temperature scaling (logit std scales proportionally), while top_p/min_p candidate counts vary significantly with T.
- **Argmax-invariant** — the top-1 token always survives (0 std from itself), so greedy decoding is unaffected.

## Proposal

Add `TopNSigmaLogitProcessor` as a **built-in** `CustomLogitProcessor` in `python/sglang/srt/sampling/custom_logit_processor.py`, following the same pattern as the existing `ThinkingBudgetLogitProcessor` and `DisallowedTokensLogitsProcessor`.

### Implementation characteristics

- **Fully vectorized** across the batch (no per-row Python loop)
- **std computed once** and reused for both the `std==0` guard and the threshold formula (avoids a duplicate vocab-wide reduction)
- **Argmax-invariant** by construction

### Edge cases handled

| Case | Behavior |
|------|----------|
| `top_n_sigma <= 0` | Request skipped |
| `top_n_sigma` is None / non-numeric | Request skipped |
| `std == 0` (all logits equal) | Row skipped (no filtering) |
| NaN/Inf logits | Row skipped (finite guard) |
| Empty / None param list | Logits returned unchanged |

### Usage

```python
import requests
from sglang.srt.sampling.custom_logit_processor import TopNSigmaLogitProcessor

# Server must be started with --enable-custom-logit-processor
response = requests.post("http://localhost:30000/generate", json={
    "text": "The capital of France is",
    "sampling_params": {
        "temperature": 0.8,
        "custom_params": {"top_n_sigma": 2.0},
    },
    "custom_logit_processor": TopNSigmaLogitProcessor.to_str(),
})
```

## Scope

- New processor class in `custom_logit_processor.py` (~50 lines)
- Unit tests in `test/registered/unit/sampling/test_custom_logit_processor.py`
- No changes to `SamplingParams`, `SamplingBatchInfo`, or the sampler — uses the existing custom processor framework as-is

## Related PR

- #TBD — implementation

## References

Tang et al., "Top-nσ: Not All Logits Are You Need", ACL 2025. [arXiv:2411.07641](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.07641)

title: [RFC] Generalize cuda_graph_* server args / runner naming to a device-agnostic scheme (device_graph_*)
author: siju-samuel
body:
### Checklist

- [x] If this is not a feature request but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [x] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

### Motivation

Graph capture/replay is no longer CUDA-exclusive in SGLang. We now have four graph runners that are conceptually the same feature — capture/replay on a device backend:

- CudaGraphRunner (CUDA/ROCm/MUSA)
- NPUGraphRunner
- CPUGraphRunner
- XPUGraphRunner (proposed in [#29053](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/29053))




### Related resources

## Current state (post-`CudaGraphConfig` [refactor](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/28107))


### 1. The config object — `CudaGraphConfig`
File: `python/sglang/srt/model_executor/cuda_graph_config.py`

- `CudaGraphConfig` (dataclass) — top-level config: one `PhaseConfig` per phase (`decode`, `prefill`)
- `PhaseConfig` (dataclass) — per-phase: `backend`, `max_bs`, `bs`, `tc_compiler`
- `Phase` (class) — `DECODE`, `PREFILL`, `ALL`
- `Backend` (class) — `FULL`, `BREAKABLE`, `TC_PIECEWISE`, `DISABLED`
- `default_cuda_graph_config()` (fn) — decode → `full`, prefill → `tc_piecewise`
- `parse_cuda_graph_config_arg()` (fn) — `--cuda-graph-config` JSON parser
- `check_cuda_graph_backend()` (fn) — runtime backend query

### 2. `ServerArgs` fields — `python/sglang/srt/server_args.py`

**Canonical config input**
- `cuda_graph_config` : `Optional[CudaGraphConfig]` — the canonical object; everything else folds into it

**Per-phase convenience fields** (fold into `cuda_graph_config`)
- `cuda_graph_backend_decode` : `Literal["full","breakable","tc_piecewise","disabled"]`
- `cuda_graph_backend_prefill` : `Literal["breakable","tc_piecewise","disabled"]`
- `cuda_graph_max_bs_decode` : `Optional[int]`
- `cuda_graph_max_bs_prefill` : `Optional[int]`
- `cuda_graph_bs_decode` : `Optional[List[int]]`
- `cuda_graph_bs_prefill` : `Optional[List[int]]`
- `cuda_graph_tc_compiler` : `Literal["eager","inductor"]`
- `disable_prefill_cuda_graph` : `bool`
- `disable_decode_cuda_graph` : `bool`

**Debug / profiling fields**
- `disable_cuda_graph_padding` : `bool`
- `enable_profile_cuda_graph` : `bool`
- `enable_cudagraph_gc` : `bool`
- `debug_cuda_graph` : `bool`

**Legacy field** (kept, folds into config with a deprecation warning)
- `disable_cuda_graph` : `bool`

### 3. Live CLI flags
```
--cuda-graph-config            (JSON, canonical)
--cuda-graph-backend-decode
--cuda-graph-backend-prefill
--cuda-graph-max-bs-decode
--cuda-graph-max-bs-prefill
--cuda-graph-bs-decode
--cuda-graph-bs-prefill
--cuda-graph-tc-compiler
--disable-prefill-cuda-graph
--disable-decode-cuda-graph
--disable-cuda-graph-padding
--enable-profile-cuda-graph
--enable-cudagraph-gc
--debug-cuda-graph
```

### 4. Deprecated CLI aliases (already warn-and-forward via `DeprecatedAliasStoreAction` / `DeprecatedStoreTrueAction` / `DeprecatedStoreConstAction`)
| Deprecated flag | Forwards to |
|---|---|
| `--cuda-graph-max-bs` | `--cuda-graph-max-bs-decode` |
| `--cuda-graph-bs` | `--cuda-graph-bs-decode` |
| `--disable-cuda-graph` | `--cuda-graph-backend-{decode,prefill}=disabled` |
| `--enable-breakable-cuda-graph` | `--cuda-graph-backend-prefill=breakable` |
| `--disable-piecewise-cuda-graph` | `--cuda-graph-backend-prefill=disabled` |
| `--enforce-piecewise-cuda-graph` | `--cuda-graph-backend-prefill=tc_piecewise` |
| `--piecewise-cuda-graph-tokens` | `--cuda-graph-bs-prefill` |
| `--piecewise-cuda-graph-compiler` | `--cuda-graph-tc-compiler` |
| `--piecewise-cuda-graph-max-tokens` | `--cuda-graph-max-bs-prefill` |

### 5. Environment variables (`python/sglang/srt/environ.py`)
| Env var | Generalize? |
|---|---|
| `SGLANG_ENABLE_CUDA_GRAPH_CAPTURE_TRACE` | ✅ device-agnostic capture trace |
| `SGLANG_VIT_ENABLE_CUDA_GRAPH` | ✅ |
| `SGLANG_MEMORY_SAVER_CUDA_GRAPH` | ✅ |
| `SGLANG_PREP_IN_CUDA_GRAPH` | ✅ |
| `SGLANG_USE_BREAKABLE_CUDA_GRAPH` | ✅ |

### 6. Internal naming — what is already generic vs. what is still CUDA-named

**Already device-agnostic (the precedent to extend):**
- `torch.get_device_module(device)` → `self.device_module` — set once in `runner/base_runner.py`, used in ~50 files across CUDA/NPU/XPU/speculative/scheduler. This is the real anchor for the rename.
- Graph-capture log string: `f"{current_platform.device_name} graph"` (`model_runner.py`).

**Still CUDA-named internally (would also need renaming for full consistency — see follow-on):**
- `ModelRunner.init_decode_cuda_graph()` / `init_prefill_cuda_graph()` → `init_decode_device_graph()` etc.
- `self.decode_cuda_graph_runner` attribute.
- `CudaGraphConfig` / `runner/*CudaGraphRunner` / `runner_backend/*CudaGraphBackend` classes.

**Not a general seam (do NOT cite as evidence):**
- `_create_device_graph()` — defined only in `NPUGraphRunner`; the proposed `XPUGraphRunner` copies it and marks it dead code. The base runner and CUDA path don't use it.

---

## Proposal

Introduce a canonical, device-agnostic scheme; keep all `cuda_graph_*` names as deprecated aliases.

**Config object**
- `CudaGraphConfig` → `DeviceGraphConfig`
- `cuda_graph_config` → `device_graph_config`
- file `cuda_graph_config.py` → `device_graph_config.py`
- `--cuda-graph-config` → `--device-graph-config` (alias the old)

**Per-phase fields / flags** (mechanical 1:1 rename, `cuda_graph` → `device_graph`)

| Current | New |
|---|---|
| `cuda_graph_backend_{decode,prefill}` | `device_graph_backend_{decode,prefill}` |
| `cuda_graph_max_bs_{decode,prefill}` | `device_graph_max_bs_{decode,prefill}` |
| `cuda_graph_bs_{decode,prefill}` | `device_graph_bs_{decode,prefill}` |
| `cuda_graph_tc_compiler` | `device_graph_tc_compiler` |
| `disable_{prefill,decode}_cuda_graph` | `disable_{prefill,decode}_device_graph` |
| `disable_cuda_graph_padding` | `disable_device_graph_padding` |
| `enable_profile_cuda_graph` | `enable_profile_device_graph` |
| `enable_cudagraph_gc` | `enable_device_graph_gc` |
| `debug_cuda_graph` | `debug_device_graph` |

**Env vars**
- `SGLANG_ENABLE_CUDA_GRAPH_CAPTURE_TRACE` → `SGLANG_ENABLE_DEVICE_GRAPH_CAPTURE_TRACE`
- `SGLANG_VIT_ENABLE_CUDA_GRAPH` → `SGLANG_VIT_ENABLE_DEVICE_GRAPH`
- `SGLANG_MEMORY_SAVER_CUDA_GRAPH` → `SGLANG_MEMORY_SAVER_DEVICE_GRAPH`
- `SGLANG_PREP_IN_CUDA_GRAPH` → `SGLANG_PREP_IN_DEVICE_GRAPH`

`device_graph_*` is chosen to match existing internal naming (`init_device_graphs`, `_create_device_graph`, `device_module`) rather than introducing a new concept. Every `--cuda-graph-*` flag stays as a back-compat argparse alias (warn-and-forward) — the codebase **already has** `DeprecatedAliasStoreAction` / `DeprecatedStoreConstAction`, so extending it to `cuda_graph → device_graph` follows an established pattern. Existing scripts, docs, tests, and benchmarks keep working unchanged.

---

## Optional follow-on: class / file naming

For end-to-end consistency, the base `CudaGraphRunner` could become `DeviceGraphRunner` (with `CudaGraphRunner` kept as a subclass/alias), and the device-specific hooks (`_create_device_graph`, `_capture_graph`, profiling) lifted into the base so per-device subclasses shrink toward near-zero. Likewise the `runner/` / `runner_backend/` file and class names (`*CudaGraphRunner`, `*CudaGraphBackend`) could follow. Larger change; can be split out.

---

## Alternative names considered

Two candidate schemes are on the table; the rest are rejected.

- **`device_graph_*`** (the primary proposal) — matches the one existing device-agnostic seam in the code (`device_module` / `torch.get_device_module`) and the generic capture log string (`f"{current_platform.device_name} graph"`). Emphasizes *which hardware* runs the graph; extends an existing identifier rather than minting a new concept.
