| Worker install | `publish(..., role="scheduler"|"tokenizer"|…)` — if the bag was already materialized by a parent publish + pickle, skip re-running the pipeline (idempotent) |

v1 may run the **same** pipeline for all roles (parity with today’s construct-time full `__post_init__`), then project by role. Role-specific pipeline thinning is a follow-up.

---

## 6. Lifecycle details

### 6.1 What moves out of `__post_init__`

Everything that is not “store the field the user set”:

- Model-specific declarations / registry application
- Post-process passes (backend auto-selection, page size, …)
- Cross-field validation that needs a resolved view
- Materialization of resolvable whitelist fields
- Remaining imperative “`server_args.x = …`” adjustments in hooks

`ServerArgs` may keep **dataclass defaults** and **argparse registration**. Construction initializes declaration stash only; it does not resolve.

Parent/CLI paths that need resolved fields before workers start call **`publish(..., role="launcher")`** at a documented boundary (`from_cli_args`, `Engine`, `launch_server`, …) — never a separate resolve helper.

### 6.2 After publish

| Event | Mechanism |
|-------|-----------|
| Weight load discovers `kv_cache_dtype` | Load-time declaration / audited write into `model` — not a second `publish` |
| Spec draft narrows graph batch sizes | Namespace override on `exec.graph` / `spec` (draft still must not clobber target publish) |
| Tests force a path | `get_exec().moe.override(...)` (and peers); fixtures use `role="test"` |

### 6.3 Transition dual-write (temporary)

```text
publish(role=...):
  run private resolution pipeline if needed
  write context namespaces for role   # new source of truth
  optionally keep ServerArgs fields filled for dual-read
```

Exit when business reads of `get_server_args().` for that domain are gone (ratchet); then stop depending on bag fields for reads.

---

## 7. Migration plan

| Step | Work |
|------|------|
| **0** | Nested namespace types + getters + `publish(..., role=...)` skeleton (may project full tree; store role) |
| **0b** | Hollow `__post_init__`; resolution **only inside** `publish`; CLI/Engine/launch call `publish(role=…)` (no public `ServerArgs.resolve`) |
| **0c** | Thread `role` through shims and every production install site (`tokenizer` / `scheduler` / `encoder` / `expert_backup`) |
| **0d** | Enforce per-role namespace sets (fail closed on missing getters); stop full-tree projection if still used |
| **1** | Migrate `parallel` readers |
| **2** | Migrate `device` + `model` |
| **3** | Migrate `exec.*` |
| **4** | Migrate `schedule` + `memory` |
| **5** | Migrate `spec` + `lora` + `mm` |
| **6** | Migrate `disagg` + `serving` + `observe` (role-sensitive) |
| **7** | Close dual-write; namespace override as business mutation API |
| **8** | In-tree business `get_server_args` → 0; docs/skill; optional out-of-tree shim |

**Ordering:** 0 → 0b → 0c before domain reader flips that assume role-aware getters. 0d can trail early reader flips if full-tree projection remains temporarily.

### 7.1 Compatibility

- Public CLI unchanged.
- Out-of-tree `get_global_server_args()` shim may remain; install shims pass fixed roles.
- In-tree: decrease-only ratchets; no new production `get_server_args().` reads.

### 7.2 Testing

- Raw construct does not materialize; `publish(..., role="test")` resolves + projects.
- Each production role has a smoke that install entry passes the correct `role`.
- Getter for a namespace omitted by role raises.
- Draft path still does not publish over target.
- Unit suite + multi-GPU smokes on large flip PRs.

---

## 8. Alternatives considered

| Alternative | Why rejected / deferred |
|-------------|-------------------------|
| Keep resolved values on `ServerArgs`, only rename the getter | Does not fix structure or bag overload. |
| `publish` without `role` (full tree every process) | Simpler, and OK for early dual-read — but erases process identity already present in dual setters and blocks safe namespace pruning / fail-closed getters. |
| Separate publish functions per process (`publish_tokenizer`) | Verbose; `role` keeps one entry and one dual-write path. |
| Hoist hot-path reads to instance attrs only | Does not retire `ServerArgs` as the config API. |
| Flat ~400 fields on `RuntimeContext` | New god object. |
| Mirror resolved config into `flags` | Dual source of truth. |
| Keep `__post_init__` as permanent thin `publish()` | Hides process boundaries; target is explicit `publish(role=...)`. |
| Public `ServerArgs.resolve()` separate from `publish` | Two entrypoints re-create “when is config ready?” ambiguity; parent/CLI should `publish(role="launcher")` instead. |

---

## 9. Risks and mitigations

| Risk | Mitigation |
|------|------------|
| Missing `publish` → empty context | Fail loud on first config `get_*`; checklist of process entries |
| Wrong `role` at call site | Type/Literal + unit tests per entrypoint; shim hard-codes role |
| Role set too small → missing leaf at runtime | Start full-tree projection; tighten sets with audit + ratchet |
| Behavioral drift when moving resolve | Parity tests; dual-write window |
| Dual-write never ends | Per-domain ratchets; step 7 closes bag reads |
| Draft clobbering target | Draft continues to skip publish; never `role=` install on draft |
| `torch.compile` storage sensitivity | Existing runtime-context storage rules for hot ints |

---

## 10. Open questions

1. Final name of the publish API (`publish` vs `publish_context` vs `install_runtime_config`)?
2. `get_model()` vs `get_model_cfg()` naming?
3. Keep raw `ServerArgs` on context for debugging (`ctx.raw_server_args`)?
4. Exact v1 namespace set per role (table in §5.3) — freeze after one audit PR?
5. Leaf name shortening under nested groups — late cleanup or never?
6. Exact when parent uses `role="launcher"` vs skipping parent publish entirely (workers only)?

---

## 11. Success criteria

- [ ] No in-tree production business read of resolved config via `ServerArgs` accessors (shim only if required out-of-tree).
- [ ] `ServerArgs.__post_init__` contains no resolution pipeline.
- [ ] No public `ServerArgs.resolve()` (or equivalent) — only `publish`.
- [ ] Every long-lived process that installs config calls `publish(..., role=...)` exactly once (or equivalent shim).
- [ ] Context records `role`; getters fail closed for namespaces outside that role’s set (after 0d).
- [ ] Domain namespaces match the census classification.
- [ ] Developer docs describe `publish(role=...)` + namespace overrides.
- [ ] Unit parity with pre-migration resolved behavior; smokes green on large flip PRs.

---

## Appendix A — Example call-site migration

**Before**

```python
from sglang.srt.server_args import get_global_server_args

sa = get_global_server_args()
if sa.moe_runner_backend == "auto":
    ...
backend = sa.attention_backend
```

**After**

```python
from sglang.srt.runtime_context import get_exec

exec_cfg = get_exec()
if exec_cfg.moe.moe_runner_backend == "auto":
    ...
backend = exec_cfg.kernel.attention_backend
```

**Process install**

```python
# tokenizer process
publish(server_args, role="tokenizer")

# scheduler process (target ModelRunner)
publish(server_args, role="scheduler")
```

---

## Appendix B — `exec` subgroup sizes (approx.)

```text
kernel ~20 · moe ~32 · graph ~19 · comm ~12 · mamba ~14
overlap ~3 · offload ~5 · dllm ~2 · deterministic ~2 · features ~11
```

A complete field→namespace assignment table can ship as a follow-up checklist in the implementation PR series (generated from `ServerArgs` annotations) so it stays in sync with main.

title: [RFC] Position-Independent KV Cache Reuse for Agentic/RAG Workloads
author: krakhit
body:
### **Summary**

RadixAttention reuses KV cache only when a request's prefix is byte-identical and at the same absolute offset as something already cached. In agentic/RAG traffic shared system prompts, tool schemas, retrieved documents, and multi-turn history routinely put identical content at different offsets across requests. This causes a guaranteed cache miss even though the content itself hasn't changed.

_Three recent approaches tackle this differently. Wanted to check if this is on anyone's radar before digging further._

- **Irminsul** ([arXiv:2605.05696](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.05696)) (sglang-targeted but no code). Exploits MLA's factorization into a position-free latent ($$c_{KV}$$) and a small rotatable slice ($$k_r$$). The idea is that reusing a cached span at a new offset only requires a closed-form "delta-rotation" on the small rotatable slice. it is  MLA-specific,  though the same split exists in any partial-RoPE model (rotary_dim < head_dim), not just MLA, so the mechanism plausibly generalizes further than the paper states explicitly. 

- **MiniPIC** ([arXiv:2606.13126](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.13126)) ( vLLM).  Stores unrotated K, defers RoPE to attention-read-time. More general ( RoPE models) but touches every attention backend, conflicts with fused write-path kernels, and needs new per-token position plumbing through CUDA-graph-captured decode. Code exists ([IBM/vllm](https://github.com/IBM/vllm), traced to the actual authors' commits). It is worth knowing that it went through two implementation strategies, and the first one ([PR #88](https://github.com/IBM/vllm/pull/88)) shipped with an acknowledged accuracy bug from concurrent requests reusing the same span at different positions, serious enough that they abandoned it for a different strategy rather than patch it. Real, useful precedent for anyone attempting this class of feature. In principle this can be applied on top of sglang, but requires substantial engineering. I wonder if it is worthwhile.

- **COMB** ([arXiv:2602.01519](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.01519)) — a third, different category: trains a dedicated encoder component into the model rather than changing only the inference engine. Claims 51-94% TTFT reduction, 3x throughput, tested on DeepSeek-V2-Lite-Chat. Code released: [github.com/shijuzhao/Comb](https://github.com/shijuzhao/Comb).

### **What's been looked into so far**

Confirmed against current sglang code that RoPE is baked into K at write time and the radix-cache hash chain is explicitly position-coupled.  today's architecture can't do any of the above without new work. All three are recent (Feb-June 2026) with limited independent validation, so there are potential bugs, 

I searched existing issues/PRs and didn't find prior discussion of this specific angle. Closest related work is #27574 / #24656 (agent-aware/session KV cache hints), but that's a different problem targeting cache locality/lifecycle, not reuse across a shifted position with identical content.

**Questions for the community**

Has anyone evaluated any of these for sglang already, even informally?
Is there a reason this hasn't come up that isn't obvious from the papers?

Would a narrow, opt-in delta-rotation implementation (gated to MLA/partial-RoPE models, feature-flagged behind a --radix-cache-backend variant) be a welcome contribution, or better suited as an external/experimental extension?

Happy to share more detailed technical notes if there's interest.
speedup_claims: Claims 51-94% TTFT reduction, 3x throughput, tested on DeepSeek-V2-Lite-Chat

title: [Feature] RFC: SGLang KV Indexer for Distributed KV Cache Placement Metadata
author: wuyl1
body:
### Checklist

- [x] If this is not a feature request but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [x] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

### Motivation

cc: @isytwu @TianDi101

## Summary

This RFC proposes a SGLang KV Indexer for collecting and querying distributed KV cache location metadata. The indexer does not store KV cache bytes. It tracks which worker holds which KV block hash and at which storage tier, so schedulers and routing components can make cross-worker KV reuse decisions.

SGLang workers already emit KV cache lifecycle events such as `BlockStored`, `BlockRemoved`, and `AllBlocksCleared`. A bridge component converts these events into indexer metadata updates. Query clients can then ask the indexer which workers may hold a given set of KV block hashes.

The initial project will be implemented out of tree as an independent Rust service. It integrates with SGLang through the existing KV event stream and gRPC APIs, without requiring the indexer code to live inside the SGLang source tree.

## Goals

1. Collect KV location metadata from SGLang workers.

   The bridge subscribes to SGLang KV events and converts them into metadata operations such as `report`, `revoke`, and `revoke-all`. The indexer maintains a location index in the form of `hash -> worker -> tier`.

2. Provide cross-worker KV location lookup.

   Schedulers or query clients can ask the indexer where a list of KV block hashes may be found. The response includes worker IDs and storage tiers, and can optionally update hit-count statistics for scheduling policies.

## Architecture

```text
+------------------+        +----------------------------+
|      SGLang      |        |           Bridge           |
|------------------|        |----------------------------|
| KV Cache         | ZMQ    | - subscribe KVEventBatch   |
| Event Publisher  +------->| - decode KV events         |
| BlockStored      | events | - map hash / medium / tier |
| BlockRemoved     |        | - batch report / revoke    |
| AllBlocksCleared |        |                            |
+------------------+        +-------------+--------------+
                                           |
                                           | gRPC metadata API
                                           v
+------------------------+  +-------------+--------------+
|     Metadata Store     |<-|          KV Indexer        |
|------------------------|  |----------------------------|
| hash -> worker         |  | location index             |
| worker -> tier         |  | hit-count index            |
| hit counts             |  | query API                  |
|------------------------|  |                            |
| possible backends:     |  |                            |
| - in-memory            |  |                            |
| - Redis                |  |                            |
| - MySQL / PostgreSQL   |  |                            |
| - RocksDB              |  |                            |
+------------------------+  +----------------------------+
```

The data flow is metadata-only. The bridge sends KV block location updates to the indexer. The indexer stores and serves location metadata. KV bytes remain owned by SGLang workers and are not transferred through the indexer.

## KV Indexer

The indexer is a standalone metadata service. Its core responsibility is to maintain KV block location state and expose query APIs.

| Function | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Location update | Record that a worker holds a set of KV block hashes at a specific tier. |
| Location revoke | Remove specific hashes, or remove all hashes from a worker at a specific tier. |
| Location lookup | Return workers and tiers that may hold requested KV block hashes. |
| Hit counting | Optionally count real lookup hits for scheduling or monitoring. |
| Store abstraction | Persist metadata in memory, Redis, SQL, RocksDB, or another backend. |

The primary data model is:

```text
hash -> worker_id -> set<tier>
```

This allows a KV block hash to exist on multiple workers and on multiple tiers of the same worker.

## Bridge

The bridge adapts SGLang KV events into indexer metadata operations. The initial implementation will run out of tree, most likely as a sidecar near each SGLang worker. This avoids changes to the SGLang worker process and keeps the indexer deployable independently while the API stabilizes.

| Function | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Event subscription | Subscribe to SGLang ZMQ `KVEventBatch`. |
| Event decoding | Decode `BlockStored`, `BlockRemoved`, and `AllBlocksCleared`. |
| Tier mapping | Map SGLang storage medium to indexer tier, for example GPU -> HBM, CPU pinned memory -> DRAM, disk -> SSD. |
| Hash normalization | Convert SGLang block hashes into the indexer hash format. |
| Batching | Group updates by action and tier before sending gRPC requests. |
| Observability | Track decode errors, sequence gaps, and report / revoke failures. |

Event mapping:

| SGLang event | Indexer operation |
| --- | --- |
| `BlockStored(block_hashes, medium)` | `ReportExternalKvBlocks(hashes, tier)` |
| `BlockRemoved(block_hashes, medium)` | `RevokeExternalKvBlocks(hashes, tier)` |
| `AllBlocksCleared()` | `RevokeAllExternalKvBlocksAtTier(tier)` for configured tiers |

For multi-worker or DP-rank deployments, the bridge can manage multiple event sources. Each source has its own worker ID, endpoint, topic, and sequence tracking.

## Metadata Store

The metadata store is the persistence layer behind the indexer. It stores location metadata and optional hit-count data. The indexer should keep the store behind an interface so deployments can choose a backend based on latency, durability, and operational requirements.

| Store backend | Suitable use case |
| --- | --- |
| in-memory | Prototype, single indexer, fastest lookup, no persistence. |
| Redis | Shared low-latency metadata service. |
| MySQL / PostgreSQL | Durable state, operational visibility, SQL queries. |
| RocksDB | Embedded persistent KV store for a single indexer node. |

The initial implementation can use an in-memory store and keep the backend abstraction stable. Redis, SQL, or RocksDB can be added later without changing the gRPC API.

## gRPC API

The indexer exposes a small set of metadata update and query APIs. The API operates on hashes, worker IDs, and tiers. It does not expose KV bytes.

### API Overview

| RPC | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `ReportExternalKvBlocks` | Report that a worker holds hashes at a tier. |
| `RevokeExternalKvBlocks` | Remove hashes from a worker at a tier. |
| `RevokeAllExternalKvBlocksAtTier` | Remove all hashes for a worker at a tier. |
| `MatchExternalKv` | Query which workers and tiers hold requested hashes. |
| `GetExternalKvHitCounts` | Query accumulated hit counts for hashes. |

### Proto Sketch

```proto
enum TierType {
  TIER_UNKNOWN = 0;
  TIER_HBM = 1;
  TIER_DRAM = 2;
  TIER_SSD = 3;
}

service KVIndexer {
  rpc ReportExternalKvBlocks(worker_id, hashes, tier) returns (Empty);
  rpc RevokeExternalKvBlocks(worker_id, hashes, tier) returns (Empty);
  rpc RevokeAllExternalKvBlocksAtTier(worker_id, tier) returns (Empty);
  rpc MatchExternalKv(hashes, count_as_hit) returns (matches);
  rpc GetExternalKvHitCounts(hashes) returns (hit_counts);
}
```

`MatchExternalKv` returns matches grouped by worker and tier, for example `worker_id -> tier -> hashes`. `GetExternalKvHitCounts` returns `hash -> hit_count_total`.

`count_as_hit` is used to distinguish real scheduling lookups from diagnostic queries. When it is true, only matched hashes should increase hit-count statistics.

## Implementation Approach

The indexer service will be implemented in Rust. Rust provides near-C++ performance, strong memory and thread-safety guarantees, and a mature async / gRPC ecosystem. This is a good fit for a high-QPS metadata service with concurrent location updates and lookups.

The first implementation can use `tonic` for gRPC, `tokio` for async runtime, and an in-memory metadata store. The project should remain out of tree from SGLang and keep the store interface stable so Redis, SQL, or RocksDB backends can be added later without changing the gRPC API.

## Open Questions

- Should the out-of-tree bridge remain a sidecar long term, or should parts of it be upstreamed into SGLang after the API stabilizes?
- Should the indexer store only block-level hashes initially, or also accept prefix-chain information for future prefix-aware routing?
- What consistency guarantees are required between SGLang KV events and indexer metadata?
- Which metadata store backend should be recommended for production deployment?

### Related resources

_No response_

title: [RFC] Backend, KV dtype and platform compatibility is checked case by case, and the responses are inconsistent
author: mosya415
body:
### Motivation

While fixing #31346 I noticed that the bug I was fixing is one instance of a pattern, and that the project handles that pattern in at least four different ways depending on who wrote the code.

The concrete bug: `--kv-cache-dtype fp8_e4m3` together with `--dsa-decode-backend tilelang` is accepted on CUDA. The tilelang sparse kernel only has an fp8 path under ROCm, and on CUDA the kernel is compiled for bfloat16, so the server boots, loads the weights, and dies at decode CUDA-graph capture with `kernel main input KV dtype expected bfloat16, but got float8_e4m3fn`. I verified this on H100 at kernel level and on a DSA model across 4 nodes. The fix is three lines in argument resolution.

That fix is fine on its own. What bothers me is how it got there.

### The pattern

Constraints of the form "backend X only works on platform Y" or "backend X only supports kv-cache-dtype Z" are written by hand, one at a time, usually inside the PR that integrated the backend. `arg_groups/overrides.py` currently has 13 `raise ValueError` guards and `server_args.py` has 98 plus 101 asserts. Two of the DSA ones sit a few hundred lines below the guard I added and have exactly the same shape:

```python
if not is_blackwell_supported():
    raise ValueError("TRTLLM MLA backend is only supported on Blackwell GPUs (SM100/SM12x). Please use a different backend.")
if view.kv_cache_dtype not in ["fp8_e4m3", "fp4_e2m1", "bf16", "auto"]:
    raise ValueError("TensorRT-LLM MLA backend only supports kv-cache-dtype of fp8_e4m3, fp4_e2m1, bf16, or auto.")
```

Because each one is added independently, two things drift.

**The coverage is uneven.** In the DSA arm, of the 7 entries in `DSA_CHOICES` only 3 appear in any validation condition at all. `flashmla_sparse`, `flashmla_kv`, `flashmla_auto` and `trtllm` have none. This is awkward in my own case, because the error message I just added tells users to switch to `flashmla_kv` on Hopper or `trtllm` on Blackwell, and nothing checks that those accept what the user passes.

**The response is inconsistent.** Looking at merged PRs that deal with an unsupported combination, there are at least four different behaviours, all reasonable in isolation:

#23903 rejects the combination with an error. #31532 silently auto-disables one of the two features. #30463 keeps going and logs a warning. #23139 silently falls back to a different backend. #28689 is interesting because it was explicitly about deduplicating such asserts and filling one missing guard, which suggests I am not the first person to notice the shape.

From a user's point of view these are very different contracts. One tells you to fix your flags, one changes your configuration without asking, one changes it and mentions it in the log, and one changes it quietly. Today which of the four you get depends on which subsystem you happened to touch.

### Why it costs something

Because the check is missing rather than wrong, the failure surfaces late. In my case the server allocated the KV pool and reached decode CUDA-graph capture first, so on a multi-node deployment every attempt costs a full model load. Related reports look similar from the outside: #22277 is an fp8 KV dtype mismatch in Triton extend attention, #5700 is an fp8 KV cache producing nonsense output on fa3, #20163 is about incompatible KV layouts between trtllm and flashMLA.

### Prior work I found

#20481 refactored `server_args.py` and mentioned that each argument group could own its validation, but it was about code organisation rather than about whether the matrix is complete. #29630 is about the kernel namespace and notes in passing that backend coverage is hard to inspect. I did not find anything that treats the compatibility matrix itself as a thing to be filled in, so please point me at it if it exists.

### What I propose

Two steps, deliberately small, and the second one does not depend on the first.

**Step 1: fill one arm and see whether the shape holds.** Make the DSA compatibility matrix explicit as a declarative table living next to `_dsa_split_backend_resolution`, covering the 7 entries of `DSA_CHOICES` against the KV dtypes and platforms, with unit tests for every cell and hardware checks for the cells I can reach. Scope stays inside the DSA arm, nothing else changes, and it is easy to revert if the shape turns out to be wrong. The point of starting here is that the gaps are already known and I can verify them rather than guess.

**Step 2: write down which response is correct.** Independently of any table, agree on when an unsupported combination should raise, when it should auto-disable a feature, when it should fall back to another backend, and when a warning is enough. This costs almost nothing, it is a paragraph in the contribution guide plus review attention, and it stops the four behaviours above from multiplying further.

If step 1 works out, the natural continuation is to push the declarations from the table into the backends themselves, so each backend states its own platforms and dtypes and the resolver checks generically. I am deliberately not proposing that now: the DSA backends are plain strings in `DSA_CHOICES` dispatched through if/elif rather than registered objects, so doing it properly means introducing a registry first, and that is a much larger change than the problem currently justifies. Attention backends are in better shape for it, since they already have classes.

I also considered simply continuing to add guards by hand as gaps are found. That is the status quo, it is cheap per fix, and it needs no agreement from anyone, but the gaps keep being found by users in production and the inconsistent response stays. My own fix was found that way, which is what prompted this.

### What I am asking

Does this seem worth doing, or is case-by-case the deliberate choice here? If it is worth doing, is step 1 scoped the way you would want it, and does anyone object to starting in the DSA arm specifically? I am happy to write it, and I have hardware to verify the DSA cells on.

title: [RFC] An NPU-Native, Sparsity-Driven KV Offloading SubSystem for Efficient LLM Decoding
author: nzbej
body: # **RFC: An NPU-Native, Sparsity-Driven KV Offloading SubSystem for Efficient LLM Decoding** USTC: Yinhe Chen, Chengru Yang, Chengjie Tang(SXU, intern at USTC-IAI), Youhui Bai, Cheng Li Ascend NPU Network Lab\*\*: Ning Zhao, Heyuan Li, Biao Wang, Pengcheng Wang, Chen Sun ## Motivation Autoregressive decoding is a major bottleneck in LLM serving\. Unlike prefill, which processes prompt tokens in parallel, decoding generates tokens sequentially and repeatedly accesses the KV states of all preceding tokens\. Serving systems such as SGLang and vLLM maintain a KVCache to avoid recomputing these historical states, but its bandwidth and capacity costs grow linearly with sequence length and batch size\. Consequently, KVCache has become a primary constraint on decoding efficiency, maximum context length, and serving concurrency\. To reduce GPU HBM pressure from the growing KVCache, recent GPU\-oriented subsystems offload the full KVCache to host memory and fetch only the top\-k states selected by sparse attention at each decoding step\. This reduces device\-resident KV memory and supports longer contexts and higher concurrency, but relies on GPU\-specific kernels, transfer primitives, and runtime support\. NPUs are increasingly deployed in large\-scale LLM training and serving, including production stacks at major technology companies such as ByteDance and Tencent\. However, existing KVCache subsystems remain largely GPU\-oriented and cannot be directly ported to NPUs\. Beyond shared challenges such as cache management and data transfer hiding, NPUs introduce several platform\-specific issues\. First, efficient index\-driven Host–Device transfer primitives are not readily available in current NPU software stacks\. Second, NPU graph execution favors fixed\-shape buffers and device\-side control, which conflicts with the data\-dependent access patterns and variable transfer demands of dynamic top\-k sparsity\. Third, NPUs lack a mature, drop\-in Unified Memory abstraction, requiring explicit management of host memory, device\-visible addresses, and KV movement\. Despite these challenges, an NPU\-native KVCache subsystem for efficient LLM decoding in online serving is essential to establish NPUs as a first\-class alternative to GPUs\. ## **Proposal** To our knowledge, this RFC introduces the first NPU\-native KVCache subsystem for efficient LLM decoding\. It combines top\-k sparse attention with host\-backed KV offloading to reduce device\-resident KV memory while preserving the original sparse\-attention semantics\. The subsystem is compatible with NPU graph execution and existing serving optimizations, such as continuous batching and chunked prefill\. For clarity, the figure below compares the original execution path of NPU sparse attention with the data path introduced by our subsystem\. The dashed arrows denote the original path, while the solid arrows denote the new path\. ### Original Sparse\-Attention Data Path The original execution path consists of four steps: 1. **Prepare attention inputs\.** The attention frontend computes the query, KV states, and top\-k indices for the current token\. 2. **Append the current KV\.** The newly generated KV states are written to the Full Paged KVCache resident in NPU HBM\. 3. **Form the full KV input.** After appending the current KV states, the device\-resident cache contains the complete KV history for the request\. 4. **Execute sparse attention\.** The full KVCache, query, and top\-k indices are passed to the backend sparse\-attention kernel, which accesses the selected KV states\. Although the attention kernel accesses only top\-k KV states, the complete KV history remains resident in NPU HBM\. ### Sparsity\-Driven KV Offloading Data Path We add `SparseKVCacheManager` between the attention frontend and the sparse\-attention backend\. It stores the complete KV history in host memory while maintaining only a bounded KV working set and its metadata in NPU HBM\. The manager maintains three KV data structures: - **Host KV Store:** stores the complete KVCache and serves as the source of truth\. - **NPU Cached KV Buffer:** caches hot KV states likely to be reused across decoding steps\. - **NPU Selected Top\-K KV Buffer:** stores the compact set of KV states required by the current attention step\. It also maintains one device\-side metadata structure: - **NPU Slot Map:** records whether a logical KV position is cached in NPU HBM and, if so, its physical slot in the NPU Cached KV Buffer\. The proposed subsystem modifies only Steps 2 and 3 of the original execution path\. Step 1, attention\-input preparation, and Step 4, sparse\-attention computation, remain unchanged\. 2. **Offload the current KV\.** The newly generated KV states are written to the Host KV Store instead of being appended to the full KVCache in NPU HBM\. 3. **Materialize the selected KV\.** `SparseKVCacheManager` queries the NPU Slot Map using the top\-k indices\. Cache hits are copied from the NPU Cached KV Buffer, while cache misses are fetched from the Host KV Store\. The selected entries are assembled in the NPU Selected Top\-K KV Buffer, after which the cached buffer and Slot Map are updated according to the cache\-management policy\. The resulting selected KV buffer is passed to the original sparse\-attention kernel together with the query and top\-k indices\. Since the subsystem changes only KV placement and movement while preserving the selected KV states and attention computation, it is a lossless system\-level optimization and introduces no additional inference accuracy loss\. ## **System Optimizations** We introduce four Ascend\-friendly kernels to implement the modified KV data path efficiently: - **Slot\-Map Lookup Kernel:** performs device\-side cache lookup using the top\-k indices and NPU Slot Map, producing cache\-hit slots, miss indices, and valid masks without CPU intervention\. - **UniDex Copy Kernel:** provides a unified indexed\-copy primitive for KV offload, cache\-hit gathering, cache\-miss fetching, and cache updates\. Fixed\-shape inputs and valid masks make it compatible with NPU graph execution\. - **Shared\-Memory Allocator:** allocates and registers the Host KV Store during initialization, exposing stable device\-visible addresses and avoiding runtime memory registration\. - **Sparse\-Attention Backend Adapter:** connects the NPU Selected Top\-K KV Buffer to the existing sparse\-attention kernel while preserving its query, top\-k index, and output interfaces\. ## **Functional Scope and Compatibility** - **NPU MLA sparse attention scope:** This RFC focuses on the NPU MLA sparse attention path and is not intended to replace general KVCache management, HiCache, or non\-sparse attention paths\. - **Compatible with existing serving patterns:** The sparse KV offload path supports chunked prefill, mixed sequence lengths, padding requests, and invalid or partially valid top\-k selections\. - **Compatible with NPU graph execution:** Fixed\-shape buffers, valid masks, and sentinel entries ensure that graph capture and replay do not depend on the number of valid requests or selected tokens in a batch\. - **Compatible with chunked prefill layouts:** Newly generated KV can be offloaded from both compact ragged layouts and graph\-style padded layouts\. ## Evaluation We evaluate DeepSeek\-V3\.2\-W8A8 deployed with TP16 on a single Ascend 910C server with 16 NPU dies, 64 GB HBM per die, and 2 TB host memory\. The experiments use colocation deployment with graph optimization enabled\. We compare sparse KV offloading against the baseline with the feature disabled\. Both correctness and performance experiments use the same model, prompt format, sparse policy, sampling settings, and serving configuration unless otherwise noted\. ### Accuracy We evaluate model quality on GSM8K using the same model, prompt format, sparse policy, sampling settings, and serving configuration for both runs\. The baseline with sparse KV offload disabled achieves a score of **0\.98**, while sparse KV offload achieves **0\.97**\. Sparse KV offloading is lossless with respect to the underlying sparse\-attention algorithm\. It changes only KV placement and data movement, while preserving the same top\-k selections, KV values, and attention computation\. Therefore, it introduces no additional approximation or accuracy loss beyond that already incurred by sparse attention\. ### Online Serving Throughput We evaluate aggregate decoding throughput under increasing client concurrency with a fixed sequence length of 32K tokens, where concurrency denotes the number of submitted requests that have not yet completed\. The baseline reaches a peak decoding throughput of **44\.70 tokens/s**\. Its concurrency is limited by the device\-resident KVCache capacity, preventing it from running the higher\-concurrency configurations supported by sparse KV offload\. With sparse KV offload enabled, throughput continues to increase as concurrency grows and reaches **113\.97 tokens/s**, which is about **2\.55×** the baseline peak\. These results show that sparse KV offload relieves the NPU HBM capacity bottleneck and allows the serving system to sustain a larger decode batch\. The throughput gain mainly comes from the increased achievable concurrency rather than from reducing the cost of decoding an individual request\. ## Future Work - **Cache\-miss prefetching:** predict future top\-k accesses and prefetch missing KV states to keep Host\-to\-NPU transfers off the critical path\. - **PD disaggregation:** integrate sparse KV offloading with disaggregated prefill and decode serving\. - **Supernode support:** adapt KV placement, transfer, and cache management to Ascend supernode architectures\. - **Supernode memory pools:** extend the Host KV Store to supernode\-native memory\-pool semantics, enabling shared and elastic KV capacity across devices\. - **Ascend 950D support:** optimize the subsystem for the memory hierarchy, interconnect, and execution features of next\-generation Ascend 950D hardware\. - **UB\-aware execution:** exploit expanded Unified Bus capacity to improve KV staging, data reuse, and transfer\-compute pipelining\. - **DeepSeek\-V4 support:** extend the subsystem to the sparse\-attention mechanism introduced by DeepSeek\-V4\.

title: Deprecate CUTLASS MLA attention backend
author: b8zhong
body:
To reduce the complexity of the MLA attention backend paths, we plan to deprecate `--attention-backend cutlass_mla`.

| Quantization/Backend | What it is | Why it's removable |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Cutlass MLA** | Decode-only MLA kernel, gated to exactly SM 10.0 (B200); already disabled on SM 10.3 (GB300) | `CutlassMLABackend` only overrides `forward_decode` — prefill, extend, verify, and draft-extend all fall through to its own parent class, `FlashInferMLABackend`. It's also locked to `page_size=128` and blocks tree speculative decode. It hasn't had a functional change in ~10 months (the only recent touch was disabling it on newer Blackwell hardware), and it isn't exercised by any CI workflow. |

We recommend `trtllm_mla` or `tokenspeed_mla` as the supported replacements for MLA decode. Their perf. is much better.

Feedback time: 3 weeks.

title: Deprecate legacy (non-Marlin) GPTQ kernel and Dual Chunk Flash Attention backend
author: b8zhong
body:
To reduce the complexity of the quantization and attention backend paths, we plan to deprecate these two features.

| Feature | What it is | Why it's removable |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **GPTQ (non-Marlin)** | Original desc_act/exllama-style GPTQ CUDA kernel (`gptq_gemm`, `gptq_shuffle` in `sgl-kernel/csrc/gemm/gptq`), only reached when a GPTQ checkpoint isn't Marlin-compatible | `GPTQMarlinConfig` already auto-upgrades any Marlin-compatible checkpoint to `gptq_marlin` by default, which is the actively maintained path (fully migrated to JIT). This plain kernel only serves the shrinking set of checkpoints that fall outside Marlin's supported bits/group_size/desc_act combinations, and it has no JIT/Triton replacement of its own. |
| **Dual Chunk Flash Attention** | Sparse attention kernels (`fwd_sparse`, `varlen_fwd_sparse`, `convert_vertical_slash_indexes`/`_mergehead`) backing `--attention-backend dual_chunk_flash_attn`, added for Qwen/Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct-1M 1M-context support | Purely opt-in — no model registers or auto-selects this backend. The underlying kernel hasn't had a functional change in about a year. Now we have many more options for efficient sparse attention. |

Feedback time: 3 weeks.

title: [RFC][PD] Seamless P-to-D handoff via token replay
author: catyans
body:
# [RFC][PD] Seamless P-to-D Handoff via Token Replay

## Summary

This RFC proposes an opt-in seamless handoff mode for PD-disaggregated serving.
While the immutable prompt KV cache is transferred from the Prefill worker to
the Decode worker, the Prefill worker temporarily continues decoding and emits
tokens to the client. The Decode worker then replays the emitted token log as a
short extend to reconstruct only the post-prefill KV tail, catches up with the
Prefill worker, and atomically becomes the sole output owner.

The proposal does not replace Mooncake KV transfer and does not change
attention math. It removes the transfer handoff bubble by replacing
post-prefill delta-KV migration with a small token log plus deterministic
replay.

## Motivation

The current disaggregated Prefill lifecycle is:

```text
prefill forward
  -> sample one handoff token
  -> transfer prompt KV
  -> wait for transfer completion
  -> release Prefill KV
  -> return/continue on Decode
```

SGLang already overlaps parts of KV transfer with chunked prefill and supports
incremental transfer. Those optimizations reduce the remaining transfer tail,
but Decode still cannot continue until the required KV state is available.

The proposed path is:

```text
Prefill:
  prompt forward
    -> emit t1, t2, ... while prompt KV transfer is in flight
    -> append emitted token IDs to a monotonic handoff log
    -> stop only after Decode acknowledges the exact committed prefix

Decode:
  receive frozen prompt KV
    -> replay t1..tn with a short extend
    -> catch up with newly appended tokens
    -> atomically acquire output ownership at token boundary n
    -> generate t(n+1)
```

Token replay is useful because the token log is tiny, while the corresponding
per-layer KV tail is larger. More importantly, a short extend can process
multiple replay tokens in parallel and may catch up with token-by-token source
decoding.

## Relationship to Existing SGLang Work

This proposal is intentionally narrower than a generic adaptive PD runtime.

| Existing work | What it does | Difference in this RFC |
|---|---|---|
| Layerwise KV transfer | overlaps layer/chunk transfer with Prefill compute | emitted tail KV is reconstructed from token IDs |
| Incremental PD transfer | avoids retransmitting a Decode-resident prefix | still transfers KV; this RFC replays the live post-prefill tail |
| Optimistic Prefill | starts Prefill before bootstrap fully completes | does not keep Prefill as temporary output owner |
| Runtime role switching | changes an entire idle instance between P and D | this RFC transfers one live request |
| PD true-retraction rebootstrap (#25372) | recomputes a retracted Decode request through Prefill | provides reusable replay/commit semantics, but is not an online P-to-D catch-up |

The implementation should reuse the correctness lessons and data structures
from PD true-retraction rebootstrap instead of creating a second incompatible
token replay contract.

## Goals

1. Hide the remaining P-to-D KV handoff tail when Prefill has temporary Decode
   headroom and Decode can replay faster than Prefill emits.
2. Preserve exactly-once token streaming with an explicit output owner.
3. Preserve the standard Mooncake transfer path for immutable prompt KV.
4. Fail back to source-side continuation before commit.
5. Keep the feature default-disabled and make normal PD behavior unchanged.

## Non-goals

- Eliminating prompt KV transfer.
- Supporting different P/D model versions or KV layouts in the first version.
- Moving arbitrary sampling, grammar, or speculative-decoding state in the
  first PR.
- Providing Decode failback after ownership has committed.
- Claiming that the mode improves throughput for every workload.

## Protocol

### Request identity

Every handoff attempt is identified by:

```text
(request_id, bootstrap_room, handoff_epoch)
```

Messages from an older epoch are ignored. Retrying a failed handoff increments
the epoch.

### Monotonic token log

The Prefill owner publishes:

```text
TokenLogAppend {
  request_id
  handoff_epoch
  first_output_index
  token_ids[]
}
```

The receiver accepts an append only when `first_output_index` equals its current
log length. Duplicate appends are idempotent only when the payload matches;
gaps or conflicting payloads fail the attempt.

### Replay acknowledgement

Decode publishes:

```text
ReplayAck {
  request_id
  handoff_epoch
  replayed_output_count
}
```

`replayed_output_count` is cumulative and monotonic. It means Decode has
materialized KV for exactly that many already-emitted output tokens.

### Commit

Decode can request commit only when:

```text
replayed_output_count == Prefill.produced_output_count
```

Prefill compares the requested count against its current log length. If another
token was emitted after the ACK, commit is rejected as `BEHIND` and Decode
replays the new suffix. On success:

1. Prefill stops emitting after output index `n - 1`.
2. Prefill publishes `Commit(epoch, n)`.
3. Decode becomes the sole owner and generates output index `n`.

The client-facing stream must be owned by one side at all times. A router may
proxy both workers, but it must deduplicate by `(request_id, output_index,
handoff_epoch)` and accept data only from the current owner.

## KV Snapshot Boundary

The prompt KV transferred to Decode must be immutable while Prefill performs
bridge Decode. Paged KV allocators make the last prompt page important:
Prefill may otherwise append the first output token into the same physical page
that Mooncake is reading.

The first implementation must use one of:

1. freeze the final prompt page and allocate a fresh page for bridge Decode; or
2. copy-on-write the final partial page before the first bridge token.

This is a correctness requirement, not a performance optimization.
Until freeze/COW exists, an initial experimental path may reject
`page_size > 1` and run only with token-granular pages. It must fail closed
rather than silently enabling the handoff on paged MLA backends.

## Catch-up Admission

Let:

- `R_p` be Prefill bridge Decode tokens/s;
- `R_r` be Decode replay tokens/s;
- `T_copy` be remaining prompt KV transfer time.

At replay start the expected backlog is approximately:

```text
B0 = R_p * T_copy
```

Catch-up requires:

```text
R_r > R_p
```

and the idealized additional catch-up time is:

```text
T_catch = B0 / (R_r - R_p)
```

The runtime should use measured EWMA values, include fixed replay startup and D
queue delay, and enforce a maximum bridge-token budget. If admission fails, the
request follows normal PD handoff.

## Failure Semantics

| Failure point | Required behavior |
|---|---|
| Prompt KV transfer fails before commit | P remains owner and continues or returns the existing transfer error policy |
| Token-log transport fails | abort handoff attempt; P remains owner |
| Decode replay fails | abort handoff attempt; P remains owner |
| Stale/duplicate ACK | ignore without changing ownership |
| EOS before commit | finish on P and cancel outstanding transfer when supported |
| Commit succeeds | P must never emit another token for this epoch |
| Decode fails after commit | out of scope for v1; use existing request failure policy |

## MVP Scope

The first implementation is limited to:

- Mooncake transfer backend;
- 1P1D;
- identical P/D model, TP size and KV layout;
- greedy decoding;
- no speculative decoding;
- no multimodal input;
- feature flag default off.

The existing PD path remains the fallback.

## Proposed Implementation

### Step 1: protocol and deterministic tests

- Add a private handoff state model with epoch fencing, monotonic append/ACK and
  exact-count commit.
- Add deterministic race, duplicate, stale epoch, cancel and failure tests.
- Add a cost-model helper used by benchmarks and later admission policy.

### Step 2: restricted end-to-end path

- Preserve the Prefill request after its first token and place it in a
  bridge-decode queue while Prompt KV transfer remains in flight.
- Freeze/COW the Prompt KV boundary.
- Let Decode schedule an actual extend over token-log suffixes after Prompt KV
  commit; replay logits are discarded.
- Add atomic output-owner switch and E2E exact-output tests.

The current disaggregated Prefill loop cannot be reused unchanged: it limits
the request to one new token, parks the request in the transfer-inflight queue,
and releases its KV as soon as transfer succeeds. The experimental path needs
a bounded bridge-decode queue, must retain the source KV until commit, and must
not make generic PDMux a prerequisite.

### Step 3: production compatibility

- Counter-based sampling RNG keyed by request and output index.
- Grammar/logprob/stop-state transfer.
- Speculative decoding and multi-rank compatibility.
- Adaptive admission and observability.

## Evaluation

### Correctness

- Exact greedy-output parity with normal PD.
- No duplicate/missing token under randomized append/ACK ordering.
- Fault injection at transfer, replay and pre-commit stages.
- KV/page leak and repeated bootstrap-room reuse tests.

### Performance

Report:

- TTFT;
- first-to-second-token latency;
- P50/P95/P99 ITL;
- Prefill goodput impact;
- Prompt KV transfer latency and bytes;
- replay throughput and bridge-token count;
- GPU and NIC utilization.

Use 8K/32K/64K prompts, 1/8/32/64 replay tokens, low and saturated load, and
separate RDMA from TCP results.

## Open Questions

1. Should bridge Decode run in the Prefill scheduler event loop or through a
   small role-agnostic generation subqueue?
2. Can the existing page allocator expose a cheap freeze/COW primitive for the
   last partial prompt page?
3. Should token-log control messages reuse the bootstrap channel or use the
   router stream?
4. What is the minimum sampling state needed after the greedy MVP?
5. Should a future Mooncake intent mark the frozen Prompt KV transfer as
   latency-critical while making cancellation best-effort after early EOS?

title: [RFC][Feature] Topology-transparent multi-NIC HTTP ingress with a single logical scheduling queue
author: catyans
body:
## Checklist

- [x] This is a feature request rather than a general question.
- [x] This issue is written in English.

## Motivation

### Summary

This RFC proposes topology-transparent multi-NIC HTTP ingress for the SGLang
router/server:

> Requests arriving through multiple host-facing NICs should converge into one
> logical scheduling queue, without changing the OpenAI-compatible API or
> application request path.

This is useful on inference nodes equipped with multiple front-side
NICs/DPUs/ENIs. A single ingress NIC can become a bandwidth or packets-per-second
bottleneck even when the Prefill/Decode and KV-transfer data planes have spare
capacity on other NICs.

### What Linux already provides

With one wildcard listener (`0.0.0.0:PORT` or `[::]:PORT`), Linux already
accepts connections addressed to any matching local interface into the same
listen socket and accept queue. Therefore, the baseline multi-NIC fan-in path
does **not** require per-NIC listeners or changes to SGLang's request API.

There are two important qualifications:

1. The accept queue is ordered by TCP handshake completion, not by client send
   time or SYN arrival time. This RFC does not promise a strict total order
   across NICs.
2. `SO_REUSEPORT` or multiple server workers create multiple kernel accept
   queues. If those modes are used for higher PPS, SGLang still needs one
   logical fan-in point before request scheduling to preserve global admission,
   priority, and fairness semantics.

### Current gap

Today this behavior is implicit. Operators lack:

- an explicit and tested multi-homed ingress contract;
- startup diagnostics confirming which addresses/interfaces can reach the
  listener;
- per-ingress-interface observability for connection rate, request rate,
  errors, and queueing;
- a benchmark that compares 1/2/4 ingress NICs and detects whether traffic
  actually spreads across them;
- a supported scale-up path when one accept queue or one HTTP worker becomes
  the bottleneck;
- a documented guarantee that optional multi-listener ingress converges before
  SGLang's scheduling/admission policy.

### Proposed design

#### Phase 0: Define and validate the zero-change baseline

- Document wildcard binding as the default multi-NIC ingress mode.
- At startup, report the bound address family, port, and whether the listener is
  wildcard-bound.
- Warn when configuration unintentionally binds to one specific host address.
- Add an integration test using two local destination addresses to verify that
  both paths reach the same SGLang endpoint and scheduler.

No request schema, OpenAI-compatible API, or model-worker change is required.

#### Phase 1: Add ingress observability

Expose optional, low-overhead metrics such as:

- accepted connections and HTTP requests by local destination
  address/interface;
- accept/HTTP queue depth or queueing delay where available;
- connection errors and resets by ingress path;
- aggregate versus per-path throughput and PPS.

Interface attribution may use the accepted socket's local address plus a cached
address-to-interface mapping. It should not add per-request routing decisions to
the model-serving hot path. If reliable attribution is unavailable on a
platform, metrics should fall back to local-address or aggregate labels instead
of guessing.

Suggested metric labels must remain bounded; raw client addresses must never be
used as labels.

#### Phase 2: Optional multi-listener fan-in for PPS scaling

If profiling shows that one accept queue/HTTP worker is the bottleneck, add an
opt-in ingress mode:

```text
NIC/IP A ─ listener/worker A ─┐
NIC/IP B ─ listener/worker B ─┼─> bounded MPSC fan-in ─> one logical
NIC/IP C ─ listener/worker C ─┘                         admission/scheduling queue
```

Possible implementations include `SO_REUSEPORT` workers or explicitly bound
per-address listeners. The implementation choice should be hidden behind the
router/server boundary.

Required semantics:

- existing endpoints and request schemas remain unchanged;
- all ingress paths share the same admission, priority, deadline, and fairness
  policy;
- bounded backpressure prevents one NIC from exhausting global queue capacity;
- no strict ordering is promised across independent TCP connections;
- failure or removal of one ingress NIC does not stop healthy listeners;
- the default remains the current single wildcard listener unless benchmarks
  justify enabling another mode.

### Alternatives considered

- **Linux bonding/LACP:** useful when available, but often unavailable for cloud
  ENIs, SR-IOV VFs, or independently managed DPUs. It also hides per-path
  observability.
- **External L4/L7 load balancer:** valid for cluster-level routing, but it does
  not remove the need to validate and observe multiple local ingress paths.
- **One SGLang instance per NIC:** duplicates serving state and fragments
  admission/scheduling queues, which is the opposite of the desired contract.
- **DPDK/XDP in the first version:** significantly increases operational
  complexity. The kernel wildcard-listener baseline should be measured first.

### Non-goals

- Configuring cloud ENIs, IP addresses, routes, bonding, or DPU firmware.
- Reordering packets or connections across NICs.
- Changing Mooncake/TENT KV-transfer path selection.
- Claiming bandwidth scaling when upstream routing still sends traffic to only
  one destination IP.

### Validation plan

On a node with 1/2/4 routable host-facing NICs:

1. Send independent HTTP workloads to each NIC's local IP and the same SGLang
   port.
2. Verify that all requests reach the same logical scheduler and preserve
   existing API behavior.
3. Measure aggregate requests/s, goodput, p50/p95/p99 latency, CPU utilization,
   accept/queue delay, drops, and fairness per ingress path.
4. Compare:
   - specific-address bind;
   - one wildcard listener;
   - optional `SO_REUSEPORT`/multi-listener fan-in.
5. Disable one ingress path during load and verify bounded impact on the others.

### Open questions

1. Should the first contribution be documentation + diagnostics + benchmark
   only, with multi-listener fan-in gated on evidence?
2. Is the SGLang Router the preferred single logical queue, or should the HTTP
   server expose a generic fan-in abstraction reusable without the router?
3. Which existing queue-delay/admission metrics should be reused to avoid a
   second ingress-only metric model?

## Related resources

- Linux `ip(7)`: binding to `INADDR_ANY` accepts traffic addressed to any local
  interface.
- Linux `socket(7)`: `SO_REUSEPORT` permits multiple sockets bound to the same
  address and port and distributes incoming connections.
- SGLang HTTP server entry point:
  `python/sglang/srt/entrypoints/http_server.py`.
- Related but separate work: #28631 proposes propagating request priority into
  the KV-transfer layer. This RFC concerns HTTP ingress before that scheduling
  and transfer path.

title: [RFC] Add CI Infrastructure for the SGLang MLU Backend
author: chenxb002
body: ## 1. Motivation The SGLang MLU backend needs a CI mechanism to keep its functionality continuously usable. Changes to MLU-specific code, as well as changes to shared SGLang components used by the MLU backend, can introduce regressions. Relevant pull requests therefore need to trigger MLU tests so that functional correctness is validated before the changes are merged. The MLU hardware and its supporting execution environment are accessible only from Cambricon's internal network and cannot be attached directly to GitHub-hosted runners. This RFC proposes a CI architecture that connects the public SGLang GitHub workflows to the internal Jenkins and MLU cluster while preserving the internal network boundary. The resulting CI lane makes MLU validation visible to the SGLang community and helps maintain the backend's functional availability as the project evolves. ## 2. Summary This RFC proposes community-visible PR and Nightly CI infrastructure for the Cambricon MLU backend in SGLang. The integration connects GitHub Actions to an internally operated Jenkins and MLU cluster without exposing Jenkins or internal infrastructure to the public Internet. The corresponding implementation is tracked in [sgl-project/sglang#26898](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/26898). The proposed CI infrastructure has these properties: - Pull requests run only after the existing `run-ci` gate and the `run-ci-mlu` opt-in label pass. - During the initial observation period, the PR lane is a non-required check and does not block pull requests from being merged. - Test failures fail the GitHub job and remain visible as code-related failures. - Infrastructure failures and MLU resource queue timeouts are reported with a warning annotation, while the GitHub job concludes successfully because contributors cannot repair the private CI infrastructure. - Nightly and trusted manual/default-branch runs remain strict. - Results distinguish test failures, infrastructure failures, and timeouts. - Jenkins logs and structured result metadata are uploaded as GitHub artifacts when the GitHub job has started and reaches the upload step. - PR and Nightly jobs use separate labels in a dedicated runner group and run on one-job ephemeral self-hosted GitHub Actions runners on the VPS. - The PR workflow runs with `pull_request_target`, so its YAML and reusable gate come from the reviewed base branch. - The self-hosted runner never checks out or executes client code from the pull request. The proposal is intended to begin with an observation period. It does not ask SGLang maintainers to make the MLU lane required at initial rollout. ## 3. Proposed Architecture The architecture consists of four modules across three trust zones: public GitHub, the VPS, and the trusted internal network containing the controller, Jenkins, and MLU resources. ### 3.1 GitHub Community The SGLang-side integration includes PR and Nightly workflows, the existing `run-ci` gate and the `run-ci-mlu` opt-in label, and a reliability reporting workflow. GitHub Actions dispatches eligible MLU CI jobs and displays their status, annotations, logs, and artifacts to contributors. ### 3.2 VPS The VPS hosts: - a GitHub Actions runner provisioner; - one PR runner slot and one Nightly runner slot; - a task submission bridge and task/status store; - a trusted, preinstalled `sglang-mlu-ci` client. `sglang-mlu-ci` is an operator-installed command-line client invoked by the GitHub workflow. It submits validated task metadata, polls for progress, and publishes the final result without fetching or executing pull request code. ### 3.3 Internal Controller The internal controller retrieves pending tasks from the VPS, coordinates their execution in Jenkins, and returns status and logs. It also provides a runner broker that issues restricted JIT configurations for ephemeral runners. GitHub Actions has no direct access to Jenkins or MLU resources, and communication with internal services is initiated from within Cambricon's network. ### 3.4 Jenkins / MLU Cluster Jenkins receives the repository URL, immutable commit SHA, task ID, and trigger type. It checks out the exact SHA in an isolated MLU pod, prepares the MLU backend dependencies, and runs the registered PR or Nightly test suites. Execution status and logs are returned through the internal controller. ## 4. GitHub Workflow Policy ### 4.1 Trigger Policy The workflow uses `pull_request_target` so the workflow definition and reusable gate are loaded from the reviewed base branch. It never checks out the pull request or executes repository code on the self-hosted runner. The untrusted repository URL and immutable head SHA are passed only as data to the trusted client, and PR code is executed later in the isolated Jenkins MLU pod. The MLU PR job is entered only when: 1. the PR targets `main`; 2. the PR has the `run-ci-mlu` label, an explicit opt-in for the MLU lane; 3. the PR is not a draft; 4. the PR has the `run-ci` label; 5. the existing PR gate and rate-limit policy pass. The label check runs at gate time with a live fetch of the pull request's current labels, so a rerun after adding `run-ci-mlu` picks up the new label set; the workflow also re-fires when `run-ci` or `run-ci-mlu` is added. > [!IMPORTANT] > SGLang maintainers must review and merge the MLU workflow files into the default branch before the PR and Nightly lanes can run. GitHub loads `pull_request_target`, `schedule`, and `workflow_dispatch` definitions from the default branch. This bootstrap also prevents a pull request from replacing the commands executed on the self-hosted runner. ### 4.2 Lane Isolation The Organization runner group is named `mlu-ci` and is restricted to the SGLang repository. The jobs select it as follows: ```yaml # Pull requests runs-on: group: mlu-ci labels: mlu-pr # Nightly runs-on: group: mlu-ci labels: mlu-nightly ``` Separate labels prevent a long Nightly GitHub job from occupying the PR runner slot. Each lane has one provisioner in the initial deployment, so the maximum GitHub-side concurrency is one PR job and one Nightly job. ### 4.3 Initial Observe-Only PR Policy During the initial observation period, the MLU PR lane is a non-required check. Its result policy is: | Result | GitHub annotation | PR job conclusion | Reason | | ---------------------------------- | ----------------- | ----------------- | ------ | | Success | none | success | MLU validation completed successfully. | | `test/pytest` | error | failure | A test executed and failed, indicating a possible code regression. | | Invalid request or source metadata | error | failure | The requested source cannot be safely or correctly tested. | | `infrastructure/*` | warning | success | Private CI infrastructure is unavailable and cannot be repaired by the contributor. | | `timeout/mlu_resource_queue` | warning | success | No MLU resource became available within the queue time budget. | | `timeout/external_task` | warning | success | The VPS task did not reach a terminal state within its active-task time budget. | | `timeout/github_client` | warning | success | The GitHub-side client did not receive a terminal result within its time budget. | | `timeout/jenkins_task` | error | failure | An executing Jenkins task exceeded its time budget, which may indicate a hung or regressed test. | Test failures remain visible as failing checks, but they do not block merging while the lane is non-required. Infrastructure failures conclude successfully with a warning because contributors cannot repair the private CI infrastructure. `timeout/jenkins_task` remains a failure because it indicates that an executing test may have hung or regressed. MLU resource queue timeout is advisory because a contributor cannot make internal hardware available. No automatic retry is proposed during the initial observation period. Returning a warning avoids blocking the PR, while not retrying prevents duplicate Jenkins work and makes infrastructure reliability visible in the data. An automatic single retry can be considered after the observation period. Nightly, default-branch, and trusted manual runs use strict conclusions so infrastructure operators still receive a red signal when the lane is unhealthy. ## 5. Test Scope PR validation currently uses: - `pr-test-1-mlu`: tests requiring one MLU device; - `pr-test-2-mlu`: tests requiring two MLU devices. Additional test cases and suites can be added as MLU coverage requirements evolve. Nightly uses the independent `nightly-test-mlu` suite. ## 6. Failure Classification and Reporting The status is not limited to pass/fail. The task result carries: ```json { "status": "error", "failure_type": "timeout", "failure_stage": "mlu_resource_queue", "observe_only": true, "github_conclusion": "success", "task_id": "" } ``` The main classifications include: | Failure type | Example stages | Meaning | | --- | --- | --- | | `test` | `pytest` | A test executed and failed | | `infrastructure` | `jenkins_connect`, `internal_poller`, `runner_client`, `vps_bridge` | CI infrastructure could not execute or report the test normally | | `timeout` | `mlu_resource_queue`, `jenkins_task`, `external_task`, `github_client` | A named layer exceeded its time budget | | `request` | `task_submission` | The submitted repository/ref/SHA metadata was invalid | The classification is emitted in four places: 1. the live Actions console log; 2. a GitHub warning or error annotation; 3. the GitHub step summary; 4. `result-.json` in the uploaded artifact. An example line is: ```text MLU CI failure classification: type=timeout, stage=mlu_resource_queue ``` ## 7. Log Streaming, Artifact Upload, and Retention The internal master incrementally reads the Jenkins console log and sends log chunks to the VPS task store. The trusted client polls for new log bytes and prints them to the GitHub Actions console. At terminal status, it downloads the complete log and writes: ```text jenkins-.log result-.json ``` The workflow upload step uses `if: always()` and `actions/upload-artifact@v4`. Result metadata is also uploaded as a separate small `mlu-ci-result-pr--` artifact with 30-day retention, so the weekly reporter does not need to download the complete Jenkins log. Artifact upload is best-effort rather than unconditional. It works for normal success, test failure, classified infrastructure failure, and classified timeout after the GitHub job has started. It cannot run when: - no runner ever claims the GitHub job; - the runner host or runner process is terminated before the upload step; - GitHub's artifact service itself is unavailable. To provide a recovery window, failed tasks and their logs remain on the VPS for 72 hours by default. The duration is configurable by the operator. Successful tasks are removed after complete log download. A successful task with incomplete log download is also retained for the recovery window. GitHub artifact retention remains controlled by the SGLang repository's Actions retention setting. ## 8. Timeout Budget The PR timeout budget is intentionally ordered from the execution layer outward: | Layer | PR timeout | | --------------------------------------------- | ----------: | | Internal poller claim | 5 minutes | | Continuous Jenkins unavailability | 5 minutes | | Jenkins pipeline, including MLU resource wait | 100 minutes | | VPS active task | 105 minutes | | Trusted GitHub client | 110 minutes | | GitHub Actions job | 120 minutes | This leaves time for the inner layer to publish a classified terminal result and for outer layers to drain logs and upload artifacts. Nightly has an independent longer budget: | Layer | Nightly timeout | | --------------------- | --------------: | | Jenkins Nightly task | 420 minutes | | VPS active task | 435 minutes | | Trusted GitHub client | 450 minutes | | GitHub Actions job | 480 minutes | ## 9. Ephemeral Runner Provisioning Each ephemeral runner requires a fresh GitHub JIT configuration, and the GitHub API that issues this configuration requires Organization-level self-hosted runner management permission. To keep this permission off the VPS, an internal broker uses a GitHub App with only: ```text Organization permission: Self-hosted runners, read and write Repository permissions: no additional permissions ``` The broker fixes the Organization, runner group, and allowed lane labels. The VPS can request only an `mlu-pr` or `mlu-nightly` JIT configuration and cannot use the broker to create runners with arbitrary access. The GitHub App credentials remain inside the internal network. Each runner is configured as ephemeral and processes at most one GitHub job. After it exits, the provisioner uses the broker to remove the old registration and obtain a JIT configuration for its replacement. Stale registrations are also removed without affecting runners outside the configured group and label boundary. The expected steady state is two registered runners: one PR runner and one Nightly runner. Runner IDs changing after jobs is expected; an ever-growing list of offline runners is not. > [!IMPORTANT] > Production rollout requires cooperation from `sgl-project` Organization administrators to authorize the restricted `mlu-ci` runner group and install the runner-provisioning GitHub App. SGLang repository maintainers must also keep the MLU PR check non-required during the initial observation period, as described in Section 4.3. ## 10. Security Model ### 10.1 GitHub Permissions and Credentials - The workflows declare explicit, minimal, read-only `GITHUB_TOKEN` permissions. - No repository write credential is installed on the self-hosted runner or passed to pull request code. - The runner-provisioning GitHub App has no repository permissions; it has only the Organization-level self-hosted runner permission required to manage ephemeral runners. - The VPS has no GitHub Organization credential and can request runners only for the predefined MLU runner group and lane labels through the broker. As a result, the MLU CI infrastructure cannot modify repository code, pull requests, or issues. An infrastructure outage can affect only the availability and reporting of the MLU lane. A compromise of the runner-provisioning GitHub App could affect Organization runner registrations, but it would not grant access to repository content or repository write operations. ### 10.2 Trusted Runner Code The self-hosted job does not run `actions/checkout` for the pull request. It invokes a preinstalled `sglang-mlu-ci` command deployed from a trusted infrastructure revision. The workflow passes only validated metadata: repository name, GitHub HTTPS clone URL, and full commit SHA. The `pull_request_target` workflow and its local reusable gate are loaded from the base branch. A pull request therefore cannot replace the `run:` block that invokes the trusted client. The workflow has explicit read-only permissions and does not expose repository or infrastructure secrets. The pull request code is fetched and executed only inside the isolated Jenkins MLU pod. Jenkins checks out the immutable SHA and verifies that `HEAD` matches it. ### 10.3 Remaining Trust Assumptions - The VPS, internal controller, Jenkins, and MLU pod isolation are managed by the Cambricon MLU CI maintainers and are treated as trusted infrastructure in this proposal. - The MLU workflow on the default branch has passed normal SGLang review. - The dedicated runner group remains restricted to the intended repository/workflow. ## 11. Operations and Response SLA The proposed primary community contact is `@chenxb002`. The response target applies to infrastructure-classified failures, repeated MLU resource queue timeouts, and runner unavailability. It does not apply to test failures caused by the code under test. During the observe-only period, the Cambricon MLU CI maintainers will: - acknowledge a reported or monitored infrastructure incident within one business day; - restore the affected lane, temporarily disable it, or publish a status update within two business days (worst case); - publish a follow-up when service is restored. While an infrastructure incident remains unresolved, the PR lane remains non-required and infrastructure-classified results do not block pull requests. These are proposed response targets rather than an uptime guarantee and should be confirmed by the named contact and SGLang maintainers during RFC review. ## 12. Reliability Visibility Infrastructure failures remain visible even when the PR conclusion is successful. A scheduled workflow aggregates only PR-lane runs and appends a reliability report to the public RFC issue. The report is published weekly while the lane remains observe-only. The report includes: - total triggered, started, completed, cancelled, and unclaimed jobs; - success and test-failure counts; - counts grouped by `failure_type` and `failure_stage`; - MLU queue timeout count; - median and p95 queue/completion time where available; - artifact and structured metadata coverage among jobs that started. Failure classifications come from the structured result artifact and are combined with GitHub run and job metadata. Jobs that never receive a runner or never upload result metadata are reported separately rather than silently excluded, allowing the community to distinguish runner assignment, reporting coverage, and classified CI reliability. The reporter runs only on GitHub-hosted runners. Report collection is read-only, while a separate publishing job receives `issues: write` only to append the report comment; the MLU PR workflow remains read-only. Every report is also available in the step summary and as Markdown/JSON artifacts. Each run creates a new issue comment so the community can compare historical snapshots. ## 13. Demonstrated Behavior > [!NOTE] > The following evidence was collected in the public [`sglang-mlu/sglang`](https://github.com/sglang-mlu/sglang) fork, which deploys the trusted-workflow, observe-only policy, and ephemeral-runner architecture proposed in this RFC. All demo pull requests, workflow runs, jobs, annotations, and artifacts linked in this section come from that fork. ### 13.1 Successful PR Run The final trusted-workflow and ephemeral-runner architecture successfully validated pull request [#5](https://github.com/sglang-mlu/sglang/pull/5): - [workflow run](https://github.com/sglang-mlu/sglang/actions/runs/30064140061), triggered by `pull_request_target` for commit `58bef9b52280d8637867bdb7e64608c35d8e2f4d`; - [`pr-test-mlu` job](https://github.com/sglang-mlu/sglang/actions/runs/30064140061/job/89391687467), completed successfully on an ephemeral runner with label `mlu-pr` in the dedicated `mlu-ci` runner group; - the MLU task, result metadata upload, and Jenkins log upload steps all completed successfully; - both `mlu-ci-result-pr-30064140061-1` and `mlu-jenkins-log-pr-30064140061-1` artifacts were created. ### 13.2 Successful Nightly Run The strict Nightly lane successfully validated the same commit: - [workflow run](https://github.com/sglang-mlu/sglang/actions/runs/30064649714), manually triggered for commit `58bef9b52280d8637867bdb7e64608c35d8e2f4d`; - [`nightly-test-mlu` job](https://github.com/sglang-mlu/sglang/actions/runs/30064649714/job/89393132734), completed successfully on an ephemeral runner with label `mlu-nightly` in the dedicated `mlu-ci` runner group; - the Nightly MLU task and Jenkins log upload steps both completed successfully; - the `mlu-jenkins-log-nightly-30064649714-1` artifact was created. ### 13.3 Intentional Test Failure Pull request [#6](https://github.com/sglang-mlu/sglang/pull/6) added a deterministic failing test to verify that a pytest failure remains red and is propagated through Jenkins: - [workflow run](https://github.com/sglang-mlu/sglang/actions/runs/30065563358), triggered by `pull_request_target` for commit `2400a0a9cd73c11540923a765787f4ce53fc2c2b`; - [`pr-test-mlu` job](https://github.com/sglang-mlu/sglang/actions/runs/30065563358/job/89395751493), failed as expected while both artifact upload steps completed successfully; - the Actions log identified `TestMLUCIFailureDemo::test_intentional_failure_reaches_github_actions` and showed the intentional `AssertionError`; - the failure annotation reported `MLU CI failure classification: type=test, stage=pytest`; - both `mlu-ci-result-pr-30065563358-1` and `mlu-jenkins-log-pr-30065563358-1` artifacts were created. This confirms that observe-only handling does not mask test failures: a code-related test failure still produces a failing GitHub conclusion. ### 13.4 Jenkins Unavailable Pull request [#7](https://github.com/sglang-mlu/sglang/pull/7) validated the observe-only behavior when the internal controller could not connect to Jenkins. For this experiment, the controller was temporarily pointed at an unreachable local endpoint; the Jenkins service itself was not stopped: - [workflow run](https://github.com/sglang-mlu/sglang/actions/runs/30068996587), triggered by `pull_request_target` for commit `42bfa1145c3a6a770a923844ccb954fb754dc1a3`; - [`pr-test-mlu` job](https://github.com/sglang-mlu/sglang/actions/runs/30068996587/job/89405643748), completed successfully after the five-minute Jenkins availability deadline; - the warning annotation reported `MLU CI failure classification: type=infrastructure, stage=jenkins_connect`; - the MLU task step and both artifact upload steps completed successfully under the observe-only policy; - both `mlu-ci-result-pr-30068996587-1` and `mlu-jenkins-log-pr-30068996587-1` artifacts were created. This confirms that an internal Jenkins outage remains visible as a warning and structured infrastructure result without making the contributor's PR job fail. ### 13.5 MLU Resource Queue Timeout Pull request [#8](https://github.com/sglang-mlu/sglang/pull/8) validated the observe-only behavior when Jenkins accepted the build but could not schedule an MLU worker. For this experiment, the pipeline temporarily used an unavailable MLU label and a five-minute outer timeout: - [workflow run](https://github.com/sglang-mlu/sglang/actions/runs/30069671544), triggered by `pull_request_target` for commit `a01f381b84b04c5e28197e2f88669c0f3515f240`; - [`pr-test-mlu` job](https://github.com/sglang-mlu/sglang/actions/runs/30069671544/job/89407780967), completed successfully after the Jenkins resource queue timeout; - the warning annotation reported `MLU CI failure classification: type=timeout, stage=mlu_resource_queue`; - the MLU task step and both artifact upload steps completed successfully under the observe-only policy; - both `mlu-ci-result-pr-30069671544-1` and `mlu-jenkins-log-pr-30069671544-1` artifacts were created. This confirms that unavailable internal MLU capacity remains visible as a classified timeout without blocking the contributor's PR. ### 13.6 Internal Poller Unavailable Pull request [#9](https://github.com/sglang-mlu/sglang/pull/9) validated the observe-only behavior when the VPS accepted a task but the internal controller was unavailable to claim it.
