For this experiment, only the internal task poller was stopped; the GitHub runner, VPS services, runner broker, and Jenkins remained available: - [workflow run](https://github.com/sglang-mlu/sglang/actions/runs/30070992748), triggered by `pull_request_target` for commit `1ff76ae934036c7aed99d497b35c60b327d824b1`; - [`pr-test-mlu` job](https://github.com/sglang-mlu/sglang/actions/runs/30070992748/job/89411696723), completed successfully after the five-minute task claim deadline; - the warning annotation reported `MLU CI failure classification: type=infrastructure, stage=internal_poller`; - no Jenkins build was created because the task was never claimed by the internal controller; - both `mlu-ci-result-pr-30070992748-1` and `mlu-jenkins-log-pr-30070992748-1` artifacts were created. This confirms that an unavailable internal poller is reported as a visible infrastructure warning without blocking the contributor's PR or silently losing the task. ## 14. Feedback Requested Feedback and suggestions are welcome. This proposal will be revised based on community discussion and the refreshed demonstration results.

title: [RFC] Apple Silicon serving redesign: Torch-owned SRT path with an exported whole-model MLX region (roadmap)
author: noob-se7en
body: **Jump to:** [Roadmap](#user-content-roadmap) · [Design](#user-content-design) · [Evidence](#user-content-evidence) · Implementation PR: #36164 This updates the original proposal (can be found in previous edited version) after the Torch/MLX interoperability work in [#32984](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/32984). The stub problem remains, but zero-copy access to Torch MPS storage gives us a smaller solution: keep one standard SRT serving path and use MLX or Metal only for computation. The architecture below has been implemented and validated behind a default-off flag in the accompanying draft PR, [noob-se7en/sglang#2](https://github.com/noob-se7en/sglang/pull/2) (branch `rfc-whole-region-mlx-clean`, stacked on the #32984 bridge): none of it is upstream yet; measured results are in the Evidence section. **Implementation.** The core stack of this RFC — capture → lowering → serving — is under review upstream as sgl-project/sglang#36164 (three commits on current `main`, off by default behind `SGLANG_ENABLE_MLX_WHOLE_REGION`). The full RFC branch with every measurement quoted below is [noob-se7en/sglang#2](https://github.com/noob-se7en/sglang/pull/2); [noob-se7en/sglang#3](https://github.com/noob-se7en/sglang/pull/3) is the extraction that became #36164. Follow-up items and their PRs are tracked in the [Roadmap](#user-content-roadmap). ## Why this matters MLX compatibility bugs have repeatedly reached users through startup failures, request-time attribute errors, incomplete feature paths, lifecycle leaks, and configuration drift. Examples include #26882, #29681, #30181, #30389, #30547, #32115, #32445, #32446 and #32447. The same split also creates review burden. A scheduler or `ModelRunner` change may not mention MLX, but an MLX reviewer still has to check whether the new path reaches the stub, whether the required field was initialized, whether the MLX worker intercepts the operation, and whether copied framework calculations still match core. In #30547, for example, MLX silently ignored the configured `max_running_requests` because its stub maintained a separate calculation. #32115 then had to update that copied behavior again. As long as SGLang has two owners for serving state, fixes in the standard path can continue to drift from MLX. ## Current flow Today Apple Silicon serving has two execution paths selected at the backend level: ```text Scheduler | +-- Standard Torch path | TpModelWorker | Torch ModelRunner | Torch model | Torch request tables and KV cache | +-- Native MLX path MlxTpModelWorker MlxModelRunnerStub: Torch-shaped bookkeeping MlxModelRunner: model execution mlx-lm model separate request and KV lifecycle ``` `MlxModelRunnerStub` exists because generic serving code still expects a Torch-shaped `ModelRunner`, while the actual model is loaded and executed by a separate MLX runner. The arrangement is safe only for fields and paths that have already been mirrored and reviewed. The problem is not simply that the stub is incomplete. The framework has two implementations of model loading, request state, KV ownership, feature handling, and lifecycle behavior. ## Proposed flow Apple Silicon should use the standard Scheduler, worker, and Torch `ModelRunner` as the only owners of serving state: ```text Standard Scheduler Standard TpModelWorker Torch ModelRunner Torch-owned model, weights, requests and KV cache +-- eager Torch MPS forward (always available; also serves any | batch the region rejects before launch) +-- direct Metal AOT/JIT operators (existing fused-op dispatch) +-- exported whole-model MLX region (standard graph-runner slot; eligibility and export checked per batch before any device work) ``` Torch owns the model and storage. Metal and MLX are computation backends behind the two dispatch points SGLang already has: the fused-operation dispatch for individual operators, and the graph-runner slots for the exported region. They may read or update Torch-owned buffers through an explicit contract, but they do not load a second model or own another scheduler, request table, KV pool, sampler, or weight-update lifecycle. Models the region cannot serve continue to use the complete Torch MPS path. ## Design ### One owner for serving state | Concern | Authoritative owner | | --- | --- | | Scheduling, batching, request lifecycle and Radix cache | Standard SGLang Scheduler | | Model loading, parameters, request tables and KV allocation | Torch `ModelRunner` | | Logits, sampling, logprobs, grammar, LoRA and weight updates | Existing standard SRT components | | Operator dispatch and region selection | Existing fused-op dispatch and the standard graph-runner slot | | Accelerated computation | Torch MPS, Metal AOT/JIT or MLX | Neither dispatch point introduces a second copy of framework state. New Scheduler and `ModelRunner` behavior is inherited automatically because Apple Silicon uses the standard implementations. ### Direct Metal for small operations Model-independent operations such as RMSNorm, fused add and RMSNorm, and SiLU-and-multiply should use the existing fused-operation dispatch mechanism: ```text SGLang operation +-- supported Metal AOT/JIT kernel +-- otherwise Torch implementation ``` These kernels operate directly on Torch MPS buffers and do not cross into MLX. A separate model registry is not needed for this level. ### Capture-and-lower MLX region MLX becomes useful when a sufficiently broad region can remain in MLX long enough to amortize framework dispatch and synchronization. The region is not assembled from per-model MLX blocks. It is captured from the standard Torch model and lowered to MLX. Support for a new architecture is gated by lowering coverage of the ATen ops in its graph. #### Region construction by torch.export Non-strict `torch.export` captures the loaded model's forward (transformer body plus LM head) as one ATen FX graph, traced with a real serving `ForwardBatch` for a given batch shape (decode batch size or a Prefill token bucket). Attention layers emit a semantic custom op, `sglang::unified_attention_with_output`, carrying `k_cache`, `v_cache`, `req_to_token` and `seq_lens`. The op is only emitted under `torch.compiler.is_exporting()`, so eager execution is unchanged. #### FX-to-MLX lowering The lowering (`python/sglang/srt/hardware_backend/mlx/fx_backend.py`) walks the exported graph once: - Generic ATen ops map to `mx` ops. The mapping is written per ATen op, not per model, so coverage added for one architecture carries over to any other that uses the same ops. - The attention op lowers to a deferred radix-attention Metal kernel (`python/sglang/kernels/ops/attention/_deferred_radix_attention_mlx.py`), templated on head counts and head dim taken from the KV-pool shapes. No per-model kernel code. - KV pool buffers bind as persistent zero-copy DLPack views of Torch MPS storage. Fusion (fused QKV post-processing, RMSNorm chains) belongs in the lowering, as ATen-subgraph pattern matches to custom MLX kernels. The hand-fused blocks in yeahdongcn/sglang#7 show the available headroom; a pattern match gives the same win to every model whose graph contains it. #### Execution and deferred KV commit Execution is one lazy MLX region per step. The step's new K/V leaves the region as small delta outputs rather than in-place pool writes; a Torch-side Metal-JIT commit kernel (`python/sglang/kernels/ops/kvcache/_deferred_kv_commit_metal_jit.py`) scatters the deltas into the Torch-owned pool. #### Serving runner `MlxRegionRunner` (`python/sglang/srt/hardware_backend/mlx/region_runner.py`) occupies both graph runner slots, selected in `model_runner_components/cuda_graph_setup.py` behind the env flag `SGLANG_ENABLE_MLX_WHOLE_REGION` (default off). - Export is lazy, one executor per batch size or prefill token bucket (about 1.9 s for Qwen3-0.6B); the executor is reused across steps. - Guards: decode batch size up to 16, and no LoRA (the region binds views of the base weights, so adapted requests must stay on Torch). Speculative decoding, encoder inputs, and hierarchical sparse attention are also rejected, though none of these are available on Torch MPS today anyway. - A batch size whose export fails is blacklisted and served transparently by eager Torch. A pool-identity check re-exports if the KV pool is reallocated. Export temporarily swaps fused custom ops for their plain-Torch forms and restores them afterwards, so the eager path is untouched. ### Executor lifecycle Operators route through the existing fused-operation dispatch. The exported region occupies the standard graph-runner slot and is built lazily, one executor per batch shape. An executor checks request eligibility before device work, invalidates its views when Torch weights change or the KV pool is reallocated, and releases compiled graphs and borrowed views on replacement or shutdown. Construction is atomic: views, lowering and a KV write-verify pass complete before the executor serves traffic, and a failed export rolls back and blacklists that batch size. An executor must never use a view after Torch replaces or releases the storage. ### Fallback behavior Torch is the complete correctness fallback. - Static model or runtime incompatibility leaves the graph-runner slot empty at startup. - Request-specific incompatibility (mode, batch size, speculative decoding, encoder inputs, LoRA) is rejected by the runner's eligibility check before any device work. - Export failure for a batch shape blacklists that shape; it is served by eager Torch from then on. - A Metal operator outside its kernel contract falls back to the Torch implementation through the fused-op dispatch. - Failure after the region launches or KV state is committed is surfaced; it must not retry the same forward through Torch. Which path executed should be visible through the fused-op trace and runner logs so tests can prove it. ## Why this removes the stub failure class This proposal removes the second runner instead of adding more fields or methods to its compatibility adapter. - Scheduler and `ModelRunner` state no longer needs to be copied into MLX. - Shared calculations such as request-capacity resolution have one implementation. - Radix caching, sampling, logprobs, grammar, LoRA and weight updates stay on their standard paths. - MLX and Metal review is limited to lowering coverage, numerical behavior, storage lifetime, and kernel performance. MPS testing remains necessary because core code can still introduce CUDA-only assumptions. The change removes the more fragile requirement to mirror ordinary serving behavior into a partial `ModelRunner` subclass and a parallel lifecycle. ## Evidence **Interoperability** (#32984, merged): Torch-owned MPS storage is borrowed by MLX with no payload-sized copies; owned copies and borrowed views have separate lifetime contracts; unsupported runtime pairs fail before model loading. The same work showed that zero-copy is not zero-overhead — per-op crossings still pay dispatch and synchronization — which is why MLX runs one broad region here rather than one op at a time. **End-to-end serving**, Qwen3-0.6B bf16, 512 in / 65 out, Apple M3 Pro, real scheduler, fresh random prompts (no radix short-circuit), medians of warm runs. Base-commit columns measure the pre-existing paths; the region column is the only one containing this proposal's code (measured on the RFC branch, noob-se7en#2; the same region code is upstream as #36164). | Qwen3-0.6B, 512 in / 65 out | SGLang Torch eager (base commit) | SGLang MLX lane + overlap (base commit) | SGLang MLX region (this branch) | mlx-lm (standalone) (not SGLang) | Region vs Torch eager | | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | | Time to first token (ms, lower is better) | 318 | 157 | 233 | 135 (prompt processing only) | 1.4x faster | | Batch 1 (output tok/s, higher is better) | 18.1 | 75.7 | 58.7 | 80.8 | 3.2x | | Batch 4 (output tok/s) | 39.2 | 95.5 | 115.3 | — | 2.9x | | Batch 8 (output tok/s) | 49.0 | 126.8 | 167.8 | 228.6 | 3.4x | | Batch 16 (output tok/s) | 57.4 | 130.0 | 204.9 | 251.0 | 3.6x | The lane leads at batch 1 (its `mx.async_eval` hides per-step host work the region still exposes — overlap scheduling is a roadmap item); the region leads from batch 4 and keeps scaling while the lane goes flat. At the region boundary, exported decode runs at 12.19 ms vs 11.31 ms for a native `mlx_lm` forward (~93 %); prefill at 142 ms vs 126 ms (~89 %), the remainder being un-fused norm/rope chains. **Correctness.** Server-level greedy A/B against the eager path: exact token match for decode; with prefill in the region, one divergence traced to an exact bf16 logit tie (both engines' top-1 margins 0.0625). The validation harness on the RFC branch passes logit cosine/top-5 gates, exact KV commit, and 17-step lockstep parity; #36164 adds a serving-boundary test that uses `LogitsProcessor` itself as the oracle on a padded-vocabulary fixture. **Architectures**, no model-specific code (flag off is this branch's Torch MPS path, flag on is the exported region; both include sampling and scheduler overhead): | Model | Family | Q/KV heads | Head dim | Lockstep parity (17 steps) | Decode per step, batch 1 (flag off to on) | Speedup | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | ---: | ---: | | Qwen3-0.6B | qwen3 | 16/8 | 128 | match | 44.0 to 13.8 ms | 3.2x | | Qwen2.5-Coder-1.5B | qwen2 | 12/2 | 128 | match | 58.3 to 27.1 ms | 2.15x | | SmolLM2-360M-Instruct | llama | 15/5 | 64 | match | 31.6 to 8.7 ms | 3.6x | ## Roadmap Two review units carry the architecture change; everything else plugs into a stable seam of the core stack and proceeds independently. Work items carry the PR that implements them once it exists. ### 1. Core stack - [x] **Runtime pair + Torch–MLX tensor-bridge contract** (Torch 2.13 / MLX 0.32; independent copies, scoped/persistent zero-copy borrows, DLPack result export): @yeahdongcn #32984 - [ ] **Whole-model MLX region** — capture → lowering → serving, decode + single-request prefill, `SGLANG_ENABLE_MLX_WHOLE_REGION` (off by default), eager fallback per batch: @noob-se7en #36164 *(in review)* - [x] semantic attention op under `torch.export`; structural decoder-body resolution (no per-model adapters) - [x] FX→MLX lowering; deferred paged-attention kernel; deferred KV commit with startup write-probe - [x] startup export ladder (`SGLANG_MLX_REGION_STARTUP_EXPORT`: OFF / DECODE / ALL), CUDA-capture parity - [x] serving-boundary oracle test (`LogitsProcessor` as oracle on a padded-vocab fixture) - [ ] **Native MLX lane removal** (2–3 PRs, after parity sign-off on #36164): `MlxTpModelWorker` / `MlxModelRunner` / scheduler mixin; `mlx/kv_cache`, `layers/quantization/mlx.py`, `mlx/models`; `SGLANG_USE_MLX` and the `mlx` CI suite → `mps` - [ ] **Torch eager path on MPS (flag-off serving)** — three independent PRs, none a dependency of the region: - [ ] platform device lifecycle (`platforms/mps.py`, `get_device`/`set_device`/`create_stream`/memory queries on the platform interface; retires the `_mps_stub` monkeypatching) - [ ] direct Metal semantic ops for eager (RMSNorm, SiLU-and-mul Metal-JIT; `fused_op` `"mps"` dispatch entry) - @ItsOdeLeo - [ ] torch-native LoRA on MPS (lm_head-pruned batch metadata; CPU-only metadata on MPS) ### 2. Kernels and lowering (the op table) - [ ] **Kernel tuning + benchmarking PR** (separate from the region, per review): paged *prefill* kernel for radix-prefix batches (currently the weak kernel; proposed for #36164: the region declines prefix-hit prefills until it lands); block-table decode kernel from #32451 retargeted to the Torch pool behind `mlx_radix_attention`; AOT Metal build path from #32451 (first-request latency, replaces `torch.mps.compile_shader` for the KV commit); `index_copy_` fallback for the commit - [ ] **`mx.fast.rope` / RMSNorm-chain pattern matching** in the lowering — prefill region 142 → ~126 ms; benefits every architecture - [ ] **Logits path**: return hidden states and run the real `LogitsProcessor`, or capture through it — lifts logit-scale/softcap rejection and enables prompt logprobs (~30 rejected architectures: Gemma, Cohere, Granite, InternLM2, …) - [ ] **Packed multi-request prefill** (per-request segmenting in the prefill graph) - [ ] **MoE ops lowering** (`FusedMoE` routing/experts → `mx`; unlocks 40 registered MoE architectures) - [ ] **Attention variants**: sliding-window, MLA (split QK/V head dims), attention logit cap - [ ] **SSM / linear-attention layers** for hybrid stacks (Qwen3-Next, NemotronH, Qwen3.5) - [ ] **Quantized serving** (Torch-side quantized checkpoint format + `mx.quantized_matmul` lowering) — the one capability lost with the native lane ### 3. Model coverage: (1) eager Torch path vs (2) region, per architecture One matrix, two columns per architecture: correctness (greedy token match between the eager path and the region on the same prompts) and speed (decode step and TTFT, flag off vs on). Each family is either verified, or blocked on one named item from §2 — never on per-model code. - [ ] Run both paths across the architecture families below and publish the matrix - [x] correctness verified, exact match: Qwen3 (Qwen3-0.6B), Qwen2 (Qwen2.5-Coder-1.5B), Llama (SmolLM2-360M), GPT-2, OPT, Phi (phi-1_5) — padded-vocab and non-standard body signatures included - [ ] speed per family (measured so far at batch 1: Qwen3 3.2×, Qwen2.5-Coder 2.15×, SmolLM2 3.6×) - [ ] Qwen3-MoE, Mixtral, OLMoE, DBRX, GLM4-MoE — *blocked on MoE lowering* - [ ] Gemma 2/3, Cohere, Granite, InternLM2 — *blocked on the logits path (+ sliding window for Gemma)* - [ ] Qwen3-Next, NemotronH, Qwen3.5 — *blocked on SSM/linear-attention lowering* - [ ] DeepSeek V2/V3, MiMo-V2 — *blocked on MLA kernels* - [ ] Qwen3-VL / Qwen2.5-VL text-only requests — *blocked on the `input_embeds` path* - [x] Static classification of all 239 registered architectures against the region's startup gates: 43 pass, 40 MoE lowering-gap, 149 rejected → eager ### 4. Performance - [x] Baseline (Apple M3 Pro, Qwen3-0.6B bf16, 512 in / 65 out): 3.2–3.6× e2e decode tok/s over eager, TTFT 318 → 233 ms; decode region ~93 % of `mlx_lm`, prefill ~89 % - [ ] Overlap scheduling on MPS (hide per-step host work — the largest remaining e2e decode lever; scheduler seam, independent of the region) - [ ] Decode batch padding to the export ladder (fewer executors, CUDA-graph-style) - [ ] In-tree region validation harness (`bench_export_region`: logit gates, exact KV commit, lockstep parity) + `bench_one_batch --skewed-input-lens` - [ ] Alternative executors in the same graph-runner slot, benchmarked as drop-ins when available: torch.mps graph capture (pytorch/pytorch#180397), Inductor-Metal (`torch.export` + Inductor) ### 5. Testing and CI - [x] `register_mps_ci` marker (additive; in #36164) - [ ] MPS CI workflow + self-hosted Apple Silicon runner; model-free MPS tests automatic - [ ] Documented repeatable real-model validation path until CI hardware exists - [ ] Weight-update lifecycle end-to-end test against the storage-identity re-export ### 6. Documentation - [ ] Apple Silicon serving guide: region flag, startup-export knob, supported-architecture matrix, fallback behavior ## Alternatives considered ### Keep the native MLX runner behind a stronger worker contract This was the original proposal. It remains the fallback if the unified Torch-owned path cannot meet serving or performance requirements. It improves the boundary but preserves two model and KV lifecycles. ### Dispatch individual Torch operations through MLX This is generic but pays the framework boundary repeatedly. Direct Metal kernels are a better fit for small operations. ### Model adapters plus reusable MLX blocks An earlier revision of this proposal built the region from per-architecture adapters: a declarative model descriptor resolved through a registry, composing reusable MLX normalization, attention and MLP blocks. The adapter layer was introduced to cut the per-model duplication of the provider approach below. It has real advantages: block-level fusion is available immediately and nothing depends on `torch.export`. But the descriptor and blocks are still a second implementation of the model math, per architecture, which is the drift class this document exists to remove. The exported region keeps the Torch model as the single source of truth and moves fusion into the lowering. ### Per-model MLX and Metal implementations behind providers The parallel draft (yeahdongcn/sglang#7) takes this shape: a provider registry resolves a typed model-family plan, and each supported family carries its own MLX/Metal implementation. It produces a broad execution region and its hand-fused variants show the available fusion headroom (90%+ of `mlx_lm` prefill on M1), but common transformer logic is duplicated across architectures and every family is a separately maintained rewrite. The exported region preserves the broad region without either.

title: [RFC]: Native Heterogeneous Weight Conversion in SGLang
author: Bo-Vincent
body:
## Motivation SGLang can already load or update weights from checkpoints and remote instances, but these paths mainly assume compatible source and target layouts. That assumption does not hold when scaling, failover, RL training/inference transitions, or resource scheduling changes TP, PP, EP, and DP at the same time. SGLang needs a native, backend-neutral way to convert weights between these layouts. The full workflow needs to: 1. Export stable logical semantics for every runtime tensor. 2. Describe the actual sharding, ownership, and physical location of source and target tensors. 3. Jointly plan N-D resharding across TP, PP, EP, and DP. 4. Bind the logical plan safely to live GPU, Store, or checkpoint data. 5. Execute transfers through pluggable backends. 6. Keep the source serving read-only traffic and activate the target only after full validation. Without a shared conversion layer, model semantics, parallel layouts, and backend details remain scattered across `load_weights`, `ModelRunner`, distributed workers, and remote loaders. A transfer backend can move bytes, but it should not infer model structure from names such as `q_proj`, `down_proj`, or `expert`. This RFC proposes a complete **SGLang-native heterogeneous weight conversion layer**. Runtime manifests, physical bindings, snapshot leases, and model adapters are components of this capability rather than separate end goals. ## Proposal ```mermaid flowchart TB P["Source Placement + Target Placement"] L["LogicalTransferPlan
address-independent"] B["Source Binding + Target Binding"] T["TransferPlan
executable"] E["TE / Store executor"] P -->|"N-D planning"| L L --> T B -->|"bind and validate"| T T --> E ``` Placement is address-independent and is the only input to N-D planning. Runtime Binding adds the current addresses, endpoints, generation, and lease immediately before execution. Address changes therefore require rebinding, not replanning. For a Store source, the stored fragment/object-range mapping acts as the source binding; only the target requires a live Runtime Binding. ### Scope This proposal covers: * Byte-compatible weight conversion when TP, PP, EP, and DP change together. * Live runtime, Store/L3, and checkpoint/OSS sources. * Model semantics, the canonical transfer plan, and target activation owned by SGLang. * Pluggable execution through Mooncake, local CUDA, NCCL M2N, or other backends. * Compatibility with existing one-dimensional TP, checkpoint loading, and remote update paths. The first version does not perform arbitrary dtype conversion, quantization, swizzling, or backend-private packed-layout transforms. It also does not make Mooncake, NCCL M2N, or any transfer runtime a hard dependency. ### Architecture | Component | Responsibility | | --- | --- | | Model adapter | Export tensor semantics, Placement, and Binding from the actual runtime | | Snapshot/lifecycle | Pin the source generation and manage leases and target activation | | N-D planner | Jointly plan TP/PP/EP/DP changes and produce backend-neutral regions | | Binder/validator | Bind current physical locations and validate layout, coverage, and bounds | | Executor provider | Lower validated regions to TE, CUDA, or another backend | ```text source/target Placement -> N-D planner -> LogicalWeightTransferPlan current Bindings -> bind/validate -> executor -> barrier/activate ``` The model adapter and runtime manifest are the sources of truth for model semantics and physical locations. The planner does not read addresses, and the executor does not reinterpret model structure. ### Core contracts | Contract | Content | | --- | --- | | Placement | model/revision, tensor ID, global/local box, layer/expert ownership, shard dimensions, dtype/layout | | Binding | placement ID, generation/lease, and a GPU address, Store object range, or checkpoint range | | LogicalWeightTransferPlan | tensor/fragment IDs, overlap offset/shape, base offsets, inner bytes, outer loops, and strides | Placement is address-independent. Binding refers to one concrete resource instance. The logical plan contains no address, object key, lease, or backend handle, so the same plan can run against live G2G, Store/L3, or checkpoint/OSS sources. Target parallelism values alone are not enough. SGLang must first create the non-serving target model and its final buffers, then export the actual target Placement and Binding. This is necessary for fused tensors, separate expert allocations, packed layouts, and real buffer addresses. ### Joint TP/PP/EP/DP planning | Axis | Planning semantics | | --- | --- | | TP | N-D logical-box intersections, including TP4 to TP8, TP8 to TP4, and cross-dimension sharding | | PP | Routing by explicit layer/tensor ownership through `(src_pp, dst_pp)` groups | | EP | Expert ID as a leading logical coordinate, including EP8 to EP2 and EP/TP cross-dimension sharding | | DP | Source replica selection without sharding weight contents; every target replica receives full coverage | For `TP4/PP2/EP8/DP2 -> TP8/PP4/EP2/DP4`, the planner directly combines DP replica selection, PP routing, and expert/TP intersections. It does not build intermediate TP, PP, or EP layouts. PP does not rely on benchmark-specific layer formulas, and EP does not require independent allocations to be packed or all-gathered. The legacy single `partition_dim` is adapted into a one-dimensional logical box, preserving the current TP4 to TP8 and TP8 to TP4 behavior. ### Execution and lifecycle Before submission, the binder validates revision/layout compatibility, lease/generation state, physical bounds, full target coverage, and the absence of overlapping writes. Executors follow a common lifecycle: ```text probe -> prepare -> submit -> wait/cancel -> synchronize -> release ``` Providers advertise capabilities such as G2G, Store ranges, scatter, strided regions, and cancellation. Lowering must keep the operation count bounded and must not expand a plan into one operation per row or element. SGLang provides a local/mock executor as the baseline. The current N-D planner reference implementation is in Mooncake; SGLang will implement the same canonical planning semantics. Mooncake TE/Store remains an optional provider, and NCCL M2N can be used as an optional executor when its constraints are met. A live source may continue serving read-only inference while its snapshot lease is valid, but the referenced weights cannot be modified, released, or reallocated. The target follows this flow: ```text allocate final buffers -> export manifests -> plan/transfer -> validate/world barrier -> commit revision and activate ``` Failures, timeouts, stale generations, revoked leases, coverage gaps, and out-of-bounds regions fail closed. The target must not enter serving in any of these cases. ### Model and layout extensibility Model adapters are implemented per architecture family. The first version only supports byte-compatible resharding. A future extension may add an explicit `LogicalWeightTransformPlan`: ```text WeightConversionPlan = optional LogicalWeightTransformPlan + LogicalWeightTransferPlan ``` This can cover dtype conversion, W31/W13 transforms, fuse/split, pack/swizzle, and delta reuse. Each transform must be declared explicitly by the model adapter. ## Compatibility and failure behavior * Disabling the feature leaves normal serving and loading unchanged. * Legacy `runtime_v1` manifests and single `partition_dim` inputs remain available through adapters. * Existing loaders continue to own quantization, fuse, pack, and swizzle logic. * Schema or capability mismatches return explicit errors instead of falling back to an unvalidated copy. * Mooncake and other providers remain optional dependencies. ## Phasing | Phase | Scope | | --- | --- | | 1. Core contract | Stabilize Placement, Binding, tensor identity, N-D regions, and legacy manifest compatibility | | 2. Native planner | Implement joint TP/PP/EP/DP planning, coverage validation, bounded lowering, and a local/mock executor | | 3. Executors and storage APIs | Provide backend-neutral loading from a live runtime, Store/L3, or checkpoint/OSS into a target runtime, as well as staging runtime snapshots or checkpoint/OSS weights into Store/L3 | | 4. Models and transforms | Extend the Qwen baseline to DeepSeek, Llama/Mistral, Mixtral, multimodal models, and explicit transforms | These phases are incremental steps toward one complete capability. The core contract is foundational infrastructure for the conversion layer, not a standalone end state. ## Acceptance criteria * TP4 to TP8 and TP8 to TP4, PP2 to PP4 and PP4 to PP2, and EP8 to EP2 and EP2 to EP8. * Dim0 to dim1 and dim0 to dim2 for `[experts, out, in]`. * `TP4/PP2/EP8/DP2 -> TP8/PP4/EP2/DP4`. * Regression coverage for live G2G, Store, checkpoint, and legacy manifests. * Byte-exact target tensors with full coverage and no overlapping writes. * Bounded operation counts, source-serving continuity, and successful target activation/rollback behavior. ## Open questions 1. Should this design eventually support broader reuse scenarios such as FP16 to FP8 conversion? 2. Should the first schema reserve a `LogicalWeightTransformPlan`? ## Related resources * [Mooncake heterogeneous weight transfer companion RFC](https://github.com/kvcache-ai/Mooncake/issues/3111)

title: [RFC] Define Metadata, Workspace, and Stream-Ownership Contracts for Dynamic CUDA Graph Replay
author: Phoenix3334
body:
## Summary

This RFC proposes explicit runtime contracts for dynamic CUDA Graph paths that reuse Graph-static metadata, workspaces, request/KV slots, captured buffers, kernel-produced plans/indices, and alternate streams across asynchronous iterations.

The original motivation came from the DSpark compact ragged target-verify investigations in #31023 / #33356. Since this RFC was opened, that investigation has separated several **different correctness layers** that originally surfaced through similar CUDA illegal-memory / graph failures:

```text
control-plane consistency
  -> kernel-produced plan correctness
  -> capture-initialization ordering
  -> replay-time ownership / stream / lifetime contracts
```

The current evidence is useful precisely because these mechanisms are no longer being conflated:

- **#31195** addresses cross-TP verify-budget / target-Graph-tier consistency.
- **#32467** addresses a producer-side race in `plan_compress_prefill_kernel0` that can emit invalid ragged plans.
- **#33795** proposes the final warmup-to-capture completion boundary for `FullCudaGraphBackend` and has independent H200 evidence.
- **#34286** applies and regression-tests the same capture-initialization invariant for `BreakableCudaGraphBackend`.

The B300 investigation therefore no longer supports treating generic metadata/workspace lifetime reuse as the default explanation for every observed failure. At the same time, the fact that the same warmup-to-capture invariant appears independently in both Full and Breakable graph backends strengthens the case for making these contracts explicit and eventually sharing enforcement where appropriate.

This RFC is **not** a claim that all DSpark failures have one common root cause. It is a proposal to make the assumptions required by asynchronous graph capture/replay reviewable, testable, and enforceable across backends.

---

## Evidence update — 2026-08-10

### 1. Cross-TP control-plane inconsistency is a separate contract

PR #31195 fixes a real control-plane bug in which TP ranks could independently resolve different verify budgets and therefore choose different target CUDA-Graph tiers for the same decode step.

Observed before the fix:

```text
TP0 target Graph key = 160
TP1 target Graph key = 144
raw batch size = 32 on both ranks
```

After broadcasting TP0's final verify budget, the tested TP8 matrix completed:

```text
no-overlap, same service:          30/30
no-overlap, restart per workload:  30/30
overlap, same service:             30/30
overlap, restart per workload:     30/30
Total:                            120/120

verify_token_budget divergence: 0
sum(verify_lens) divergence:     0
target Graph-key divergence:    0
```

This belongs to a **distributed control-plane consistency contract**, not to workspace ownership or kernel-memory lifetime.

### 2. B300 producer-side plan corruption is directly observed

PR #32467 targets `plan_compress_prefill_kernel0`.

The original kernel initializes every `warp_min` / `warp_max` scratch slot from warp 0 and then lets each warp overwrite its own slot during Stage B. Without ordering between those operations, warp 0 can clobber another warp's already-written reduction result. A genuinely ragged `extend_lens` vector can then appear uniform and select the MTP-uniform fast path, producing `ragged_id` from `B * s_max` rather than the actual ragged row count.

The direct single-GPU B30Z regression originally showed:

```text
unpatched: 2592 bad plans / 6000 calls
patched:      0 bad plans / 30000 calls
```

Characteristic corruption:

```text
rmax = 383 = B * s_max - 1
actual ragged rows = 360
```

Full-model B300/TP8 validation with #32467 alone also passed the tested startup and sustained-replay paths:

```text
startup capture: 3/3 READY, 35/35 shapes each
runtime Gate 1:  320/320, Graph replay observed, no GPU fault
strong path:     512/512, compact + SPS + c256 + 60k/1k, no GPU fault
```

This establishes a producer-side correctness failure **before** downstream Triton / TRT-LLM / DeepGEMM / cuBLAS sites surface the sticky CUDA error.

#### Reviewer simplification: remove the redundant initialization

@DarkSharpness later asked whether the scratch initialization can be dropped entirely, because the launch is structurally 1024 threads / 32 warps and every warp overwrites its own slot before the existing post-reduction `__syncthreads()`.

A same-session A/B/C kernel experiment tested exactly that proposal, 10,000 calls per case / 30,000 per variant:

| Variant | scratch init | extra pre-reduction barrier | OOB plans |
|---|:---:|:---:|---:|
| A: original | ON | OFF | **13111 / 30000** |
| B: current #32467 | ON | ON | **0 / 30000** |
| C: reviewer variant | OFF | OFF | **0 / 30000** |

Inputs:

```text
[4] * 96
[4] * 72 + [3] * 24
[3] * 104 + [2] * 24
```

Core oracle:

```text
max(valid ragged_id) < sum(extend_lens)
```

This supports the simpler no-initialization formulation under the current fixed launch geometry. If that implementation is adopted, the dependency on the 32-warp launch invariant should be made explicit with a comment/assertion so a future dynamic launch change cannot silently invalidate it.

The broader RFC lesson is unchanged: **kernel-produced plans/indices need their own correctness contract**; perfectly stable metadata ownership cannot compensate for a producer that emits an invalid index.

### 3. FullCudaGraphBackend has a separate capture-initialization gap

#33795, authored by @Leoyzen, identifies the following boundary in `FullCudaGraphBackend.capture_one()`:

```text
warmup forward / post_warmup_hook
  -> no final device/TP completion boundary
  -> graph construction / capture
```

The proposed correction is:

```python
self._device_module.synchronize()
self._tp_group.barrier()
# then enter CUDA Graph construction/capture
```

H200/TP4 has independent evidence that this boundary matters in that environment.

On the tested B300/TP8 reproducer, however:

```text
#33795 only: 1/6 READY
#32467 only: 3/3 READY + sustained replay clean
```

Therefore #33795 is not the primary B300 producer fix and should not be used to reinterpret the #32467 kernel evidence. It exercises a separate **capture initialization contract**.

### 4. BreakableCudaGraphBackend has the same structural boundary

#34286 extends the capture-initialization invariant to `BreakableCudaGraphBackend`.

Current structure before the fix:

```text
warmup 1: sync -> TP barrier -> forward -> hook
warmup 2: sync -> TP barrier -> forward -> hook
                                      |
                                      +--> directly construct BreakableCUDAGraph
```

The PR adds:

```text
final warmup / hook
  -> device synchronize
  -> TP barrier
  -> BreakableCUDAGraph construction
```

and adds a CPU-only deterministic ordering regression that requires:

```text
final post_warmup_hook
  < synchronize
  < barrier
  < BreakableCUDAGraph construction
```

The regression was first run against unpatched production code and failed specifically on the missing boundary; after the production change it passed. The relevant runner-backend suite passed 5/5 and pre-commit was clean after rebasing onto current main.

Scope matters: #34286 does **not** claim a natural BCG crash reproducer and does **not** claim to fix the #32467 B300 producer bug. Its value is that the same capture-initialization invariant is now visible in a second backend and protected by a focused regression.

### 5. What this changes for the RFC

Originally, several contracts in this RFC were motivated by a broad search for the cause of #31023. The evidence now supports a cleaner decomposition:

```text
#31195
  distributed control-plane consistency

#32467
  kernel-produced plan/index correctness

#33795
  FullCudaGraphBackend capture initialization

#34286
  BreakableCudaGraphBackend capture initialization

#32432
  shared vocabulary / review contracts / future reusable helpers
```

This makes the RFC stronger rather than weaker: concrete incidents now map to distinct contracts instead of one vague "CUDA Graph lifetime" category.

---

## Investigation lineage and contributions

The current picture was built collaboratively across several reproductions and review cycles:

- **@EanWang211123** authored #31195 and #32467, providing the concrete fixes for cross-TP graph-tier alignment and the ragged prefill-plan race.
- **@Leoyzen** independently reproduced the H200/TP4 capture problem, developed the warmup/JIT-to-capture ordering hypothesis, and authored #33795 for the Full CUDA Graph backend.
- **@hassellof** independently validated #32467 on RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell / SM120, contributed a separate shape/allocator failure matrix, and helped cross-check the interaction between #32467 and #33795 across hardware.
- **@DarkSharpness** reviewed #32467 and proposed removing the redundant warp scratch initialization rather than adding another barrier; the resulting A/B/C regression validated that simplification on B30Z.
- **#31023 / #33356** supplied the B300/TP8 startup and sustained-replay isolation matrices, direct producer regression, four-arm #32467 × #33795 comparison, and cross-version follow-up that separated downstream surfacing sites from producer evidence.

The purpose of recording this provenance is not to imply that every contributor endorses every hypothesis in this RFC; it is to make clear which observations and fixes established each layer of the current model.

---

## Motivation

A dynamic speculative-verification path maps runtime decisions into reusable GPU state:

```text
per-request verify length / layout
  -> verify_lens / qo_indptr / positions / request + KV locations
  -> Graph tier selection
  -> Graph-static metadata + workspace refresh
  -> CUDA Graph replay
```

Overlap scheduling may prepare the next batch while previous GPU work is still in flight:

```text
replay stream:        execute batch N
plan/copy/aux stream: prepare batch N+1
```

Correctness depends on more than Python call order. A safe implementation must make clear:

- which distributed decisions must be identical across ranks;
- which object identities / addresses are capture-stable;
- which contents may change on replay;
- whether updates happen in place or by object replacement;
- who owns reusable storage at each generation;
- which stream produces an update and which stream consumes it;
- when a request slot, KV location, or workspace can be reused;
- whether one-time JIT / module loading / lazy initialization has completed before capture;
- which dimensions require a distinct Graph key versus only larger capacity;
- what structural invariants kernel-produced plans/indices must satisfy.

---

## Proposed runtime contracts

### 1. Distributed control-plane consistency contract

Before TP/DP/EP ranks enter collectives or select captured Graph variants for the same logical step, all layout-defining distributed decisions must agree.

Examples include:

```text
verify-token budget
graph_num_tokens / target Graph tier
collective token shape
layout mode / path selection
```

Core invariant:

> Two ranks participating in the same logical collective/captured step must not independently choose incompatible layout dimensions.

#31195 is a concrete example of enforcing this contract by broadcasting the final verify budget before Graph-tier selection.

### 2. Graph-static metadata contract

For every metadata field consumed by a captured Graph, define:

- whether Python object identity must remain stable;
- whether backing storage address must remain stable;
- whether contents are refreshed before every replay;
- whether refresh is in-place or object-replacing;
- whether nested metadata is recursively refreshed;
- whether the value is prepared outside the Graph or produced inside capture;
- minimum storage capacity for all layouts sharing the Graph.

Core invariant:

> Before replay starts, every dynamic value consumed by the Graph must be fully initialized, visible to the consumer stream, and backed by storage valid for the complete replay lifetime.

### 3. Workspace ownership contract

Every reusable workspace should expose or internally enforce:

```text
workspace identity
capacity
owner component
owner replay/batch generation
producer stream
consumer stream(s)
reuse-completion condition
```

Core invariant:

> A workspace must not be overwritten, resized, rebound, or reassigned until its last GPU consumer has completed.

Possible implementations include per-stream workspaces, double buffering, generation-tagged ownership, or event-guarded reuse. This RFC does not prescribe one universal mechanism.

### 4. Stream-ordering contract

Cross-stream dependencies should be explicit rather than inferred from host execution order.

A proven dependency may look like:

```python
ready_event.record(producer_stream)
consumer_stream.wait_event(ready_event)
```

The contract should cover:

- metadata / plan preparation streams;
- graph replay streams;
- result / copy streams;
- graph-internal alternate streams used by attention, indexer, compressor, communication, or custom kernels;
- one-time warmup/JIT work before capture.

A host-side event does not automatically prove correctness for graph-internal alternate-stream work, so internal dependencies must remain auditable.

### 5. Capture initialization contract

Backends should explicitly define when capture may begin.

Core invariant:

> All asynchronous work triggered by eager warmup, lazy initialization, module loading, first-use JIT, or warmup hooks that is not capture-safe must complete before entering the capture region; distributed ranks that must capture coherently must rendezvous at the same boundary.

This contract is now exercised independently by:

```text
#33795 -> FullCudaGraphBackend
#34286 -> BreakableCudaGraphBackend
```

This is the strongest current candidate for a future shared backend helper, but extracting one should wait until the exact semantics of both backends are reviewed and the individual fixes land.

### 6. Graph/cache-key contract

Graph state should distinguish:

1. **Capture-shape dimensions** — require a distinct captured graph.
2. **Capacity dimensions** — may share a graph only when static storage/workspaces cover the worst case.
3. **Per-replay mutable contents** — may vary if completely refreshed and correctly ordered.

The audit should consider dimensions such as:

```text
graph_num_tokens
raw batch size
verify_lens distribution
qo_indptr/layout shape
page-table dimensions
workspace requirement
attention/indexer/compressor variant
stream index
backend variant
```

Not every field belongs in the key. If a field is omitted, the implementation should make explicit why sharing is safe.

### 7. Request/KV-slot lifetime contract

Request-pool entries, KV locations, page-table entries, and output-cache locations must not be recycled while any in-flight Graph or alternate-stream consumer can still reference them.

Core invariant:

> CPU/scheduler logical completion is not sufficient for reuse unless GPU consumer completion is also established.

### 8. Kernel-produced plan/index contract

The #32467 investigation demonstrates that Graph metadata may be perfectly owned and ordered while a producer kernel itself emits invalid indices.

For index/plan producers, debug or regression coverage should assert structural invariants such as:

```text
index < backing capacity
ragged_id < real ragged row count
batch_id < batch size
workspace offset < allocated workspace
```

Where possible, these invariants should be testable with small kernel-level regressions rather than only full-model stress tests.

Kernel scratch initialization/reduction assumptions should also be explicit. If correctness depends on fixed launch geometry (for example, every scratch slot being overwritten by exactly one warp), encode that dependency in a static assertion/comment or derive the implementation so the invariant is structurally unavoidable.

### 9. Debuggability contract

Dynamic Graph backends should provide opt-in, synchronization-free tracing for:

```text
replay sequence
rank
Graph key
batch/request generation
metadata identity
data_ptr / shape / stride / storage capacity
workspace identity / capacity / generation
producer and consumer stream identity
```

Debug logging should avoid CUDA tensor `.item()` or unconditional device synchronization because observer effects can suppress timing-sensitive failures.

Observations should be labeled by scope, for example:

```text
PROVEN: covers whole captured graph completion
PARTIAL: does not identify a component's exact last-consumer point
UNKNOWN: internal lifetime not exposed by host instrumentation
```

---

## Non-goals

This RFC does not propose:

- an unconditional hot-path `torch.cuda.synchronize()`;
- one universal workspace implementation for every backend;
- converting every dynamic layout field into a Graph key;
- treating old diagnostic synchronization switches from #31455 as a production fix;
- claiming that metadata/workspace lifetime caused the #32467 B300 plan-kernel corruption;
- claiming that #32467 explains the independent H200 warmup/capture ordering behavior;
- claiming that #33795 or #34286 explains every DSpark CUDA-Graph failure;
- prematurely merging Full and Breakable capture logic before their backend-specific semantics are reviewed.

---

## Proposed phased adoption

### Phase 1 — Document and assert local invariants

- document distributed layout decisions that must agree across ranks;
- document metadata ownership and capture-stable addresses;
- document capture-initialization boundaries;
- assert workspace / plan / index capacity assumptions where cheap;
- add deterministic regression tests for known producer bugs such as #32467;
- add ordering regressions for backend capture boundaries such as #34286;
- identify graph-internal alternate-stream dependencies.

### Phase 2 — Localized correctness fixes

When evidence identifies a violated contract, implement the smallest correction:

- cross-rank broadcast / agreement point;
- missing kernel barrier or removal of a racy redundant initialization;
- targeted stream event dependency;
- complete nested metadata refresh;
- workspace ownership/reuse guard;
- capacity correction;
- Graph/cache-key refinement;
- request/KV lifetime correction;
- explicit post-warmup completion boundary.

### Phase 3 — Shared backend helpers

Extract common helpers/interfaces only after the same invariant appears in more than one backend/path and the local semantics are understood.

The Full/Breakable capture-initialization pair (#33795 / #34286) is now a concrete candidate for evaluating this phase.

Potential surfaces include:

- capture-initialization helper;
- Graph-static metadata refresh protocol;
- event-aware reusable workspace wrapper;
- generation/ownership tracing helper;
- Graph-key capacity assertions;
- distributed layout-agreement helper where applicable.

---

## Open questions

1. Should Full and Breakable CUDA Graph backends share an explicit `finish_warmup_before_capture()`-style helper once #33795 / #34286 semantics are settled?
2. Which ownership/generation state belongs in the Graph runner versus the attention/indexer/compressor backend?
3. Which graph-internal streams are guaranteed by current capture semantics and which need explicit events?
4. Should capacity dimensions participate directly in Graph keys or be enforced through worst-case allocation + assertions?
5. Can request/KV-slot reuse be tied to existing completion events without a scheduler-wide synchronization point?
6. Which index/plan invariants can be checked cheaply in GPU CI?
7. If #32467 adopts the no-initialization variant, where should the fixed 32-warp launch invariant be asserted so future launch changes fail loudly?
8. What tracing can remain compiled into production with near-zero cost while disabled?

---

## Relationship to existing work

- #31023 — historical compact target-verify runtime evidence and B300 sustained-replay isolation.
- #33356 — startup-capture evidence, B300/H200 separation, and cross-version follow-up.
- #31195 — cross-TP verify-budget / Graph-tier planning fix.
- #32467 — concrete plan-kernel race, direct OOB-plan regression, and reviewer-driven no-init simplification experiment.
- #33795 — FullCudaGraphBackend warmup-to-capture ordering boundary with H200 evidence.
- #34286 — BreakableCudaGraphBackend warmup-to-capture ordering invariant + deterministic CPU regression.
- #31455 — historical diagnostic synchronization / metadata tracing work.

## Expected outcome

SGLang dynamic CUDA Graph paths should have explicit, reviewable invariants for distributed layout agreement, capture initialization, metadata refresh, storage capacity, plan/index validity, stream ordering, workspace ownership, and request/KV lifetime.

The goal is to preserve asynchronous overlap and CUDA Graph performance while preventing both **producer-side invalid state** and **consumer-side stale/early-reused state**, without relying on global synchronization as a blanket fix.

title: [RFC] A Unified KV-Cache Sparsity Framework for Post-Hoc Sparse Attention
author: magicYang1573
body:
## Motivation

An increasing number of KV-cache sparsification methods can be applied to existing dense-attention checkpoints without training a model-native sparse indexer. Examples include fixed-pattern selection, KV-derived selection, and current-query-aware retrieval.

We refer to this family as **post-hoc or non-native KV sparsity**:

- the model was not trained with a native sparse-attention architecture;
- the sparse policy is attached at inference time;
- the policy decides which cached KV entries are visible to an existing attention backend;
- the same framework can potentially support many dense MHA/GQA model families.

This scope is broader than a model-specific sparse implementation. A unified framework would make it possible to:

- experiment with new sparse methods on existing dense checkpoints;
- share request, decode-step, and layer lifecycle hooks;
- reuse logical-to-physical KV translation;
- reuse attention-backend integration and CUDA Graph support;
- compare methods under the same serving conditions;
- add a new method without modifying the model runner and attention backend again.

Today, SGLang does not yet provide a complete runtime framework for this use case. Some abstractions have been merged, and several Quest/HiSparse efforts are in progress, but the common interface and serving integration remain incomplete or method-specific.


## Current State

### Existing `mem_cache/sparsity` interfaces

SGLang `main` already contains a sparse algorithm skeleton under:

```text
python/sglang/srt/mem_cache/sparsity/
├── algorithms/
│   ├── base_algorithm.py
│   ├── quest_algorithm.py
│   └── deepseek_dsa.py
├── backend/
│   └── backend_adaptor.py
├── core/
│   └── sparse_coordinator.py
└── factory.py
```

The existing code introduces several useful ideas:

- `BaseSparseAlgorithm` for representation construction, updates, and retrieval;
- `SparseCoordinator` for request/forward/attention lifecycle hooks;
- logical sparse indices independent of physical KV locations;
- `BackendAdaptor` for translating a logical selection into backend metadata;
- an initial Quest implementation and FlashAttention adaptor.

These pieces were introduced mainly by:

- [#14741 — Add Sparse Interface](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/14741)
- [#16086 — Init sparse coordinator](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/16086)

They provide a useful starting point, but the current implementation has several limitations.

#### 1. It is not connected to the live inference path

`create_sparse_coordinator()` has no serving caller in `main`, and the coordinator's attention hooks are not invoked by the normal model execution path. As a result, enabling the existing configuration does not make a dense model execute Quest or another post-hoc sparse policy end to end.

#### 2. The interface contract is underspecified

The current interface does not completely define:

- whether indices are logical tokens, logical pages, or physical locations;
- how policy granularity is matched to backend granularity;
- how ragged, multi-token, speculative, or padded query layouts are represented;
- how dense and sparse requests coexist in the same batch;
- how fixed-capacity outputs are represented for CUDA Graph;
- when a selection may be reused across requests, steps, or layers;
- who owns and restores dense backend metadata;
- which runtime evidence a policy requires.

#### 3. Request lifecycle correctness is incomplete

Sparse state is indexed primarily by `req_pool_idx`, but request-pool slots are reused. The framework does not currently use `ReqToTokenPool.req_generation` as part of request identity, and request begin/end hooks are not wired into all serving paths.

Without a generation-aware state contract, a reused request slot can inherit stale sparse representations.

#### 4. Forward and offload responsibilities are mixed

The coordinator contains hierarchical/offload-oriented fields and TODOs such as:

- `device_buffer_size`;
- `host_to_device_ratio`;
- `swap_in_block_size`;
- `forward_begin/end` descriptions for KV offloading.

However, the current implementation does not provide a working hierarchical placement path. These fields make the core sparse-selection interface appear coupled to HiSparse/HiCache even though logical HBM-only selection does not require either subsystem.

#### 5. Backend support is incomplete

The current framework contains an initial FlashAttention adaptor, while other backend contracts are missing or incomplete. The DSA adaptor is still a placeholder, and there is no common capability negotiation between policy output and backend metadata.

#### 6. The reference selection path is not graph- or performance-ready

The current Quest/reference retrieval path contains Python request loops, host scalar reads, and dynamic output shapes. These are useful for validating semantics, but they cannot be placed directly inside a captured decode graph.

#### 7. Memory accounting and tests are incomplete

Algorithm representation pools consume HBM and must be included in KV pool sizing. The current `main` implementation does not yet provide a complete memory accounting contract or end-to-end tests for generic post-hoc sparse serving.

### HiSparse and Quest

HiSparse provides an important production reference for host-backed sparse serving, including:

- request admission and cleanup;
- host/device KV pools;
- sparse working-set materialization;
- asynchronous transfers;
- scheduler integration;
- CUDA Graph-compatible buffers.

There are also active Quest-related efforts:

- [#30277 — Quest runtime integration](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/30277)
- [#29666 — Optimize Quest sparse page selection](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/29666)
- [#31790 — Quest GPU kernel primitives](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/31790)
- [#31951 — Breakable CUDA Graph runtime variants](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/31951)

These implementations are valuable and should be reused where possible. However, the current runtime/configuration path is centered on HiSparse and Quest, with backend- and method-specific eligibility checks. It does not yet establish a stable, method-independent contract for adding different post-hoc sparse policies.

HiSparse itself also has a different primary objective: reducing HBM residency through a host-backed working set, especially for model-native sparse attention. The first version of the framework proposed here instead keeps the complete KV cache in HBM and changes only the logical KV set visible to attention.

The goal of this RFC is therefore not to replace HiSparse. It is to make `mem_cache/sparsity` the common **policy and logical-selection layer**, which can initially run on HBM and later connect to HiSparse/HiCache through a separate placement interface.

## Proposal

We propose evolving the existing `mem_cache/sparsity` package into a complete, unified KV-sparsity framework. The overall design follows the KSE style:

1. a lifecycle controller;
2. a pluggable sparsity policy;
3. a backend-independent logical selection result;
4. a backend-specific metadata adaptor.

The framework should be default-off and should not change dense inference when no sparse policy is configured.

## Four Classification Dimensions

Every policy should explicitly declare its position in four dimensions. These dimensions describe algorithm semantics and determine the required serving interfaces.

### D1 — KV-state action

What happens to KV entries that are not selected?

- **Visibility-only**: all KV remains allocated, but attention sees only a selected subset.
- **Physical eviction/compaction**: unselected KV is removed or compacted and its storage is reclaimed.
- **Others**: hierarchical migration, recall, reconstruction, or a combination of state actions.

The initial framework supports only **visibility-only** policies.

This keeps physical KV ownership unchanged and allows dynamic selections to change between decode steps or layers.

### D2 — Backend output granularity

What unit does the policy expose to the attention backend?

- **Token**
- **Page/block/chunk**
- **Others** for mixed or uncommon output units

The policy always returns logical request-relative indices. A backend adaptor is responsible for translating them to physical KV locations and backend metadata.

The initial framework should support token and page/block outputs where a lossless backend mapping exists:

- a page selection may be expanded for a token-indexed backend;
- a token selection cannot be represented by a page-only backend unless explicit over-selection is allowed;
- algorithm page size and physical backend page size must have a validated mapping.

### D3 — Selection evidence

What runtime information determines the selection?

- **Position-only/fixed**
- **KV-derived and query-independent**
- **Current-query-aware**
- **Attention-history-dependent**
- **Others**, including learned selectors and multi-stage hybrids

The initial framework supports evidence already available outside the fused attention matrix:

- position and sequence metadata;
- current query tensors;
- K/V tensors or derived summaries;
- policy-owned auxiliary representations.

The initial framework does **not** support attention-history/attention-score-based policies.

### D4 — Decision scope

When is the selection produced and how long can it be reused?

- **Request-level**: established after prefill and reused for the request;
- **Step-level**: computed once per decode step and reused across layers;
- **Layer-level**: computed before each layer's attention.

This dimension should be part of the policy contract rather than implemented independently by every method. The controller can then cache or invalidate `SelectionResult` at the correct lifecycle boundary.

## Supported Initial Design Region

The first implementation targets:

| Dimension | Initial support |
|---|---|
| D1: state action | Visibility-only |
| D2: granularity | Token and page/block where the backend mapping is lossless |
| D3: evidence | Fixed/position, KV-derived, and current-query-aware |
| D4: scope | Request-level, step-level, and layer-level |
| KV placement | Complete KV resident in HBM |
| Model scope | Existing dense MHA/GQA checkpoints without a native sparse indexer |

Representative initial policies can include:

- a Quest-style current-query-aware page selector;
- a StreamingLLM-style **visibility pattern** using sink and recent tokens;
- future KV-derived selectors that do not require attention matrices or physical eviction.

The StreamingLLM-style policy in this scope emulates only the visible sink/window pattern. It does not implement the original paper's rolling physical cache.

## Explicit Non-Goals

### 1. No physical KV eviction or compaction

The first version will not:

- call the KV allocator to free unselected entries;
- compact `req_to_token`;
- update scheduler KV ownership;
- reclaim HBM capacity;
- claim increased request concurrency from reduced KV residency.

Methods such as H2O, physical StreamingLLM, SnapKV, PyramidKV, and other bounded-cache algorithms require scheduler/allocator coordination and are outside the initial implementation.

Visibility-only selection may reduce attention computation and memory traffic, but the complete KV cache remains allocated in HBM.

Physical retention/eviction should be proposed separately after the logical selection framework is stable.

### 2. No attention-score- or attention-history-based policies

The first version will not require the attention backend to expose:

- a full attention matrix;
- observation-window attention scores;
- accumulated per-token attention history;
- per-head historical attention statistics.

Modern fused attention kernels normally do not materialize these values. Supporting such methods would require new kernel statistics, recomputation, or an approximation contract.

This excludes the complete semantics of methods such as:

- Scissorhands;
- H2O;
- TOVA;
- SnapKV;
- PyramidKV;
- attention-derived ChunkKV.

Attention-score support should be designed as a separate evidence-provider extension.

### Additional initial non-goals

- CPU/NVMe KV offload or hierarchical retrieval;
- HiCache/HiSparse admission and transfer scheduling;
- model-native sparse architectures such as DSA;
- learned selectors that require training or checkpoint changes;
- lossy granularity conversion hidden inside a backend adaptor.

## Proposed Interfaces

### `SparsityPolicy`

Each policy declares:

- KV-state action;
- output granularity;
- required evidence;
- decision scope;
- backend or layout capabilities;
- auxiliary representation memory requirements.

The policy consumes logical request/layer context and returns a `SelectionResult`. It does not rewrite backend metadata and does not mutate the KV allocator.

Conceptually:

```python
class SparsityPolicy(ABC):
    @property
    def capabilities(self) -> SparsityCapabilities: ...

    def on_request_begin(self, request_state) -> None: ...
    def on_request_end(self, request_state) -> None: ...
    def on_prefill_complete(self, layer_context) -> None: ...
    def begin_forward(self, forward_context) -> None: ...

    def select(self, selection_context) -> SelectionResult: ...

    def on_attention_complete(self, layer_context) -> None: ...
```

### `SelectionResult`

`SelectionResult` is the backend-independent sparse view:

```python
@dataclass
class SelectionResult:
    granularity: Granularity
    logical_indices: torch.Tensor
    valid_lengths: torch.Tensor
    sparse_mask: torch.Tensor
    layer_id: Optional[int]
    capacity: int
```

Required semantics:

- indices are logical positions within each request;
- invalid entries use a documented sentinel;
- `valid_lengths` is device-resident;
- sparse and dense requests may coexist;
- output capacity is fixed when required by graph capture;
- no allocator ownership is transferred through this object.

### `KVSparsityController`

The controller owns:

- request state and generation validation;
- policy lifecycle hooks;
- request/step/layer selection caching;
- dense fallback;
- policy/backend compatibility validation;
- coordination between policy, placement, and adaptor;
- representation-memory accounting.

Request state should use `(req_pool_idx, req_generation)` rather than only `req_pool_idx`.

### `MetadataAdaptor`

The adaptor:

- translates logical indices through `ReqToTokenPool`;
- validates policy/backend granularity compatibility;
- prepares backend-specific metadata;
- preserves and restores dense metadata;
- owns backend-specific fixed-capacity graph buffers where appropriate.

Examples:

- FA3: `page_table`, `cache_seqlens`, and related metadata;
- FlashInfer/Triton: CSR-style `kv_indptr` and `kv_indices`.

### Optional future `KVPlacementProvider`

The initial provider is `HBMResidentPlacement`:

- all KV is already in HBM;
- logical indices are mapped to physical slots;
- no transfer or allocation is performed.

A future hierarchical provider may use the same logical `SelectionResult` to:

- check residency;
- materialize missing KV into an HBM working set;
- return a completion event;
- release placement-specific request resources.

This extension point leaves room for HiCache/HiSparse without making them a dependency of the core policy interface.

## Runtime Integration

The integration should follow the current SGLang execution model rather than the older KSE prototype call sites.

Proposed ownership and hook placement:

1. `ModelRunner` creates and owns the sparsity controller after KV pools are initialized.
2. The controller is published through `ForwardContext`.
3. `RadixAttention.forward` checks whether the current layer/path is eligible.
4. Before attention, the controller obtains a logical selection and the adaptor prepares metadata.
5. The existing attention backend executes normally.
6. After attention, the policy updates incremental representations.
7. Request state is reset or released using generation-aware lifecycle handling.

The first implementation should explicitly reject unsupported combinations instead of silently producing an approximate mapping.

## Development Plan

The implementation should begin with one simple end-to-end reference method,
then add more demanding algorithms and placement paths without changing the
main inference flow.

### PR 1 — Common framework with a StreamingLLM reference path

- Define the common `SparsityPolicy`, `SelectionResult`, `KVSparsityController`, `MetadataAdaptor`, capability, configuration, and lifecycle contracts.
- Define the optional placement boundary, with `HBMResidentPlacement` as the only implementation.
- Wire the framework through `ModelRunner`, `ForwardContext`, and `RadixAttention`.
- Add a position-based, visibility-only StreamingLLM policy with one working FA3 adaptor.
- Keep the feature disabled by default, preserve dense fallback, and explicitly reject unsupported configurations.

StreamingLLM is used here because it exercises selection, metadata adaptation,
request lifecycle, and the serving path without first requiring a KV-derived
representation or attention-score history.

### PR 2 — Quest and additional sparse policies

- Add Quest as the first KV-derived policy on the same HBM + FA3 path.
- Implement its representation construction/update, query-conditioned selection, memory accounting, and optimized selection path.
- Reuse or coordinate with [#30277](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/30277), [#29666](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/29666), [#31790](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/31790), and [#31951](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/31951).
- Add each further policy or backend as an independent end-to-end PR following the same pattern; do not combine multiple new algorithms in one PR.

### PR 3 — Hierarchical KV path

- Implement one working hierarchical configuration by connecting the placement-provider boundary to HiSparse/HiCache.
- Reuse an existing policy, preferably Quest, without changing the policy-selection contract.
- Keep HBM-resident KV as the default and preserve the existing HBM-only execution path.
- Split this stage into a short PR series if scheduler, transfer, and placement changes cannot remain independently reviewable.

Every PR should include:

- one documented launch or test command for its supported configuration;
- an end-to-end smoke test and policy/adaptor conformance tests;
- dense-path regression coverage and explicit unsupported-configuration checks;
- a short correctness or performance result demonstrating the new path.

Physical eviction/compaction and attention-score/history-based selection remain separate future RFCs.


## Relationship to Existing Work

Related issues and PRs:

- [#10585 — Integrate KVPress](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/10585)
- [#22452 — Sparse Attention for non-DSA models](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/22452)
- [#22865 — Extend framework to support non-NSA sparse algorithms](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/22865)
- [#28874 — HiSparse roadmap](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/28874)
- [#28882 — Experimental Quest FlashAttention serving path](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/28882)
- [#30277 — Quest runtime integration](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/30277)
- [#29666 — Quest selection optimization](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/29666)
- [#31790 — Quest GPU kernels](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/31790)
- [#31951 — Breakable CUDA Graph runtime variants](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/31951)


The proposed work should reuse the existing `mem_cache/sparsity` package and collaborate with the active Quest/HiSparse PRs. The intended contribution is a stable common framework, not a second parallel Quest runtime.

title: [Feature] [RFC] SharedEP: a zerocopy execution model for MoE Expert Parallelism
author: foraxe
body:
### Checklist - [x] If this is not a feature request but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed. - [x] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed. ### Motivation # RFC: SharedEP: a zerocopy execution model for MoE Expert Parallelism ## Overview SharedEP is a shared-memory execution model for MoE Expert Parallelism. Instead of: ```plain pack tokens → dispatch → materialize receive buffer → expert compute → combine → return output ``` SharedEP uses directly addressable peer memory: ```plain publish activations and routing metadata → expert directly reads routed token rows → expert computes → writes results directly to token-owner output slots ``` ```mermaid flowchart LR A["Token owner publishes
activation + route metadata"] B["Expert directly reads
selected token rows"] C["Expert computation"] D["Direct-write contribution
to token-owner slot"] E["Owner performs Top-K reduction"] A --> B --> C --> D --> E ``` SharedEP removes dispatch/combine payload materialization and CPU-side communication orchestration. Remote memory traffic still occurs over the scale-up interconnect. ## Platform Mapping | Platform | Memory mechanism | Interconnect | Kernel/runtime requirements | Status | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | NVIDIA CUDA | CUDA VMM peer mappings | NVLink / NVSwitch | CUDA kernels, GPU release/acquire epochs, CUDA Graph-safe buffers | Implemented by PR #32482 | | AMD ROCm | HIP VMM peer mappings | Infinity Fabric / XGMI | gfx950 kernels, wave64-aware scheduling, HIP Graph-safe synchronization | Implemented by PR #32619 | | Huawei Ascend | Fabric memory or VMM-style peer mappings | HCCS scale-up fabric | AscendC kernels directly consuming remote tensors, device-side publish/completion flags, graph-safe fixed buffers | Proposed backend | - [ ] CUDA: #32482 - [ ] ROCm: #32619 - [ ] ASCEND: Todo ## Ascend Design The Ascend implementation should preserve the same SharedEP protocol: 1. Allocate rank-owned activation, routing, and output objects. 2. Map peer objects into every EP rank. 3. Publish valid rows and routing metadata using device-visible epochs. 4. Let expert kernels directly load routed rows from local or remote HBM. 5. Write W2 contributions directly into token-owner output slots. 6. Let each token owner reduce its local Top-K contributions. The critical Ascend requirement is not only shared allocation. The expert kernel must be able to directly dereference peer-memory addresses. If the platform only supports explicit `put/get` or SDMA copies, it implements SharedEP’s layout but not its full direct-compute execution model. ## Scope Initial scope: + decode-oriented MoE execution; + one directly addressable scale-up domain; + fixed model and topology profiles; + FP8/MXFP4 or platform-equivalent quantization; + existing EP backend remains the prefill fallback. Enablement interface: ```bash --moe-a2a-backend shared_ep ``` Unsupported models, quantization formats, or topologies must fail during server initialization rather than silently falling back in the decode hot path. ### Related resources _No response_

title: [RFC] [MLX] Write down the per-step contract that a replacement event loop must satisfy
author: jlee5814
body:
`Scheduler.run_batch` runs the torch forward and performs the per step bookkeeping backend neutral readers depend on. `event_loop_overlap_mlx` replaces the first and inherits the second, with nothing enforcing the inheritance. Four bugs across July hit four of the five clauses below: `TypeError` at startup, silent cache loss, silent wrong output, a segfault behind a flag pair.  The fifth returns the right answer by accident.

The pattern is older than those. #29217, merged in June, states in its own root cause section: the MLX loop bypasses `run_batch`, where `forward_ct` is incremented and the profiler predicate is called. Its fix mirrored the missing write inside the loop. Clause 3 then broke again in July and was fixed the same way by #32447.

Line numbers anchored to `50029f0`, which predates #32447; the `scheduler_mixin.py` anchors have drifted by a couple of lines since.

## The contract

A step that emits tokens must leave the following true when it ends.

1. Slots recorded. `alloc_for_decode` writes `req_to_token[row, position]` (`allocation.py:578`), read back as a pool slot id by `_sync_decode_kv_to_pool`.
2. Counters advanced. `seq_lens`, `kv_committed_len`, `kv.kv_allocated_len` (`schedule_batch.py:2884-2892`), read by radix insertion as the visibility bound.
3. Step stamped. `forward_ct`, `forward_iter`, `launch_ts` (`scheduler.py:3371-3373`), read by the watchdog, the profiler and the SWA eviction cadence.
4. Relays published or provably unread. `future_map.output_tokens_buf` is written only from the torch branch of `run_batch` (`scheduler.py:3460`).
5. In flight predicates test any overlap loop. `enable_overlap` and `enable_overlap_mlx` are mutually exclusive by construction (`scheduler.py:382`).

| Clause | On the MLX loop | Status |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Skipped on the chained path | Sync side clamped by #30147; open allocation |
| 2 | Skipped on the chained path | Open, #30093 |
| 3 | Fixed | #29217, #32447 |
| 4 | Never published; inert for pure decode, live for a mixed batch | Path disabled on MLX by #32591 |
| 5 | Wrong flag, masked | #32934 |

## Clause 2

The `seq_lens` undercount never self corrects, since the next fresh `prepare_for_decode` adds one regardless of chain length and `get_next_batch_to_run` returns `running_batch` by identity (`scheduler.py:2883`), so the stale value sits on the live object for the request's lifetime. #30093 documents the per chain skip; the permanence is what makes it a contract violation rather than a transient. #30147 clamps the sync to the committed bound and does not advance it, so clause 2 stays open after the PR lands.

The retraction budget reads these counters, but chained steps never allocate, so `kv_committed_len` tracks real pool occupancy and `check_decode_mem` stays self consistent. The measured cost is radix truncation, not a memory pressure miscalculation.

## Clause 5

`is_fully_idle` (`scheduler.py:3814`) checks `not self.enable_overlap or len(self.result_queue) == 0`, so MLX never inspects the queue. It returns the right answer anyway because `running_batch` is non empty whenever the queue is. Nothing enforces coupling and `release_memory_occupation` asserts on this predicate.

## Scope

#32321 closes reaching through the worker, which produces absence bugs; this is state never written, which produces staleness. Nothing asks chained decode to change.

## Proposed enforcement

One registered unit test driving a short prefill and decode workload through both loops and asserting all five clauses at each step boundary, failing with the clause number and the field name rather than a downstream symptom. #32934 is a worked example of the shape at one clause: five lines of production change, three cases, red on the parent and green on the branch.
