Adding the other four is incremental, one clause per commit, and none of it requires a model.

title: [RFC] Asynchronous completion handling for the HiCache NIXL storage backend
author: aaltinsoy
body:
Follow-up to my [comment on #26693](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/26693#issuecomment-5110159045): the full writeup plus measurements for the "Asynchronous backend" roadmap item. cc @lluki as the item's owner; this also builds directly on @ccs1112's #27359 poll-cost measurements.

## Summary

The NIXL storage backend polls each transfer to completion inside `_xfer_and_wait`, one transfer in flight per direction, at a fixed 100 us interval. Measurements below show the poll loop is load-bearing for correctness (it drives I/O submission past 64 descriptors), costs ~8% of a core per in-flight transfer at the shipped interval, adds 2.4x latency to small O_DIRECT transfers and caps disk-true bandwidth at a flat depth-1 ceiling regardless of batch size. This RFC proposes splitting submit from completion, sweeping all outstanding handles from one place, tying NIXL registration lifetime to handle lifetime and adding ring-buffer bounce slots so more than one batch can be in flight. It also settles two design questions from the roadmap discussion: notifications cannot replace polling for storage plugins, and `useProgThread` is not an available escape hatch.

## Background and constraints

All verified in source; permalinks in the [#26693 comment](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/26693#issuecomment-5110159045).

1. Storage plugins (POSIX, OBJ, GDS, GDS_MT, HF3FS) return `supportsNotif() == false`; notifs on a non-supporting backend are a hard error and the notif registry is gated on `supportsRemote()`. An event/notification design is structurally unavailable. Polling stays; the question is only where and how cheaply.
2. POSIX `checkXfer` is the submission pump: `poll()` calls `post()` first, which submits at most `MAX_IO_SUBMIT_BATCH_SIZE = 64` I/Os per call. A transfer with more than 64 descriptors cannot finish submitting without repeated polling.
3. The POSIX io_queue is engine-wide under one lock, so a single poller advances all in-flight requests.
4. `useProgThread` only becomes `enableProgTh` in backend init params and only the ucx and libfabric plugins read it. Moving polling to the C side would need NIXL-side work (in the spirit of #27060).
5. Today's structure serializes: the `_page_transfer`/`_page_backup` loops and single-slot `_bounce_set`/`_bounce_get` buffers give in-flight depth 1 per direction.

## Measured baseline

GCP c3-standard-8-lssd, nixl 1.3.2, POSIX plugin, WRITE, 256 KiB pages, median of 9 rounds per cell. Script, raw data and full analysis: [aaltinsoy/nixl-posix-bench](https://github.com/aaltinsoy/nixl-posix-bench).

| Finding | Number |
|---|---|
| Submission staircase | polls to DONE = ceil(K/64) + 1 exactly; each 64-descriptor boundary costs one full poll interval of wall time |
| Poll floor, single O_DIRECT op | 206 us busy-polled vs 502 us at the shipped 100 us interval (2.4x) |
| CPU per in-flight transfer | ~8% of a core at the shipped interval (K=64, O_DIRECT); busy-poll pins a full core. Consistent with #27359 |
| Depth-1 bandwidth ceiling | ~0.41 GB/s O_DIRECT, flat across K = 8..256; buffered runs additionally lose 11.3 -> 6.9 GB/s from K=64 to K=256 waiting on the pump |

## Proposed design

### Core: split submit from completion
- `batch_set`/`batch_get` submit transfers and return handles; a completion sweep polls all outstanding handles (same pattern as `disaggregation/nixl/conn.py`).
- The sweep must call `check_xfer_state` repeatedly per handle until fully submitted; the staircase finding makes this a correctness requirement, not a latency choice.
- One sweeper covers everything (constraint 3): sweep cost is amortized across all in-flight transfers instead of one poll loop per transfer.

### Placement of the sweep: two options, decidable by measurement
- Option A: dedicated reaper thread in the backend. Simple, contained, keeps HiCacheController unchanged. GIL cost: one polling thread total instead of one per transfer; #27359's scheduler-interference numbers bound the impact.
- Option B: fold submissions and polls into the main scheduler loop (@lluki's suggestion on #26693). No extra thread, no lock handoff, but couples backend cadence to scheduler iteration time; needs a measurement of scheduler iteration jitter under load to size that risk.
- The interfaces are identical either way. I propose landing A first (smaller diff) and keeping B open as a follow-up once measured.

### Registration lifetime
- Replace the per-transfer register/deregister context manager with acquire/release tied to handle lifetime. This also gives runtime `detach_storage_backend` (recently asked about on Slack) its prerequisite: drain outstanding handles, then release.

### Bounce buffers
- A ring of N bounce slots per direction instead of the single `_bounce_set`/`_bounce_get` tensors, so depth >1 is possible on the non-zero-copy path. N is a config knob; default to be picked from the depth-sweep measurements.

### Rollout: staged PRs, each mergeable alone
1. Registration acquire/release refactor (no behavior change, mechanical, unit-testable).
2. Submit/sweep split behind a flag, depth still 1 (behavior-equivalent; validates the sweep).
3. Ring bounce slots + depth >1 (the perf change; benchmarked).
4. Optional: scheduler-loop placement (Option B) if measurements justify it.

## Validation plan

Follows the conventions of #25173 / #27060.

- Tier 1 (CPU-only): re-run the staircase and baseline suites on the new backend; add bandwidth and CPU/GB vs in-flight depth 1/2/4/8; batch_exists latency vs key count.
- Tier 2 (GPU): warm TTFT with L2 cold / L3 warm, ctx 1k/8k/16k/32k, median over 4+ rounds, tp=1 and tp=4; decode ITL interference while a large prefetch runs; backup drain rate under sustained load.
- Report the config where async should NOT help (large batches, single stream, disk-bound) and expect parity there.
- Accuracy is unaffected (no change to inference mechanisms).

## Open items

- fio iodepth control run on the same device class, to bound the device's own headroom above the 0.41 GB/s depth-1 ceiling (treat the absolute number as provisional until then; the flatness across batch sizes is the structural result).
- Pin which POSIX io queue implementation (io_uring vs aio) the PyPI wheel selects; the 64-per-post constant is identical in all three queue impls, so the staircase is impl-independent.
- Scheduler iteration jitter measurement to evaluate Option B.

## Open questions for maintainers

1. Reaper thread vs scheduler-loop as the first landing point (this RFC proposes reaper first).
2. Is a NIXL-side C polling home worth pursuing in parallel (extends #27060's direction)? It would benefit all NIXL consumers, not just SGLang.
3. Default in-flight depth, and whether it should adapt per plugin/backing store.
4. Should detach/attach support land as part of stage 1 (registration lifetime) or separately?

I'm happy to take the implementation through the staged plan above.

## Related

- #26693 roadmap item and discussion (@ccs1112's #27359 benchmarks, @lluki's GIL analysis)
- #32693 / #32705 (clear() scoping) and #32702 (cleaner grouping): shared-mount hygiene issues found during this investigation
- #21891 SGLang Simulator: the baseline table doubles as ground truth for a faithful L3 storage timing model
speedup_claims: 4x latency to small O_DIRECT transfers and caps disk-true bandwidth at a flat depth-1 ceiling regardless of batch size

speedup_evidence.claim: 4x latency to small O_DIRECT transfers and caps disk-true bandwidth at a flat depth-1 ceiling regardless of batch size

title: [RFC] KVCR as a HiCacheStorage backend for peer-to-peer KV reuse
author: linhu-nv
body:
## Summary SGLang's HiCache already supports pluggable L3 storage backends (mooncake, hf3fs, eic, …) behind a stable `HiCacheStorage` interface. This RFC adds KVCR as one more such backend. KVCR is a multi-tier KV cache management solution from NVIDIA. The integration totally follows the integration and design of hicache storage — we register a `"kvcr"` backend and implement the same `batch_set_v2 / batch_get_v2 / batch_exists_v2` contract the other backends already implement. This backend also aligns with the router-initiated hint model in **[#27574 — Programmatic KV Cache for Agentic Workloads](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/27574)**, which defines a provider-neutral hint taxonomy (Share / Prefetch / Demote / Pin / Retain). KVCR fits the **`Share`** intent — *"reuse a prefix that already lives on another worker... pull the prefix from the old one"* — but does not depend on that RFC: it is a self-contained mechanism any router emitting such a hint can drive. Following the Dynamo DEP (ai-dynamo/dynamo#11673), the near term goal is **direct worker-to-worker (host memory) KV reuse**: a prefix computed on one worker is served to another without recomputation or a round-trip through a global pool. When a request lands on a worker lacking a prefix another worker holds, KVCR fetches it **peer-to-peer** — an asymmetric, directed transfer, not a symmetric external store. Selecting *which* peer holds the prefix is a decision only a router can make well. So the router hands the target worker a small piece of per-request metadata — a **hint** — naming the peer. "Router" here means any orchestrator above the engine: the router (flash indexer) is the first target, SGLang's own router a later one, and the same carrier serves both. The rest of this RFC covers (1) that hint and (2) how KVCR plugs into HiCache to act on it. ## Part 1 — Router Hint ### Why a hint is needed HiCache storage is content-addressed: the controller asks `get(block_hash)` and the backend is expected to know where the bytes live. That works for a global pool. It does **not** work for P2P reuse, where the same prefix may sit on any one of N peer workers. The only component that knows which one is the **router** — it made the routing decision that sent this request here in the first place. The hint will directly tell the node where target kvcache sits. ### Why decide this at the router Putting the source-selection decision at the routing stage — rather than probing peers after a request lands — is what makes the hint valuable beyond avoiding a broadcast: - **It enables a routing cost function that can grow over time.** The hint is the input to a decision the router makes; that decision can start *simple* (route on load only, ignoring cache residency) and evolve to *rich* (weigh prefix cache residency, estimated transfer time, distance/topology, and thresholds that decide when a P2P fetch is even worth it versus recomputation). - **It lets us prefetch and shape system behavior.** Because the router decides before the request is admitted, the target can begin fetching the prefix ahead of time, and the router — with its global view — can steer placement to balance load and reuse across the fleet, rather than reacting locally after the fact. ### Carrier We do **not** widen the `HiCacheStorage` signature. Every v2 call already threads a free-form `HiCacheStorageExtraInfo.extra_info` dict from the controller into the backend. The hint is the `Share` case of #27574's provider-neutral hint envelope and rides in that dict; the key name below is a placeholder pending #27574's envelope: ``` # placeholder key — to be aligned with #27574's KvHintEnvelope extra_info.extra_info["kvcr_router_hint"] = { "source_control_endpoint": "host:port", # ZMQ control endpoint of the peer holding the prefix "block_hashes": [...], # root-aligned block hashes for the shared prefix } ``` ### Propagation path The hint travels from the router down to the backend without widening any interface — it rides the `extra_info` dict every layer already passes through: 1. **router → scheduler.** The router attaches the hint to the request's `extra_info`; the scheduler stashes it into the prefetch request. 2. **scheduler → controller.** `HiCacheController.prefetch(...)` carries it into the daemon `prefetch_io_aux_func` thread (`managers/cache_controller.py`). 3. **controller → backend.** `_page_transfer → page_get_func(op, hashes, host_idx, extra_info)` hands it to `KVCR.batch_get_v2(...)` (`storage/kvcr/kvcr_store.py`). 4. **backend → decision.** `RouterHint.maybe_from_extra_info(extra_info)` (`storage/kvcr/router_hint.py`) parses it: - hint **absent/malformed** → fall back to local-only (deposit/local-get), never raises; - hint **present** → drive a directed P2P fetch from `source_control_endpoint`. The parser is **fail-closed**: a missing or malformed hint degrades to local-only behavior, it never crashes a prefetch, and the backend is safe to ship before the any router side lands (dynamo pr here https://github.com/ai-dynamo/dynamo/pull/11695). ## Part 2 — KVCR Integration Architecture ### Where it sits ```mermaid flowchart LR SCH[Scheduler] --- HRC[HiRadixCache] --- HCC[HiCacheController] HCC -->|HiCacheStorage iface| KS[KVCR
thin adapter] subgraph core[KVCR core · vendored] LD[local DRAM tier
deposit / get] CC[control channel
ZMQ peer] PT[progress thread
owns NIXL agent] end KS --> core ``` `KVCR` is a thin adapter. It owns no transfer threads of its own — kvcr's core runs **one** daemon "kvcr-progress" thread that exclusively holds the NIXL agent and control socket. The store advances state only by calling `poll_completed()` from the HiCache controller's existing prefetch thread. No new threading model is introduced into SGLang. ### Get path (with router hint) — sequence ```mermaid sequenceDiagram participant AUX as prefetch aux thread participant KS as KVCR participant PT as KVCR progress thread participant SRC as source worker participant SCH as scheduler AUX->>KS: batch_get_v2(hashes, host_idx, extra_info) Note over KS: hint = maybe_from_extra_info(...) KS->>PT: submit_hint(source_endpoint, keys) Note over PT: register source peer KS->>PT: h = deliver(blocks) PT->>SRC: START_WRITE (ctrl) Note over SRC: search_and_pin SRC-->>PT: NIXL WRITE (UCX) → host pages (direct DMA) SRC-->>PT: send_notif("write_done") Note over PT: _poll_notifications
_TargetDeliverOp: WAITING→FINISHED PT-->>KS: _completion_queue.append(OpResult) Note over KS: poll_completed(): match r.op_handle == h KS-->>AUX: [per-page success bools] Note over AUX: operation.increment(page_size × hits) SCH->>SCH: check_prefetch_progress(req_id)
polls completed_tokens (hiradix_cache.py) Note over SCH: True → req admitted into batch ``` - **A single KVCR daemon thread owns the whole P2P mechanism.** It handles all KVCR↔KVCR message send/recv, maintains the internal op state machine, and drives the interaction with NIXL transfers. When a transfer finishes it does not push anything — it just appends the result to a completion queue; the store itself spawns no extra thread. - **The KVCR thread never touches the scheduler main thread or the prefetch thread.** It runs entirely on its own, so neither of SGLang's threads is blocked or slowed by how KVCR does its work. - **The existing completion-notification model is unchanged.** A finished transfer sits on that queue until the prefetch daemon thread actively drains it via `poll_completed()` and turns it into `completed_tokens`; the scheduler main thread, one level up, only reads the resulting boolean tick (`check_prefetch_progress`) — the same KVPoll-style poll as today. ### Non-goals - No changes to HiRadixCache or the scheduler cache path. - No new SGLang-side transfer threads. - Shared-HiCache serving (source pins from HiRadixCache via `TreeNode.protect_host`) is a future swap of the pin adapter only — out of scope here.

title: [RFC] Push-based Engine Load Reporting and Router Load Monitoring
author: Bakerjc-bgner
body:
## Abstract Load-aware routing needs a fresh and engine-authoritative view of scheduler pressure. Router-side request counters, periodic HTTP polling, and Prometheus scraping each provide useful signals, but none gives the Router a consistent, low-latency view of every data-parallel rank inside an Engine. This RFC proposes an opt-in, two-sided load reporting architecture: 1. An **Engine Load Reporter** samples already-published scheduler snapshots and pushes complete per-DP-rank reports over long-lived gRPC streams. 2. A **Router Load Monitor** discovers workers, asks them to start or renew reporting, validates incoming streams, aggregates rank values, and publishes an immutable, versioned snapshot for diagnostics and future policies. The first two implementation stages deliberately do **not** change request routing. They establish the control plane, wire contract, freshness semantics, and read-only snapshot boundary first. Load-aware policies and additional metrics can then be reviewed separately. ## Motivation ### Why Router-local state is not enough A Router can observe when it forwards a request and when an HTTP response finishes, but it cannot reliably infer the Engine's scheduler state: - requests may queue, retract, abort, or move between PD-specific queues after admission; - KV-cache pressure and pending uncached Prefill tokens are only known inside the Engine; - one worker may contain multiple DP ranks with very different instantaneous pressure; - PP and PD execution make a single request count an incomplete approximation of actual work; - Engine restarts and topology changes can invalidate Router-side counters. The scheduling source of truth therefore has to originate from the Engine. ### Multi-node, multi-replica, and HA deployments magnify partial visibility In HA deployments, each Router replica sees only its own traffic while sharing the same Engine fleet. Local counters and asynchronous polling miss peer traffic, Engine-internal queues, DP-rank imbalance, and rapid failover shifts. Independent Routers can therefore make locally reasonable but globally poor choices, causing herd effects and hotspots. This proposal does not attempt global coordination. It gives every Router replica fresh, Engine-authoritative load signals, reducing decisions based on fragmented local views. ### Why not poll every worker Polling `/v1/loads` is useful for diagnostics, but it has undesirable control plane properties at larger scale: - the Router creates repeated connection and request fan-out across all workers; - polls complete at different times, so one routing decision can combine snapshots from different sampling windows; - short queue spikes can occur between polling rounds; - timeout and retry behavior is duplicated for every poll; - multiple Routers multiply the polling load on every Engine. A persistent push stream amortizes connection setup, lets the Engine publish at millisecond-resolution intervals, and makes sequence, restart, and lease semantics explicit. ### Why not use Prometheus as the routing control plane Prometheus remains the right tool for historical monitoring, alerting, and capacity analysis. A routing control plane has different requirements: bounded freshness, direct worker identity, complete DP-rank snapshots, restart detection, and deterministic handling of missing or stale data. Routing should not depend on scrape intervals, external storage availability, or time-series query latency. ## Goals - Export scheduler-authoritative load without blocking model execution. - Preserve complete per-DP-rank detail rather than only a worker average. - Support millisecond-resolution report intervals over persistent connections. - Make freshness, restart, ordering, and topology changes explicit. - Support one Engine reporting independently to multiple Routers. - Give every HA Router replica an Engine-authoritative fleet view instead of relying only on its own fragment of request history. - Keep regular SGLang installs and routing behavior unchanged by default. - Provide one immutable snapshot version per Router read or future routing decision. - Split implementation into reviewable PRs with clear dependency boundaries. ## Non-goals - Changing model outputs, kernels, batching, or scheduler behavior. - Claiming an inference-throughput improvement from reporting itself. - Replacing `/v1/loads`, `/metrics`, or Prometheus observability. - Enabling a new load-aware policy in the initial Reporter or Monitor PR. - Providing historical storage, replay, acknowledgements, or exactly-once delivery. - Making the initial internal h2c protocol suitable for an untrusted public network. ## Proposed Architecture ```mermaid flowchart LR subgraph Engine["SGLang Engine"] Schedulers["Schedulers / DP ranks"] SnapshotSource["Existing SHM or ZMQ
LoadSnapshot source"] Hints["Request lifecycle
refresh hints"] Sampler["Single-flight sampler"] Store["Validated immutable
latest snapshot"] Builder["LoadReport builder
source + sequence"] Streams["Persistent gRPC stream
per Router target"] StartAPI["POST /v1/start_reporting"] Schedulers --> SnapshotSource --> Sampler --> Store --> Builder --> Streams Hints -. "coalesced, non-blocking" .-> Sampler StartAPI --> Streams end subgraph Router["experimental/sgl-router"] Discovery["Worker discovery"] Reconcile["Registration / lease
reconciliation"] GRPC["LoadMonitorService.Report"] Validate["Identity, sequence,
rank and freshness validation"] RankStore["Per-worker + per-rank store"] Aggregate["Derived worker aggregates"] Snapshot["GET /v1/load_monitor/snapshot
immutable + versioned"] Policies["Future load-aware policies"] Discovery --> Reconcile GRPC --> Validate --> RankStore --> Aggregate --> Snapshot Snapshot -. "future stage" .-> Policies end Reconcile -- "start / renew reporting" --> StartAPI Streams -- "client-streaming gRPC" --> GRPC ``` The architecture intentionally separates two directions: - **Control plane, Router to Engine:** worker reconciliation and lease renewal through `POST /v1/start_reporting`. - **Data plane, Engine to Router:** long-lived client-streaming gRPC reports. This lets the Router control which discovered workers should report, while the Engine remains authoritative for what each DP rank is doing. ## End-to-end Lifecycle ```mermaid sequenceDiagram participant D as Worker discovery participant M as Router Load Monitor participant E as Engine /start_reporting participant R as Engine Reporter participant G as Router gRPC ingest participant S as Immutable snapshot store D->>M: Reconcile current workers M->>E: POST /v1/start_reporting(ip, port, interval, lease) E->>R: Upsert reporting target and activate sampler E-->>M: Accepted lease and renewal time R->>R: Sample complete DP-rank snapshot R->>G: Open stream and send first report immediately G->>S: Validate identity, source, sequence and ranks loop Fixed cadence while lease is renewed R->>G: Send latest complete snapshot G->>S: Latest valid sequence wins M->>E: Renew reporting lease end D->>M: Worker removed or identity changed M->>M: Cancel renewal and reconcile store R->>R: Lease expires and target stream closes ``` ## Key Design Decisions 1. **Router initiates, Engine reports.** Discovery tells the Router which workers should participate; only the Engine can provide scheduler truth. 2. **Persistent streams instead of polling.** A long-lived stream reduces connection churn and gives every report an explicit source/session context. 3. **Latest-wins instead of replay.** Routing needs the newest trustworthy state. Sequence IDs reject regression without building a historical log. 4. **Complete ranks plus aggregates.** Raw DP-rank data preserves imbalance; derived worker values make common consumers simpler without discarding it. 5. **Immutable consumer views.** One snapshot version prevents a request from observing half-old, half-new worker state during a routing decision. 6. **Leases instead of a required stop RPC.** If a Router disappears, Engine tasks converge automatically. Multiple Routers remain independent targets. ## Engine Load Reporter ### Snapshot source and validation The Reporter does not synchronously query GPU execution. It consumes the Engine's existing `LoadSnapshot` publication path: - single-tokenizer mode uses `TokenizerManager.get_loads(include=["core"])`; - multi-tokenizer mode reads through the single Python `MultiTokenizerRouter` owner; - SHM/ZMQ transport remains internal to the Engine. Each sample is validated as one complete expected DP-rank set before it becomes the latest immutable view. Invalid or incomplete samples never partially replace a previously valid view. ### Single-flight sampling Timer wakes and request lifecycle hints share one sampler state machine. At most one `get_loads()` call is in flight. Notifications that arrive during a sample coalesce into at most one additional refresh, preventing request bursts from spawning unbounded background work. The inference request path only emits a lightweight, synchronous wake hint. It does not await sampling or network I/O. ### Runtime ownership - With one tokenizer worker, the HTTP process owns one `LoadReporterRuntime`. - With multiple tokenizer workers, the Python `MultiTokenizerRouter` is the sole runtime owner. HTTP workers use correlated IPC control messages and coalesced refresh notifications. This boundary prevents N HTTP workers from creating N duplicate report streams for the same Engine. ### Stream management Each Router target owns an independent task and gRPC stream: - send the first report immediately after connecting; - send the latest snapshot on a fixed millisecond-resolution cadence; - skip missed periods after backpressure instead of replaying old reports; - retry transient gRPC failures with bounded exponential backoff and jitter; - wait for a renewed registration after permanent/protocol failures; - expire the target when its lease is not renewed; - use bounded, ordered shutdown so background tasks cannot leak. Sampling and transport failures are isolated from inference requests. ### Optional dependency boundary The Reporter uses the optional `sglang[load-reporter]` dependency extra, which contains compatible `grpcio` and `protobuf` versions across supported wheel variants. Normal SGLang installations do not gain mandatory gRPC dependencies. When the extra is unavailable, normal serving still starts and the registration endpoint reports that the feature is unsupported. ## Router Load Monitor ### Listener and worker reconciliation Load monitoring is opt-in. The Router binds an independent gRPC listener before registering workers. Port `0` is supported; the actual selected port is sent to the Engine. A separately configured report IP must be reachable from workers. The Monitor continuously reconciles the complete discovery result: - new workers get a missing-load entry and a registration-renewal task; - unchanged worker identities preserve report and sequence state; - removed or identity-changed workers lose old state and renewal tasks; - duplicate normalized worker origins are rejected rather than guessed. The initial implementation uses a 1-second report interval, 3-second freshness window, 15-second lease, and 2-second registration timeout. The wire/control API already represents intervals in milliseconds; configuration policy can be expanded after the first implementation is stable. ### Stream binding and validation The first report binds a stream to a discovered worker using normalized origin, worker role, and `source_instance_id`. The Monitor validates: - the worker exists in the current discovery view; - reported regular/Prefill/Decode role matches discovery; - stream identity remains stable; - source IDs are non-empty and retired sources cannot return; - sequence IDs move forward; - DP ranks are unique and non-negative; - counters and capacities are internally consistent; - floating-point metrics are finite where required. Duplicate or out-of-order sequences are ignored. A newly accepted source retires the prior source, making Engine restarts explicit and preventing a late old stream from overwriting a new process. ### Freshness model Freshness is evaluated from **Router receipt time**, not solely from Engine wall clock, so clock skew cannot make an old report appear fresh. Each worker is one of: - `missing`: discovered but no accepted report yet; - `fresh`: healthy and received within the freshness window; - `stale`: explicitly stale, locally invalid, or too old; - `unreachable`: the Engine explicitly cannot produce an authoritative load. Stale and unreachable entries remain visible for diagnostics but must not be silently treated as fresh scheduling data. ### Immutable snapshot boundary `GET /v1/load_monitor/snapshot` returns a fully owned, deterministically sorted, versioned capture. Freshness is computed once at capture time. All consumers of that object therefore see the same worker set and freshness decision even if a new report arrives concurrently. The first Monitor PR exposes this read-only diagnostic boundary and keeps all existing routing policies unchanged. A future policy can pin one snapshot per request and define an explicit fallback for missing/stale workers. ## Wire Protocol The shared package is `router.loadmonitor.v1`: ```protobuf service LoadMonitorService { rpc Report(stream LoadReport) returns (google.protobuf.Empty); } ``` ### Report envelope | Field | Purpose | | --- | --- | | `source_instance_id` | Distinguishes one Reporter process lifetime from another. | | `sequence_id` | Monotonic latest-wins ordering within a source. | | `report_time_unix_ms` | Engine-side report creation time for diagnostics. | | `worker` | Canonical worker address, role, optional model, and zone. | | `status` | `HEALTHY`, `STALE`, or `UNREACHABLE`. | | `last_error` | Diagnostic reason when the Engine cannot produce a healthy snapshot. | | `ranks` | Complete per-DP-rank values for healthy/stale reports. | ### Per-rank fields | Field | Meaning | | --- | --- | | `dp_rank` | Rank identity within the Engine's DP topology. | | `snapshot_time_unix_ms` | Time when that scheduler snapshot was produced. | | `num_running_reqs` | Requests in the scheduler's current running batch. | | `num_waiting_reqs` | Requests waiting across the applicable normal/PD queues. | | `num_waiting_uncached_tokens` | Pending Prefill tokens that still require computation. | | `num_used_tokens` | KV token slots currently used by the relevant pool accounting. | | `num_total_tokens` | Used KV tokens plus not-yet-allocated pending sequence length. | | `max_total_num_tokens` | KV token-slot capacity. | | `max_running_requests` | Scheduler request-slot capacity. | | `token_usage` | Current token-pool usage ratio. | | `gen_throughput` | Recent Decode generation throughput. | | `cache_hit_rate` | Recent effective Prefix Cache hit ratio. | | `utilization` | Existing Engine utilization signal; retained for compatibility, not proposed as the sole policy score. | These are transport signals, not a universal load score. For example, PD Prefill may not express active forward work through `num_running_reqs`; pending uncached tokens and future role-specific Engine signals may be more useful for that role. Likewise, the current `utilization` field should not be used as the only scheduling input. Fields 1-13 and existing enum values form the initial contract. Field numbers must never be renumbered or reused. Additive fields remain backward compatible because older protobuf readers ignore unknown fields. ## Aggregation Semantics The Monitor retains complete rank values and also derives a worker aggregate: - sum request counts, pending uncached tokens, used/total/capacity tokens, request capacity, and generation throughput; - derive saturating free-token and available-request-slot capacity; - compute request utilization from running requests and request capacity; - compute capacity-weighted token usage and retain maximum rank token usage; - compute queue pressure from waiting uncached tokens and throughput only when the denominator is meaningful. The aggregate is a convenience, not a replacement for rank detail. Future policies should be able to account for a hot rank instead of hiding imbalance behind a worker average. ## Correctness and Failure Semantics | Condition | Expected behavior | | --- | --- | | Router target is unavailable | Reporter reconnects with bounded exponential backoff while the lease remains valid. | | Sampling fails | Reporter never publishes a partial rank set. If no authoritative sample has ever succeeded it reports `UNREACHABLE`; otherwise the last complete view can age to stale with diagnostic error context. | | Snapshot is old | Engine may report `STALE`; Router also enforces receipt-time freshness independently. | | Slow gRPC write | Reporter skips missed deadlines and sends the latest view; it does not replay history. | | Engine restarts | New `source_instance_id` supersedes and retires the old source. | | Duplicate/out-of-order report | Router ignores the sequence without regressing state. | | Worker disappears from discovery | Router cancels renewal and removes/reinitializes identity-bound state. | | Router shuts down | Router stops renewals and waits up to one lease TTL for streams to converge. | | Multiple tokenizer workers | Exactly one Python owner samples and streams; HTTP workers only send IPC hints. | Delivery is intentionally **latest-wins**, not exactly-once. Routing needs the newest trustworthy state, not replay of every intermediate sample. ## Security and Trust Boundary The initial implementation is for a trusted internal serving network: - gRPC uses h2c without TLS, mTLS, or per-stream authentication; - `/v1/start_reporting` has no dedicated load-reporter admin credential; - the Router sends no authorization header when registering an Engine; - worker identity is bound to the discovery-normalized origin and role; - forwarded HTTP headers are not trusted to construct worker identity. Deployments should bind the listener to a private interface and restrict both the registration endpoint and gRPC port with cluster/network policy. The registration endpoint can cause the Engine to connect to a supplied IP/port, so it must not be exposed to untrusted callers. The snapshot endpoint also reveals capacity and load data and should remain internal. Authentication, target allowlisting, and TLS/mTLS are explicit hardening items rather than properties of the first PRs. Engines protected by a global HTTP API key may currently reject the Router's unauthenticated registration; that integration also requires an agreed credential mechanism. ## Performance Characteristics The design keeps hot-path work intentionally small: - request lifecycle hooks only set/coalesce an event; - sampling reuses already-published scheduler snapshots; - there is at most one sampler call per Engine at a time; - each Router target reuses one long-lived connection; - Router ingestion performs bounded validation and one short store update; - consumers read a fully owned snapshot without holding a live store reference. No inference speedup is claimed. Before a load-aware policy is enabled by default, we should measure CPU use, event-loop delay, report bandwidth, and request latency across worker count, DP size, interval, and multiple Router targets. ## Compatibility and Rollout - Both sides are disabled by default. - A normal Engine does not require the optional Reporter dependencies. - Existing Router policies behave exactly as before. - Reporter and Monitor share the same IDL but have no source-code dependency; they can be reviewed and merged in either order using fake peers in tests. - High-value load signal extensions should follow both base implementations and evolve the protocol additively on both sides. - Future policy integration depends on the Monitor snapshot API and needs a separately reviewed fallback design. ## Roadmap and PR Plan Following the staged approach used by other SGLang architecture efforts, each stage should stay independently reviewable and update this checklist as it lands. - [ ] **Stage 1 — Engine Load Reporter.** Add the optional Python Reporter, shared v1 protocol, snapshot validation, single-flight sampling, resilient streams, multi-tokenizer single ownership, tests, and documentation. Tracking PR: #32523 - [ ] **Stage 2 — Router Load Monitor.** Add the opt-in gRPC listener, discovery-driven registration/lease reconciliation, stream validation, per-DP aggregation, immutable snapshot API, Rust/unit/Kubernetes tests, and documentation. Existing routing policies remain unchanged. PR: #32927 - [ ] **Stage 3 — High-value load signal extensions.** Add Engine-authoritative fields that materially improve Router scheduling decisions. Select signals by worker role and measured decision value, and define their units, sampling, aggregation, freshness, compatibility, and validation before adoption. PR(s): TBD; depends on Stages 1 and 2. - [ ] **Stage 4 — Load-aware policy integration.** Define scoring, snapshot pinning, stale/missing fallback, PD role-specific signals, and rollout controls in a separate RFC/PR. Depends on Stage 2; no implicit policy change is part of this RFC's first implementation series. - [ ] **Stage 5 — SLA-aware service governance.** Use load and health signals in the Router Load Monitor to adaptively remove overloaded or unhealthy workers from routing and restore them after recovery. Define thresholds, hysteresis, fallback behavior, and observability to avoid flapping and protect the Engine fleet from cascading overload or failure. - [ ] **Stage 6 — Production hardening.** Add scale/overhead benchmarks, configurable timing policy, Router/Engine observability, multi-Router HA tests, and an agreed authentication/TLS or target-allowlist design. Stages 1 and 2 are parallel review tracks. Stage 3 is the first ordered dependency. Stage 4 depends on a stable immutable snapshot contract, Stage 5 builds service governance on that contract, and Stage 6 hardens the full path. ## Validation Plan ### Engine Reporter - store validation, timestamp fallback, and complete-rank publication; - report construction and source/sequence allocation; - single-flight sampling and event coalescing; - initial send, fixed cadence, backpressure, reconnect, lease, and shutdown; - IPC correlation and one runtime owner across multiple tokenizer workers; - optional dependency behavior and generated protobuf compatibility; - GPU E2E proving multiple HTTP workers establish one report stream. ### Router Monitor - CLI/config validation and ephemeral-port binding; - worker reconciliation, renewal, retry, topology change, and shutdown; - first-message stream binding, source retirement, ordering, and malformed data; - rank aggregation and freshness classification; - immutable snapshot versioning and deterministic ordering; - fake-worker Kubernetes E2E covering registration, reporting, renewal, and worker removal. ### Integrated and performance validation - container/image deployment with real Engine-to-Router registration; - observe fresh snapshot versions and running-load transitions under requests; - Engine restart, Router restart, target unreachability, and lease expiry; - multiple DP ranks, multiple tokenizer workers, PD roles, and multiple Routers; - CPU, bandwidth, event-loop latency, and request-latency measurements at several reporting intervals. A combined prototype has already been exercised in a container deployment to validate registration, continuous reporting, fresh snapshot publication, and request-driven load transitions. Community CI and the staged PR-specific tests remain the merge gates. ## Alternatives Considered ### Router polling `/v1/loads` This requires less Engine integration, but scales polling fan-out, introduces sampling skew, and duplicates connection/retry behavior. It remains useful as a diagnostic and compatibility fallback, not the proposed primary control plane. ### Router-maintained active request counters These are cheap and useful for lifecycle diagnostics, but they cannot represent internal queues, KV capacity, uncached Prefill work, rank imbalance, or Engine restarts. In a multi-Router HA deployment, each replica also counts only its own traffic contribution while sharing the same Engine fleet with its peers. A locally optimal choice from those fragmented counters can still be globally poor, so these counters should not be confused with scheduler-authoritative load. ### Prometheus queries Prometheus provides rich history and alerts but adds scrape/query latency and an external availability dependency. It is intentionally decoupled from per-request routing decisions. ### Short-lived HTTP pushes or a shared broker Per-report HTTP requests add connection churn and make stream identity less explicit. A broker improves decoupling but introduces another operational dependency before the basic in-process protocol and semantics are proven. ## Open Questions 1. Should the v1 protobuf remain embedded in Python and Rust with compatibility tests, or move to one repository-level canonical IDL/codegen location? 2. Which timing values should become public Router configuration after the initial fixed defaults? 3. Should `/v1/load_monitor/snapshot` remain a diagnostic/internal API or become a documented stable interface? 4. What authentication model best fits both open-source clusters and secured deployments: global API key, dedicated token, mTLS, target allowlist, or a combination? 5. Which raw and derived fields should the first load-aware policy use for regular, Prefill, and Decode workers, and what is the exact stale fallback? 6. Should protocol metadata eventually include SDK/build version and explicit topology generation, or are source ID, sequence, discovery identity, and lease sufficient? ## Requested Feedback - Is the push/lease split the right ownership model for SGLang deployments? - Are the v1 identity, ordering, freshness, and per-rank semantics sufficient? - Is the Reporter/Monitor/metric/policy PR boundary small enough for review? - Which security hardening item is required before broader production use? - Which routing policy should be the first consumer of immutable snapshots? ## References - Engine Load Reporter implementation: #32523 - Router Load Monitor implementation: PR #32927 - High-value load signal extensions: PR(s) TBD CC @merrymercy @hzh0425 @whybeyoung

title: [RFC][sgl-router] Recoverable KV Placement State with Snapshots and Event Replay
author: skajre
body: ## Background KV-aware routing relies on an accurate view of which KV blocks are available on each KV cache replica. Today, the Router builds this view incrementally from live `BlockStored` and `BlockRemoved` events. This works when the Router starts before the Workers and receives every event, but it cannot reliably recover when: - the Router or KV Indexer starts after caches have already been populated; - the placement-state consumer—either the Router’s embedded index or an external KV Indexer—restarts, loses its in-memory placement view, and must reconstruct it from replica snapshots before safely serving cache-aware routing decisions; - events are lost because of backpressure, network interruption, or subscriber restart; - a KV cache replica restarts and its previous placement state becomes invalid; - an event gap is older than the replay buffer. These cases do not affect inference correctness, but they may leave the placement view incomplete or stale, resulting in suboptimal routing and lower KV cache hit rates. ## Proposal Each independently routable KV cache replica should provide: - a **live event stream** for steady-state updates; - a **replay journal** for repairing short event gaps; - a **snapshot endpoint** for initialization and full recovery. The replica is identified by the same Worker endpoint and DP or attention-DP rank used by the existing KV-event subscription. No additional cache-group abstraction is introduced. ## Tensor Parallelism A KV cache replica may contain multiple TP ranks. KV tensors are physically sharded across those ranks, while their logical block hashes and block lifecycle are expected to remain synchronized. For example: ```text TP=4, DP=1 → 1 KV cache replica → 1 snapshot TP=4, DP=2 → 2 KV cache replicas → 2 snapshots ``` The Router selects a replica, not an individual TP rank. Therefore, one logical snapshot is exposed per replica rather than one snapshot per TP rank. A designated metadata leader, currently equivalent to: ```text pp_rank == 0 attn_tp_rank == 0 attn_cp_rank == 0 ``` represents the replica and owns: - snapshot generation; - event sequencing; - replay retention; - live event publication. This follows the ownership model already used by the current KV event publisher and avoids duplicate snapshots from TP ranks. ## Snapshot Semantics Each replica maintains: - `epoch`: changes whenever the replica is restarted or rebuilt; - `seq`: monotonically increases within one epoch. The epoch should be assigned by the replica lifecycle owner and propagated to the metadata publisher, rather than being generated only by the metadata leader. If any required TP rank is restarted or replaced, the replica must use a new epoch, even if the metadata leader itself did not restart. A snapshot contains: ```text worker endpoint dp_rank or attn_dp_rank epoch resume_seq active block records ``` Each active block record must include the parent relationship required to rebuild the placement index. The format may reuse `BlockStored`-compatible records: ```text parent_block_hash block_hashes ``` An equivalent chain representation is also acceptable as long as the consumer can reconstruct the same logical prefix tree. The consistency requirement is: > A snapshot with `resume_seq = N` reflects the effects of all placement events with sequence numbers smaller than `N`. Events starting from `N` can be recovered from the replay journal or live event stream. The snapshot contains placement metadata only. It does not transfer KV tensors. ## Architecture The placement-state consumer may be the Router’s embedded HashTree or an external KV Indexer. ## Main Flow During initialization or full recovery, the consumer: 1. Subscribes to the live event stream and buffers incoming events. 2. Fetches the replica snapshot. 3. Builds a staging placement view from the snapshot block records. 4. Replays events starting from `resume_seq`. 5. Applies buffered live events in sequence order and verifies that no sequence gap remains. 6. Atomically publishes the recovered view and marks the replica as `READY`. Snapshot, replay, and live events are independent inputs to the synchronization controller. They are not processed as a serial pipeline. Only `READY` replica views are used for cache-aware routing. During steady-state operation, live events are applied incrementally using `(epoch, seq)` for ordering and deduplication. ## Recovery Behavior - **Sequence gap:** stop using the affected replica for cache-aware routing and request replay from the missing sequence. - **Replay unavailable:** discard the affected view and fetch a new snapshot. - **Epoch change:** remove the old placement state and resynchronize the replica. - **Duplicate event:** ignore it using `(epoch, seq)`. - **Invalid or incomplete snapshot:** do not publish the staging view and retry synchronization. - **Recovery failure:** temporarily fall back to normal load-aware routing. - **Placement-state consumer restart:** fetch a fresh snapshot for every discovered replica, replay events from each replica’s `resume_seq`, and mark each replica as `READY` only after catch-up completes. Recovery stays outside the inference request path and should not block normal request processing. ## Expected Outcome After this change: - a newly started Router can discover KV blocks that already exist; - a restarted placement-state consumer can reconstruct its placement view before resuming cache-aware routing; - short event gaps can be repaired through replay; - gaps outside replay retention can be repaired through a new snapshot; - the parent relationships required by the HashTree can be restored; - multiple TP ranks expose one logical snapshot per KV cache replica; - replica restarts cannot leave stale placement state behind; - cache-aware routing safely degrades to load-aware routing during recovery. ## Related Work This proposal complements the ongoing [external KV Indexer work](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/33370) and [event-gap replay work](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/32729). It focuses on the missing full-state bootstrap and recovery mechanism.

title: [RFC] Distributed multimodal preprocessing for large multi-image requests in multi-node TP deployments
author: frankjoey2048
body:
## Summary

I'd like to discuss adding native support for distributed multimodal preprocessing in multi-node tensor-parallel deployments, particularly for requests that contain hundreds of images.

On the Kimi-K3 deployment we tested, one model instance spans four nodes with TP32/EP32. The API server and tokenizer manager run on rank 0, so image loading and preprocessing are naturally coordinated there. Increasing `--mm-processor-worker-num` improves concurrency on rank 0, but it does not use the CPU capacity available on the other TP nodes. For very large multi-image requests, rank 0 becomes the preprocessing bottleneck while the CPUs on the other nodes stay mostly idle.

The core requirement is not just distributing independent requests. A *single* request containing hundreds of images should be divisible into bounded chunks that can be processed across all nodes and then merged back in the original image order.

## Deployment context

```text
Model:                       Kimi-K3
Nodes:                       4
GPUs per node:               8 x H200
CPU per node:                150 cores
Memory per node:             1500 GB
Tensor parallel size:        32
Expert parallel size:        32
Maximum images per request:  512
Typical stress-test image:   512 x 512
Multimodal feature transport: CPU
```

All four Pods run the same startup command, and the node rank is assigned by the orchestration platform. The four nodes form one TP32 model instance, not four independent replicas, and rank 0 remains the API and request-lifecycle coordinator.

## Current challenge

For a request containing 512 images, preprocessing involves image download or byte loading, JPEG/PNG decode, resize, normalization, patchification, image-grid calculation, final image-token expansion, and construction of the multimodal scheduler inputs.

Processing all 512 images as a single unit has several drawbacks: only one node performs most of the CPU preprocessing; the request is too large to schedule fairly alongside smaller requests; request-count limits don't reflect actual preprocessing cost; implicit queues make timeout and cancellation behavior hard to control; a failure late in preprocessing can waste substantial CPU work; and the large preprocessed outputs need clear ownership and lifecycle rules.

Request-level load balancing alone does not solve this. A single 512-image request must itself be shardable.

## Prototype design

I implemented a Kimi-K3-specific prototype using an external multimodal processor plus one CPU preprocessing worker service on each TP node. Rank 0 stays the control plane:

```text
Client request
  -> rank-0 API / TokenizerManager
  -> weighted admission queue
  -> split images into ordered chunks
  -> distribute chunks to CPU workers on all nodes
  -> collect per-chunk tensors and metadata
  -> sort by original image index
  -> merge processor outputs
  -> construct final input_ids once from the complete prompt
  -> submit one multimodal request to the TP32 scheduler
```

The remote CPU workers do preprocessing only:

```text
image decode -> resize -> normalize -> patchify
  -> return pixel_values, image_grid_thw, original image sizes
```

ViT, projector, and model inference all remain on the GPUs.

## Prototype scheduling configuration

For a 512-image request:

```text
Images per RPC chunk:            16
Chunks per request:              32
Max parallel chunks per request: 16
Max in-flight RPCs per endpoint:  8
Endpoints:                        4
Max global in-flight RPCs:       32
```

Admission is weighted by image count rather than request count alone:

```text
Max admitted image credits: 8192
Max admitted requests:        16
Queue timeout:              1800 seconds
```

So `16 requests * 512 images = 8192 admitted images`, and additional requests wait in a FIFO queue. The 16 admitted requests do not create 256 simultaneous RPCs — remote execution stays bounded by `4 endpoints * 8 RPCs = 32` global in-flight RPCs.

## Admission lifecycle

A preprocessing-only semaphore isn't enough, because completed features may still be retained while waiting for GPU scheduling and generation. In the prototype, admission credit is held from the start of multimodal preprocessing until one of: generation completes, request processing fails, the request is cancelled, or the client disconnects. For a batch request, credits are released for all corresponding request IDs. This prevents preprocessing from producing an unbounded number of completed feature tensors ahead of the GPU scheduler.

## Chunk merge requirements

Each chunk carries its original image offset and returns:

```text
chunk index
original image start index
pixel_values
image_grid_thw
original image sizes
```

Rank 0 sorts chunk results by original image index and verifies there are no missing or duplicated ranges. The final `input_ids` is constructed only once, using the complete original prompt, the complete ordered image-grid list, and the complete ordered original image-size list. Constructing `input_ids` independently inside each chunk would lose the relationship between the original prompt and the image placeholders.

This merge is model-specific today. A generic upstream design would likely need a processor-defined interface for: split request, process shard, merge shard outputs, and rebuild final prompt tokens.

## Failure semantics

The prototype uses strict failure behavior: no automatic chunk retry; no fallback to rank-0 local preprocessing; one failed chunk fails the whole multimodal request; unsent chunks are cancelled immediately; queue waiting does not mark an endpoint unhealthy; HTTP 4xx is treated as a request error; connection errors, processing timeouts, and HTTP 5xx trigger endpoint cooldown; and endpoint queue time is excluded from the remote processing timeout.

Automatic retry is intentionally disabled because a timed-out worker may still be processing the original chunk, and retrying large chunks on another node can multiply CPU, memory, and network work.

## Offline stress-test results

The prototype was tested without starting SGLang inference or an HTTP service.

```text
Submitted requests:            512
Admitted requests:              16
Queued requests:               496
Images per admitted request:   512
Total real images preprocessed: 8192
Image size:                    512 x 512
Chunks processed:              512
```

Observed limits:

```text
Max global RPC concurrency:  32
Max concurrency per endpoint: 8
Endpoint chunk distribution:  128 / 127 / 128 / 129
```

Performance on one 128-core, 1500 GB host simulating four endpoint pools:

```text
Elapsed time:                62.731 s
Throughput:                 130.59 images/s
Encoded request traffic:      6.007 GiB
Returned processor output:   25.912 GiB
Merged output retained (rank 0): 25.912 GiB
Peak process RSS:            31.664 GiB
```

All request and image credits were released after the test.

This was an offline CPU/control-plane test only. It did **not** include physical cross-node network transfer, ViT execution, TP32 scheduler behavior, GPU prefill, or end-to-end TTFT. The results demonstrate bounded preprocessing and memory behavior, but not final end-to-end model throughput.

## Design questions

**1. Should distributed preprocessing be a native SGLang abstraction?** Would it make sense to add a processor interface along the lines of `estimate_cost(request)`, `split_multimodal_request(request)`, `process_multimodal_shard(shard)`, and `merge_multimodal_shards(results)`? The model-specific processor would define how image outputs and prompt tokens are merged, while SGLang provides admission, endpoint scheduling, and lifecycle management.

**2. What should admission measure?** Image count is enough for the current workload but may not generalize. Candidate cost metrics include image count, decoded pixel count, estimated patch count, estimated vision tokens, video frame count, and expected processor-output bytes. A processor-provided cost estimate may be more appropriate than a global image-count limit.

**3. Where should processed features be aggregated?** The prototype returns all features to rank 0 because rank 0 owns the TokenizerManager and the scheduler submission path. That's the simplest incremental design, but it creates a rank-0 network and memory aggregation point. A more scalable design could have the CPU worker store the processed feature locally and return a handle; the scheduler then assigns images to encoder/TP ranks, and target ranks retrieve the corresponding feature. That would require scheduler-aware feature ownership, cancellation, cache lifetime, and transport support. Would rank-0 aggregation be acceptable as an initial implementation, or should the design start with distributed feature handles?

**4. Where should request-lifecycle credits be released?** The credit must survive beyond preprocessing and be released after generation completes or the client disconnects. Is there an existing generic request-finalization hook an external multimodal processor should use, or would a new TokenizerManager lifecycle hook be appropriate?

**5. How should sessions and multimodal feature caching interact with admission?** The current prototype targets ordinary non-session OpenAI-compatible requests. Long-lived sessions may retain image features after generation and need a different ownership model. It would help to clarify whether session-held features should consume the same admission budget or a separate cache budget.

## Possible incremental implementation

**Phase 1:** keep rank 0 as the feature aggregation point; add weighted multimodal admission; add bounded intra-request shard scheduling; add processor-defined split/merge callbacks; add explicit cancellation and lifecycle release; and support external worker endpoints.

**Phase 2:** add shared-memory or remote feature handles; allow scheduler or encoder ranks to retrieve features directly; integrate feature placement with multimodal caching; and avoid returning all processed tensors through rank 0.

## Attached prototype patch

I can attach the current Kimi-K3 deployment patch as a reference implementation. It includes a versioned preprocessing protocol, node-count-independent endpoint discovery, FIFO weighted admission, image chunking, explicit per-endpoint capacity, strict cancellation and failure behavior, ordered tensor/metadata merging, and request-lifecycle credit release.

It's a deployment prototype, **not** a proposed upstream patch — the goal of attaching it is to provide concrete behavior and test data for the design discussion.

```text
Reference implementation / RFC prototype — not a proposed upstream patch
```

## Environment

```text
SGLang branch:  origin/kimi-k3
SGLang commit:  15fa94d2c6724999c299996fe40a5b276a559812
Python:         3.12.13
PyTorch:        2.11.0+cu129
Model:          Kimi-K3
Deployment:     4 nodes, TP32/EP32
GPUs:           32 x H200
CPU MM workers: 4 per node
I/O workers:    16 per node
```

Prototype patch (based on commit `15fa94d2c6724999c299996fe40a5b276a559812`, branch `origin/kimi-k3`): [kimi_k3_distributed_cpu_preprocess_full.patch](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/30669680/kimi_k3_distributed_cpu_preprocess_full.patch)

## Related upstream discussions

- #28669 proposes a standalone/disaggregated request preprocessing abstraction, but leaves heavy multimodal preprocessing placement open.
- #33035 covers bounded pre-scheduler multimodal admission and the CPU memory retained before requests reach the scheduler.
- #24945 covers EPD-side parallel decode, GPU preprocessing, pipelining, and encoder DP.
- #16787 covers efficient ownership and transport of large multimodal tensors between TokenizerManager and Scheduler.

This RFC focuses on the remaining case: sharding one very large multi-image request across the CPU resources of all nodes in a multi-node TP instance, followed by ordered processor-defined merging and lifecycle-scoped admission accounting.

title: [RFC] Allow prefill CUDA graph bs below chunked_prefill_size under post-capture KV sizing
author: hnyls2002
body:
## Summary

Post-capture KV sizing currently requires the prefill CUDA graph to have captured every reachable prefill shape. This RFC proposes relaxing that to the treatment the decode side already uses: allow the prefill bucket list to top out below `chunked_prefill_size`, and reserve activation headroom for the eager prefill instead of disabling the feature.

## Current behavior

`post_capture_kv_sizing_planned()` in `python/sglang/srt/server_args.py` bails out entirely when the largest reachable prefill forward batch is not already captured:

```python
if (
    prefill_cfg.backend == Backend.DISABLED
    or self.chunked_prefill_size <= 0
    or self.max_prefill_buffer_tokens() > max(prefill_cfg.bs or (0,))
):
    return False
```

`max_prefill_buffer_tokens()` is `chunked_prefill_size` outside PP dynamic chunking, and `prefill.max_bs` defaults to `chunked_prefill_size`, so the condition holds under default settings. It stops holding as soon as anyone passes `--cuda-graph-max-bs-prefill` below `chunked_prefill_size`, at which point the feature turns off with no log saying why.

## Why the constraint is stronger than the requirement

**The two values are independent knobs.** `chunked_prefill_size` is a scheduling ceiling; prefill `max_bs` is capture coverage. Requiring the latter to be >= the former makes "capture covers every reachable prefill shape" a precondition of post-capture sizing. That is an implementation convenience, not something the mechanism needs.

**What the mechanism needs is a bound on eager activation, not the absence of eager forwards.** The benefit of post-capture sizing is that graph memory is *measured* rather than *estimated*. That benefit is orthogonal to whether some forwards run eager. The decode side already operates on exactly this reading: `compute_post_capture_kv_resize()` in `python/sglang/srt/model_executor/model_runner_components/kv_pool_runtime.py` accepts a captured decode `max_bs` below `max_running_requests` and raises the reserve instead of bailing out.

```python
eager_decode_gap = (... and decode_max_bs < running_requests)
if eager_decode_gap or mambaish_config(...) is not None:
    headroom_gb = max(headroom_gb, ...pre_capture_activation_reserve_mb(...) / 1024)
```

**The current gate makes two legitimate goals mutually exclusive.** Lowering prefill `max_bs` is a reasonable thing to want: the bucket list runs to `chunked_prefill_size` and its largest buckets cost seconds each to capture. Today you can have a shorter capture or post-capture sizing, never both.

The one defensible argument for the status quo is that the eager prefill activation peak is hard to estimate, and under-reserving means OOM. But decode carries the same uncertainty and chose to reserve. That argues for a more conservative formula, not for a hard gate.

## Proposal

Move the prefill condition out of the gate and onto the headroom path that `eager_decode_gap` already uses:

- keep `backend == DISABLED` and `chunked_prefill_size <= 0` as hard gates, since those are genuinely inapplicable
- when `max_prefill_buffer_tokens() > max(prefill_cfg.bs)`, warn and raise `headroom_gb` to cover the eager prefill activation peak

No new estimate is needed: `pre_capture_activation_reserve_mb()` already has a prefill branch keyed on `chunked_prefill_size`. Its 10GB floor on large-memory GPUs makes the relaxed path less profitable than the fully-captured one, but still better than the current fallback, which on top of the same activation reserve also *estimates* graph memory via `reserve_for_graph_mb()`.

A tighter variant would reserve only the delta between the eager prefill peak and the largest captured bucket's peak, since the latter is already reflected in the measured free memory. That needs a model of how activation scales with token count, so it seems worth doing only if the simple version proves too conservative in practice.

## A smaller item that can land independently

Whichever way the above goes, the gate should not be silent. Passing `--cuda-graph-max-bs-prefill` below `chunked_prefill_size` today disables post-capture KV sizing with no diagnostic at all. A single `logger.warning` naming the two values would have saved the debugging in #33847 and costs nothing.

## Context

This surfaced in #33847, where a CI-wide `--cuda-graph-max-bs-prefill 1024` default silently gated the feature off on H100-class GPUs, on which `chunked_prefill_size` defaults to 8192.

title: [RFC] PD disaggregation: single protocol layer, per-backend transport
author: hnyls2002
body:
## Summary

The three PD transfer backends (mooncake, nixl, mori) each implement the full bootstrap + transfer control protocol independently: ZMQ socket loops, message dispatch, room/state lifecycle, staging glue, TP/DCP slice orchestration, timeouts, failure handling. They describe the same protocol but have drifted apart.

This RFC proposes a **target end state** where the protocol exists once and a backend only implements data movement. It is an early proposal: the interface below is a sketch, and whether the end state is reachable exactly as drawn is open.

## Why

The divergence is not cosmetic -- each copy is missing something the others have. Examples from comparing the three:

- mori's decode manager never starts the heartbeat checker thread, so a dead prefill peer is never detected (mooncake and nixl both start it).
- nixl's sender never enforces the bootstrap timeout, and prefill-side transfer failures are not propagated to decode -- requests hang until the generic waiting timeout instead of failing fast.
- The transfer-info message swaps two frame positions between mooncake and nixl; both frames hold integers, so a mismatch would silently exchange two fields rather than fail cleanly.

Every protocol fix or feature is currently written up to three times (staging exists in mooncake+nixl only, DCP relayout in mooncake+nixl only, session blacklisting in mooncake only), and the per-backend classes are dispatched through an enum-keyed `get_kv_class` table that erases static typing.

## Target end state (sketch, open to change)

One concrete set of protocol classes -- `KVManager` / `KVSender` / `KVReceiver` / `KVBootstrapServer` -- with no backend subclasses. Socket loops, parsing/dispatch, room lifecycle, staging, chunking, TP/DCP slice math, timeouts, heartbeat, failure propagation live there, once. A backend provides only a transport object, injected at construction:

```python
class BaseTransport(ABC):
    def init_engine(self): ...
    def register_memory(self, kv_args): ...
    def local_desc(self) -> bytes: ...            # opaque, carried in the register message
    def open_peer(self, session_id, desc: bytes) -> Peer: ...
    def submit(self, peer, blocks) -> Handle: ... # blocks = [(src_ptr, dst_ptr, len)]
    def poll(self, handle) -> KVPoll: ...
```

Boundary: protocol decides which bytes go where and when; transport moves `(src_ptr, dst_ptr, len)` and names remote memory. Backend directories shrink to thin wrappers around their engines (today mooncake calls 5 engine methods, nixl 14, mori 8). `get_kv_class` / `KVClassType` are replaced by a typed `make_transport(backend)`. The `fake` backend becomes a null transport, which also makes the whole protocol layer testable in CPU-only CI.

There is no big-bang refactor implied: the intended path is many small PRs -- behavior alignments (individually reviewable fixes) and mechanical hoists of already-identical code. Wire-format unification goes last and needs its own migration story, since there is no version negotiation today.

## Open questions

- Completion signaling: mooncake/mori report status to decode over ZMQ; nixl uses in-band transport notifications with a passive decode side. Which model should the unified layer own?
- Is the 6-method transport interface sufficient? (nixl's prepped descriptor lists need per-peer cached state; mixed VRAM/DRAM pools are nixl-only today.)
- `is_dummy` / abort-ack / guard-frame semantics differ subtly across the three; each needs a call on which behavior is intended.
- Wire migration: flag day vs a version frame with a dual-parse window.

Feedback from the mooncake / nixl / mori owners is the main ask -- especially whether this target shape conflicts with anything planned for the backends.

title: [RFC] Remove the torchao integration (`--torchao-config`)
author: b8zhong
body:
## Summary

`--torchao-config` has been **broken since 2026-04-19** — every accepted value raises
`ImportError` — and the breakage went undetected for ~4 months. The feature has had no new
capability since 2024-09-28, no commit from its upstream author since 2024-12-20, and no CI
coverage at any point.

I propose we remove it outright — no deprecation period — and drop `torchao` from the core
dependency block of `python/pyproject.toml`. A deprecation window exists to give working behavior
time to migrate; there is no working behavior here, so it would only delay the cleanup.

## 1. It is currently broken, not merely unused

`python/sglang/srt/layers/torchao_utils.py:47-56` imports five snake_case factory functions.
torchao renamed all of them to `*Config` dataclasses and removed the old names — and that landed
**before** the version we pin, not in a later one:

```console
$ python -c "import torchao; print(torchao.__version__)"
0.17.0+cu130

$ python -c "from torchao.quantization import int4_weight_only"
ImportError: cannot import name 'int4_weight_only' from 'torchao.quantization'
```

The import block pulls all five names at once, so this is not a partial breakage — every
documented value fails identically:

| `--torchao-config` | result |
| --- | --- |
| `int8wo` | `ImportError` |
| `int8dq` | `ImportError` |
| `int4wo-128` | `ImportError` |
| `fp8wo` | `ImportError` |
| `fp8dq-per_row` | `ImportError` |

<details>
<summary>Reproduction</summary>

```python
import torch
from sglang.srt.layers.torchao_utils import apply_torchao_config_to_model

m = torch.nn.Sequential()
m.add_module("proj", torch.nn.Linear(64, 64))
for cfg in ["int8wo", "int8dq", "int4wo-128", "fp8wo", "fp8dq-per_row"]:
    try:
        apply_torchao_config_to_model(m, cfg)
        print(cfg, "OK")
    except Exception as e:
        print(cfg, "FAIL:", type(e).__name__, str(e)[:80])
```

All five print `FAIL: ImportError`.
</details>

### How it broke, and why nobody noticed

```
2026-04-19  #23119  "[CI] Add per-job uv venv isolation and upgrade CI version to Cuda 13"
            -  "torchao==0.9.0",
            +  "torchao==0.17.0",
```

The pin jumped eight minor versions as **collateral of a CUDA-13 CI upgrade**, not as a deliberate
torchao upgrade, so nobody audited the API surface.

Two things kept it silent afterwards:

- **No CI coverage.** The only tests are `test/manual/quant/test_torchao.py` and the torchao case in
  `test/manual/test_srt_engine_with_quant_args.py`. `test/README.md:15` documents `manual/` as
  "Non-CI tests for local debugging or special setups."
- **#17626 (2026-01-22, "Lazy import torchao")** moved the `if torchao_config == "": return` guard
  *above* the import block. Intended to suppress import-time warnings, it also means the
  `ImportError` only fires for users who actually pass the flag, rather than at startup.

No issue has been filed in those four months. That is the usage signal.

## 2. Development history

Full history of `torchao_utils.py` — 16 commits:

| Period | What happened |
| --- | --- |
| 2024-09-09 → 2024-12-20 | Real development. 6 of 8 commits by Jerry Zhang (torchao maintainer), who built it upstream-in. |
| **2024-09-28** | `Add float8 dynamic quant to torchao_utils` (#1528) — **last time the feature gained a capability.** The `int8dq/int8wo/int4wo/fp8wo/fp8dq` menu has been frozen for ~23 months. |
| **2024-12-20** | #2528 (gemlite) — **last commit by torchao upstream.** |
| 2025-01-22 → 2026-01-22 | Three maintenance commits, net **negative** LOC: layered-loading plumbing (#3061, generic on-the-fly quant, not torchao work), a Conv3d skip for VLMs (#13508, +14/−3), and `clean up gemlite usage` (#14444, **−41 lines, pure deletion**). |
| 2026-01-22 | `Lazy import torchao` (#17626), +4/−3 — see above. |

The two most recent commits are a backend removal and an import deferral. Nothing has been added
since 2024.

## 3. It was never a first-class quantization path

- **Not registered.** `torchao` is absent from `QUANTIZATION_METHODS`
  (`python/sglang/srt/layers/quantization/__init__.py:72`). It is a bolt-on flag that rewrites
  modules after load, selecting layers by substring match (`"proj" in fqn`) rather than by any
  checkpoint-declared config.
- **Dead branch.** `python/sglang/srt/models/paddleocr_vl.py:293` tests
  `quant_config.get_name() in ["bitsandbytes", "torchao"]` — unreachable, since no such name is
  registered.
- **No checkpoint support.** sglang cannot load torchao-serialized HF checkpoints (the `pytorch/*`
  org). That is vLLM's torchao backend; sglang never had an equivalent.

## 4. At the current frontier (NVFP4 / MXFP8 / MXFP4), torchao offers nothing we lack

This is the decisive point. The `--torchao-config` menu is int8/int4/fp8 only — **no fp4, no mx
formats at all.** torchao's work on those formats lives elsewhere in the library and is behind what
we already ship (checked against torchao `main`, v0.19.0):

| | torchao | sglang today |
| --- | --- | --- |
| status | `torchao/prototype/mx_formats/` — not exported from `torchao.quantization` | registered: `modelopt_fp4`, `nvfp4_online`, `petit_nvfp4`, `mxfp4`, `mxfp8`, `mxfp_w4a8`, `quark_mxfp4` |
| NVFP4 linear | `torch._scaled_mm` (cuBLAS) + mslk triton quant | flashinfer `mm_fp4`, trtllm-gen, cutlass, marlin fallback |
| MXFP8 / MXFP4 | `_addmm_mx_dispatch` → `_scaled_mm` | flashinfer / trtllm-gen, `triton_kernels`, aiter on ROCm |
| MoE | `aten._grouped_mm` → `scaled_grouped_mm` only | flashinfer-cutlass + trtllm-gen fused MoE runners |

torchao's genuine state-of-the-art contributions are **training-side** — float8/MXFP8 pretraining,
MXFP8 MoE training, QAT, PARQ. None of that is reachable from an inference server.

**Most importantly, owning these paths is what lets us write faster kernels.** Every row above where
sglang wins is a row where we call a kernel we can tune, autotune, and specialize per shape and per
architecture — flashinfer, trtllm-gen, cutlass, cute-dsl. torchao's inference path bottoms out in
`torch._scaled_mm` / `_addmm_mx_dispatch`, which hands the shape to cuBLAS and ends the conversation:
no tactic selection, no epilogue fusion, no per-model tuning, no ability to fix a bad shape without
waiting on an upstream release. A dependency that can only ever be as fast as the default cuBLAS
kernel is not a quantization backend we want on the critical path.

And this is where the hardware is going, not a niche: **future architectures prioritize NVFP4 /
MXFP8 / MXFP4** — Blackwell and beyond put the block-scaled 4- and 8-bit formats in the tensor cores
as the first-class datapath, with hardware scale-factor handling, and that is where the remaining
perf is.

**int8 and int4 are legacy formats.** They were the answer when tensor cores had no sub-8-bit float
support and quantization had to be integer; that constraint is gone. On current and future hardware
int8/int4 are emulated or de-prioritized paths, they carry accuracy penalties that block-scaled fp4
does not, and no frontier checkpoint ships in them. The entire `--torchao-config` menu —
`int8wo`, `int8dq`, `int4wo-128`, plus per-tensor `fp8wo`/`fp8dq` — is the previous generation's
frontier, and where users still want int4 we already serve it better through AWQ and GPTQ-marlin.
Carrying a broken dependency for legacy formats while the formats that matter are served by kernels
we control is exactly backwards.

## 5. What keeping it costs

- **`torchao==0.17.0` is a hard pin in the core `dependencies` block** of `python/pyproject.toml:80`
  — every CUDA install pays ~21 MB and a version constraint for a feature that raises `ImportError`.
- **The pin drags others.** `python/pyproject_other.toml` pins
  `peft>=0.18.0,<0.19.0  # Pin to <0.19.0 due to torchao incompatibility` in two places.
- **Dedicated noise suppression** exists only to hide torchao's import-time warnings:
  `python/sglang/srt/utils/hf_transformers_patches.py:76-88` and `:224-230`, plus
  `python/sglang/multimodal_gen/runtime/utils/logging_utils.py:565`.
- `python/sglang/check_env.py` lists `"torchao"` twice (lines 29 and 43).

## 6. Prior art: how vLLM handles it

Worth comparing, because vLLM's integration is the one people cite — and it is a different thing,
built differently.

**vLLM does not depend on torchao.** No occurrences in `requirements/`, `setup.py`,
`pyproject.toml`, or `docker/`. It is a lazily-imported optional backend gated on
`find_spec("torchao")`; the docs instruct users to install it themselves.

| | sglang | vLLM |
| --- | --- | --- |
| entry point | `--torchao-config` flag, on-the-fly quant post-load | `quant_method: "torchao"` in HF config |
| in quant registry | ✗ | ✓ `"torchao": TorchAOConfig` |
| checkpoint loading | none | `is_checkpoint_torchao_serialized`, safetensors, `ModuleFqnToConfig` regex |
| layer skipping | substring `"proj" in fqn` | `modules_to_not_convert` + `should_skip()` |
| API drift handling | pinned, broken | `torchao_version_at_least("0.15.0")` runtime gates |
| dependency | hard pin, core deps | not a dependency |

That last row is why theirs still works and ours does not.

**But vLLM's backend is also in maintenance mode.** Last substantive change: `update torchao
safetensors impl` (2025-12-08). The ~8 months since are janitorial — typo fixes,
`Optional[X]` → `X | None`, torch-version cleanup, one error-message bugfix (2026-05-23), and a
ROCm CI skip (2026-07-27). Jerry Zhang's last vLLM torchao commit was 2025-11-04.

Notably, the one idea that grew out of it — `Support RL online quantization with torchao`
(2025-10-01) — was generalized into vLLM-wide **layerwise reload / QeRL** infra, actively developed
through 2026-07-25 and no longer torchao-specific. The reusable concept outlived the backend.

## 7. Proposal

Remove it in the next release. No deprecation window — every code path already raises `ImportError`,
so there is nothing working to give users time to migrate off.

**Remove:**

- `python/sglang/srt/layers/torchao_utils.py`
- the `torchao_config` server arg (`python/sglang/srt/server_args.py:2015-2019`)
- `python/sglang/srt/model_executor/model_runner.py:83` and `:752-755`
- the layered-loading torchao branch, `python/sglang/srt/model_loader/loader.py:907-960`
- the dead `"torchao"` name at `python/sglang/srt/models/paddleocr_vl.py:293`
- `test/manual/quant/test_torchao.py` and the torchao case in `test/manual/test_srt_engine_with_quant_args.py`
- the duplicate `check_env.py:43` entry

**Dependencies:** move `torchao` out of the core `dependencies` block. The diffusion path keeps it
transitively — `cache-dit==1.3.0` declares `torchao>=0.14.1; extra == "quantization"`, backing the
