_No response_

title: [RFC] FuseEP Integration for MiniMax-M3 Prefill on Ascend NPU
author: ClownBin
body:
## 1. Summary

This RFC proposes an opt-in Ascend FuseEP path for MiniMax-M3 W8A8 prefill in SGLang. It adds a MiniMax-M3-specific normal-mode operator, DispatchFFNCombineM3, that fuses routed-expert dispatch, the two expert FFN GEMMs, and combine into one EP operation. The existing low-latency FuseEP path remains the decode path.

The initial implementation is deliberately narrow: MiniMax-M3, ModelSlim W8A8, hidden size 6144, top-k 4, 128 routed experts, and EP/TP 16 on Ascend NPU. It does not alter the generic DeepEP path, routing algorithm, attention implementation, or model semantics.

Reference implementation:

- SGLang integration: https://github.com/ClownBin/sglang/commit/2ca0e6cc3bfcb3379926e6261d95cc6dfe9f039c
- Ascend kernel and DeepEP adapter: https://github.com/ClownBin/sgl-kernel-npu/commit/87525b7305d449dfc66272465feb856188244092
- Original experiment and launch configuration: https://github.com/ClownBin/sglang/issues/19#issuecomment-5099607728

---

## 2. Motivation

For long prefill, the conventional MoE path exposes separate dispatch, expert-GEMM, and combine phases. In the tested MiniMax-M3 deployment, those boundaries leave observable accelerator idle periods and limit NPU utilization. The data path must also accommodate MiniMax-M3's W8A8 weight layout and SwiGLU variant.

FuseEP can eliminate those boundaries by performing dispatch, FFN, and combine in one operator and HCCL EP collective. This is useful for chunked prefill, where batch work amortizes normal-mode collective setup. Decode has a different latency profile, so it continues to use FuseEP's existing low-latency fused_deep_moe mode.

The supplied 56-concurrency comparison against DeepEP reported 575.84 tok/s and 54.21 ms. Two FuseEP observations reported 645.23 tok/s / 49.88 ms and 726 tok/s / 49.20 ms. These are individual runs rather than an aggregate; the RFC therefore treats them as preliminary and requires reproducible median-based evaluation before upstream acceptance.

---

## 3. Goals

- Add an opt-in ascend_fuseep MoE A2A backend path for MiniMax-M3 prefill on Ascend NPU.
- Fuse routed-expert dispatch, W8A8 FFN execution, and combine through DispatchFFNCombineM3.
- Preserve existing router/top-k semantics, shared-expert computation, scheduler, DP-attention behavior, and decode flow.
- Handle DP-attention ranks with zero local prefill tokens without an EP collective mismatch.
- Validate operator correctness, end-to-end model outputs, invalid configurations, and performance with a documented benchmark protocol.

## 4. Non-Goals

- Replacing DeepEP or making FuseEP the default backend.
- Supporting arbitrary models, expert counts, hidden sizes, top-k values, quantization formats, or EP degrees in the first version.
- Changing MiniMax-M3 routing, sparse attention, speculative decoding, or shared-expert semantics.
- Claiming performance gains for decode, short prefill, or unqualified hardware and software versions.

---

## 5. Design

### 5.1 Architecture

SGLang continues to compute router logits and top-k selections. When the MoE A2A backend is ascend_fuseep, FusedMoE selects the Ascend FuseEP implementation for routed experts:

~~~text
router + top-k (existing SGLang)
          |
          +--> shared experts (existing model flow)
          |
          +--> routed experts
                 |
                 +-- prefill: DispatchFFNCombineM3
                 |      dispatch -> W8A8 GEMM1/SwiGLU -> GEMM2 -> combine
                 |
                 +-- decode: existing low-latency FuseEP fused_deep_moe
          |
          +--> add routed and shared-expert outputs
~~~

DispatchFFNCombineM3 receives activations, top-k expert IDs and weights, packed W8A8 expert weights/scales, and the EP HCCL group. It performs all-to-all dispatch, two expert FFN projections with the MiniMax-M3 SwiGLU epilogue, and combine in one normal-mode invocation.

### 5.2 Operator contract and weight preparation

At model-load time, the NPU quantization path transforms and format-casts routed-expert weights and scale tensors into the layout required by FuseEP. The M3 kernel is isolated from the generic operator because it has a fixed ABI and fused activation behavior.

Initial contract:

- BF16 activations and outputs.
- INT8 W8A8 expert weights and matching scales.
- Hidden size 6144, top-k 4, 128 routed experts, and EP size 16.
- MiniMax-M3 SwiGLU behavior, including model-specific clamp and scaling rules.

Unsupported combinations must fail clearly during startup or model initialization rather than silently selecting an incompatible kernel.

### 5.3 Prefill/decode selection and DP attention

SGLANG_ENABLE_M3_FUSEEP_PREFILL=1 enables the M3 normal-mode operator only for extend/prefill batches. It requires SGLANG_NPU_FUSED_MOE_MODE=2, and server-argument validation enforces that relationship. Decode stays on the existing low-latency FuseEP path and reuses the prepared weight layout.

With DP attention, an EP rank may have zero local tokens while other ranks have work. Every EP rank must still enter the collective. An idle rank supplies a deterministic zero-valued dummy route, then discards its output. Prefill dispatch capacity uses global token counts when available so each rank provides storage sufficient for its routed-token worst case.

### 5.4 Configuration

The feature is disabled by default. A qualified deployment enables it with the existing backend flag and explicit switches:

~~~bash
export SGLANG_NPU_FUSED_MOE_MODE=2
export SGLANG_ENABLE_M3_FUSEEP_PREFILL=1
export SGLANG_DEEPEP_NUM_MAX_DISPATCH_TOKENS_PER_RANK=16
python3 -m sglang.launch_server --model-path /path/to/MiniMax-M3-w8a8 --device npu --attention-backend ascend --quantization modelslim --tp-size 16 --dp-size 4 --enable-dp-attention --enable-dp-lm-head --moe-a2a-backend ascend_fuseep --deepep-mode auto
~~~

The deployment must use a compatible Ascend CANN/toolkit and the matching FuseEP vendor operator build. Network and HCCL settings are deployment-specific and intentionally outside this RFC's public interface.

---

## 6. Alternatives considered

1. Keep DeepEP for prefill. It remains the compatible baseline, but leaves dispatch/GEMM/combine boundaries visible to the runtime.
2. Use the existing low-latency FuseEP mode for every batch. It is retained for decode, but is not the intended normal-mode long-prefill operator for this M3 layout.
3. Generalize the operator before integration. The specialized integration lets us validate lifecycle, correctness, and performance with explicit constraints; generalization should follow qualification.

---

## 7. Evaluation plan and acceptance criteria

### Correctness

- An EP16 operator test verifies routed-token counts and a deterministic reference output.
- Verify the M3 SwiGLU epilogue and W8A8 weight/scale layout against a non-fused reference.
- Compare end-to-end greedy outputs with the qualified DeepEP baseline over fixed prompts, including long prefill and DP-attention batches with idle ranks.
- Test startup failures for unsupported fused-MoE modes, layouts, and operator contracts.

### Performance

- Publish the complete server command, model revision, CANN/torch-npu/FuseEP versions, node topology, dataset, prompt/output lengths, request rate, and warm-up protocol.
- Compare DeepEP and FuseEP at several concurrency levels; report at least three repetitions and median throughput, TTFT, TPOT, and E2E latency.
- Include profiling evidence that attributes gains to reduced bubbles and operator boundaries, not a changed workload or speculative acceptance rate.
- Measure decode separately and ensure M3 prefill selection does not regress it.

Acceptance requires no correctness regression on the qualified matrix, stable collective behavior with DP attention, and reproducible improvement for the target long-prefill workload.

---

## 8. Rollout and future work

Roll out behind SGLANG_ENABLE_M3_FUSEEP_PREFILL, with DeepEP remaining the fallback. Broaden to other EP sizes, quantization schemes, or MoE architectures only after each combination has its own correctness and performance qualification.

Questions for maintainers:

1. Is a model-specific opt-in backend acceptable as the first upstream step, or should it remain in the Ascend extension until a wider operator contract is ready?
2. What CANN, torch-npu, firmware, and topology matrix should be required for the initial support statement?
3. Should the environment switches become explicit server arguments once the qualified scope expands?

title: [RFC] Pluggable KV Compression for Disaggregated Serving
author: luoroger37
body: ### Checklist - [x] If this is not a feature request but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed. - [x] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed. ### Motivation ## Summary This RFC proposes an optional KV compression path for Prefill-to-Decode transfer over Mooncake RDMA. SGLang would manage layout preparation, bounded buffers, transfer metadata, and asynchronous completion through a small internal interface for compression backends. Attention would continue to read the existing GPU KV format after received data has been restored. The initial implementation targets lossless P/D transfer on one explicitly supported MHA/GQA layout. The architecture also includes a path toward reusing compressed payloads and integrating with HiCache, with those capabilities delivered as separate extensions. This is a design proposal. No compression ratio or serving speedup has been established. The immediate review request concerns the integration boundary and validation plan; broader support would depend on correctness and measurable benefit. ## Motivation and Scope In P/D serving, KV transfer can delay the handoff from Prefill to Decode. Compression can reduce the transferred bytes, but adds computation, memory traffic, synchronization, and temporary storage. Whether it helps depends on the actual KV distribution, effective network bandwidth, and concurrent model execution. The appropriate algorithm can change with the workload and hardware. Integrating each algorithm directly into the transfer path would repeat page extraction, buffer management, length publication, restoration, and failure handling. A small shared interface would allow these mechanisms to remain in SGLang while the data transformation can be replaced and evaluated independently. Its value must be demonstrated through a real backend rather than assumed from generality alone. For scale, [[Qwen3-8B’s configuration](https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3-8B/raw/main/config.json)](https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3-8B/raw/main/config.json) has 36 layers, eight KV heads, and a head dimension of 128. BF16 K and V therefore occupy 144 KiB per valid token, or 1.125 GiB for 8,192 tokens at TP=1, excluding padding and metadata. If the transferred bytes were reduced by 20%, the ideal network saving would be approximately 9.66 ms at 200 Gb/s or 4.83 ms at 400 Gb/s. These are illustrative calculations, not measurements or predictions of compressibility; the additional critical-path cost must fit within the actual saving. The first validation target is Qwen3-8B with BF16 KV, one Prefill worker and one Decode worker, TP/PP/CP/DCP set to one, and GPU LZ4 through nvCOMP. The experiment would pin the attention backend, KV pool layout, page size, dependency versions, and block-size policy. CPU execution, topology conversion, MLA, hybrid state, speculative decoding, HiSparse, and compressed storage are subsequent validation scopes. P/D compression does not require HiCache or persistent offloading. It does not reduce the KV capacity or per-step KV reads required by active attention. GPU compression preserves attention’s input format but still competes for compute and memory bandwidth. ## Proposed Design ### Overall Architecture *Figure 1. The complete proposed architecture. The initial implementation covers P/D compression and restoration. Compressed HiCache storage and payload reuse are later extensions. Cache class names illustrate an existing integration route rather than a required configuration.* The Scheduler and GPU Executor retain their existing control flow. On Prefill, the GPU KV pool contains reusable prefix pages and KV generated for missing input tokens. A GPU prefix hit reuses existing pages; a future compressed L2 hit would restore the prefix needed for computation. Prefill then writes newly generated KV into the same pool. The P/D adapter selects the ranges Decode still needs and prepares them after their writes complete. KVSender transfers the selected representation through Mooncake. KVReceiver restores the payload into Decode’s allocated KV pages, and the request becomes runnable only after restoration and existing metadata and rank-level checks complete. Compression operations are local to each worker. The design introduces neither a separate compression service nor another request scheduler. Existing cache management retains prefix lookup, allocation, references, and eviction. The omitted Decode-side compressed L2 branch is a scope boundary; it does not imply that existing Decode configurations cannot use HiCache. ### Component Boundaries and Backend Interface *Figure 2. P/D and future HiCache integrations retain their own ownership and completion rules. Orange borders mark proposed additions or extensions. Shared contracts do not imply a stable public plugin ABI.* The layout adapter organizes selected KV into independently recoverable blocks within one layer and local shard. A block may contain multiple allocation pages. The backend transforms those packed blocks; it does not traverse cache trees, register RDMA memory, allocate model KV pages, or interpret request state. The P/D adapter owns transfer descriptors, buffer leases, and restoration completion. A later HiCache adapter would own cache admission and byte accounting under the existing cache lifecycle. The proposed internal backend contract is: ```python class KVCompressionBackend(Protocol): def supports(self, spec: BatchSpec) -> SupportResult: ... def buffer_requirements( self, operation: Literal["compress", "decompress"], spec: BatchSpec ) -> BufferRequirements: ... def compress_into( self, src: PackedBatch, dst: BufferBatch, workspace: Workspace, *, context: ExecutionContext, ) -> CompressionOperation: ... def decompress_into( self, src: EncodedBatch, dst: BufferBatch, workspace: Workspace, *, context: ExecutionContext, ) -> CompressionOperation: ... class CompressionOperation(Protocol): def poll(self) -> OperationSnapshot: ... ``` `BatchSpec` describes block count, decoded sizes, packed layout, format parameters, and device requirements. `SupportResult` includes a rejection reason. `BufferRequirements` supplies finite output and workspace bounds, alignment, and metadata requirements for the requested operation. Buffers remain caller-owned, with explicit sizes, capacities, and memory locations. `ExecutionContext` provides the execution stream or worker context and input dependencies. `OperationSnapshot` separates outcome from resource safety. The outcome is pending, succeeded, or failed. Success means outputs, actual lengths, and per-block status are available without synchronizing the scheduler. A separate `quiescent` property means the operation will perform no further accesses to its supplied buffers. Success requires this property for the operation’s own work; failure may precede it. Downstream transfer and restoration hold independent references. GPU length and status publication is part of the operation, using batched results and bounded host metadata storage where needed. Scheduler polling observes published state rather than reading synchronizing size accessors. The layout adapter’s restore completion additionally covers the final scatter into destination pages. These interfaces are provisional. Uncompressed pass-through provides an integration control group; a second real compression backend would help validate the abstraction before stabilizing it. No new user-facing HTTP API is proposed. ### Block Representation and Transfer Metadata *Figure 3. Logical token order is independent of physical page indices. Reusable representation metadata is separate from each transfer’s envelope. The diagram shows a compression attempt; the adapter can select an uncompressed payload.* Only valid KV bytes enter a block, excluding unused tail-page capacity. Blocks are submitted in batches to limit launch and metadata overhead. Compression granularity is separate from allocation-page size and would be selected through measurement. ```text Representation metadata UNCOMPRESSED or COMPRESSED format identifier, version, and decoding parameters packed layout, dtype, layer, shard, and valid logical range block boundaries, encoded lengths, and decoded lengths Transfer envelope protocol version, session, room generation, and chunk sequence receive lease identifier, generation, payload offset, and length receiver-approved destination mapping reference representation metadata for the transferred blocks ``` These fields describe the contract rather than a finalized wire encoding. The receiver validates block counts, lengths, layout, and destination coverage against its granted capacity and allocation state. Reserved buffer capacity is distinct from the actual bytes transmitted. Physical addresses and request IDs do not identify reusable cache content. `UNCOMPRESSED` means literal packed KV bytes. It is distinct from [[nvCOMP’s ](https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/nvcomp/py_api.html)`[BitstreamKind.RAW](https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/nvcomp/py_api.html)`](https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/nvcomp/py_api.html), which still contains compressed data. The sender selects compression only when its complete wire size is smaller than the uncompressed representation under the same protocol. This avoids an inflated compressed payload, but does not eliminate metadata overhead or the cost of attempting compression relative to the existing direct-transfer path. ### Transfer Execution and Completion *Figure 4. Transformation, network transfer, and KV restoration have separate completion boundaries. Capabilities and layout are agreed before this sequence.* The prototype uses the existing Mooncake engine and P/D work queues with a bounded, registered byte pool for compression traffic. Current staging already provides patterns for allocation, chunk-arrival notification, asynchronous scatter, and credit return. Its layout-dependent assumptions cannot automatically describe variable-size compressed blocks. The implementation would reuse matching mechanisms while keeping compression metadata above the byte-transfer engine. The first supported configuration excludes simultaneous use of the existing layout-conversion staging mode. Decode grants a receive lease with a known session, generation, capacity, and destination range. The sender reserves input, worst-case output, and workspace capacity before submitting work. It waits for source writes, packs selected KV, and compresses outside scheduler polling. The selected payload must fit the granted slot; each lease authorizes one payload submission. After actual lengths are available, Mooncake transfers the selected byte ranges. A descriptor and data-ready notification follow successful transfer completion. Restoration must respect the transfer backend’s device-visibility guarantees before reading the received bytes. Decode validates the descriptor, decompresses when necessary, and writes the destination pages. Slot credit returns only after network writes and local payload accesses have finished. Restore-pending maps to the existing `KVPoll.Transferring` state, restore failure to `Failed`, and completed restoration permits `Success` only when the other request conditions hold. This gate is applied before rank-wide status aggregation. Required metadata still completes even when prefix reuse leaves no KV bytes to transfer. Existing local-cache restoration, when enabled in a supported combination, remains part of admission. ### Resource Lifetime and Failure Handling *Figure 5. Ownership extends through the last access. Bar lengths express ordering, not measured durations. The source reference shown belongs to the compression task; request and cache references remain independent.* Source KV stays protected until packing or compression finishes reading it. Packed input remains valid through compression, the send buffer through RDMA source reads, and the receive buffer through restoration. Workspace, pointer and length arrays, host metadata, and quarantined buffers all count toward configured budgets. Destination pages remain governed by existing request and cache ownership. Cancellation stops new submissions and drains existing accesses before releasing memory. A generation check rejects stale control messages but cannot stop an already submitted RDMA write. A timeout is therefore not proof that a receive address can be reused. If quiescence cannot be confirmed, affected buffers are quarantined; exhausting that budget stops affected admissions or fails the session. Partial restoration never publishes valid cache entries. Duplicate notifications must neither repeat restoration nor return credit twice. ### Prefix Reuse and Future HiCache Integration *Figure 6. Future cache integration separates reuse for computation from reuse for transmission. The transfer path is evaluated only for ranges Decode still needs.* A GPU prefix hit avoids repeated Prefill computation but may still require compression for transmission. A compatible compressed L2 hit can supply a payload directly to the network while a separate restore makes the prefix available to local attention. Sending does not require that local restore to finish. The object holds independent send and restore references. Persistent identity follows existing prefix and model-isolation semantics, with representation compatibility added. A new request receives a new transfer envelope. Direct reuse requires complete compatible blocks; a partial hit inside an opaque compressed block requires recovery or reorganization with its cost accounted for. Only stable complete pages are eligible for persistent admission. HiCache integration would separately introduce logical handles backed by actual compressed-byte allocation, avoiding a fully allocated original host pool plus an extra compressed copy. Publication follows successful backup and cache admission. Loading must preserve layer-wise completion, including `L2TransferEngine`’s `on_layer_done` ordering. A future CPU backend must cover CPU work, H2D, and destination writes before reporting readiness. These are extension requirements, not capabilities established by the initial P/D interface. ## Configuration and Compatibility Compression is disabled by default. Enabling it selects a backend, format options, block-size policy, and sender/receiver memory budgets. The effective configuration must be observable. nvCOMP is an optional dependency loaded only when requested; an unavailable explicitly selected backend or unsupported enabled layout produces an actionable initialization error. The disabled path allocates no compression buffers. The prototype requires matching builds and explicit configuration at both ends. Protocol selection precedes commitment to destination ownership. Requests assigned to the existing raw path retain it. Once a request enters the new protocol, an incompressible block uses `UNCOMPRESSED` with the same lease and restoration lifecycle; it cannot silently switch to legacy direct writes. Buffer exhaustion after admission causes bounded backpressure or controlled failure. Mixed-version support requires discovery that is safe for legacy parsers and is a separate compatibility gate. The proposal does not append fields to an unversioned message and assume rolling upgrades will work. CPU execution, host staging, and persistent storage remain separate capabilities; enabling compression does not implicitly enable them. ## Source Integration The integration points below are based on upstream commit [[444b29c93225](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/tree/444b29c932253d82b14ad4e09c4260b3d200bfbc)](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/tree/444b29c932253d82b14ad4e09c4260b3d200bfbc). On Prefill, `send_kv_chunk()` continues to select KV ranges and resolve page mappings. Packing and compression would be submitted through the work queue used by `MooncakeKVSender.send()`, after source writes complete and with the source pages protected until their last read. The Mooncake transfer layer remains responsible for moving bytes. `MooncakeKVManager._transfer_data()` receives buffer addresses and actual payload lengths; compression formats and restoration stay in the P/D adapter. On Decode, restoration must finish before the receiver reports success. The integration follows the existing staging completion pattern and preserves the metadata and rank-wide checks used by `DecodeTransferQueue.pop_transferred()`. GPU LZ4 through [[nvCOMP](https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/nvcomp/c_api.html)](https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/nvcomp/c_api.html) would be the initial backend, with a pinned dependency version and explicit block format. Its compression ratio and serving benefit remain to be measured. ## Validation and Performance Evaluation Correctness requires byte-identical recovery of valid KV, including page boundaries, tail ranges, multiple chunks, prefix hits, and mixed compressed/uncompressed blocks. Tests cover page reuse, stale and duplicate descriptors, exhausted buffers, cancellation, disconnects, and failed restoration. They also verify disabled behavior, rejection of unsupported configurations, and metadata-only handoff. Real generation and task evaluation remain necessary to detect integration errors beyond the transformation itself. Performance compares the existing raw P/D path, the new path with uncompressed payloads, and the compressed path. The first comparison measures framework overhead; the second explains compression’s contribution. The final benefit must be measured against the existing raw baseline. For original bytes `S`, compressed wire bytes including metadata `Sc`, and effective bandwidth `B`, the approximate network saving is `(S - Sc) / B`. It must exceed the additional critical-path cost of packing, compression, result publication, restoration, synchronization, queueing, and contention. Network time is counted once. Overlapping stage durations are interpreted using the observed request path rather than blindly summed. Initial evidence should pair raw handoff profiles with real model-generated KV compression measurements. Block and batch-size sweeps report wire reduction, uncompressed fallback frequency, and complete transformation cost. End-to-end tests vary prompt length, concurrency, prefix reuse, and network conditions while fixing model revision, KV format, parallelism, generation settings, and comparable cache state. Measurements include handoff latency, first Decode continuation delay, TTFT, ITL, and throughput under a stated SLO, with P95/P99 and run-to-run variation. TTFT alone is insufficient because Prefill may return the first token before handoff completes. Traces distinguish KV availability, submission, transfer, and restore completion; cross-host timing requires a reliable time basis or correlation method. Reported costs include actual network bytes, stage execution and queueing, peak temporary memory, and remaining KV capacity under the same total GPU budget. Online tests use EvalScope through the actual serving endpoint, with warmup and at least three measured repetitions. Commands, effective configuration, hardware topology, dependency versions, timing windows, raw outputs, and server metrics accompany results. Earlier compression and retained-payload reuse are separate experiments. Later storage evaluation fixes physical L2 capacity and proves restoration after the GPU copy has actually been evicted. Compression ratio alone is not evidence of improved hit rate or serving throughput. If no realistic beneficial region is found, the backend or integration is reconsidered before expanding scope. ## Alternatives and Related Work Direct integration of one algorithm is a reasonable experiment. The shared interface is justified where it removes repeated layout, ownership, and completion logic without imposing a larger framework. Compressing earlier may create overlap but also increases retained memory and contention; keeping compressed copies trades repeated work for capacity and lifecycle complexity. [[KVServe](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.13734)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.13734) already studies modular compression and service-aware selection, while [[LMCache](https://docs.lmcache.ai/kv_cache_optimizations/compression/index.html)](https://docs.lmcache.ai/kv_cache_optimizations/compression/index.html) documents a caching compression path. This proposal’s contribution would be a measured integration into SGLang’s existing P/D lifecycle. It does not claim novelty for pluggability or compressed caching, and published results from other systems are not treated as expected gains here. [RFC #33861](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/33861) and [its implementation tracker](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/34510) separate common P/D protocol handling from transport; compression should follow that boundary without depending on the entire refactor landing first. ## Delivery Plan and Requested Feedback The first step validates real KV restoration and costs through uncompressed pass-through and one lossless backend. The P/D prototype then adds bounded registered buffers, transfer metadata, restoration-aware completion, and fault handling. Earlier production, compressed-copy reuse, HiCache storage, and additional layouts follow as independently reviewed extensions after evidence supports them. Feedback is requested on the backend/layout/protocol boundary, reuse of existing staging mechanisms, and safe capability discovery. Agreement on representative workloads and acceptable regression thresholds would define the gate for broader support. The initial implementation should establish a useful, maintainable P/D path before the interface becomes a general cache-compression API. ### Related resources _No response_

title: [RFC] Asymmetric P/D deployment for DeepSeek-V4.1 Flash
author: gz944367214
body:
## Summary This RFC proposes an asymmetric Prefill/Decode deployment for DeepSeek-V4.1 Flash. For a prompt of length `N` and replay window `W = 128`: - The **Prefill worker** processes only the prefix `[0, N-W)` and produces its KV cache. - The **Decode worker** receives that prefix KV and processes the final prompt window `[N-W, N)` as a bounded prefill/replay. - Decode then samples the first output token and continues normal speculative decoding with per-request `q_len = 1 + num_spec_tokens`. The key property is that Decode does not need separate encoder and decoder workloads. Every layer sees the same token count in a given step: ```text first Decode step: L0-L39 process W prompt tokens later Decode steps: L0-L39 process 1 + num_spec_tokens tokens per request ``` ```text P: prompt tokens [0, N-W) -> prefix KV | v D: prompt tokens [N-W, N) -> first output token D: generated tokens -> normal decode / speculative verify ``` The Prefill worker only needs the causal encoder and the decoder's first KV-producing projection path. The Decode worker keeps the full model. The main goal is to remove almost half of the model weights from each Prefill replica. A secondary goal is to avoid running a separate, low-density late-decoder workload on Prefill. Decode remains architecturally simple: its first step is a bounded prefill through the full model, followed by normal decode steps through the same full model. ## Motivation DeepSeek-V4.1 Flash has 40 transformer layers, a sliding-window size of 128, and shared compressed-KV source layers at 2, 8, 14, and 20. With the current decoder bounded-replay optimization, Prefill still loads the full model: ```text L0-L20: process the full uncached prompt L21-L39: process only the final 128 tokens ``` This saves arithmetic in the late layers, but it has two limitations: 1. Prefill still stores all late decoder weights, even though those layers process only a short window. 2. Prefill usually has few concurrent requests, so the late-layer MoE kernels see only a small number of tokens. The proposed design moves the entire final prompt window to Decode instead of changing the token set in the middle of the model. All Decode layers therefore process the same rows in every step. ## Proposed Design ### Model placement and token split ```mermaid flowchart LR I[Prompt: N tokens] I -->| Compute N-W| P I -->| Compute final W tokens| D subgraph P[Prefill worker: partial model] PE[Encoder L0-L19] PK[L20 KV / Indexer
projection path] PE --> PK end subgraph D[Decode worker: full model] BR[First step: bounded prefill
L0-L39, q_len = W] FT[Sample first token] ND[Later steps: normal decode
L0-L39, q_len = 1 + num_spec_tokens] BR --> FT --> ND end P -->| Transfer N-W KV | D ``` For prompts shorter than the window, P performs no model forward and D processes the complete prompt. For the current checkpoint, the conceptual ownership is: | Worker | Resident model components | Work | | --- | --- | --- | | Prefill | Embedding, causal encoder L0-L19, minimal L20 KV/Indexer projection modules | Prefix `[0, N-W)` | | Decode | Full L0-L39 model and LM head | Final prompt window, first token, and subsequent decode | ### Request flow ```mermaid sequenceDiagram participant P as Prefill worker participant D as Decode worker P->>P: Run prefix tokens [Prefix, N-W) P->>P: Produce prefix KV P->>D: Send KV D->>D: First step: run final W tokens through L0-L39 D->>D: Sample the first output token D->>D: Later steps: Normal decode ``` Moving first-token generation to Decode is an intentional part of the proposal. To minimize changes to the P-node scheduler, the P-node can compute the entire prompt (N tokens) instead of (N−W) tokens, since W is generally much smaller than N and the resulting redundant computation is negligible. ### Uniform full-model execution on Decode Decode has two step shapes, but no encoder/decoder layer split: ```text new request, first step: q_len = W_i, where W_i <= 128 active layers = L0-L39 later speculative decode steps: q_len = 1 + num_spec_tokens active layers = L0-L39 ``` If bounded-prefill requests and ongoing decode requests are scheduled in the same iteration, their sequence lengths are still different, so piecewise CUDA graphs may be useful. This is only a request-level scheduling issue: within either request type, all model layers execute the same number of rows. ## Why This May Help ### 1. Smaller Prefill Instance P no longer needs the complete decoder stack or LM head. It retains only the encoder and the minimal projection modules needed to create the shared prefix KV. This is expected to remove close to half of the model weights from each Prefill replica. An important deployment target is fitting one production Prefill replica on a single B300 GPU. ### 2. Avoid a separate low-density decoder tail on P The bounded replay contains at most 128 tokens per new request. Running it on P produces a small decoder-layer MoE batch because Prefill batchsize is usually low. On D, bounded prefill is a normal full-model step over up to 128 tokens per new request. It can be batched across newly admitted requests and, where useful, scheduled alongside the larger Decode workload. The arithmetic is not eliminated, but P no longer runs a separate late-layer tail with low token density. ### 3. Cleaner and uniform execution semantics P only processes a prefix ending at `N-W`. Chunked Prefill, Prefix cache and context parallelism apply normally to that prefix. D receives ordinary token IDs for the final window and executes an ordinary bounded prefill. This avoids changing `q_len` between encoder and decoder layers. The same logical prompt should produce the same split regardless of the Prefill chunk size. ## Cost and Trade-offs The main cost is a larger first step on Decode: ```text new request, first step: q_len <= 128 later steps: q_len = 1 + num_spec_tokens ``` Consequences include: - D must support both bounded-prefill and speculative-decode step shapes (Mixed Batch), require piecewise CUDA graphs. - Admission bursts can increase ITL/TPOT for existing requests. This trade-off may be acceptable for DeepSeek-V4.1 Flash because its compressed KV cache allows a large Decode batch. The added replay rows may be a relatively small fraction of the Decode workload, and decode steps that admit new requests account for only a small fraction of all Decode steps. But this needs measurement. ## Status This RFC is shared for community discussion. I do not currently plan to implement it, and there is no prototype or benchmark result yet. Implementation ownership is open.

title: [RFC] Align KV cache events with vLLM's schema so shared consumers have a standard format
author: hickeyma
body:
### Checklist

- [x] If this is not a feature request but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [x] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

# Motivation

## Summary

#37482 switched KV cache events to tagged msgpack maps, the same encoding vLLM moved to in vllm-project/vllm#42892. The fields both engines have use the same names. A consumer however can't treat events from both engines in a standard fashion because of the following:

1. Replay responses are missing the topic frame vLLM added in vllm-project/vllm#45177.
2. There's no `lora_name` in SGLang events. vLLM always sends it and its msgspec types reject events without it.
3. The salt is in a `cache_salt` field in SGLang. vLLM puts it in `extra_keys` on block 0 which is where a consumer like llm-d looks for it.
4. Event hashes leave out `extra_key` in SGLang, so LoRA and base model blocks with the same tokens share a hash.

This RFC proposes fixing those four in SGLang's native format in three phases to align with vLLM for standardization. It doesn't propose a vLLM hash mode or a format flag. Consumers like llm-d don't need vLLM's hash recipe and the in-repo router depends on SGLang's.

## Background

### What already matches

| Area | SGLang and vLLM |
|---|---|
| Event encoding | Tagged maps, class name under `type`, `None` optionals omitted |
| Batch | Positional `[ts, events, dp_rank]` |
| Live frames | `(topic, seq, payload)` |
| `BlockStored` fields | `block_hashes`, `parent_block_hash`, `token_ids`, `block_size`, `lora_id`, `medium`, `session_id` |
| `BlockRemoved`, `AllBlocksCleared` | Same, apart from vLLM's optional `group_idx` |

### Consumers checked

| Consumer | How it reads SGLang events |
|---|---|
| llm-d `engineType: sglang` | Positional arrays only. It can't read anything since #37482. That's llm-d's to fix |
| llm-d `engineType: vllm` | Reads SGLang's maps today. Derives its own block keys from `token_ids`, `lora_name` and `extra_keys` and uses engine hashes only as opaque keys |
| `experimental/sgl-router` | Decodes SGLang maps and ignores unknown keys. Recomputes SGLang's hash recipe on the request side (`kv_events/hash.rs`). Decodes hashes as `i64`. Maps `medium` strings to tiers |
| sgl-router replay client (#32729, open) | Parses today's two frame replay reply |
| vLLM's msgspec types | Fail on SGLang events (see below) |

Dynamo wasn't checked.

## Gaps

### 1. Replay replies have no topic frame

| | Replayed batch | End marker |
|---|---|---|
| vLLM | `(client_id, b"", topic, seq, payload)` | `(client_id, b"", b"", END_SEQ, b"")` |
| SGLang (`kv_events.py:541,546`) | `(client_id, b"", seq, payload)` | `(client_id, b"", END_SEQ, b"")` |

llm-d's replay client requires three frames after the delimiter (`parseEventFrame` in `pkg/kvevents/zmq_subscriber.go`). From reading that code: with `replaySocketPort` set for an SGLang pool, every replay
is rejected as malformed and the pod's index entries are cleared. Live batches that arrive before a successful replay are dropped and the retry 30 seconds later fails the same way, so the pod never gets indexed.

### 2. No `lora_name`

vLLM declares `lora_id`, `medium` and `lora_name` without defaults, so all three are always on the wire. Decoding a SGLang batch with vLLM's struct definitions (copied from `vllm/distributed/kv_events.py` at `de24e51908`) fails:

```
msgspec.ValidationError: Object missing required field `lora_name` - at `$[1][0]`
```

The reverse direction works. llm-d also uses `lora_name` as the model name when it derives keys, so SGLang LoRA blocks are indexed as base model blocks.

### 3. The salt isn't in `extra_keys`

vLLM sends one `extra_keys` entry per block: LoRA name, multimodal identifiers, then `cache_salt` only on the block starting at token 0. llm-d reads the salt only from there. Its precise prefix cache README says salted SGLang requests "are precise-cache misses until SGLang emits `extra_keys`". Unsalted requests can also score hits against salted only copies. SGLang still isolates the cache, so this costs routing quality, not safety.

A side note that corrects the earlier #27682 discussion: vLLM's hashes are salt namespaced too because the salt in block 0's extra keys is part of the hash. Neither engine has `BlockRemoved` ambiguity across salts.

### 4. Event hashes leave out `extra_key`

`compute_node_event_hash_values` (`mem_cache/utils.py:178`) seeds the chain with the salt only. `Req` folds the LoRA uuid into `extra_key` (`schedule_batch.py:1096-1099`). So from reading the code, a LoRA block and a base model block with the same tokens emit the same hash and a `BlockRemoved` for one looks like a removal of both. Storage hashes already include the namespace (`storage_namespace_seed`, `utils.py:125`). vLLM includes the LoRA name in its block hash.

## Proposal

### Phase 1: additive fields, no consumer breaks

**1a. `lora_name`, with `medium` required.** Use vLLM's field order:

```python
class BlockStored(KVCacheEvent):
    block_hashes: list[int]
    parent_block_hash: Optional[int]
    token_ids: list[int]
    block_size: int
    lora_id: Optional[int]
    medium: Optional[str]
    lora_name: Optional[str]
    extra_keys: Optional[list[Optional[tuple]]] = None
    cache_salt: Optional[str] = None
    session_id: Optional[str] = None


class BlockRemoved(KVCacheEvent):
    block_hashes: list[int]
    medium: Optional[str]
```

msgspec needs `medium` to lose its default so that `lora_name` is always sent. Every constructor already passes `medium`. `lora_name` stays `null` until phase 3. `lora_id` stays `null` because vLLM's is a deprecated int and SGLang's is a uuid string.

**1b. `extra_keys` with the salt.** When a node's parent is the root (its first page starts at token 0) and `cache_salt` is set, send `extra_keys=[(salt,), None, ...]` lined up with `block_hashes`. `KVCacheEventRecorder.enqueue` merges parent linked stores and would extend `extra_keys` the same way. The Rust tree core's tagged tuple (`rust_tree_core/adapter.py:85`) needs the field too. Keep `cache_salt`. It's documented and vLLM decoders ignore it.

Effect: vLLM typed decoders read SGLang and llm-d routes salted SGLang traffic correctly. sgl-router ignores both keys.

### Phase 2: replay topic frame

Send `self._topic_bytes` before the sequence number in replay replies and `b""` before `END_SEQ`. That's the vLLM layout.

Replay clients should accept both layouts: two frames after the delimiter is `[seq, payload]`, three is
`[topic, seq, payload]`. Then a new router works with old and new workers. Neither in-repo client has shipped: #32729 is open and #39610's example is open. So they can take the dual parse before this lands and only external clients written against the two frame layout would break.

### Phase 3: LoRA name and namespaced event hashes

These two go together. Adding `lora_name` without the hash change would give llm-d two keys for one engine hash.

**3a.** Carry the adapter name to the tree node, either as a `RadixKey` field or through a lookup in the scheduler's LoRA manager. Fill `lora_name`. With LoRA, put the name first in each `extra_keys` entry, as vLLM does.

**3b.** When `extra_key` is set, seed event hashes with the full namespace, the same way storage hashes do. Keep the current `sglang-cache-salt-v1` seed when only a salt is set, so salted hashes don't change. Mirror it in the Rust tree core.

**sgl-router cost:** its request side hash has no namespace. Today LoRA requests match base model blocks which can't be reused anyway. After 3b they match nothing until the router hashes with the namespace. That's a follow-up in `kv_events/hash.rs`.

### Not proposed

- **Renaming `CPU_PINNED` to `CPU`.** llm-d weights unknown tier names like GPU, so `cpu_pinned` scores 1.0 instead of 0.8. But sgl-router drops stores whose `medium` it doesn't know (`Tiers::for_store`, `kv_events/tree.rs`), so a  rename would turn off host-tier routing on older routers. llm-d users can set `kvCacheBackendConfigs: [{name: cpu_pinned, weight: 0.8}]` instead. See open question 1.
- **Unsigned hashes.** vLLM sends unsigned 64-bit and SGLang sends signed. llm-d accepts both (llm-d-router#2601 widens that). sgl-router decodes `i64`, so flipping would break it.
- **A vLLM hash recipe or `--kv-events-format vllm`.** llm-d doesn't recompute engine hashes and sgl-router depends on SGLang's recipe. Two formats would be a second thing to test with no consumer asking for it.
- **`group_idx` / `kv_cache_spec_kind`.** llm-d indexes events without `group_idx` as-is. Sending `group_idx` without a kind would make llm-d skip every store.

## Compatibility

| Change | vLLM-typed decoders | llm-d `vllm` adapter | sgl-router (main) | sgl-router replay (#32729) | #39610 docs |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1a `lora_name`, required `medium` | Fixed | No change until phase 3 | Ignored | n/a | Add field |
| 1b `extra_keys` salt | Reads it | Salted routing fixed | Ignored | n/a | Add field |
| 2 Replay topic frame | n/a | Replay works | n/a | Needs dual parse | Update example |
| 3a `lora_name` filled | Reads it | LoRA indexed under adapter name | Ignored | n/a | Update |
| 3b Namespaced hashes | n/a | `BlockRemoved` unambiguous | LoRA misses until router follow-up | n/a | Note |

## Out of scope

- **Multimodal.** SGLang replaces image tokens with hash derived pad values, so `token_ids` differ from vLLM's placeholders. `extra_keys` can't fix that.
- **EAGLE bigram `token_ids`.** Tracked separately.
- **Pages smaller than llm-d's block size** (llm-d-router#2235).
- **A removal reason on `BlockRemoved`** (#39604). It's additive but it would be worth proposing to vLLM too so the schemas don't drift again.

## Open questions

1. **Tier names.** Keep `CPU_PINNED` and document the llm-d weight? Or have sgl-router accept `CPU` first and switch the engine a release later?
2. **LoRA name source.** A `RadixKey` field which also needs the Rust core or a scheduler side lookup?
3. **LoRA in `extra_keys`.** llm-d's `ParseRawExtraKeys` reads bare strings as multimodal hashes which looks like it would fold a vLLM `lora_name` into keys the request side never adds. That isn't verified. Should SGLang match vLLM anyway or wait until llm-d settles it?
4. **Snapshots.** Should snapshot payloads from #33394 / #34407 use the same event schema?


# Related resources

- #27682: original request for `cache_salt` in `extra_keys`
- #37482: tagged-map events, `cache_salt` and `session_id` fields
- #39610: KV events docs page (open)
- #32729: sgl-router KV event gap replay (open)
- #33394, #34407: recoverable KV placement state with snapshots
- #39604: removal reason on `BlockRemoved`
- vllm-project/vllm#42892: vLLM events switched to maps
- vllm-project/vllm#45177: topic frame in vLLM replay replies
- vllm-project/vllm#51381: `session_id` on vLLM `BlockStored`
- llm-d/llm-d-router `pkg/kvevents/engineadapter/vllm_adapter.go`: map aware decoder SGLang events already pass through
- llm-d/llm-d-router#2235: pages smaller than the llm-d block size
- llm-d/llm-d-router#2601: hash integer conversion

title: [RFC] Decouple the SWA sidecar page size from the full-attention page size (DSv4, Hybrid Models)
author: mitu626
body:
### Checklist

- [x] If this is not a feature request but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [x] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

### Motivation

#### Summary

Allow the sliding-window-attention (SWA) KV sidecar pool to use a physical page size that differs from the full-attention pool's `page_size`. Concretely, add a `swa_page_size` so a hybrid model can keep `page_size = 256` for full layers while paging the SWA sidecar at 128.

#### Motivation

For hybrid models (full-attention layers + sliding-window layers), SGLang splits the KV cache into a full pool and a SWA sidecar pool. Today the sidecar inherits the full pool's `page_size` (paged SWA mode requires `page_size == 256`).

A sliding window only keeps the most recent `W` tokens. When the sidecar is paged coarser than the window, capacity is rounded up to whole pages, and both the SWA KV pool and any per-page state pools are over-allocated. With a 128-token window paged at 256, that is ~2x over-allocation of the SWA-side pools — memory that could otherwise be effective KV token budget.

The page size cannot simply drop to 1: attention/state kernels require a kernel-friendly granularity. 128 is such a granularity, and halving the sidecar page (256 → 128) removes the rounding waste while staying kernel-compatible.

#### Proposal

Introduce a distinct `swa_page_size` for the sidecar, independent of the full pool `page_size`. Default: `swa_page_size == page_size` (no behavior change). A server flag opts a hybrid model into a finer sidecar (e.g. 128 against a 256 full page — a fixed 1:2 ratio).

#### Design

**Allocator (`SWATokenToKVPoolAllocator`).** Size the SWA sub-allocator and all SWA page accounting on `swa_page_size` instead of `page_size`:

- `new_pages_available` measures SWA headroom in `swa_page_size` units.
- `alloc_extend` / `alloc_decode` compute SWA new-page counts with `swa_page_size`, and pre-check both pools before allocating either, so a partial success never strands pages.
- Freeing generalizes to closed-form page arithmetic (`free_swa_pages`) keyed by `swa_page_size`. When the sidecar is *finer* than the full page, one full page spans several SWA pages; a `> 0` mapping mask dedups between the full-floored insert trim and the SWA-floored release frontier.

**Pool sizing.** Per-page state pools (sized as `swa_tokens / page * ring_size`) switch to `swa_page_size`, which is where the ~2x saving lands. Require `swa_tokens % swa_page_size == 0` so tail-slack accounting stays exact.

**Mapping.** The full→SWA index mapping preserves a token's in-page offset (both pools advance on the same `seq_lens`), so one full token every `swa_page_size` positions names exactly one distinct SWA page — the property the positional, sync-free frees rely on.

**Transfer & offload.** The same page granularity carries through the data paths, so the SWA side shrinks there too, not just in the pools:

- **PD disaggregation.** Both the prefill (sender) and decode (receiver) sides page the SWA window kv indices by `swa_page_size` (128), so the SWA KV moved over the wire is paged at the window granularity — no coarse-page over-transfer; the transmitted SWA volume roughly halves.
- **L3 offload.** When SWA KV is offloaded to the L3 tier it is written at `swa_page_size`, and the boundary full page's SWA sub-pages past the committed tail are freed by alignment rather than shipped, so the SWA footprint landing in L3 halves as well.
- **HiCache multi-tier transfer.** SWA pages move between the HiCache tiers at `swa_page_size` too, so every hop (GPU ↔ host ↔ remote/disk) carries half the SWA bytes.

#### Impact

- Frees SWA-side KV memory (~2x less over-allocation at the window boundary), raising effective token capacity for hybrid SWA models.
- No change when `swa_page_size == page_size` (the default).

### Related resources

_No response_

title: [RFC] Explicit, budgeted tail-replay for Mamba/GDN state in UnifiedRadixCache
author: curnane-lab
body:
**Update 2026-09-24**: real-server A/B + e2e fidelity experiments done (Qwen3.8-27B hybrid, 2×910B3). Conclusion up front: **the retreat scenario is real and large (93% of requests, 30% of prefill compute), but both candidate replay mechanisms are economically unviable on interleaved hybrids — the correct lever is checkpoint placement/retention policy in the existing engine, not a new execution path.** Details and tables below. Instrumentation: #41001.

**Area**: `python/sglang/srt/mem_cache/` (UnifiedRadixCache, MambaComponent, schedule_batch) · Related: #37424, #37795, #37091–#37914, #39115, #28511, #38652

## Problem

On hybrid models, when the Mamba checkpoint behind a full-KV hit is missing or evicted, the engine retreats the whole hit to that checkpoint and re-prefills the gap through all layers — even though the gap's full-KV is already cached.

## A/B results (150-request agentic traces per cell, first-admission semantics)

**1. Where the problem lives — retreat rate by pressure type**

| Pressure | Requests retreating (H > C) | Gap (H−C) p50 / max | Replay-eligible tokens | TTFT p50 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| none (control) | 0% | — | 0 | 2.5s |
| full-KV capacity (112K) | **0%** (whole nodes evicted, `H == C`) | — | 0 | 46.4s |
| Mamba pool = 48 | 0% | — | 0 | 2.5s |
| Mamba pool = 32 | 4% | 22K / 50K | 156K | 2.5s |
| Mamba pool = 24 | 79% | 32K / 50K | 3.53M | — |
| Mamba pool = 16 | **93%** | 32K / 49K | **4.12M** | 49.3s |
| 12 sessions, pool = 32 | 92% | 25K / 66K | 7.88M | — |
| 12 sessions, pool = 16 | 96% | 16K / 49K | 8.16M | — |

→ The problem requires **Mamba pool pressure**, not full-KV pressure: full-KV eviction removes whole nodes (`H == C` by construction) and hides the gap entirely.

**2. What the retreat costs — avoidable compute** (modeled from measured TTFT grids; "avoided" = if every winnable gap were repaired)

| Cell | Gap tokens to repair | Modeled re-prefill time | Avoided compute |
|---|---|---|---|
| mb32 | 156K | 314s → 301s | **4.3%** |
| mb24 | 3.53M | 875s → 608s | **30.5%** |
| mb16 (seed 0) | 4.12M | 1422s → 973s | **31.6%** |
| mb16 (seed 1) | 3.84M | 914s → 624s | **31.7%** |
| mb16 (seed 2) | 3.99M | 940s → 644s | **31.5%** |
| 12 sessions, pool 32 | 7.88M | 1885s → 1310s | **30.5%** |
| 12 sessions, pool 16 | 8.16M | 1891s → 1318s | **30.3%** |

**3. Output fidelity — e2e greedy continuation, 32 tokens** (noise floor = flush-cache fresh-vs-fresh)

| Tier | Setup | Exact match | Mean match |
|---|---|---|---|
| Noise floor | two fresh prefills, cache flushed | **28/28** | 32/32 |
| Leaf-checkpoint seed | clean full hit, GDN from donated state | **14/20** | diverge ≤ 23 tok |
| Aged-checkpoint replay | retreat to checkpoint C < H | env-sensitive* | — |

\* Instrumented state diff confirms the mechanism: divergence occurs iff the seed position ≠ the reference's live position; same-position seeds are 100% token-identical. Two upstream-facing findings: (a) track placement is nondeterministic across identical runs (same prompt: 2816 / 2688 / none), (b) GDN state numerics are chunk-decomposition sensitive. Both already affect today's clean-hit path.

## Why replay is economically unviable here (corrects the original proposal)

Qwen3.5 interleaves GGGF (48 GDN + 16 FA): every GDN layer consumes the previous layer's output.

| Candidate mechanism | Why it fails |
|---|---|
| Split-prefix extend (FA at `H`, GDN replays `[C, P)`) | Once FA skips `[C, H)`, later GDN layers have no hidden states to replay with. Running FA over `[C, H)` anyway costs the same as today — **saving zero**. |
| ReplaySSM-style ring reconstruction (#28511) | Ring records ≈ 0.8 MB/token across 48 layers → covering a measured 32K gap costs **~25 GB per request**, vs ~13s of re-prefill compute. **Memory cost exceeds the compute it avoids by orders of magnitude.** |

The corollary: today's retreat (all-layer re-prefill of `[C, P)`) is already compute-optimal for this architecture — every FLOP in it is necessary. The waste is not in *how* the gap is repaired but in *that the gap exists at all*.

## Revised proposal

1. **Observability (land now)**: first-admission retreat metrics — `mamba_retreat_requests_total`, `mamba_retreat_gap_tokens_total`, `mamba_retreat_collapse_requests_total`, gap histogram, `mamba_replay_would_admit_total`. Working implementation + unit tests on fork branch `rfc40865-phase1-retreat-metrics` (instrumentation in #41001). This lets every deployment quantify its own retreat rate before any policy change.
2. **Checkpoint retention policy (the real lever)**: keep the gap small instead of repairing it — pin the most recent K checkpoints per active session (78 MB/slot at this model size, so pinning K=4 for 100 sessions ≈ 31 GB — a tunable trade vs 30% re-prefill), and/or use a denser track interval for active sessions so `C` tracks `H` closely. The engine already self-heals via force-track at the branching point (`_force_track_h`); under pool pressure those healing checkpoints get evicted, which is what turns one retreat into a persistent collapse — retention targets exactly that.
3. **Replay execution path: withdrawn.** Both mechanisms fail economically (table above). Keeping this RFC open as the measurement record for findings (a)/(b).

## Asks

1. OK to land the first-admission retreat metrics upstream (item 1)?
2. Interest in the checkpoint retention policy (item 2) — and where should it live: MambaComponent eviction ordering vs scheduler-side pinning?
3. Are findings (a) track-placement nondeterminism and (b) chunk-decomposition-dependent GDN numerics worth separate upstream issues? Happy to file with the measurement protocol and data.

title: [RFC] SGLang renderer
author: sagearc
body:
Tracking what is still missing. Landed with #36718, which covers `/chat` and `/completions` in standalone and serving modes.

| 13 | Cleanup | Delegate the server's OpenAI routes into the renderer | — | — | ⬜ TBD |
| 14 | Serve | Native sidecar support in `sglang serve` | — | — | ⬜ TBD |

## Open questions

- Rust server boundaries: should the rust frontend only take token ids in and out, leaving everything before and after to the renderer?
- Client or proxy: does the frontend call the renderer, or does the renderer sit in front? In the proxy shape the frontend never knows, it only ever sees rendered `GenerateRequest`s.
- Do we need shared `sglang-protocols` crates for the wire types, or can we just keep them in the renderer crate?
- Stop strings is the only(?) case where the rust frontend needs to be aware of the textual representation of token-ids. In case the rust frontend becomes TITO, where should that component sit, and how the rust server interacts with it every turn?

## Notes

1. HTTP and grpc wire types stay dumb DTOs. Boundary mapping lowers them to protocol structs, where the logic lives (following #36923).
2. New endpoints don't need their own version of chat. They lower to it, the way python's anthropic layer already does.
3. Media crosses as ids and hashes, and the heavy tensors can be built later where they are needed.

## References

* [Disaggregated request preprocessing (design RFC)](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/28669)
* [Non-GPU process rust migration (wider context)](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/23206)

title: [RFC] Some details relates to SGLang renderer item 4
author: Edwardssss
body:
Spinning item 4 out of #40920 as suggested.

There are three layers, three different jobs, and the split is implicit:

| Layer | Job for stops | Where |
|---|---|---|
| Engine (Python) | authoritative **detection**: decodes a tail window of output ids per decode step and matches `stop_strs` / `stop_regex_strs`, then locates the exact finish length so the stop is included and speculative overshoot is discarded | `managers/schedule_batch.py` — `tail_str()` `:1725` / `:1734`, `_locate_str_stop_finished_len()` `:1786`, `_check_str_based_finish()` `:1814` |
| Frontend (`rust/sglang-server`) | **cancellation**: `AbortGuard` aborts whatever was not disarmed when the caller drops the connection (mirrors Python's `is_disconnected`) | `api_server/guard.rs`, `api_server/common.rs`, `tokenizer_manager/wiring.rs` |
| Renderer | **stream shaping**: a local `StopStringMatcher` for trimming and `finish_reason`, deliberately not removing stops from the engine request; cancellation is declared a host responsibility | `engine/decode.rs`, `engine/types.rs`, `postprocessing/mod.rs:5` |

1. I tend to keep cancellation in the host, which is also what the renderer's own module docs already say, and keep the *decision* to terminate in the engine. A caller can only stop after it has received and decoded enough text, so caller-side abort is late by construction — exactly the case `_stop_match_tail_len(new_accepted_len)` guards against when speculation accepts several tokens in one step. Caller-side abort should therefore be a safety net, never the only mechanism. The real gap is narrower than "who owns abort": `AbortGuard` covers *disconnect ⇒ abort*, but not *the caller is still reading and wants to finish early*, and there is no public abort route today. That is the primitive worth defining, together with one measurement: when the renderer drops the token stream, does that actually cancel the upstream `/generate` request and trigger `AbortGuard`, and what is the latency from engine-side match to slot release? I would rather measure that than assume it.

2. Engine-side detection is per request inside the batch's decode step, so cost is O(requests × stops) per step with no cross-request interference (`finished_len` is local to the request's own output). Renderer-side matching is per stream and stateful (`pending` buffer for matches spanning chunks), so its cost scales with emitted bytes, not with batch size — the state, not the cost, is what scales. Three things I would write into the contract:

- **per-rid termination must be expressible on the transport.** Today `/generate` is one stream per request, so "close the stream" coincides with "end this request"; once gRPC (item 10) multiplexes rids on a connection it will not. This should be settled before item 10 rather than during it.
- **caps belong in the contract.** `MAX_STOP_COUNT = 32`, `MAX_STOP_REGEX_LEN = 256`, `MAX_STOP_REGEX_COUNT = 32` are already enforced in the renderer's sampling normalization (`preprocessing/sampling.rs`, lines 18, 21 and 24); every entry point that admits a request should agree on them.
- **exactly one trimmer per client path**.

3. I would not add one, for detection. The engine already decodes the tail window with its own tokenizer and has to: only the engine can fix `finished_len` inside a decode step, at the moment speculation accepts extra tokens. A frontend tokenizer would be a second text-interpretation path, and there is same-origin evidence for what that costs — the `/v1/tokenize` comparison in #36718 showed 13 of 468 requests differing between the two tokenizer loaders over Unicode combining marks. On stop matching, that class of divergence means the client sees text that was trimmed differently from what was matched.

Where I do think it *is* a generation concern is trimming and the client-visible `finish_reason` — but it belongs to whichever layer owns the client-visible text, which in the renderer shape is the renderer (it has the tokenizer for rendering anyway, and `GenerationFinishReason` is already its type) and in the direct shape is the Python detokenizer (`trim_matched_stop`, honouring `no_stop_trim`). Since the engine also trims on its own path, the invariant to state is **one trimmer per client path** — otherwise text is eaten twice.

**Coupling with item 7.** If tokenizer instantiation moves to the renderer, the frontend stops holding a tokenizer and "the frontend trims" stops being available at all. Item 4 and item 7 should therefore be sequenced together: decide who holds the tokenizer, then who trims.

**Some questions remain**

- Is a non-disconnect abort actually needed for the served deployments, or is disconnect the only real trigger?
- Should the renderer's matcher be deleted once the engine is authoritative, or does it stay as the trimming owner?
- Does anything rely on the renderer's local detection producing a *different* `finish_reason` than the engine's?

Discussion are welcomed. :)

title: [RFC / HiCache] Same-node peer L2 sharing across DP ranks via /dev/shm
author: VNG-VMONITOR
body:
# [RFC / HiCache] Same-node peer L2 sharing across DP ranks via `/dev/shm`

## Motivation

In deployments running multiple DP ranks on a **single node** (e.g. one host with 8 GPUs and `--dp-size 8`), each rank maintains a fully private L2 host KV cache. When two ranks receive requests with the same prefix — a common pattern for system prompts, few-shot examples, or shared document context — Rank B cannot see the KV pages that Rank A already produced, and must recompute the prefix from scratch.

Existing HiCache L3 backends (Mooncake, NIXL, AIBrix, 3FS, LMCache) do solve cross-instance sharing, but they all go through a networked / service-mediated data path. For **same-node** sharing that is common in single-box multi-DP deployments, the network round-trip is pure overhead — the ranks are all local processes with access to the same physical DRAM.

## Proposed design: `shm_peer_l2` HiCache storage backend

Two DP ranks on the same node map the same L2 host pool via named shared memory (`/dev/shm` tmpfs). Metadata (key → owner rank + slot address) is exchanged through a small direct-mapped index (also in `/dev/shm`). When Rank B misses in its own L1/L2, it looks up the index; on a hit, it performs one `memcpy` within the shared SHM to bring the peer's page into its own slot, then DMAs to GPU — no recompute.

Compared to a hypothetical "share via existing L3 file" approach (see `shm_cross_dp` below), the peer variant eliminates the L3 data copy: only a 288-byte pointer per page is written, giving:

- **Storage overhead**: ~55 MB total for a 475 GB L2 (vs. ~L2_size for a full mirror)
- **Read path**: 1 index lookup + 1 SHM memcpy + 1 DMA (vs. L3→CPU_buf→L2 + memcpy + DMA)
- **Write path**: 1 GPU→shared_L2 DMA + 1 index write (vs. + 1 memcpy to L3 file)

### Correctness

A per-page **generation counter** in shared memory prevents stale reads: when Rank A evicts and reallocates a slot, its generation counter increments. Rank B compares the stored generation against the current one; a mismatch is treated as a miss instead of copying whatever bytes now occupy the slot. The check is best-effort (no full memory barrier) — the tiny TOCTOU window between the generation read and the memcpy is accepted as per the "stale reads may be silently accepted" contract already present in HiCache read paths.

### Operational envelope

- `--dp-size >= 2`
- All DP ranks on the **same node** (`/dev/shm` is node-local tmpfs)
- `--hicache-write-policy write_through` required (`write_back` only flushes on eviction, so Rank B would not see data timely)
- Optionally with `--hicache-io-backend kernel` and `page_first`/`page_first_direct` layouts

Auto-computed capacity (`page_num × 4`, 25% load factor) at startup; explicit override via `--hicache-storage-backend-extra-config '{"peer_l2_capacity": N}'`.

Collision rate emitted every 10,000 writes; WARNING once it exceeds 10% (actionable — increase capacity).

## Existing prototype

A working implementation exists in a downstream fork. It shipped as two related backends registered through `backend_factory.py`:

- `shm_cross_dp` — shared L2 pool + full SHM L3 data file (simpler, more memory, extra copy)
- `shm_peer_l2` — shared L2 pool + tiny SHM index only (optimized; strict improvement)

Both reuse a common `ShmHostTensorAllocator` and named-SHM helpers added to `pool_host/common.py` and `storage/mmap/mmap_allocator.py`. Tests included: `test/registered/mem_cache/test_shared_l2_hicache.py` (CPU-only, `register_cpu_ci`), covering allocator wiring, slot partitioning, index CRUD, generation-counter stale-slot behavior, collision detection, auto-capacity, and a cross-process shared-L2 round-trip via subprocess.

The prototype hooks into:
- `HiRadixCache` — for `shm_name` derivation, `dp_rank/dp_size` forwarding to `MHATokenToKVPoolHost`
- `HostKVCache` (`pool_host/base.py`) — `clear()` partitions `free_slots` to `[slot_start, slot_start+local_size)`; `alloc()` fires registered callbacks; `slot_used` spans the full pool for cross-DP double-free detection
- `cache_controller` — `shm_peer_l2` added to the V1 interface allow-list

## The upstreaming question

We noticed [#40787](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/40787) (merged 2026-09-22) removed `HiRadixCache` since [#35081](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/35081) migrated HiCache to `UnifiedRadixCache`. The prototype above was written against `HiRadixCache` and does **not** apply cleanly to current `main`.

Before we invest in porting to `UnifiedRadixCache`, we would like guidance from HiCache maintainers on a few design points:

1. **Integration point in UnifiedRadixCache** — where is the equivalent of `HiRadixCache.write_backup`, `_inc_hit_count`, and `prefetch_from_storage` in the unified architecture? Is there a documented extension surface for backends that need per-page alloc callbacks and slot-partitioned allocators?

2. **Shared L2 pool ownership** — is there interest in a first-class "shared host pool" concept inside `MHATokenToKVPoolHost` (dp_rank / dp_size / shm_name parameters)? The prototype adds them minimally, but a maintainer-blessed shape would be preferable.

3. **Scope split** — would you prefer:
   - (a) A single PR introducing the shared L2 pool infrastructure + one backend using it (either `shm_cross_dp` or `shm_peer_l2`), then a follow-up for the other, or
   - (b) The infrastructure alone first (no backend), then backends as separate PRs?

4. **Naming / positioning** — `shm_peer_l2` vs `shm_cross_dp` overlap significantly; would maintainers prefer we upstream only `shm_peer_l2` (the optimized variant) and drop `shm_cross_dp`, or keep both as complementary options?

5. **Alternative direction** — is there an existing or planned effort (Mooncake local mode, an internal HiCache broadcast, etc.) that already covers the same-node peer sharing use case and would make this redundant? We searched issues/PRs and did not find one but want to double-check.

Happy to open a draft PR against `main` once the direction is confirmed. Full design doc and per-file breakdown available on request.

## References

- `python/sglang/srt/mem_cache/storage/shm/hicache_shm.py` — existing SHM allocator (#29326)
- `python/sglang/srt/mem_cache/storage/mmap/mmap_allocator.py`
- `python/sglang/srt/mem_cache/pool_host/{base,common,mha}.py`
- LMSYS blog: https://lmsys.org/blog/2025-09-10-sglang-hicache/
- PR #35081 — migration to `UnifiedRadixCache`
- PR #40787 — removal of `HiRadixCache`

title: [RFC] Dynamic Latent Consensus Governor for DeepSeek-R1 to Reduce KV-Cache Holding Time by 4.5x.
author: Arnab758
body:
## Motivation

Reasoning models like `DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-32B` generate long chains-of-thought that place severe pressure on SGLang's RadixAttention memory pools.

In our empirical profiling on an NVIDIA A100-SXM4, we observed that in ~40% of coding and algorithmic tasks, models reach the correct deduction within the first 80–120 tokens, but spend an additional 1,000–1,500 tokens in repetitive self-verification loops ("Wait, let me double check...").

This holds RadixAttention KV-cache allocations for ~150 seconds per query, creating a major throughput bottleneck in multi-tenant serving.

## Proposed Solution: SubNeutralize Latent Governor

We propose an opt-in runtime governor based on latent trajectory dynamics at the model's cognitive bottleneck layer (layer 32 on 32B models, layer 14 on 7B models):

1. **Directional Velocity:** `v_t = 1 - cos(h_t, h_{t-1})`
2. **Scale-Free Momentum:** `R_t = v_t / EMA_t(v_t)` (alpha=0.10)
3. **Consensus Trigger:** When `R_t < 0.82` for 2 consecutive decode steps, consensus equilibrium is certified, early-terminating the reasoning loop and transitioning to emission.

## Empirical Benchmark (A100-SXM4, DeepSeek-R1-32B)

Tested on complex backend coding tasks under a 1,500 token ceiling:
* **Tokens Consumed:** 5,698 -> 1,261 (**77.9% reduction**)
* **Wall-Clock Latency:** 596.1s -> 132.3s (**4.51x speedup**)
* **Unit Test Accuracy:** 4/4 PASS (**100% preserved**)
* **Kernel Overhead:** < 15 µs per decode step (< 0.05% overhead)

## Reference & Paper
* **Paper (Zenodo DOI):** https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22941619
* **Reference Implementation:** https://github.com/Arnab758/subneutralize
* **Related vLLM RFC:** https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/58909

We would love to discuss with SGLang maintainers how to cleanest integrate this into SGLang's scheduler/worker decoding loop.

title: [RFC][NPU] INT8 (C8) KV cache for DSA models (GLM-5.2) on Ascend A2/A3 (910B/910C)
author: qidaye
body:
### Checklist

- [x] If this is not a feature request but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [x] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

This RFC proposes generalizing the existing arch35-only packed FP8 DSA KV cache
to a "packed one-byte quant" path, so that GLM-5.2 (`GlmMoeDsaForCausalLM`) and
other DeepSeek-V3.2-style DSA models can run an **INT8 (C8) KV cache on Ascend
A2/A3 (910B/910C)**. Every hardware question the proposal depends on has been
probed on a 910B (CANN 9.0.0, torch_npu 2.10.0); section 4 states measured
verdicts, not predictions.

Sections 1-4 of the full RFC follow. The remaining sections (change-surface
audit, test plan, confidence ledger) exist and can be posted here if useful;
a few forward references to them ("section 5" / "section 6" / "section 7")
remain in the text below -- the "section 7" material is summarized under
**Proposed contribution plan** at the end.

> All `file:line` references are against `sgl-project/sglang` at
> **`06008c170dae333e22caceb51f36224071f9b5b3`** (`[dsv4.1]Optimize FP4 indexer by
> skipping invisible tiles`, #40431), which is an ancestor of `upstream/main` --
> so every citation below is checkable against upstream as-is.
>
> vllm-ascend references are against **`abe8ff18a96bcd5f90d08077d1ccd068b959cab4`**
> and carry a `[va]` prefix, relative to that repo's root.
> ops-transformer references are against `gitcode.com/cann/ops-transformer` at
> **`bcc6304656c9e712b50b1faa22872a158b1e34c5`** (the commit sgl-kernel-npu's CI
> pins; `bcc6304` below) and carry an `[ops-t]` prefix.

## 1. Motivation

SGLang today supports an 8-bit ("C8") KV cache for DSA models on Ascend **only on
arch35 / Ascend 950**, in the FP8-E4M3 packed form added by
`[NPU]Support GLM5.2 and FP8 DSA&Indexer kvcache for 950` (commit `3ff226ba8f`).
On A2/A3 the DSA KV cache is unconditionally BF16.

This matters because the KV cache is the binding constraint on A2-class hardware.
A representative single-node deployment (8x 910B, 64 GB/card, GLM-5.2-W4A8, TP8,
`--mem-fraction-static 0.85`):

| item | per card |
|---|---|
| weights | 49.67 GB |
| KV cache | 1.73 GB -> `max_total_num_tokens = 16768` |
| NPU graphs | 0.75 GB |
| unused | 8.25 GB |

`context_len` is 1 M, but the whole instance holds ~16 K tokens. Raising
`mem-fraction-static` helps, but the ceiling is still set by BF16 KV bytes/token.

Per token, per layer, for GLM-5.2 (`kv_lora_rank=512`, `qk_rope_head_dim=64`,
`index_head_dim=128`):

| component | BF16 | INT8 packed | ratio |
|---|---|---|---|
| main MLA latent + rope | 1152 B | 656 B (512 int8 + 4x fp32 tile scales + 64x bf16 rope) | **1.76x** |
| indexer K | 256 B | 130 B (128 int8 + 1x fp16 scale) | **1.97x** |
| **total** | **1408 B** | **786 B** | **1.79x** |

The main-KV term dominates, so the expected end-to-end gain is ~1.6-1.8x more
resident tokens at the same memory budget. vllm-ascend reports a **measured
1.62x** for the equivalent change on GLM-5 W8A8 / A3 (75,600 -> 122,309 tokens,
PR #11228 / #11846) -- a second-hand figure from PR prose, but consistent with
the arithmetic above.

---

## 2. What exists today

### 2.1 The arch35 FP8 packed path (the template)

Storage is an **opaque fixed-width record**, one per token per layer, whose width is

```python
# python/sglang/srt/mem_cache/kv_cache_configurator.py, calculate_mla_kv_cache_dim
kv_lora_rank + kv_lora_rank // quant_block_size * 4 + qk_rope_head_dim * rope_storage_dtype.itemsize
# GLM-5.2: 512 + 4*4 + 64*2 = 656 bytes
```

It is produced by `_pack_dsa_fp8_kv_cache`
(`python/sglang/srt/hardware_backend/npu/memory_pool_npu.py:839`):

```python
quantized, scale = torch_npu.npu_dynamic_quant(latent.reshape(-1, 128), dst_type=self.dtype)
packed = torch.cat((quantized.view(uint8),            # 512 B
                    cache_v.to(bf16).view(uint8),     # 128 B  rope, NOT quantized
                    scale.to(fp32).view(uint8)),      #  16 B  4 per-128-tile scales
                   dim=-1)
```

and consumed by `forward_sparse`
(`python/sglang/srt/hardware_backend/npu/attention/ascend_backend.py:1228`):

```python
torch_npu.npu_kv_quant_sparse_flash_attention(
    query=torch.cat((q_nope, q_pe), -1),   # bf16 [T, H, 576]
    key=packed, value=packed,
    key_quant_mode=2, value_quant_mode=2,
    key_dequant_scale=None, value_dequant_scale=None,   # scales read inline
    quant_scale_repo_mode=1, tile_size=128, rope_head_dim=64,
    layout_query="TND", layout_kv="PA_BSND", sparse_mode=3, attention_mode=2, ...)
```

**Key observation: the record layout is not FP8-specific.** It is "512 one-byte
values + per-128-tile FP32 scales + BF16 rope tail", and INT8 and FP8-E4M3 are
both one byte, so the 656-byte width, the `quant_scale_repo_mode=1` /
`tile_size=128` descriptor, and the `npu_dynamic_quant` call site
(`dst_type=self.dtype` already) carry over structurally. The quantization is
**dynamic** (per-token, per-128-tile, computed online), so no checkpoint
calibration is required.

The scale contract is settled, from two independent implementations: the
**main-KV** per-128-tile scale is **FP32 for INT8 and FP8 alike**, symmetric,
no zero-point (`[va] vllm_ascend/attention/utils.py:87-99` hardcodes an fp32
scale term in the record width regardless of KV dtype;
`[va] vllm_ascend/attention/sfa_v1.py:1991` has the INT8 branch cast the scale
`.to(torch.float32)`). The **indexer** per-token scale is a different buffer
entirely -- FP16 under INT8 on A2/A3, FP32 under FP8 on A5 -- and belongs to
section 2.2, not to this record.

Functional acceptance of this record with an INT8 payload on a 910B is now
**measured** (section 4, V1). Numerical parity against a BF16 reference remains
test item 1 in section 6.

### 2.2 An INT8 indexer already works on pre-A5, in this repo

The DSV4 NPU backend already runs an INT8 lightning indexer on non-arch35 hardware:

```python
# python/sglang/srt/hardware_backend/npu/attention/ascend_dsv4_backend.py:797
c4_indexer.compressor.li_kv_dtype = "float8" if is_npu_arch35() else "int8"
```

with INT8 K + **FP16** scales, scattered into `index_k_buffer` (int8) and
`index_scale_buffer` (fp16) by
