A later `add_tokens` or a changed flag puts the wrapper into passthrough for the life of the process. Anything else goes to the Hugging Face tokenizer: an unsupported call shape, a chunk with no safe cut, a request whose stored state does not verify. The per-request cost of these decisions is a hash comparison. The adapter's own call is about 2 ms at 100K tokens, most of it spent returning the ID list.

### Non-goals

- No change to the radix cache, session references or KV layout; our output is their input.
- No GPU code and no change to sgl-router in this PR (see Roadmap).
- No new request or response fields; `--skip-tokenizer-init` with client-supplied `input_ids` remains the route for applications that run toktier themselves.

### Measurements

We ran SGLang v0.5.19 with Qwen3-8B (bf16) on an RTX PRO 6000, with the HTTP process pinned to 16 cores of an AMD EPYC 9115 (Zen 5) and Hugging Face `tokenizers` 0.22.2 as the reference, which is also SGLang's default. The numbers are warm turns only, from two or three server processes per configuration. The adapter ran in process except where the pool is named. Full tables, the gpt-oss-120b runs and a repeat on a GH200 node are in the paper; the serving scripts and the exactness checks ship with toktier 0.3.0 under `docs/integration/sglang.md`.

| Setting | Reference | toktier |
|---|---|---|
| Median TTFT, 400-character appends, 8K / 32K / 100K tokens | 29.1 / 55.7 / 136.8 ms | 29.2 / 37.5 / 53.7 ms |
| P99 TTFT at 100K tokens | 158.5 ms | 75.0 ms |
| Median TTFT through the chat interface, 100K tokens (reference from a separate set of runs) | 145 ms | 60 ms, 59% lower |
| P99 TTFT, twelve 100K-character sessions, 24 warm turns/s | 995 ms | 103 ms (in process), 105 ms (pool) |
| P99 TTFT, same sessions at 8 turns/s, plus four one-million-character stateless requests every 8 s (over the model's context, declined after tokenization, so they load only the front end) | 1,441 ms | 166 ms (in process), 63 ms (pool) |
| P99 TTFT, same sessions, plus a repeated ~100K-token document served from the prefix cache | 498 ms | 66.5 ms (in process), 67.5 ms (pool) |

On gpt-oss-120b, median TTFT fell by 24, 42 and 45% at about 26K, 64K and 90K tokens. When every long document is new, GPU prefill sets the tail and the reference and toktier land within 5% of one another.

We also checked exactness in these runs. Every prompt-token count SGLang reported equalled the reference, 2,195 and 2,268 independent re-encodes of served text across the two sets of serving runs found no difference, and 550 greedy completions were identical to the unpatched server's. Outside SGLang, the fast encoder matched the reference on 41.8 billion whole encodes over eleven tokenizers, and on 409.6 million web documents split at the backend's cuts under four of them.

### Compatibility

- toktier is an optional dependency (`pip install toktier`, Apache-2.0), and 0.3.0, the version the PRs require, is on PyPI. Nothing changes when the backend is not selected.
- Today the backend admits eleven tokenizer files (twelve model families), covering Qwen3, Llama-3.1, gpt-oss, DeepSeek-V3 and others. A public repository that ships one of these files byte for byte is admitted by content hash. Everything else runs the Hugging Face tokenizer through the same wrapper.
- `--tokenizer-worker-num N` works, but each worker holds its own session state, so a session whose turns reach different workers is encoded in full more often. `--enable-dynamic-batch-tokenizer` works too; its executor thread does not carry context variables, so keyed requests use content lookup there.

### Relationship to existing work

Two upstream changes have since moved in the same direction. #41259, merged on October 9, encodes a rendered chat prompt in parallel: it cuts at added-token boundaries for any fast tokenizer whose added tokens match independently, and inside a message only for the exact Llama-3 and GLM pre-tokenizer with no normalizer, then runs the pieces through the backend's `encode_batch`. #42187, still open, keeps a per-handler LRU of prompt segments cut at added-token boundaries and reuses their IDs, with periodic full-encode checks. This proposal covers what both leave out. It admits tokenizers with a normalizer or a different pre-tokenizer regex, among them Qwen3, gpt-oss and DeepSeek-V3, which neither change can cut inside a message or reuse. It repairs appends that do not end at a special token, such as a tool result streamed into the same message, `continue_final_message`, or `/generate` text. It splices at any boundary the check accepts rather than only at added tokens, keeps state per session rather than in a global cache, and carries a correctness argument for each path rather than sampled checks. When the toktier backend is on, #41259 sees a wrapped tokenizer and defers to it, so the two do not stack; when it is off, nothing changes. Separately, #44392 extends #41259's own intra-message cuts to the Qwen2/Qwen3, o200k and DeepSeek-V3/V4 pipelines with the cut conditions from our paper, so that path improves for those tokenizers whether or not this backend is used.

`--tokenizer-backend fastokens` set the pattern of swapping the encode behind the same tokenizer object, and #43104 keeps it current; this proposal follows the same wiring. #41268 added an opt-in fast backend and a bounded prefix token cache to sgl-router. That reuse lives in the router, while this proposal lives in the engine's tokenizer stage and decides the splice point per request from the tokenizer's own rules, so the two can coexist. #34533 proposed a gigatoken backend through the same `tokenizer_backend` choice. #34513 motivates session affinity from the same agent workloads; its concern is which worker a turn reaches, ours is what the tokenizer does once the turn arrives. The adapter's per-request timing log records SGLang's tokenize window next to its own, which may help with the metrics asked for in #43304.

### Roadmap

1. This PR adds the backend option and the session-key binding, off by default, with tests that compare IDs against the Hugging Face tokenizer on the admitted families and on each fallback path. toktier 0.3.0, released on PyPI and crates.io on October 15, ships the adapter, the patch rebased onto current main and the exactness scripts.
2. A worker pool with session affinity. Keyed requests go to a home worker that holds their state, and stateless requests enter a shared shortest-first queue as chunks, so a short append does not wait behind a whole long request. This needs one further hook, an awaited encode in `_tokenize_texts`, and we would like your view on its shape before proposing it. Draft PR: #44382.
3. A GPU route for fresh long inputs. toktier's CUDA path encodes a new long request on the GPU, exact to the same references and described in [our TokTier paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.29678) (arXiv:2607.29678), and would attach behind the same wrapper for requests with no state to reuse. That will be a separate RFC and PR, so that this one stays small.
4. The Rust front end. The same library is a Rust crate, and since 0.3.0 the crate exposes chunk-parallel encoding through `Tokenizer::chunked()`, admitted under the default policy for the four certified families (Qwen3-8B, Llama-3.1-8B, DeepSeek-V3 and gpt-oss-120b). The PR against `experimental/sgl-router` is #44558. It brings the incremental repair and the chunk-parallel encode to SGLang's Rust front end, the tokenizer path of sgl-router (#41268), with the same admission and fallback behavior, so deployments that tokenize before the engine get the same IDs the same way.

For new models, the admitted list lives in toktier, so supporting a new tokenizer never touches SGLang. We will keep adding families as models ship. The next toktier releases also move admission from a list of frozen files to a check of the loaded configuration itself, probing the boundary rules against the Hugging Face object at startup, so that a new checkpoint of an admitted family needs no release at all.

### Open questions

1. Is a third `tokenizer_backend` value the right home, or would you prefer a generic hook for tokenizer wrappers that other backends could use too?
2. Should the session key reach the tokenizer through a context variable, as in the patch, or as an explicit argument of `_tokenize_texts`?
3. Is `session_id`, then `cache_salt`, the right precedence, and is content lookup acceptable as the default when neither is present?
4. Environment variables for the first PR, or server arguments from the start (chunk threshold, worker count)?

### References

- Paper: [Delta Tokenizer: Reference-Identical Tokenization of Session Deltas and Segment-Parallelism for Long Prompts on Multicore CPUs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.19801) (arXiv:2610.19801). The SGLang integration is in §3.4, §4.2, §4.5 and §4.6, with details in the supplement, §S6.3 and §S6.7.
- toktier: https://github.com/asu-idi/toktier
- Authors: Zhenyu Zhang (zzhan641@asu.edu), Zhichao Cao (Zhichao.Cao@asu.edu), Arizona State University.

title: [Feature] [RFC] Ownership boundaries for externally orchestrated checkpoint and restore
author: leeZardNav
body:
### Checklist

- [x] If this is not a feature request but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [x] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

### Motivation

**The use case.** Start an SGLang replica from a checkpoint of a warm server instead of a cold start. On a cluster, the replica that restores is rarely the one that was captured. It runs in a new container, often on another node.

**System context.** [Snapshot](https://github.com/ai-dynamo/snapshot) is a Kubernetes-native system that checkpoints and restores GPU workloads from outside the process:

- A node agent captures the whole container, CPU and GPU memory, with [CRIU](https://criu.org) and [cuda-checkpoint](https://github.com/NVIDIA/cuda-checkpoint).
- Snapshot stores the image and restores it into a new container on a compatible node.
- The privileged work stays in the node agent. SGLang runs unprivileged and never links CRIU.
- SGLang doesn't need to know it runs on Kubernetes.

In the rest of this RFC, Snapshot is the orchestrator. It can't make a running server safe to capture. Only SGLang can drain its requests, tear down its communicators, and decide what stays in GPU memory. After the restore, only SGLang can rebuild its communicators and start serving again.

**The gap.** SGLang already has most of the parts: `pause_generation` and `continue_generation`, and `release_memory_occupation` and `resume_memory_occupation` under `--enable-memory-saver`. What it lacks is a contract for who starts a capture, how SGLang says it is safe to capture, and how it hears it may resume. Without one, each orchestrator wraps SGLang in its own program, as [Dynamo's SGLang wrapper](https://github.com/ai-dynamo/dynamo/blob/9e41f306e8901f9368cda9185a8353baa2bf32d4/components/src/dynamo/sglang/snapshot.py#L43-L53) and [Snapshot's SGLang guide](https://github.com/ai-dynamo/snapshot/blob/3136f1d8dbc10bf9c93fa62adbdd308f41ac334b/docs/guides/sglang.md) do today, and other proposals define that contract differently (see Relationship to existing SGLang work).

**Deployments differ.** They differ in what they can afford to keep in GPU memory and what code of their own they need to run around a capture. The contract needs a default that works with no configuration, a few settings for the common choices, and a place for a deployment's own code.

This RFC proposes that contract: how the orchestrator talks to SGLang, what SGLang does once it gets the signal, and how a deployment configures and extends that behavior. It adds no orchestrator code to SGLang.

### Ownership

**What SGLang owns.** SGLang gets itself ready for a capture, on its own at startup or when a caller asks. It drains its requests, tears down its communicators, and releases what the deployer configured it to release, which also flushes the radix cache. Once that's done, it reports itself as `prepared`, which means it is now safe to capture. After the restore, when the orchestrator tells it to resume, it rebuilds what it released and returns to serving on its own. Its existing `/ready` tells the platform when to route traffic to it.

**What the orchestrator owns.** The orchestrator polls SGLang's status until it reads `prepared`, then captures, stores and restores the container. It holds the privileges and runs CRIU, the CUDA checkpoint and the node compatibility checks. Apart from an optional request to get ready, its only message to SGLang is the signal that SGLang may resume.

### Checkpoint API

SGLang adds three routes for checkpointing:

- `POST /checkpoint/prepare` asks SGLang to get ready for a capture.
- `GET /checkpoint/status` tells whether SGLang is `prepared`, and returns 503 when it isn't.
- `POST /checkpoint/resume` tells SGLang to go back to work after the restore.

All endpoints return 200 on success, 401 when the server has an API key and the call doesn't carry it, and 409 when the call conflicts with the current state. Any other error returns 500. The routes use the `ADMIN_OPTIONAL` auth level, like `/pause_generation` ([http_server.py](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/71a17dbc24acdac99231b166aea57763d925b89f/python/sglang/srt/entrypoints/http_server.py#L1764-L1765)), so `--admin-api-key` protects them when it's set ([auth.py](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/71a17dbc24acdac99231b166aea57763d925b89f/python/sglang/srt/utils/auth.py#L133-L143)). SGLang checks keys only with one tokenizer worker today ([http_server.py](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/71a17dbc24acdac99231b166aea57763d925b89f/python/sglang/srt/entrypoints/http_server.py#L2666-L2684)), so the routes would need that check with several workers too.

Everything is opt-in behind one flag, shown here as `--enable-checkpoint`. All names in this RFC are placeholders. SGLang already uses "checkpoint" for model weights, as in `--delete-ckpt-after-loading` ([model.py](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/71a17dbc24acdac99231b166aea57763d925b89f/python/sglang/srt/arg_groups/fields/model.py#L350-L353)), so the final names may need another word. Without the flag, nothing changes. A policy's prerequisites keep their own flags, such as `--enable-memory-saver` and `--enable-weights-cpu-backup` for the default offload-weights ([exec_.py](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/71a17dbc24acdac99231b166aea57763d925b89f/python/sglang/srt/arg_groups/fields/exec_.py#L56-L63)), and startup fails if one is missing.

**Who initiates.** Getting ready is separate from capturing. SGLang can get ready on its own at startup, or a caller can ask it while it's serving. Either way, the orchestrator only watches for `prepared` and doesn't need to know which one happened.

- **SGLang itself, at startup.** With a startup option, SGLang prepares right after its warmup request, before it marks itself up and serves any request ([http_server.py](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/71a17dbc24acdac99231b166aea57763d925b89f/python/sglang/srt/entrypoints/http_server.py#L2410-L2424)). This is the common case: capture once, then start every replica from that checkpoint.
- **A caller, while serving.** `POST /checkpoint/prepare` asks a running server to get ready. The caller can be the orchestrator, an operator, or a script.

SGLang never calls the orchestrator. It only publishes its state.

**Readiness.** Each probe answers a different question while SGLang is prepared:

- `GET /checkpoint/status` tells the orchestrator whether SGLang is `prepared`, meaning safe to capture. The orchestrator polls it until it returns 200.
- `/ready` tells the platform whether to route traffic. While SGLang isn't serving, it returns 503, and so do the inference routes, so the platform takes the replica out of rotation. `/ready` already does this while paused ([tokenizer_manager.py](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/71a17dbc24acdac99231b166aea57763d925b89f/python/sglang/srt/managers/tokenizer_manager.py#L722-L728)).
- `/health` is what a liveness probe calls to decide whether to restart the server. While prepared, it should return 200 without generating.

That last one is a change. Today `/health` fails on a prepared server either way, so a liveness probe would restart a server that is waiting to be captured:

- **Prepared at startup.** The server isn't marked up yet, so `/health` returns 503 right away ([http_server.py](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/71a17dbc24acdac99231b166aea57763d925b89f/python/sglang/srt/entrypoints/http_server.py#L719-L720)).
- **Prepared while serving.** `/health` sends a one-token generation by default ([environ.py](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/71a17dbc24acdac99231b166aea57763d925b89f/python/sglang/srt/environ.py#L341)), which waits behind the pause. After 20 seconds `/health` returns 503 and marks the server unhealthy ([http_server.py](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/71a17dbc24acdac99231b166aea57763d925b89f/python/sglang/srt/entrypoints/http_server.py#L735-L783)).

The prepare and resume calls return 200 as soon as SGLang accepts them, without waiting for the work to finish. `GET /checkpoint/status` shows when prepare is done, and `/ready` shows when resume is. A failure after the response is logged, and the status body carries the error.

**Resume.** After the restore, the orchestrator calls `POST /checkpoint/resume` on a fresh connection. Apart from the optional prepare, it's the only message the orchestrator sends.

The status and resume routes keep working while SGLang is prepared, even though inference routes return 503.

SGLang handles one lifecycle call at a time: repeating prepare or resume while it is running or already done has no extra effect, and calling one while the other is running returns 409. A prepare that arrives while SGLang is serving always starts a new cycle, so a caller should check the status before retrying one.

### Prepare and resume

**Prepare** (default, configuration in the next section):

1. Stop admitting and drain the requests in flight with `pause_generation`. Its default mode aborts them and waits until none remain ([tokenizer_manager.py](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/71a17dbc24acdac99231b166aea57763d925b89f/python/sglang/srt/managers/tokenizer_manager.py#L2277-L2290)). New requests should get 503 rather than wait at admission. A paused server holds them there today ([tokenizer_manager.py](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/71a17dbc24acdac99231b166aea57763d925b89f/python/sglang/srt/managers/tokenizer_manager.py#L948-L949)). How to drain is up to SGLang.
2. Tear down the communicators, such as NCCL and custom all-reduce ([parallel_state.py](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/71a17dbc24acdac99231b166aea57763d925b89f/python/sglang/srt/distributed/parallel_state.py#L288-L291)). SGLang has no hook for this yet (see Initial scope).
3. Release what the checkpoint shouldn't carry, per the configured policy. By default SGLang calls `release_memory_occupation`, which moves the weights to CPU memory with `--enable-weights-cpu-backup` ([load_model_utils.py](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/71a17dbc24acdac99231b166aea57763d925b89f/python/sglang/srt/model_executor/model_runner_components/load_model_utils.py#L307-L325)), frees the KV cache and CUDA graph memory, and flushes the radix cache ([weight_updater.py](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/71a17dbc24acdac99231b166aea57763d925b89f/python/sglang/srt/managers/scheduler_components/weight_updater.py#L337-L381)).
4. Run the deployment's own pre-capture code, if any (user custom code).
5. Report `prepared` and wait.

**Resume** reverses it. SGLang refreshes values that may differ on the new node, then runs the deployment's own post-restore code, if any (user custom code). Then it reloads what was released with `resume_memory_occupation`, rebuilds the communicators, resumes scheduling with `continue_generation` and reopens admission. It reports nothing further and returns to ready on its own.

### Configuration and extension

A default covers the simple case, settings cover the common choices, and a deployment's own code covers the rest.

**What survives.** The deployer picks what the checkpoint keeps with one new setting, `--checkpoint-policy` (see Settings). The table below lists the values we propose for it. They are not new `tags`. Each one is a preset over what SGLang already has: `release_memory_occupation` and its `tags` ([io_struct.py](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/71a17dbc24acdac99231b166aea57763d925b89f/python/sglang/srt/managers/io_struct.py#L2175-L2178)), the `--enable-weights-cpu-backup` flag, and `update_weights_from_disk`.

| Policy | Kept in the checkpoint | Released before capture |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| `offload-weights` (default) | Weights, in CPU memory | KV cache, CUDA graph memory, and weights from GPU memory, as `release_memory_occupation` with `--enable-weights-cpu-backup` |
| `resident` | Weights, KV cache and the radix cache | Nothing |
| `keep-weights` | Weights, in GPU memory | KV cache, as `release_memory_occupation(tags=["kv_cache"])`, which [Dynamo's wrapper](https://github.com/ai-dynamo/dynamo/blob/9e41f306e8901f9368cda9185a8353baa2bf32d4/components/src/dynamo/sglang/snapshot.py#L179-L193) uses |
| `reload-weights` | Neither | Weights and KV cache, without a CPU backup. Weights reload after restore with `update_weights_from_disk`, as in [#40736](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/40736) |

Every policy except `resident` flushes the radix cache, because releasing the KV cache does ([weight_updater.py](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/71a17dbc24acdac99231b166aea57763d925b89f/python/sglang/srt/managers/scheduler_components/weight_updater.py#L365-L366)). In-flight requests never survive, because prepare drains them first.

**Extension.** A deployment that keeps `sglang.launch_server` can supply its own hooks as a Python class, given by its import path, the way `--custom-weight-loader` takes a function today ([model.py](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/71a17dbc24acdac99231b166aea57763d925b89f/python/sglang/srt/arg_groups/fields/model.py#L286-L292)). Its `before_capture()` runs at prepare step 4 and its `after_restore()` at the start of resume. They run in addition to the configured policy, so a deployment can add its own logic without wrapping the entry point or giving up the default. A typical use is reloading credentials or a gateway address after a restore on another node.

**Settings.** Each is a server argument with a matching environment variable, so a deployment can turn this on without changing its command.

| Setting | Controls | Default |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| `--enable-checkpoint` | The `/checkpoint/*` routes and the lifecycle | Off |
| `--checkpoint-at-startup` | Preparing right after the warmup request | Off |
| `--checkpoint-policy` | What survives, from the table above | `offload-weights` |
| `--checkpoint-hooks` | The import path of the hooks class, such as `mypkg.hooks.SnapshotHooks` | None |
| `--checkpoint-prepare-timeout` | How long draining may take before prepare fails | No limit |

### Flow

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Caller (optional)
    participant S as SGLang
    participant O as Orchestrator
    alt at startup
        S->>S: load and run the warmup request
    else while serving
        C->>S: POST /checkpoint/prepare
    end
    S->>S: drain, tear down communicators, apply policy
    loop until prepared
        O->>S: GET /checkpoint/status
    end
    S-->>O: prepared
    O->>O: capture and store
    O->>O: restore into a new container
    Note over S: from here, this is the restored copy
    O->>S: POST /checkpoint/resume
    S->>S: reload per policy, rebuild communicators, reopen admission
    Note over S: serving again, /ready returns 200
```

### Failure and lifecycle handling

If prepare fails, such as a hook error or a drain that times out, SGLang stays unhealthy and never reports `prepared`, so nothing is captured. The error is logged and shown in the status body, and the platform replaces the replica. If the capture fails, the platform replaces the source. If resume fails, SGLang logs the error, shows it in the status body, and stays unhealthy. The deployment's controller can then replace the replica or start one cold. If the orchestrator never captures or never resumes, SGLang stays `prepared` and out of rotation until the orchestrator or the platform replaces it.

### Initial scope

One serving container with TP=1, including multiple tokenizer workers with `--tokenizer-worker-num` ([serving.py](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/71a17dbc24acdac99231b166aea57763d925b89f/python/sglang/srt/arg_groups/fields/serving.py#L50-L53)). SGLang already broadcasts pause and continue to every tokenizer worker ([multi_tokenizer_mixin.py](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/71a17dbc24acdac99231b166aea57763d925b89f/python/sglang/srt/managers/multi_tokenizer_mixin.py#L680-L695)). Local TP, PP and DP attention follow once SGLang can tear down and rebuild its communicators, prepare step 2. Multi-node, PD disaggregation and elastic EP come later.

### Relationship to existing SGLang work

This RFC doesn't replace any of these. It proposes the contract they could share.

| Work | State | How it relates |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| [#43965](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/43965), engine initialization snapshots, with [#40736](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/40736) | Open | SGLang runs CRIU itself and captures before HTTP binds, on the same host with TP=1. Here the orchestrator captures from outside, with HTTP up so it can poll and resume. Both could share the memory release and reload steps |
| [#33522](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/33522), Fast Engine Recovery roadmap | Open | Cuts the same startup cost inside SGLang, starting with a weight cache. Here the whole initialized process is restored, often on another node |
| [#27139](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/27139), weight cache | Merged | Shares weights with the daemon over CUDA IPC, so releasing weights is refused while it's active ([weight_updater.py](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/71a17dbc24acdac99231b166aea57763d925b89f/python/sglang/srt/managers/scheduler_components/weight_updater.py#L293-L307)). Checkpointing runs with `--weight-cache-mode off` until the two are combined |

### Prototypes

- A file-signaled version of the same lifecycle, [Snapshot's SGLang guide](https://github.com/ai-dynamo/snapshot/blob/3136f1d8dbc10bf9c93fa62adbdd308f41ac334b/docs/guides/sglang.md), captured an unmodified SGLang image with ai-dynamo/snapshot on one T4 and restored it into a new pod that served generations. It runs the lifecycle in an `app.py` mounted into the image, which is the program this RFC would remove.
- [Dynamo's SGLang wrapper](https://github.com/ai-dynamo/dynamo/blob/9e41f306e8901f9368cda9185a8353baa2bf32d4/components/src/dynamo/sglang/snapshot.py) runs the same lifecycle with file signals ([lifecycle.py](https://github.com/ai-dynamo/dynamo/blob/9e41f306e8901f9368cda9185a8353baa2bf32d4/components/src/dynamo/common/snapshot/lifecycle.py#L47-L87)), releasing only the KV cache unless the GPU Memory Service is in use.

### Related resources

- [Snapshot](https://github.com/ai-dynamo/snapshot), the orchestrator in this RFC

title: [RFC] Context-parallel support for the unified L3 key scheme
author: momaek
body:
## Summary

We propose extending `plan_unified_kv` with an explicit ownership rule for each attention-CP mode, so the unified key scheme (#33651) can lift its `attn_cp_size > 1` guard instead of falling back to rank-suffixed keys. Each mode gets a writer rule: replicated CP elects one writer, LayerSplit CP is keyed like a PP stage, and KV cache sharding has each page's owner write the whole page. We would like to agree on the design before sending PRs stacked on #39728.

cc @Shunkangz (unified key scheme, KV cache sharding) @Dovis01 (DSA cache layer split, #29421)

## Motivation

We serve GLM-5.3 (78 layers, DSA) with PD disaggregation on Hopper, using two prefill shapes that should share prefix KV through one Mooncake L3:

| Prefill shape | Parallelism |
| --- | --- |
| DP prefill | DP8 attention, one node |
| LayerSplit prefill | Interleave prefill CP8 with `--enable-dsa-cache-layer-split`; each rank stores about 1/8 of the layers |

Requests move between the two as prompts grow, so a prefix written by one shape is often read by the other. Upstream has no working path for this today:

- **HiCache L3 + LayerSplit does not start.** Mooncake forces the layout away from `layer_first`, while layer-sharded backup only supports `layer_first`. `backup_skip` also lets only `tp_rank == 0` write, which is right for replicated MLA but wrong when each rank owns different layers (details in #37122).
- **The direct linker does not know LayerSplit.** The DSA pool group in `linker_pool_assembler.py` is built over the full `layer_num`.
- **The unified key scheme rejects all CP.** `plan_unified_kv` raises `NotImplementedError` when `attn_cp_size > 1`.

We currently bridge the gap with out-of-tree patches that write per-rank shard keys and reassemble pages across topologies. That works, but each new topology pair needs its own assemble path, which is exactly the coupling the unified scheme removes. We would rather fix this in the scheme.

## Proposal: one ownership rule per CP mode

Today a rank's plan is a layer range × a set of head groups. We add the CP mode as an input; each mode then says which unified-key objects the rank holds completely, so it is their single writer. Keys stay exactly as #39727 defines them; only the writer set changes.

| CP mode | What one rank holds | Who writes each object | What it needs |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Replicated CP (every rank holds every page and layer, as #30501 describes prefill CP today) | Full pages, all layers | One elected rank, e.g. CP rank 0 | A fixed election rule; no key change |
| LayerSplit CP (`--enable-dsa-cache-layer-split`) | A contiguous layer range, all tokens of each page | Each rank, for its own layer chunks | Chunk-aligned split; the "only the last range may end short" check becomes `end == num_layers` instead of `is_final_stage` |
| KV cache sharding (`--enable-kv-cache-sharding`) | Whole physical pages, all layers | The page's owner (`owner(loc)`) | Writer filter by page owner, in step with #43778's host-page ownership |

The token-sliced CP case named in #39727's error message (ranks holding sub-page slices) stays out of scope here.

Two properties fall out of this. First, LayerSplit is PP from the storage point of view: a contiguous absolute layer range per rank, so the existing `_layer_chunks` logic applies unchanged once the split is chunk-aligned. Second, KV sharding matches on physical pages (per `page_interleave.py`), and each physical page lives on one rank with all its layers, so it writes exactly the objects a DP or TP member writes, on whatever `layer_partition` the fleet uses.

## LayerSplit: a chunk-aligned split

`get_layer_shard_range` gains a chunk size P: it cuts the layers into P-sized chunks and gives each rank a contiguous run of whole chunks. P = 1 reproduces today's split exactly, so the default changes nothing.

The change is required. Today 78 layers over 8 ranks split as 10 × 6 + 9 × 2, so ranges start at 0, 10, …, 60, **69**. `_layer_chunks` requires every start to be a multiple of `layer_partition`, which forces P = 1. With P = 1 every page becomes 78 KV objects of about 41 KiB each, plus one indexer object per indexer layer, multiplying Mooncake master RPCs and metadata by roughly 78× for every fleet member, including DP readers.

With P = 10 the max layers per rank is still 10, so memory is unchanged, and each rank writes exactly one chunk:

| CP rank | Today | P = 10 | Full indexer layers in the chunk | KV object size |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | [0, 10) | [0, 10) | 0, 1, 2, 6 | ~410 KiB |
| 1 | [10, 20) | [10, 20) | 10, 14, 18 | ~410 KiB |
| 2 | [20, 30) | [20, 30) | 22, 26 | ~410 KiB |
| 3 | [30, 40) | [30, 40) | 30, 34, 38 | ~410 KiB |
| 4 | [40, 50) | [40, 50) | 42, 46 | ~410 KiB |
| 5 | [50, 60) | [50, 60) | 50, 54, 58 | ~410 KiB |
| 6 | [60, 69) | [60, 70) | 62, 66 | ~410 KiB |
| 7 | [69, 78) | [70, 78) | 70, 74 | ~328 KiB |

Sizes assume 656 B per token per layer (FP8 MLA latent + rope) and page size 64; a whole 78-layer page is ~3.1 MiB. A DP reader on the same grid reads 8 KV objects per page instead of 1. CP4 or CP2 members get whole chunks the same way, so any CP size shares keys with DP, TP and PP members as long as the fleet agrees on P.

Other changes:

1. **PD transfer is unaffected in principle.** Prefill reports `prefill_start_layer` / `prefill_end_layer` per rank and decode pairs on those, not on the split rule. We will still run a PD regression.
2. **Host pool.** LayerSplit backs up one owned layer at a time and only supports `layer_first` today. It needs a `page_unified` per-layer write-back; the load direction already exists (#39726).

## DSA indexer and MTP draft layers

Neither is covered by the #33651 stack yet, and every CP mode needs both.

**Indexer as a second component.** We propose an `_indexer` object at the same coordinate as `_k`: `{page_hash}_{digest}_L{a}-{b}_indexer` next to `{page_hash}_{digest}_L{a}-{b}_k`. Only layers with a real indexer go into it. GLM-5.3 marks 21 of its 78 layers `full` in `indexer_types` (0, 1, 2, then every fourth from 6 to 74); the other 57 are `shared` and already get no host layer (`owned_device_layers` in `pool_host/dsa.py`). So the object for `L{a}-{b}` packs the full layers in `[a, b)` in ascending order, and is skipped when there are none. The indexer layer set is a model fact, so we would add it, or a digest of it, to `KVCacheNamespace` and bump `schema_version`; indexer bytes per token per layer (132 for GLM-5.3) would join the namespace too.

**MTP draft layers.** A draft layer is replicated on every CP rank under LayerSplit; `prefill.py` already sends draft KV from the last CP rank only. We propose a coordinate outside the target model's range, e.g. `D{depth}`, written by the last CP rank under LayerSplit and by the page owner under KV sharding. The GLM-5.2 CP8 LayerSplit recipe in the cookbook runs EAGLE on prefill, so the design should cover it.

## KV cache sharding: no new keys needed

KV sharding needs no new key shape. Allocation and prefix matching use the physical page size, so each L3 page hash covers one physical page, and that page lives on exactly one rank with all its layers. The owner writes the same objects a DP member writes on the fleet's grid (a single `L0-78` object when `layer_partition` is 0), and a DP member reads them back as is.

What it does need sits with the KV sharding work, so we list it rather than propose it:

- **Writer filter.** Only `owner(loc)` backs a page up to L3, instead of `tp_rank == 0`.
- **Prefetch placement.** A page fetched from L3 has to land in a host slot owned by the rank that will hold its device page, which ties prefetch to the rotation-aware allocation in #43778.
- **Lifting the L3 guards** in `kv_shard_hook.py` and #43778 once the two points above hold.

If L3 for KV sharding is planned, the ownership rule above gives it a home, and fleets mixing sharded and unsharded prefill share keys from day one.

## Alternatives considered

| Alternative | Why not |
| --- | --- |
| Keep LayerSplit's even split and set `layer_partition = 1` | No model-side change, but ~78 KV objects per page for every fleet member, DP readers included |
| Land #37122 as is (rank-suffixed keys under the current scheme) | Fixes LayerSplit-to-LayerSplit reuse only; cross-topology reuse still needs per-pair assemble logic, the coupling #33651 removes |
| Let each rank write chunks clipped to its own range, without aligning the split | A chunk such as `[60, 70)` would span two owners; it would need a cross-rank gather before every write, or partial objects Mooncake does not support |
| Move to KV cache sharding now and skip LayerSplit L3 | Preferable long term, since it needs no layer grid. But DSA under KV sharding currently targets the TRTLLM kernels (#42973), which as far as we know need SM100, and we run Hopper. We would like LayerSplit covered until KV sharding runs GLM DSA on Hopper |

## PR plan, stacked on #39728

1. **CP mode in `plan_unified_kv`**, plus the replicated-CP writer election. Replaces the blanket `attn_cp_size > 1` raise with a per-mode check; the token-sliced mode keeps raising.
2. **Chunk-aligned `get_layer_shard_range`** (default P = 1, no behavior change), then LayerSplit in the key plan: owned global range in, `end == num_layers` for the short tail.
3. **DSA indexer component**: the `_indexer` object, the indexer layer set in `KVCacheNamespace`, and a `schema_version` bump.
4. **`page_unified` per-layer write-back** for layer-sharded DSA host pools, alongside the load kernel from #39726.
5. **End-to-end test**: a LayerSplit CP writer and a DP reader round-trip the same pages byte-exact on a small DSA model.

We will close #37122 with a pointer here once we agree on the direction.

## Open questions

1. Do you agree that LayerSplit CP is a third case, distinct from the two in #39727's error message, and can be keyed like a PP stage?
2. Is changing LayerSplit's split rule acceptable? (@Dovis01)
3. Should the CP mode be an explicit input to `plan_unified_kv`, or derived inside it from the pool type (`LayerSplitDSATokenToKVPool`, the page-interleave pools)?
4. Indexer: a separate `_indexer` object (our proposal), or packed into the `_k` object as a second region?
5. Is a `D{depth}` coordinate for MTP draft layers acceptable, or is there already a plan for draft pools under the unified scheme?
6. Is L3 for KV cache sharding planned? If so, should it build on the same ownership rule, and does the prefetch-placement point match your view?
7. Order: wait for #39728 to merge, or open the first PR against it now?

Related: #21846 (roadmap), #33651, #39727, #39728, #39815, #30501, #43778, #42973, #29421, #37122.

title: [RFC] MoE routing simulator for prefill imbalance profiling: balanced reference and GPU-faithful replay
author: Phoenix3334
body:
## Motivation

We would like to follow up on #20307 with a narrowly scoped, opt-in profiling workflow: **compare production routing with a controlled synthetic routing reference inside the real serving pipeline, before investing in routing or load-balancing changes.**

While investigating DeepSeek-V4-Pro prefill on a single 8-GPU B300 node (TP8/DP8, MegaMoE), we found that several effects were easy to conflate:

- logical expert popularity from the learned router;
- physical placement / replica dispatch;
- grouped-GEMM block rounding and padding;
- rank-level stragglers;
- All-to-All dispatch/combine cost;
- request-supply / arrival gaps outside the MoE kernels.

A balanced grouped-GEMM microbenchmark can isolate one kernel property, but it cannot establish how much **end-to-end serving latency** is actually caused by routing imbalance. Conversely, a lower expert-count CV does not imply lower GPU work if the backend rounds each expert workload to tile/block boundaries.

This proposal therefore treats balanced routing as a **counterfactual measurement tool**, not as a production optimization. It does not change default routing, claim quality preservation, or imply that any observed synthetic gain can be recovered by EPLB or routing-bias changes.

---

## Related work and analytical framing

| Reference | Mechanism / result | Relevant lesson for this RFC |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [TensorRT-LLM Perfect Router](https://github.com/NVIDIA/TensorRT-LLM/blob/04cefe271daceb491dbdacb0fcd8f1a174c10c16/docs/source/developer-guide/perf-analysis.md#moe-expert-load-balance-analysis-perfect-router) | Retains learned-router work for timing, then substitutes precomputed/cached balanced logits | A balanced reference is useful when simulator overhead is controlled and clearly separated from production routing |
| [vLLM Routing Simulator](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/vllm/model_executor/layers/fused_moe/router/routing_simulator_router.py) | Synthetic expert IDs/weights with configurable distributions | Distribution sensitivity is useful, but runtime sampling overhead and statistical rather than exact balance must be accounted for |
| SGLang #20307 | Existing discussion around `--ep-dispatch-algorithm fake` and MoE/All-to-All coverage | Reuse existing seams where possible; first verify whether they cover V4-Pro/MegaMoE rather than adding another parallel abstraction |
| [Patel et al., *Demystifying the Mixture of Experts Serving Tax*, MLSys 2026](https://openreview.net/pdf?id=lELxqcgrsN) ([MLSys page](https://mlsys.org/virtual/2026/oral/3764)) | Decomposes the MoE serving gap into compute, communication, and token-distribution effects; shows that prefill and decode pay qualitatively different taxes | A routing experiment should measure **actual padded work, stragglers and communication**, not only FLOPs or raw token-count balance |

The MLSys'26 paper is particularly useful for scoping this RFC. Its central point is that the MoE-vs-dense serving gap is not one monolithic penalty. For our purposes, a useful decomposition is:

```text
MoE serving cost
  ├─ compute-side tax
  │    ├─ batch subdivision across experts
  │    └─ fragmented/smaller expert GEMMs
  ├─ communication-side tax
  │    └─ dispatch/combine collectives and imbalance
  └─ token-distribution tax
       ├─ rank/expert stragglers
       └─ backend-specific padding / block-rounding waste
```

This also explains why **prefill is the first target**. In prefill, expert imbalance can increase slowest-rank compute time and padding waste. In decode, skew can have the opposite sign by reducing the number of active experts and therefore the amount of expert weight loaded from HBM. A "perfectly balanced" decode router is therefore not a universally meaningful optimum and is explicitly out of scope for the first implementation.

---

## Measurement model: count-balanced is not necessarily cost-balanced

Let `N[l,e]` denote the number of valid tokens routed to expert `e` at layer `l`, and let the physical placement / replica dispatcher map those logical expert assignments to GPUs/ranks.

A raw logical or physical token count answers only:

```text
How many token-expert assignments reached this expert/rank?
```

It does **not** necessarily answer:

```text
How much GPU work did this expert/rank actually execute?
```

For a backend that independently rounds each expert workload to a block size `B`, a simple padded-work proxy is:

```text
P[l,g] = sum_{e on rank g} ceil(N[l,e] / B) * B
```

and a per-rank padding factor is:

```text
eta[l,g] = P[l,g] / max(R[l,g], 1)
```

where `R[l,g]` is the corresponding raw routed-token count.

This formula is only a **proxy** and must not be hard-coded as a universal truth: some backends use different packing, max-dimension padding, fused layouts, or replica-specific scheduling. The implementation should report the backend's actual block/tile work when that information is available.

Similarly, rank imbalance should be measured on execution time, not only counts. A useful straggler metric is:

```text
S[l] = max_g(T_moe[l,g]) / mean_g(T_moe[l,g])
```

with the slowest-rank time retained explicitly. If count CV decreases but `P[l,g]`, `S[l]`, or All-to-All time does not improve, then the serving bottleneck was not removed even though the route histogram looks better.

The initial profiler should therefore keep the following layers separate:

```text
logical routing
    -> physical placement / replica dispatch
        -> padded/tiled backend work
            -> rank-local MoE kernel time
                -> dispatch/combine communication
                    -> end-to-end serving latency
```

---

## Proposed profiling modes

Balanced simulation and replay answer different questions and should remain separate modes.

| Mode | Purpose | Evidence limit |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Production routing** | Establish the measured workload baseline | Includes the real learned router, placement, dispatch and scheduling behavior |
| **Synthetic balanced routing** | Measure sensitivity to an explicitly defined balanced token distribution | Invalid model outputs; not a quality-preserving optimization and not a strict upper bound |
| **Optional synthetic distribution sweep** | Test sensitivity to controlled skew / concentration after the balanced baseline works | Profiling-only; should not expand the initial implementation unnecessarily |
| **Unchanged GPU snapshot replay** | Verify that captured production IDs/weights can be reproduced faithfully before perturbation studies | Fixed hidden states; cannot establish full-model effects of changed routing |
| **Placement/replica comparison** | Evaluate physical balancing while preserving logical selections/weights | Requires real replica dispatch and held-out workloads |
| **Bias/routing perturbation** | Explore semantics-changing candidate routes | Requires full-model quality evaluation and is outside the first deliverable |

The first contribution should implement only what is required for the **production vs balanced** comparison, while leaving clean seams for replay later.

---

## First deliverable: serving-level balanced reference

### 1. Verify the actual V4-Pro/MegaMoE route/dispatch path

Before adding a new mechanism, trace the current path and determine:

- where the learned router produces logical expert IDs / weights;
- where group constraints and top-k semantics are applied;
- where logical IDs become physical replica/device assignments;
- whether existing `fake` dispatch already intercepts the correct boundary;
- whether the MegaMoE runner sees logical IDs, physical IDs, packed blocks, or another representation;
- whether the selected path is CUDA-Graph captured and what can safely vary at replay time.

Prefer extending an existing fake/simulator seam over introducing a parallel router abstraction.

### 2. Preserve production work that is not part of the variable under study

The balanced arm should preserve the learned router GEMM and other upstream model work when practical, then substitute only the routing decision needed to create the reference distribution.

Any bypassed work must be documented. In particular:

- do not attribute removed selection/normalization work to "better balance";
- measure simulator generation/copy overhead separately;
- avoid host-side random generation in the timed region if a deterministic cached form can be used;
- keep outputs visibly invalid / profiling-only.

The goal is not to synthesize meaningful model outputs; the goal is to change the token-to-expert distribution while disturbing the rest of the serving path as little as practical.

### 3. Define "balanced" precisely

The implementation/report must state:

- total experts and routed top-k;
- any group-limited routing constraints;
- whether balance is exact or statistical;
- global vs rank-local balancing objective;
- treatment of shared experts;
- whether duplicate expert selections for one token are forbidden;
- how routing weights are generated/assigned for the profiling path;
- whether balance is defined on logical experts or after physical replica remapping.

For the first implementation, prefer a **deterministic exact-count reference** where feasible. A seeded statistical distribution is acceptable only if achieved per-layer counts are reported.

### 4. Use identical request inputs for both arms

Production and synthetic runs should consume the same frozen token-ID requests. Fix at least:

- input IDs and lengths;
- arrival/request-supply policy;
- concurrency;
- output length (prefer a prefill-focused fixed small output such as 1 token for the first study);
- cache policy / hit rate;
- scheduler/delayer settings;
- topology and parallelism configuration;
- engine commit/container/runtime versions.

Request-supply gaps should be measured rather than assumed absent. Pretokenization removes tokenizer variance but does not guarantee that the server is continuously supplied.

### 5. Keep timing runs and profiling runs separate

Instrumentation can perturb timing. Use at least two passes:

**Timing pass**
- minimal counters;
- repeated production/synthetic A/B ordering;
- fixed warmup and steady-state window;
- throughput and latency measurements.

**Profiling pass**
- route/count recorder;
- per-rank block/padded-work counters;
- Nsight or backend timers where needed;
- dispatch/combine timing and bytes;
- no claim that profiler-on absolute latency equals profiler-off latency.

---

## Required metrics

A useful report should expose metrics at several levels rather than collapse them into one CV value.

### A. Logical routing

Per layer:

- expert token counts;
- active expert count `E_active`;
- mean / max / p95 expert load;
- CV or max/mean ratio;
- achieved synthetic-balance error from the requested distribution.

### B. Physical placement / replica dispatch

Per layer and rank:

- routed token count after placement/replica mapping;
- number of active physical experts / replicas;
- replica hit/dispatch counts where applicable;
- max/mean rank raw load.

### C. Backend-executed work

Prefer backend-native counters where available; otherwise report a clearly labeled proxy:

- per-expert block count;
- per-rank block count;
- padded token-equivalent work;
- padding ratio `eta`;
- max/mean padded work across ranks.

This is the key distinction between **token-balanced** and **cost-balanced** routing.

### D. Straggler behavior

Per layer/rank or for the aggregated MoE region:

- rank-local MoE compute time;
- slowest-rank time;
- mean rank time;
- `max / mean` straggler ratio;
- optionally p95 across iterations.

### E. Communication

For dispatch and combine separately when possible:

- bytes/messages transferred;
- per-rank send/receive volume;
- max/mean communication volume;
- collective/SendRecv duration;
- overlap with compute if the backend exposes it.

Do not fold communication into the compute result: balancing can reduce compute stragglers while simultaneously increasing communication cost.

### F. End-to-end serving metrics

At minimum:

- aggregate output/input throughput under the chosen benchmark convention;
- TTFT for the prefill-focused workload;
- end-to-end request latency;
- MoE-region latency if it can be measured without excessive observer effect;
- request-supply / idle gaps.

Every benchmark result should state the exact throughput convention; "TPS" is otherwise ambiguous.

---

## Suggested first experiment matrix

Keep the first matrix small enough to interpret.

| Arm | Routing | Placement/replicas | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A | Production | Production | Baseline |
| B | Synthetic exact/controlled balance | Same production placement path | Measure serving sensitivity to token distribution |
| C (optional, only if already supported) | Existing SGLang fake dispatch | Existing implementation | Cross-check backend coverage / simulator semantics |

For A vs B, keep everything else fixed. Run repeated paired trials rather than one long baseline followed by one long synthetic run, so thermal/runtime drift is less likely to masquerade as a routing effect.

If the first result is meaningful, a later matrix can vary placement/replication independently of logical routing. That separation is important because the following are different interventions:

```text
change logical expert selection
        !=
keep logical selection, change physical expert placement
        !=
keep both, change replica dispatch
```

---

## How to interpret the result

The balanced reference is most useful as a diagnostic decision point.

### Case 1: lower raw imbalance -> lower padded work -> lower straggler time -> E2E gain

Then token distribution is a real serving bottleneck under the tested workload. Follow-up work can ask how much of the synthetic gain is recoverable through placement/replication without changing model semantics.

### Case 2: raw counts improve, but padded/block work barely changes

Then raw token CV is the wrong optimization objective for this backend. Investigate a block/padding-aware cost metric before changing the router.

### Case 3: compute stragglers improve, but All-to-All/SendRecv grows enough to erase the gain

Then the system is trading one tax for another. The next step is communication-aware placement/replication or overlap, not a claim that balancing failed in principle.

### Case 4: kernel/MoE time improves, but end-to-end serving does not

Inspect request supply, scheduler gaps, attention/non-MoE time, and profiler overhead. Kernel-level gains are not automatically serving-level gains.

### Case 5: balanced routing provides little or no MoE/E2E improvement

Deprioritize routing changes for that workload/configuration. This is a useful result: it establishes that the remaining performance opportunity is elsewhere.

---

## Faithful replay as a separate follow-up

For replay, reuse existing SGLang mechanisms where possible:

- [expert distribution recording](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/main/python/sglang/srt/eplb/expert_distribution.py);
- [routed expert capture](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/main/python/sglang/srt/state_capturer/routed_experts.py);
- the selected production GPU gating path.

Capture bounded samples together with enough metadata to make replay interpretable:

```text
layer
valid-token count
expert IDs / weights
routing bias
scoring / grouping / normalization configuration
parallelism topology
backend / runner
physical remapping semantics
aggregation semantics
```

Do not sum a dump again if it is already globally aggregated.

Our earlier CPU top-k exploration did not reliably reproduce GPU choices near ties. Before using replay for perturbation experiments, unchanged GPU replay should reproduce captured IDs/weights; report expert-set differences and slot-order differences separately.

Snapshot replay is still not a quality experiment. It verifies the routing implementation and supports controlled sensitivity studies under fixed hidden states.

#38695 is relevant to shared gating/precision; #42188 illustrates recording/remapping coverage gaps. This proposal should reuse those efforts rather than add a parallel recorder.

---

## Historical motivation and evidence limits

This RFC is motivated by historical v0.5.17-derived V4-Pro prefill experiments, not by a current-main correctness bug.

Those experiments suggested that changes in expert/rank count balance did **not** map monotonically to end-to-end throughput, and some load-balancing configurations introduced additional communication/SendRecv work. However:

- earlier text-vs-token-ID comparisons had request-path confounds;
- clean held-out EPLB validation was incomplete before the machine was released;
- a placement-only experiment without additional replicas cannot establish EPLB's full potential;
- raw token counts did not expose backend padding/block work directly;
- the measurements were not designed to separately attribute compute, padding, straggler and communication taxes.

Therefore this RFC intentionally does **not** claim:

- a specific attainable speedup;
- a 13% recoverable routing opportunity;
- that EPLB is ineffective;
- that routing is the only remaining bottleneck;
- that a balanced synthetic route is a quality-preserving or even universally faster route.

The purpose of the simulator is to produce the missing controlled measurement.

---

## New workload study (2026-11-04): V4.1-Flash placement, dispatch, and redundancy

This follow-up measures **physical placement / replica dispatch under production-selected routing**, rather than the proposed synthetic balanced logical router. It adds workload-specific evidence; it does not implement the simulator or establish that EPLB is generally ineffective.

### Setup and independent axes

- DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, four B30Z/B300-class GPUs on one eight-GPU host; TP4 / EP4 / attention-DP4.
- A v0.5.23 deployment build with CUDA 13.0, not the v0.5.22 reference recipe and not a current-main validation. The exact source commit/container digest is not included in this summary.
- MegaMoE, total-token accounting, static memory fraction 0.8, configured prefill chunk 128K (32K per attention-DP rank), max prefill tokens 32768, max running requests 256, radix cache disabled.
- Prefill-dominated ordinary serving with output length 1: **not** a disaggregated-prefill-role or real two-node P/D experiment.
- Throughput below is **input tokens/s**, not output generation throughput.

| Independent axis | Values | Intervention |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Placement update | Frozen / online | Load a calibrated layout with --init-expert-location, versus periodically rebuild the layout with --enable-eplb |
| Replica dispatch | static / dynamic | Dispatch against the existing physical layout; additional replica choices require redundant physical experts |
| Redundancy | 0 / 8 | --ep-num-redundant-experts 8, increasing physical slots from 384 to 392 |

**Frozen is not a synonym for static dispatch; online is not a synonym for dynamic dispatch.** The random-token campaign used static dispatch throughout. The real-token campaign tested baseline plus all eight combinations.

### Initial random-token campaign

A separate statistics run calibrated layouts using 547 forward windows. Frozen timing runs performed zero runtime rearrangements. Online runs used RI=50 and reported 120 rearrangements per arm. RI=1000 was not a matched timing arm; the initial observation was only about one or two rearrangements over this workload.

The six points were 4K/C256, 16K/C32, 32K/C32, 64K/C32, 128K/C16 and 128K/C32. Nominal frozen-layout gains were **6.5–8.2%**; online arms were approximately **1–4%** above their random baselines. No confidence intervals are available.

At 64K/C32:

| Arm | Input tok/s | vs random baseline |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Baseline | 346,800 | reference |
| Frozen static r0 | 370,600 | +6.86% |
| Frozen static r8 | 370,600 | +6.86% |
| Online RI=50 static r0 | 351,800 | +1.44% |
| Online RI=50 static r8 | 354,600 | +2.25% |

Calibration and timing used the same random workload distribution. These are **in-distribution candidate gains**, not held-out performance or a mathematical upper bound.

### Real-token 64K campaign: nine arms

ShareGPT long conversations supplied 640 eligible examples of at least 65,532 tokens, truncated to that length. Chat templates were rendered to text before explicit tokenization, and the client sent frozen input_ids to /generate. A direct templating/tokenization path had returned two-token inputs in this deployment and was excluded from the final dataset.

This cohort represents **long conversations / long-context prompts**, not a representative short-request production distribution. Layout calibration and evaluation used the same source distribution; held-out/domain-shift validation remains missing.

Timing used C32 and 512 requests per arm. C32 was selected for throughput among the checked points, not as a global or SLO-constrained optimum. The real baseline at C16 was about 358.6k input tok/s with TTFT 2.84s, versus 365.2k / 5.68s at C32.

| Arm | Layout | Dispatch | Redundant slots | Input tok/s | vs real baseline |
| --- | --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Baseline | Default | Default | 0 | 365,166 | reference |
| Frozen static r0 | Frozen | static | 0 | 367,597 | +0.67% |
| Frozen static r8 | Frozen | static | 8 | 368,512 | +0.92% |
| Frozen dynamic r0 | Frozen | dynamic | 0 | 367,468 | +0.63% |
| Frozen dynamic r8 | Frozen | dynamic | 8 | 367,781 | +0.72% |
| Online static r0 | Online RI=50 | static | 0 | 348,666 | -4.52% |
| Online static r8 | Online RI=50 | static | 8 | 347,992 | -4.70% |
| Online dynamic r0 | Online RI=50 | dynamic | 0 | 351,142 | -3.84% |
| Online dynamic r8 | Online RI=50 | dynamic | 8 | 350,433 | -4.03% |

Real-token online runs reported 20 rearrangements per arm, distinct from the random campaign's totals.

Observed at this point:

- Frozen-layout throughput was only **0.6–0.9%** above baseline.
- Online RI=50 was **3.8–4.7% below** baseline.
- Eight additional replicas did not demonstrate a clear throughput benefit.
- Frozen static/dynamic differences were small. Online dynamic points were about 0.7 percentage points less negative than static, but **one run per arm cannot establish statistical equivalence or a reliable dispatcher improvement**.
- Reported median chunk-level prefill times were around 1.05–1.06s across arms. These aggregate medians are not per-layer/per-rank straggler measurements and do not prove that all MoE imbalance disappeared.

The real baseline is nominally 5.3% above the earlier random baseline (365,166 vs 346,800 input tok/s). However, content source and client preparation/request path changed, and the random/real count statistics below use different aggregation conventions. **This is not a clean content-only causal ablation.** A follow-up should hold the token-ID client path, request supply and aggregation window fixed.

### Placement-aware per-pass diagnostics

A separate instrumented campaign used real approximately-65K prompts, C32 and 96 requests. Analysis selected 48 steady-state passes using layer-0 token volume at least 50% of its peak. EP=4 and a padded-block proxy with BLOCK_M=192 were used.

The analysis was adapted from a trivial-placement assumption to the recorded physical-to-logical mapping when interpreting physical expert slots and rank ownership. The frozen layout is unchanged over these measurements. An online layout requires the mapping corresponding to each window: a final map alone cannot reconstruct past assignments. With replicas, logical totals alone also do not determine actual per-replica execution counts.

CV values are mean / maximum across the reported layer summary. Throughput comes from the separate timing campaign, not the instrumented 96-request run.

| Arm | Logical expert CV mean / max | Rank token-count CV mean / max | Rank max/min summary | Padded M-block max/mean proxy | Layers with rank CV >0.3 | Timing input tok/s |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Real baseline | 1.805 / 3.614 | 0.148 / 0.311 | 1.52 | 1.207 | 1/40 | 365,166 |
| Frozen static r0 | 1.748 / 3.451 | 0.050 / 0.109 | 1.14 | 1.062 | 0/40 | 367,597 |
| Frozen static r8 | 1.806 / 3.614 | 0.153 / 0.378 | 1.49 | 1.218 | 3/40 | 368,512 |

The key frozen-r0 observation is:

- Rank count CV: **0.148 -> 0.050**.
- Padded M-block max/mean proxy: **1.207 -> 1.062**.
- Corresponding timing-point throughput: only **+0.67%**.

This supports the distinction between **count balance, padded-work balance, and serving throughput**. The block metric is a tile-count proxy, not measured kernel latency or proof of a recoverable speedup.

Logical expert CV remains approximately similar: placement does not directly change learned logical expert selection, though scheduling/batch composition can change observed distributions. In this sample r8 did not produce better rank-count or block-proxy balance than baseline. Replica hit/dispatch counters are needed before assigning a mechanism to the extra replicas.

For trend reference only, an earlier random aggregate reported expert CV mean/max 4.13/6.28, rank CV 0.346/0.759, rank max/min 2.94, M-block proxy 1.461 and 23/40 layers above rank CV 0.3. That dump was aggregated differently from the real per-pass measurements. **Do not calculate a precise random-to-real CV reduction or infer causality from these cross-convention values.**

### Online recorder incompatibility: missing measurement

Online per-pass collection failed on the tested v0.5.23 deployment. The reported path was:

> EPLB requests an object-mode statistics dump  
> -> _PerPassAccumulator.dump expects output_mode == "file"  
> -> AssertionError / scheduler failure

This occurred in RI=50 and RI=10 diagnostic attempts. It is a separate **instrumentation compatibility observation**; current-main applicability and a standalone source-level reproducer have not been established here.

The successful online throughput runs and failed instrumented CV attempts are separate campaigns. **No valid online per-pass CV is available in this report.** Similarity to the frozen placement algorithm cannot substitute for measurement.

Rebalance-related SendRecv work was observed in the run report, making maintenance/communication cost a plausible contributor to the slowdown. Without a matched RI sweep and critical-path timing breakdown, these data do not prove that communication explains the entire slowdown or that it is pure overhead after perfect balance.

### Limits and implications

- Single host, one four-GPU topology, one timing run per arm and 512 requests per arm; no repeated paired-startup confidence intervals. An assumed noise band is not a statistical test.
- Long-context-selected inputs; short/mixed requests, bursty arrivals, held-out calibration and alternate topologies remain untested.
- Request completion or a readable sample response is not a quality evaluation. No GSM8K/full task-quality evaluation was performed for this matrix.
- Raw artifacts are retained privately. This public summary lacks an exact source commit, full client scripts, frozen-input checksums and a reproducibility archive.
- The recorder compatibility problem remains separate from the performance results and needs reduction before an upstream fix is proposed.

For the **tested real 64K/C32 workload**, default placement/dispatch is a reasonable reference; frozen layout is a small candidate improvement to repeat, and online RI=50 / extra replicas are not supported by these measurements as beneficial defaults. This is not a recommendation to disable EPLB across V4.1 or other deployment sizes/distributions.

This follow-up reinforces **logical selection -> physical placement/replica dispatch -> padded work -> rank timing -> communication -> serving latency** as separate measurement layers. Priority follow-ups are matched token-ID request paths, repeated timing orders, held-out layouts, actual slowest-rank/communication timing, and an online-compatible recorder.

---

## Additional evidence reported 2026-11-05: real-token balanced reference and GPU timelines

This is a **separate follow-up campaign**, not a replacement for the v0.5.23 nine-arm study above. It adds a reported synthetic balanced-routing reference and GPU timeline evidence to the distinction between token-count balance, MoE-region time, and end-to-end throughput.

### Campaign provenance and scope

- Model: DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash. The real-token result table uses four GPUs, TP4 / EP4 / attention-DP4, and a selected ShareGPT long-context cohort at approximately 64K input tokens, C32, output length 1. Throughput below is **aggregate input tokens/s**.
- The accompanying recipe is labeled as a v0.5.22-derived CUDA 13.0 deployment build with additional patches. Its `main` annotation is not an immutable source identity. The recipe's original host and the real-token follow-up table's host differ; the exact follow-up GPU SKU, source SHA, container digest, and flag-by-flag match are not captured in this public summary. Do not treat these values as a clean cross-version comparison against the earlier v0.5.23 campaign.
- The reference recipe uses MegaMoE, total-token DP accounting, a global prefill chunk of 131072 (32768 per attention-DP rank), max prefill tokens 32768, static memory fraction 0.8, max running requests 256, and radix caching disabled. It also documents flashmla_mega, decoder SWA bounded replay, Mega-mHC prefill, and All-to-All Engram lookup.
- The recipe's P-only benchmark uses a disaggregated-prefill role with fake bootstrap / a fake KV sender. This avoids requiring a real decode node; it does **not** measure real cross-node KV transfer or a complete P/D serving path. Confirm the real-token follow-up's request/client and role settings in its reproducibility manifest rather than assuming every recipe setting carried over.
-

title: [RFC] scheduler: Overlap prefill scheduling and KV loading with model execution
author: ttaohe
body:
**Implementation status:** local runtime integration, CPU regressions and initial PD experiments have been performed against main base 92580581da. The implementation is not pushed; the Draft PR still has an intentionally empty diff. Supporting authoring files remain local. Further investigation and validation are continuing. **Implementation tracker:** https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/44723 (Draft; local integration under validation). ## Motivation Native overlap already overlaps some CPU work with GPU execution, but the scheduler regains control only after its synchronous CPU model call returns. Preparing the next batch and submitting cached-KV loads can therefore happen late. Agent requests arriving during that call create additional useful work to advance. We propose one persistent forward thread while the scheduler remains the only owner of requests, radix state, allocation, admission, and retirement. A = current batch, B = next batch, C = an earlier batch. ```mermaid %%{init: {"theme": "base", "gantt": {"displayMode": "compact", "barHeight": 30, "barGap": 8, "fontSize": 13, "sectionFontSize": 14, "leftPadding": 190, "rightPadding": 45}, "themeVariables": {"taskBkgColor": "#dff2e8", "taskBorderColor": "#318463", "taskTextColor": "#172b4d", "activeTaskBkgColor": "#fff0bb", "activeTaskBorderColor": "#ba8a20", "critBkgColor": "#ffe5e5", "critBorderColor": "#bd5656", "doneTaskBkgColor": "#e4edff", "doneTaskBorderColor": "#3b6bb5", "sectionBkgColor": "#f7f9fc", "sectionBkgColor2": "#eff7f2", "sectionBkgColor3": "#f7f9fc", "taskTextDarkColor": "#172b4d", "taskTextOutsideColor": "#172b4d", "gridColor": "#d8e0e9"}}}%% gantt title Move preparation and KV loading into A's model-call window dateFormat YYYY-MM-DDTHH:mm:ss axisFormat %S tickInterval 10second todayMarker off section Native / Scheduler Prep A : a0, 2026-01-01T00:00:00, 5s CPU model call A : done, a1, 2026-01-01T00:00:05, 20s Retire C / prepare B : a2, 2026-01-01T00:00:25, 12s CPU call B : done, a3, 2026-01-01T00:00:40, 10s section Native / GPU A forward window : active, a4, 2026-01-01T00:00:07, 21s Exposed boundary : crit, a5, 2026-01-01T00:00:28, 14s B forward : active, a6, 2026-01-01T00:00:42, 8s section Native / B KV Load B : a7, 2026-01-01T00:00:32, 12s section V2 / Scheduler Prep A : b0, 2026-01-01T00:00:00, 5s Retire C : b1, 2026-01-01T00:00:06, 6s Receive : b2, 2026-01-01T00:00:12, 7s Prepare B : b3, 2026-01-01T00:00:19, 6s Handoff : b4, 2026-01-01T00:00:25, 5s section V2 / Forward worker CPU model call A : done, b5, 2026-01-01T00:00:05, 20s CPU call B : done, b6, 2026-01-01T00:00:30, 10s section V2 / GPU A forward window : active, b7, 2026-01-01T00:00:07, 21s Gap : crit, b8, 2026-01-01T00:00:28, 4s B forward : active, b9, 2026-01-01T00:00:32, 8s section V2 / B KV Early load B : b10, 2026-01-01T00:00:21, 12s ``` *Horizontal positions are schematic, in arbitrary units. Widths are not measured durations or continuous GPU activity. B consumes KV as the required layers become ready.* **One state owner, separate execution and loading paths** ```mermaid %%{init: {"theme": "base", "flowchart": {"htmlLabels": true, "curve": "linear", "nodeSpacing": 35, "rankSpacing": 55}, "themeVariables": {"fontFamily": "Arial, sans-serif", "fontSize": "15px", "lineColor": "#7a8699", "edgeLabelBackground": "#ffffff", "clusterBkg": "#f7f9fc", "clusterBorder": "#d8e0e9"}, "fontFamily": "Arial, sans-serif"}}%% flowchart LR accTitle: One scheduler owner, separate forward and KV loading paths S["Scheduler owner
